Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 5.4: share necessary information when the interests of patient safety and public protection override the need for confidentiality; Code 17.2 requires sharing information if you believe someone may be at risk of harm, in line with disclosure law. A specific threat to a named person justifies disclosure in the public interest, so the nurse should escalate immediately per local policy.

n.1: Confidentiality is not absolute; a serious threat to a named person justifies disclosure.
n.2: A promise does not remove the risk to the named person and is not a safe basis for withholding.
n.3: Waiting until the ward round delays action on an immediate risk of serious harm.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A caller to a surgical ward says she is the daughter of Mrs Green, 70, who had surgery today, and asks how the operation went. The nurse cannot confirm who the caller is. What should the nurse do?
o: Check Mrs Green's wishes and agreed contacts before sharing anything
Give a brief update, as the caller knows the patient's name
Ask the caller to confirm Mrs Green's date of birth, then answer
Confirm the operation went well but give no further details
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Code 5.1 requires respect for a person's right to privacy, and 5.2 that people know how and why their information is shared. The nurse should establish whether Mrs Green consents to information being given to this caller (for example agreed contacts or a password).

n.1: Knowing a patient's name does not show the caller has a right to her information.
n.2: A date of birth is easily known by others and does not establish Mrs Green's consent.
n.3: Confirming the outcome is still disclosure of confidential information without consent.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Femi, a nurse on a medical ward, notices that her neighbour has been admitted to another ward in the trust. She has access to the electronic record system and is curious about the diagnosis. She is not involved in the neighbour's care. What applies?
o: She may view it if she later offers support as a friend
She may view it if she does not share what she reads
Viewing the record breaches the need-to-know principle
She may view it because she has trust login access
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Caldicott principle 4: access to personal confidential data should be on a strict need-to-know basis. Having system access does not create a right to view records of people not in your care; this also breaches Code 5.1.

n.0: Personal support as a friend is not a care purpose that justifies access.
n.1: Accessing the record without a care purpose is itself the breach, whether or not it is shared.
n.3: System access is given for care purposes; it does not authorise curiosity viewing.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse finds a printed handover sheet listing patients' names, diagnoses and resuscitation status left on a table in the staff canteen. Which UK GDPR principle has most directly been breached?
o: Accuracy (keeping data up to date)
Storage limitation (retention periods)
Purpose limitation (use for stated purposes)
Integrity and confidentiality (security)
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: UK GDPR Article 5 requires personal data to be processed securely, protecting against unauthorised access (integrity and confidentiality). Code 10.5 also requires records to be kept securely.

n.0: Nothing suggests the content is inaccurate; the problem is security.
n.1: Storage limitation concerns keeping data no longer than necessary, not leaving it unsecured.
n.2: Purpose limitation concerns using data for the purpose it was collected; handover is a legitimate purpose.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A ward team cannot agree whether to share a patient's HIV status with a care agency that will provide personal care at home. The patient has capacity but has not been asked yet. Who in the organisation is responsible for advising on difficult decisions about confidential information?
o: The ward matron on duty
The Freedom to Speak Up Guardian
The Data Protection Officer at the ICO
The Caldicott Guardian
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: The Caldicott Guardian is the senior person responsible for protecting the confidentiality of patient information and enabling appropriate sharing; the Caldicott principles advise involving them in difficult decisions. The first step remains asking the patient.

n.0: The matron can support the team but is not the designated lead for confidentiality decisions.
n.1: Freedom to Speak Up Guardians support staff to raise concerns; they do not advise on confidentiality decisions.
n.2: The ICO is the external regulator; it does not advise on individual sharing decisions within a trust.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Wood, 82, lives alone in England and receives daily care visits for help with washing and meals. She tells the community nurse that her grandson takes her bank card and she now cannot afford food. She says she is frightened of him. Which type of abuse is most clearly described?
o: Financial or material abuse
Self-neglect by Mrs Wood
Organisational abuse by the care agency
Discriminatory abuse by a relative
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.17 lists financial or material abuse, including theft and misuse of a person's money or possessions. Taking her bank card so she cannot buy food fits this type.

n.1: Self-neglect is a person neglecting their own care; here the harm is caused by her grandson.
n.2: Organisational abuse arises within a care setting or service, not from a family member at home.
n.3: Discriminatory abuse is harm motivated by a protected characteristic; nothing suggests this.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A nurse joining a residential home notices that all residents are got up and dressed by 6 am to suit staff rotas, toileted at fixed times regardless of need, and given meals in the same order every day. Residents' preferences are not recorded. Which type of abuse does this most suggest?
o: Neglect and acts of omission
Organisational abuse
Psychological abuse
Physical abuse
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Organisational abuse (Care Act statutory guidance para 14.17) includes poor care practice within an institution or service, for example rigid routines that serve the organisation rather than the people in its care.

n.0: Fixed toileting may neglect individual needs, but para 14.17 places neglect and poor practice arising from an institution's structure, policies and routines under organisational abuse.
n.2: Psychological abuse involves emotional harm such as threats or humiliation by an individual; the problem described is a system of care.
n.3: No physical harm or force is described.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A ward nurse is completing an adult safeguarding referral in England. Under section 42 of the Care Act 2014, the local authority must make enquiries where it has reasonable cause to suspect that an adult has care and support needs and is experiencing, or at risk of, abuse or neglect. What is the third condition?
o: The adult has been assessed as lacking capacity to decide
As a result of those needs, the adult cannot protect themselves
The adult has agreed in writing to the referral being made
The abuse has been witnessed by a health or care professional
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Care Act 2014 s42(1): the duty applies where the adult (a) has needs for care and support, (b) is experiencing or at risk of abuse or neglect, and (c) as a result of those needs is unable to protect themselves from it.

n.0: Lack of capacity is not a s42 criterion; adults with capacity can also meet the criteria.
n.2: Written agreement is not a statutory condition for the enquiry duty.
n.3: Reasonable cause to suspect is enough; abuse need not have been witnessed.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Gray, 70, has capacity and a physical disability. He discloses that his son pushes him when angry, but asks the nurse to do nothing. The nurse discusses the options, and there is no apparent risk to anyone else. Which of the six adult safeguarding principles requires the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk?
o: Empowerment
Protection
Accountability
Proportionality
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: The six principles (Care Act statutory guidance ch 14) are empowerment, prevention, proportionality, protection, partnership and accountability. Proportionality means the least intrusive response appropriate to the risk presented.

n.0: Empowerment concerns person-led decisions and informed consent, not the scale of response.
n.1: Protection concerns support and representation for those in greatest need.
n.2: Accountability concerns accountability and transparency in delivering safeguarding, not the scale of the response.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mrs Ahmed, 66, has capacity and care needs after a stroke. She discloses that her husband sometimes slaps her but says she does not want any action taken. Nobody else lives in the home. Following the statutory guidance, what is the most appropriate action?
o: Make a safeguarding referral but do not let her know it has been made
Share her disclosure with relevant professionals via the safeguarding lead
Report her husband directly to the police against her wishes
Respect her wishes, taking no further action and making no record
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Care and support statutory guidance para 14.92: if an adult with capacity does not want action taken, this does not preclude sharing information with relevant professional colleagues to assess risk and check she is not being coerced. It is good practice to tell her this is being done unless that would increase the risk.

n.0: Para 14.92 says she should normally be told, unless telling her would increase the risk; nothing suggests that here.
n.2: Police involvement against her wishes is not the first step without a wider risk or public interest; colleagues should first assess the risk.
n.3: Her wishes carry great weight, but para 14.92 allows information to be shared with professional colleagues, and the disclosure must be recorded.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: In an emergency department in England, Kerry, 29, is treated for alcohol intoxication. She mentions her 3-year-old son is at home alone. She refuses to let staff contact anyone. Under the Children Act 2004 s16LA duty in force since 30 September 2026, what should the nurse do?
o: Seek Kerry's consent again and share the information if she agrees
Share once a safeguarding threshold has been reached
Record the concern and share if it happens again
Share the relevant information with children's social care now
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Children Act 2004 s16LA (inserted by the Children's Wellbeing and Schools Act 2026, in force 30 September 2026) requires bodies under the s11 duty, including NHS bodies, to share information relevant to safeguarding a child, without a threshold and without needing consent, unless sharing would be more harmful to the child. A young child alone at home needs immediate action.

n.0: Consent is not required under s16LA, and waiting for it delays protection of a child at immediate risk.
n.1: s16LA sets no threshold; the information is relevant to his safety and must be shared.
n.2: A 3-year-old alone at home is at immediate risk; waiting for a repeat leaves him unprotected.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Lee, 58, has care needs and has been financially exploited by a neighbour. At the start of the safeguarding enquiry, the social worker and nurse meet him. Which approach best reflects Making Safeguarding Personal?
o: Ask Mr Lee what outcomes he wants from the enquiry
Agree the safest plan with his family before seeing him
Move him to a care home to remove him from the risk
Complete the enquiry, then tell him what was decided
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Making Safeguarding Personal (Care Act statutory guidance ch 14) means safeguarding is person-led and outcome-focused. An enquiry 'will usually start with asking the adult their view and wishes' (para 14.93).

n.1: Planning with family before hearing from Mr Lee is not person-led.
n.2: Moving him is a highly intrusive response that ignores proportionality and his wishes.
n.3: Telling him afterwards excludes him from decisions about his own safety.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Miss Patel, 45, has a learning disability and has substantial difficulty understanding the safeguarding process. Her only relative is the person suspected of abusing her. The local authority is starting a section 42 enquiry. What should happen?
o: The local authority arranges an independent advocate for her
Her relative supports her, as her closest family member
The enquiry continues without her views, to avoid distress
The nurse acts as her advocate throughout the enquiry
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Care Act 2014 s68 and statutory guidance para 7.3: the local authority must arrange an independent advocate for a safeguarding enquiry where the adult has substantial difficulty being involved and there is no appropriate person to support them. The suspected abuser cannot be that person.

n.1: A relative suspected of abuse is not an appropriate person to support her.
n.2: Excluding her views contradicts Making Safeguarding Personal and the advocacy duty.
n.3: The nurse is not an independent advocate under the Care Act and has a different role.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Joanne, 41, is on an orthopaedic ward after a fall. She has been tearful, says she feels 'a burden to everyone' and has stopped eating. The nurse is concerned about her mood. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask the GP to review her mood once she has been discharged
Avoid asking about suicide so the idea is not suggested to her
Ask her to complete a risk scale to grade her risk of suicide
Ask her directly and compassionately about thoughts of suicide
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 (2022) rec 1.13.5 encourages professionals to use contacts to ask about thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Feeling a burden and withdrawal are warning signs; asking directly and compassionately opens the conversation and allows an appropriate response and escalation.

n.0: Deferring to the GP after discharge delays a response to warning signs present now.
n.1: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea; avoiding it leaves risk unrecognised.
n.2: NG225 recommends not using risk assessment tools and scales to predict suicide.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Liam, 22, attends an emergency department after cutting his arm. A local form asks the nurse to grade his suicide risk as low, medium or high using a scoring tool, and says 'low' scores can be discharged without referral. According to NICE NG225, how should the nurse approach this?
o: Not use the score to predict risk or decide on discharge
Complete the score and refer him to liaison psychiatry if it is high
Repeat the score each hour until he is discharged
Use the score to decide whether to refer him to liaison psychiatry
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 (2022) recs 1.6.1-1.6.3: do not use risk assessment tools and scales to predict future suicide or repetition of self-harm, or to determine who should and should not be offered treatment or who should be discharged; do not use global low, medium or high risk stratification.

n.1: Restricting referral to high scores is risk stratification, which NG225 advises against.
n.2: Repeating a tool does not make it a valid predictor; NG225 advises against using it for this purpose.
n.3: NG225 says tools must not decide who is offered treatment; liaison psychiatry referral should be offered after self-harm.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ayesha, 19, attended an emergency department after taking an overdose. Her blood results are awaited. Before the liaison psychiatry assessment she says she is going home and stands up to leave. What should the nurse do first?
o: Assess her immediate safety and mental state before she leaves
Give her a crisis line number as she walks out
Let her leave, as an adult has the right to discharge herself
Ask security to stop her leaving the department
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.5.14: if a person who has self-harmed wants to leave before a full psychosocial assessment, assess their safety and any mental health problems before they leave. Capacity, consent and duty of care also need consideration (rec 1.7.1).

n.1: A phone number alone does not assess her safety or the medical risk of the overdose.
n.2: She may be free to leave, but NG225 requires an assessment of safety and mental state first; her overdose may also affect capacity.
n.3: Restraining her is not the first step; it may be considered only if she lacks capacity and is at serious risk.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Doyle, 55, tells his community mental health nurse that he has been saving his prescribed tablets and has a large supply at home, as he 'might need them one day'. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Remove the tablets from his home while he is out of the room
Tell his GP to reduce his prescription at the next medication review
Note his comment in the record and review it at the next visit
Discuss removing the tablets with him and agree a plan to keep him safe
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.7.1: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing them with therapeutic collaboration or negotiation to keep the person safe. A stockpile with this comment is an immediate safety concern needing collaborative action and escalation.

n.0: Covert removal undermines trust; NG225 describes collaborative negotiation, not unilateral action.
n.1: Waiting for a future review leaves the means available now.
n.2: Delaying to the next visit fails to act on an immediate safety concern.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Before discharge, a nurse helps Sophie, 27, who self-harms, to develop a safety plan. Which description of the safety plan best follows NICE NG225?
o: Written with and agreed by Sophie, and held by her
Written by the team, then shared with Sophie's family
Written by Sophie, without input from services or family
Written by the nurse, kept in the notes for professionals
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.17 and 1.11.7-1.11.8: a safety plan should be written with and agreed by the person, held by the person, and shared with family and professionals as the person decides. It covers means of self-harm, triggers, coping strategies, supportive contacts, service contact details and keeping the environment safe.

n.1: A plan written for her and shared without her agreement is not collaborative.
n.2: NG225 describes developing the plan in collaboration with services and, as appropriate, family and carers.
n.3: A plan held by professionals is not accessible to Sophie at a time of crisis.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Ben, 34, is admitted to a medical ward after self-harm while intoxicated. He is now talking coherently. A doctor suggests waiting until his breath alcohol is zero before making any referral to liaison psychiatry. What does NICE NG225 recommend?
o: Refer if he repeats his self-harm while on the ward
Refer now, as alcohol levels should not delay the assessment
Wait until his breath alcohol reading has returned to zero
Refer once his physical treatment on the ward is complete
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 recs 1.5.2 and 1.5.4: do not delay the psychosocial assessment until after medical treatment is completed, and do not use breath or blood alcohol levels to delay it. Rec 1.7.21: after admission for self-harm, offer referral to liaison psychiatry as soon as possible, alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting for a repeat episode ignores the need for prompt assessment after this one.
n.2: NG225 states alcohol levels should not be used to delay the assessment.
n.3: NG225 advises not to wait until medical treatment is finished.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Kayla, 30, had a psychosocial assessment in an emergency department after self-harm and is discharged home. The team remains concerned about her safety. According to NICE NG225, within what time should initial aftercare be provided?
o: Within 14 days, at a routine outpatient clinic
Within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment
Within 7 days of the psychosocial assessment
Within 24 hours of arriving at the department
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE NG225 rec 1.10.2: if there are ongoing safety concerns after self-harm, the responsible team should provide initial aftercare within 48 hours of the psychosocial assessment.

n.0: A routine 14-day appointment is far later than NG225 recommends when safety concerns persist.
n.2: 7 days is longer than the 48-hour aftercare window in NG225.
n.3: The timing runs from the psychosocial assessment, and the interval is 48 hours.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: A district nurse visits Mr Shaw, 68, whose wife died recently. He has given his dog to a neighbour, written letters to his children and says calmly that 'everything is sorted now'. He denies any physical symptoms. How should the nurse interpret these signs?
o: They are warning signs of suicidal intent needing direct enquiry
They suggest early dementia, so a memory screen is the priority
They show he is adjusting well and needs routine follow-up
They suggest normal grief, so a bereavement leaflet is enough
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Giving away possessions, putting affairs in order and sudden calm after loss can signal suicidal intent (NMC Annexe B 1.1.6: recognise signs of self-harm and suicidal ideation). NICE NG225 supports asking about suicidal thoughts and acting on immediate safety concerns.

n.1: Nothing suggests cognitive decline; the behaviour points to risk of suicide.
n.2: Settling affairs after recent bereavement with sudden calm is a recognised warning sign, not evidence of adjustment.
n.3: A leaflet does not address possible suicidal intent, which needs direct enquiry.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Amara is a newly registered nurse on a surgical ward in England. During induction a colleague explains that one organisation sets the professional standards in the Code and can take action if a registrant's fitness to practise is impaired. Which organisation is the colleague describing?
o: The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Royal College of Nursing
The Care Quality Commission
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: The NMC is the professional regulator for nurses, midwives and nursing associates: it publishes the Code (2015, updated 2018), keeps the register and deals with fitness to practise concerns about individual registrants.

n.1: The RCN is a professional body and trade union; it supports nurses but has no regulatory powers over registration.
n.2: The CQC regulates registered providers of health and social care in England (for example enforcing regulation 20, the statutory duty of candour), not individual nurses.
n.3: NICE produces evidence-based guidance; it does not register nurses or judge fitness to practise.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: On a medical ward in England, Mr Hughes, 70, was given a tenfold insulin overdose and needed transfer to intensive care. The ward manager asks which organisation regulates the trust's compliance with the statutory duty of candour under regulation 20 of the 2014 Regulations. Which organisation is this?
o: The Care Quality Commission
The Nursing and Midwifery Council
The Health and Safety Executive
The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: The statutory duty of candour (Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, reg 20) applies to registered providers and is regulated by the CQC in England. The professional duty in Code 14 is overseen by the NMC for individual registrants.

n.1: The NMC oversees the professional duty of candour of individual registrants (Code 14), not the provider's statutory duty under reg 20.
n.2: The HSE enforces workplace health and safety law such as HASAWA 1974 and RIDDOR, not reg 20 of the 2014 Regulations.
n.3: The Ombudsman investigates unresolved complaints about the NHS; it does not regulate providers' compliance with reg 20.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Joseph, a staff nurse, is reviewing a NICE guideline with a student nurse. The student asks what legal status NICE guidance has for registered nurses caring for an individual patient. Which statement by Joseph is most accurate?
o: It replaces individual clinical judgement whenever a recommendation applies
It should be taken fully into account alongside the person's needs and preferences
It carries the same legal force as an Act of Parliament once it is published
It applies to medical staff, while nurses follow local trust policy instead
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: NICE's standard 'Your responsibility' statement (seen in NG253) says guidance is not mandatory: professionals are expected to take it fully into account alongside the individual needs, preferences and values of the person. Code 6.1 requires advice to be evidence-based.

n.0: NICE states its guidance supports, and does not replace, the professional's judgement about the individual person.
n.2: NICE guidance is not legislation; it does not have the force of an Act of Parliament.
n.3: NICE guidance applies to all health professionals, including nurses, not to medical staff alone.

Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.q: Mr Rahman, 58, is a practising Muslim admitted for a planned operation in England. He asks the nurse whether he can be helped to pray at the set times each day and have a quiet space to do so. Which Article of the Human Rights Act 1998 Schedule 1 most directly protects this request?
o: Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 14, the prohibition of discrimination
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, the right to respect for private and family life
Law, Consent, Capacity & Safeguarding.w: Article 9 protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, including manifesting religion in worship and practice. Supporting Mr Rahman to pray is a direct application (HRA 1998 Sch 1).

n.1: Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of the other Convention rights; it does not itself create the right to practise religion.
n.2: Article 5 concerns liberty and detention, not religious observance.
n.3: Article 8 protects private and family life; religious practice is protected more directly by Article 9.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A nurse has completed a detailed physical assessment of Mr Rees, 75, who is admitted after a fall at home. She has recorded his observations, skin, mobility and continence. Which further area is most needed to make the assessment holistic before discharge planning?
o: A second set of skin checks by another registered nurse
His social circumstances, support at home and his own priorities
A full list of every past hospital admission he has had
A full repeat of his observations before the end of the day shift
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Holistic assessment (P3.1, P3.4) combines physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs and the person's own goals. After a fall at home, his living situation, support and priorities are central to safe planning, and NICE NG249 includes a home hazard assessment.

n.0: A second skin check adds to the physical assessment already completed.
n.2: An exhaustive admission history adds little compared with his current social and support needs.
n.3: Repeat observations are part of physical monitoring, not the missing holistic domain.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Webb, 68, has a moderate learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. His support worker says he has become irritable and is refusing his favourite activities, which is unusual for him. Which is the most appropriate way to interpret this information?
o: As a possible sign of acute illness that needs assessment
As part of his learning disability needing no action
As evidence that he lacks capacity for all decisions
As a behavioural issue for the support team to manage
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.4.8: changes in cognitive function may present as changes in behaviour or irritability in adults with a learning disability or dementia; rec 1.4.7 says assessment should include history from family or carers. A change from his baseline is significant.

n.1: Attributing new behaviour to his learning disability (diagnostic overshadowing) risks missing illness.
n.2: Behaviour change does not establish incapacity; capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2-3).
n.3: Treating it as behaviour to manage ignores a possible physical cause.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Patel, 58, is two days after bowel surgery. Her NEWS2 is 4. On assessment the nurse notices her knees are mottled and her lips look slightly blue. How should these findings change the nurse's view of her risk?
o: Her NEWS2 of 4 shows low risk, so routine monitoring is enough
They are expected after surgery and do not change her risk
They should be rechecked once her NEWS2 rises to 5 or more
She may be at higher risk than her NEWS2 score suggests
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 rec 1.6.3: consider a higher risk of severe illness or death from sepsis than NEWS2 suggests if the person has a mottled or ashen appearance or cyanosis of skin, lips or tongue. These are signs of physical ill health (Annexe B 1.2.1) needing urgent escalation.

n.0: NG253 says these signs indicate higher risk than the score alone suggests.
n.1: Mottling and cyanosis are not normal post-operative findings.
n.2: Waiting for the score to rise delays escalation of signs that already indicate higher risk.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Ortiz, 66, is profoundly deaf and uses British Sign Language. He is being admitted for elective surgery at an English NHS hospital. Under the Accessible Information Standard, what should the nurse do as part of the admission assessment?
o: Use written notes with him, as these work for all deaf people
Identify, record and flag his communication needs and arrange support
Ask his daughter to interpret during his stay to save time
Note his deafness in the record so staff know to speak more loudly
Assessment & Care Planning.w: The Accessible Information Standard (DAPB1605, updated June 2025) requires services to identify, record, flag, share and meet information and communication needs related to disability or sensory loss. For a BSL user this means arranging a qualified interpreter and flagging the need.

n.0: BSL is a distinct language; written English may not meet his needs.
n.2: Relying on a relative does not meet his needs and compromises confidentiality and accuracy.
n.3: Speaking louder does not help a profoundly deaf BSL user and does not meet the Standard.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Nolan, 74, has cellulitis of the leg and is otherwise well. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 16, SpO2 97%, blood pressure 132/78, pulse 84, alert, temperature 39.3°C. Using NEWS2 Chart 1, what is her temperature score and her aggregate score?
o: Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 2
Temperature scores 3, giving a NEWS2 total of 3
Temperature scores 2, giving a NEWS2 total of 4
Temperature scores 1, giving a NEWS2 total of 1
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017) Chart 1: temperature 39.1°C or above scores 2; 38.1-39.0 scores 1. All other parameters score 0 (RR 12-20, SpO2 96% or above, systolic 111-219, pulse 51-90, alert, on air), so the aggregate is 2.

n.1: No temperature band scores 3 for fever; 3 is for 35.0°C or below.
n.2: The other parameters all score 0, so the total equals the temperature score of 2.
n.3: A score of 1 applies to 38.1-39.0°C; 39.3°C is in the 39.1 or above band.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Bailey, 66, has pneumonia and is breathing air. His observations are: respiratory rate 22, SpO2 95%, systolic BP 104, pulse 96, alert, temperature 38.3°C. What is his NEWS2 score and the minimum response?
o: 6; inform the medical team at once and observe at least hourly
6; continue observations every 4-6 hours and reassess the score
5; inform the nurse in charge and observe every 4 hours
7; request an emergency review by the critical care team
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NEWS2 Chart 1: RR 21-24 = 2; SpO2 94-95 = 1; systolic 101-110 = 1; pulse 91-110 = 1; alert = 0; temperature 38.1-39.0 = 1; air = 0. Total 6 (medium). Chart 4: 5 or more needs at least hourly monitoring and the RN must immediately inform the medical team and request urgent assessment by a clinician competent in acute illness.

n.1: A score of 5-6 is the key threshold for an urgent response; 4-6 hourly monitoring is for scores 1-4.
n.2: The total is 6, not 5, and a score of 5 or more requires hourly observation and medical review, not 4-hourly.
n.3: The total is 6, not 7, so a critical care emergency response is not yet the minimum required.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Fry, 45, is on a surgical ward after an appendicectomy. Her observations on air are: respiratory rate 26, SpO2 97%, systolic BP 124, pulse 88, alert, temperature 37.2°C. Which response does NEWS2 require?
o: Repeat the observations in 4-6 hours as her total is 3
Record the observations and recheck them in 12 hours
Observe at least hourly and inform the medical team
Call the critical care outreach team as an emergency
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Respiratory rate 25 or more scores 3; all other parameters score 0, giving a total of 3. NEWS2 Charts 2 and 4: a score of 3 in any single parameter is low-medium risk and requires an urgent ward-based response, at least hourly monitoring, and the RN informing the medical team.

n.0: Although the total is low, a single parameter scoring 3 triggers hourly monitoring and medical review.
n.1: 12-hourly observation applies to a total of 0, not to a score of 3 in one parameter.
n.3: An emergency critical care response is required at an aggregate of 7 or more.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Shaw, 70, is weighed as 48 kg and measured as 1.62 m tall on admission. She says her clothes have been getting looser. What is her BMI to one decimal place, and how is it interpreted under NICE CG32?
o: 18.3 kg/m²; this meets the NICE criteria for malnutrition
29.6 kg/m²; this is within the overweight range
18.3 kg/m²; this is within the healthy weight range
20.1 kg/m²; this places her at moderate risk of malnutrition
Assessment & Care Planning.w: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²: 48 ÷ (1.62 × 1.62) = 48 ÷ 2.6244 = 18.29, so 18.3 kg/m². NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as including a BMI under 18.5 kg/m², so she meets the criteria and needs nutrition support planning.

n.1: 29.6 results from dividing weight by height in metres once rather than by height squared.
n.2: The value is correct, but a BMI under 18.5 meets the CG32 definition of malnutrition, not healthy weight.
n.3: 20.1 is a miscalculation; the correct value is 18.3 kg/m².

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Mensah, 59, has Black African heritage and is recovering from pneumonia. His pulse oximeter reads 94% on air. He is a little more breathless than earlier. Which consideration is most important when interpreting this reading?
o: Oximeters underestimate saturations in people with dark skin
Oximeters can overestimate saturations in people with dark skin
His reading is within target, so his breathlessness is not significant
An SpO2 of 94% on air means oxygen therapy should be started
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 (practical information on pulse oximeters): some oximeters underestimate or overestimate saturations, especially when borderline, and overestimation has been reported in people with dark skin. His true saturation may be lower, so the reading should be interpreted with his clinical picture and escalated if concerned.

n.0: The reported error in people with dark skin is overestimation, not underestimation.
n.2: Increasing breathlessness is significant even when the oximeter reading is within target.
n.3: 94% on air is within the 94-98% target for most adults; starting oxygen is not indicated by the number alone.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Clarke, 52, is alert, warm and chatting. An automated machine records his blood pressure as 82/50 mmHg; an hour ago it was 128/76. His pulse is 78 and regular. What should the nurse do first?
o: Record it as a machine error because he looks well
Repeat the automated reading at the next routine set
Recheck the blood pressure manually and assess him now
Score it as 3 and put out a cardiac arrest call
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Annexe B 2.1 requires nurses to take and interpret vital signs manually and by device. An unexpected device reading should be checked promptly by a manual measurement alongside clinical assessment, rather than accepted or dismissed.

n.0: Assuming error without checking risks missing true deterioration.
n.1: Waiting for the next routine set may delay recognition of genuine hypotension.
n.3: He is alert and talking, so he is not in cardiac arrest; the reading needs verifying first.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Grant, 72, has COPD and is admitted with breathlessness. His SpO2 is 89% on air. No target saturation range has been prescribed or documented. A colleague says to use NEWS2 SpO2 Scale 2 because he has COPD. What should the nurse do?
o: Use Scale 2, because a diagnosis of COPD is sufficient
Use Scale 1 and ask the medical team to prescribe a target range
Use Scale 2 and give oxygen to reach 94-98% saturations
Leave the SpO2 parameter unscored until a target range is prescribed
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): Scale 2 (target 88-92%) is for people with hypercapnic respiratory failure and is used when a clinician has prescribed that target. Until then Scale 1 applies (89% scores 3), and the team should be asked to set a target.

n.0: COPD alone does not authorise Scale 2; it must be prescribed by a clinician.
n.2: Scale 2 corresponds to a target of 88-92%, not 94-98%.
n.3: Leaving the parameter unscored gives a falsely low NEWS2 and delays escalation.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Doyle, 63, is receiving 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannulae. Her observations are: respiratory rate 18, SpO2 96%, systolic BP 130, pulse 80, alert, temperature 36.8°C. Her SpO2 is scored on Scale 1. What is her NEWS2 score?
o: 1, because supplemental oxygen scores 1
3, because oxygen scores 3 on Scale 1
0, because each vital sign is in range
2, because supplemental oxygen scores 2
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NEWS2 Chart 1: SpO2 96% or above on Scale 1 scores 0, but the 'air or oxygen' parameter scores 2 for any supplemental oxygen. All other values score 0, so the total is 2.

n.0: Supplemental oxygen scores 2, not 1.
n.1: Oxygen use scores 2; 3 is not a value in the air or oxygen parameter.
n.2: The use of supplemental oxygen is scored separately and adds 2 points.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Price, 79, was alert this morning. At 14:00 his eyes are closed and he opens them and answers when the nurse speaks to him, but then drifts off again. His other observations are unchanged from earlier. How should his level of consciousness be recorded and scored on NEWS2?
o: V on ACVPU, scoring 1
V on ACVPU, scoring 3
A on ACVPU, scoring 0
P on ACVPU, scoring 3
Assessment & Care Planning.w: ACVPU: Alert, new Confusion, responds to Voice, responds to Pain, Unresponsive. He responds to voice, so V. NEWS2 Chart 1 scores any of C, V, P or U as 3, which also triggers at least hourly monitoring and informing the medical team.

n.0: V is correct, but any score other than Alert scores 3 on NEWS2, not 1.
n.2: He is not alert, as his eyes are closed until he is spoken to.
n.3: He responds to voice, so a pain stimulus was not needed; P overstates the level.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Lewis, 84, is on day 2 after a hip replacement. Her daughter tells the nurse her mother 'is not making sense today' and keeps asking where she is, which is new. Her other observations are within normal ranges. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Recheck her level of consciousness at the next routine set
Record new confusion as scoring 3 and inform the medical team
Record her as Alert, as she is awake and talking with her daughter
Reassure the daughter that this is normal after hip surgery
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NEWS2 (RCP 2017): new confusion (C on ACVPU) scores 3. A single parameter scoring 3 requires at least hourly monitoring and the RN informing the medical team. NICE CG103 also asks that changes reported by relatives prompt delirium assessment.

n.0: New confusion scores 3 and needs action now, not at the next routine check.
n.2: Being awake and talking does not make a newly confused person 'Alert' on ACVPU.
n.3: New confusion is not an expected finding and may signal delirium, sepsis or other illness.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Ito, 38, has a head injury. On assessment his eyes open to pressure on the fingertip, he is talking but disorientated about time and place, and he localises to a painful stimulus. What is his Glasgow Coma Scale score?
Assessment & Care Planning.w: GCS: eye opening to pressure = 2; confused speech = 4; localising = 5. Total 2 + 4 + 5 = 11 out of 15 (range 3-15). Any fall in GCS after head injury needs urgent escalation.

n.0: Orientated speech scores 5 and obeying commands 6; he is confused and localises.
n.1: Eye opening to speech scores 3; he opens his eyes only to pressure, which scores 2.
n.2: Inappropriate words score 3; he is talking in sentences but confused, which scores 4.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Ward, 72, is breathless with heart failure and has gained 3 kg in 4 days. On chest auscultation, which finding would the nurse most expect and report?
o: A pleural rub over the left upper zone
Fine crackles at both lung bases
Absent sounds over the whole right lung
High-pitched stridor on inspiration
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Fluid overload in heart failure causes pulmonary oedema, heard as fine crackles, usually at both bases. This fits her rapid weight gain and breathlessness (Annexe B 2.8: undertake chest auscultation and interpret findings).

n.0: A pleural rub indicates inflamed pleura, for example pleurisy, not fluid overload.
n.2: Absent sounds over one whole lung suggest pneumothorax, large effusion or collapse, not the typical bilateral picture.
n.3: Stridor is an upper airway sound suggesting obstruction, not pulmonary oedema.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Ali, 41, is given IV co-amoxiclav. Within minutes he says his throat feels tight, and the nurse hears a harsh, high-pitched noise each time he breathes in. What does this sound indicate, and what is the priority?
o: Normal breath sounds; reassure him and continue the infusion
Crackles from fluid; sit him up and recheck later
Wheeze from asthma; give his inhaler and observe him
Stridor from upper airway obstruction; call for emergency help
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A harsh, high-pitched inspiratory sound is stridor, indicating upper airway narrowing. After an IV antibiotic this suggests anaphylaxis, an airway emergency: stop the infusion, call for help and treat following the RCUK ABCDE approach and anaphylaxis algorithm.

n.0: Stridor with throat tightness is never a normal finding and continuing the drug is dangerous.
n.1: Crackles are added sounds in the lungs and are not the harsh inspiratory sound described.
n.2: Wheeze is usually expiratory from narrowed lower airways; an inhaler does not treat airway swelling in anaphylaxis.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Kerr, 66, fell and hit her head. Her GCS has fallen from 14 to 11 over an hour, and her right pupil is now larger than the left and slow to react to light. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the findings and inform the next ward round
Call for an urgent medical review as an emergency
Recheck her neurological observations in 1 hour
Dim the lights and recheck her pupils in 30 minutes
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A falling GCS with a new unequal, sluggish pupil after head injury suggests rising intracranial pressure, a neurological emergency (Annexe B 2.12). Immediate escalation is needed; she also scores 3 on NEWS2 for an altered level of consciousness.

n.0: A ward round is far too late for an acute neurological deterioration.
n.2: Waiting an hour delays treatment of possible raised intracranial pressure.
n.3: Changing the lighting does not address the deterioration and delays escalation.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A nurse is carrying out a whole-body systems assessment of Mr Burns, 80, who has been bedbound for several days. On the skin review she finds a red area over his sacrum that does not blanch with light finger pressure. What should she do?
o: Record it as a category 2 pressure ulcer and apply a dressing
Reassess it at his next weekly skin inspection
Massage the area to restore its circulation and recheck it tomorrow
Start pressure ulcer prevention and recheck the skin at least 2-hourly
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG179: use finger palpation or diascopy to test blanching; if non-blanching erythema is present, start prevention and reassess the skin at least every 2 hours until resolved. A systems assessment includes skin (Annexe B 2.7).

n.0: Intact non-blanching erythema is a category 1 finding, not category 2, which involves partial-thickness skin loss.
n.1: Weekly review is too infrequent; CG179 requires at least 2-hourly reassessment.
n.2: Massaging pressure-damaged skin can cause further harm, and a day's delay is too long.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A student nurse is about to auscultate the chest of Mrs Hall, 68, who has a productive cough. Which technique should the supervising nurse advise?
o: Listen at one point on each side for a few seconds
Listen over her clothing to protect her dignity
Listen at the front of the chest, which is enough for a review
Sit her upright and compare each side at matching points
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Chest auscultation (Annexe B 2.8) is done with the person upright where possible, the stethoscope on bare skin, comparing left with right at matching points front and back so that differences in air entry and added sounds can be detected.

n.0: A single point per side cannot detect localised changes such as basal crackles.
n.1: Clothing muffles and distorts breath sounds; dignity is maintained in other ways.
n.2: The bases are best heard from the back, so front-only listening misses findings.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A nurse is admitting four people to an acute medical unit. Using the risk factors in NICE CG103, which person is at increased risk of developing delirium and should be observed for it?
o: Mr Green, 45, admitted for a planned endoscopy
Mrs Young, 78, admitted with a urinary infection
Ms Black, 30, admitted with a simple ankle fracture
Mr White, 52, admitted for blood pressure review
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 (updated 2023) lists risk factors including age 65 or over, past or present cognitive impairment or dementia, current hip fracture and severe illness. Mrs Young is 78, so she should be observed at least daily for indicators of delirium.

n.0: At 45 and admitted for a planned procedure, Mr Green has none of the CG103 risk factors described.
n.2: An ankle fracture is not a CG103 risk factor; current hip fracture is.
n.3: At 52 with no listed risk factor, Mr White is not identified as at risk by CG103.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Daly, 81, on a general medical ward, has become muddled and restless since yesterday evening and is not sure where he is. His wife says he is 'not himself'. Which tool does NICE CG103 recommend the nurse uses to assess him for delirium?
o: The Abbreviated Mental Test score
The 4AT
The Mini Mental State Examination
The CAM-ICU
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: if indicators of delirium are identified, a competent practitioner should assess using the 4AT; in critical care or the recovery room use CAM-ICU or ICDSC instead.

n.0: The AMT is a cognitive screen, not the delirium tool recommended in CG103.
n.2: The MMSE assesses cognitive impairment and is not the CG103 delirium assessment tool.
n.3: CAM-ICU is recommended for critical care and recovery settings, not a general ward.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Ross, 77, is ventilated in the intensive care unit after major emergency surgery. Over the last few hours she has become agitated at times and keeps picking at her lines. The nurse is concerned she may be developing delirium. Which assessment tool is recommended in this setting by NICE CG103?
o: CAM-ICU or ICDSC
The Glasgow Coma Scale
The 4AT
The Abbey pain scale
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 rec 1.6.1: in critical care or the recovery room after surgery, use CAM-ICU or the Intensive Care Delirium Screening Checklist instead of the 4AT.

n.1: GCS measures level of consciousness and does not assess delirium.
n.2: The 4AT is recommended for most settings, but CG103 specifies CAM-ICU or ICDSC in critical care.
n.3: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people who cannot communicate, not delirium.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Blake, 85, has dementia and was admitted two days ago with pneumonia. Staff describe him as 'a lovely quiet man' who sleeps most of the day, eats little and is slow to respond. His family say he is usually chatty. What should the nurse suspect?
o: Hypoactive delirium needing assessment
Expected tiredness from his pneumonia
Progression of his dementia over two days
Low mood related to being in hospital
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 notes hypoactive delirium is easily missed. Recent changes in cognition, physical function (reduced movement, appetite, sleep) and social behaviour (withdrawal), reported by family, are indicators of delirium needing assessment with the 4AT (rec 1.3.1, 1.6.1).

n.1: Attributing a marked change from his baseline to tiredness risks missing delirium.
n.2: Dementia progresses gradually; a change over two days points to delirium.
n.3: Low mood may cause withdrawal, but slowed responses and drowsiness developing over days point to delirium first.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Turner, 72, had a hip replacement two days ago. Her son tells the nurse at visiting time that his mother 'seems confused and is seeing things on the curtains', which started this afternoon. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask the son to stay with her to settle her for the night
Note it and ask the night staff to see if it continues
Reassure the son that this is common after an anaesthetic
Assess her for delirium and record the reported change
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 recs 1.3.1 and 1.5.1-1.5.2: recent changes or fluctuations (including hallucinations) may be reported by relatives and should prompt assessment with an appropriate tool; changes must be documented.

n.0: Family presence can help, but it does not replace assessment of a new change.
n.1: Deferring to night staff delays assessment of an acute change.
n.2: Dismissing a new change risks missing delirium and its cause.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Moore, 83, has delirium. He is shouting, pulling at his cannula and swinging his arms at staff. No one has been hurt yet. What should the nurse do first?
o: Request haloperidol as the first step to calm him down quickly
Restrain his arms so the cannula is not pulled out
Ask security to stay with him until he settles down
Use calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation and look for causes
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103: if a person with delirium is distressed or a risk to themselves or others, first use verbal and non-verbal de-escalation; consider short-term haloperidol if de-escalation is ineffective or inappropriate. Underlying causes such as pain, retention or hypoxia should be sought (Annexe B 1.1.5).

n.0: Medication is considered when de-escalation fails or is inappropriate, not as the first step.
n.1: Physical restraint is a last resort and may worsen agitation and delirium.
n.2: Security presence is restrictive and does not address his distress or its cause.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Ford, 50, is due to have surgery this afternoon. She is restless, keeps asking the same questions and says she cannot stop thinking she will not wake up. Her observations are normal. What is the most appropriate initial nursing intervention?
o: Give her a leaflet about the operation and leave her to rest
Ask the anaesthetist to prescribe a sedative premedication
Tell her that modern anaesthetics are very safe and move on
Sit with her, explore her fears and explain what will happen
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NMC proficiency P4.8 requires nurses to initiate interventions for common symptoms including anxiety. Listening, exploring specific fears and giving clear information are first-line, person-centred interventions for pre-operative anxiety.

n.0: A leaflet without discussion leaves her specific fears unexplored.
n.1: Medication may be considered later, but non-drug measures come first for anxiety with normal observations.
n.2: Brief reassurance without exploring her fears does not address her anxiety.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A student nurse asks how to tell delirium from dementia when an older person on the ward is confused. Which feature points most strongly to delirium?
o: A long history of difficulty with word-finding
Acute onset over hours or days with fluctuation
Confusion that is stable from day to day
Gradual memory decline over several years
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE CG103 describes delirium indicators as recent changes or fluctuations, over hours or days, in cognition, perception, physical function or social behaviour. Dementia typically develops gradually over months to years.

n.0: Longstanding word-finding difficulty suggests an established condition rather than an acute change.
n.2: Stable confusion does not show the fluctuation characteristic of delirium.
n.3: Gradual decline over years is typical of dementia, not delirium.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: At 16:30 the laboratory phones the ward with a potassium result of 6.9 mmol/L for Mr Hayes, 74, who has chronic kidney disease. He feels 'a bit weak' but is otherwise as before. The doctor who requested the test has gone home. What should the nurse do?
o: Escalate to the on-call doctor now and document the result
Recheck his observations in 4 hours and escalate if they change
Record the result for the day team to review in the morning
Ask the laboratory to send the result to his GP for review
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NMC proficiency P3.12 requires nurses to interpret results and act promptly, escalating when required. A potassium of 6.9 mmol/L is markedly raised and can cause life-threatening arrhythmias, so the on-call doctor must be told now and the communication documented (Code 10).

n.1: Normal-looking observations do not exclude the risk of arrhythmia from severe hyperkalaemia.
n.2: Waiting until morning leaves a dangerous result untreated for hours.
n.3: The GP is not responsible for an inpatient's urgent results.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A nurse is about to take blood for a full blood count and urea and electrolytes from Mrs Ellis, 66. She has a peripheral cannula in her left forearm with an IV infusion of 0.9% sodium chloride running. Which site is most appropriate?
o: The cannula itself, after briefly pausing the infusion
Her left antecubital fossa, above the cannula
A vein in her right arm, away from the infusion
A vein in the back of her left hand, below the cannula
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Blood taken from a limb with an infusion running can be diluted or contaminated by the fluid, giving falsely altered results (for example sodium, potassium or glucose). The opposite arm should be used (Annexe B 2.2).

n.0: Sampling from an infusing cannula risks contaminated results and is not the most appropriate choice here.
n.1: Sampling above an infusion on the same arm risks contamination with the infused fluid.
n.3: The same limb is still affected by the infusion; the opposite arm is preferred.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Owusu, 70, has suspected sepsis from a chest infection. His NEWS2 is 8 and the FY2 doctor has reviewed him. Under NICE NG253 (2025), which set of blood tests should the nurse make sure is taken?
o: Urea and electrolytes and FBC, with lactate if the BP falls
Venous gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, FBC and CRP
Arterial gas and troponin, then cultures after antibiotics are given
FBC, CRP and liver function tests, with cultures if fever persists
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NICE NG253 recs 1.8.2-1.8.3 (high risk, NEWS2 7 or more): take a venous blood test including blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count and CRP (plus U&E, creatinine, liver function tests and a clotting screen), and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.

n.0: Lactate is part of the initial high-risk bloods and should not depend on a further fall in BP.
n.2: NG253 specifies a venous gas with lactate and blood culture as part of the initial tests; delaying cultures is not recommended.
n.3: Cultures are part of the initial bloods and should not wait for persisting fever.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Price, 59, needs a blood sample for group and screen before surgery. The nurse has confirmed her identity verbally and against her wristband. When should the sample tube be labelled?
o: In the laboratory, from the details on the request form
At the nurses' station once all samples are collected
At the bedside, straight after taking the sample
Before going to the bedside, so it is ready to use
Assessment & Care Planning.w: BSH guidance on the administration of blood components (2017) requires positive patient identification and labelling of the sample at the bedside, immediately after it is taken, to prevent 'wrong blood in tube' errors.

n.0: The sample must be labelled by the person who took it at the bedside, not by the laboratory.
n.1: Labelling away from the patient after collecting several samples increases the risk of mislabelling.
n.3: Pre-labelled tubes can be used for the wrong patient and are a recognised cause of errors.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Kaye, 61, is on a cardiac monitor. The monitor alarms and shows a chaotic trace resembling ventricular fibrillation. The nurse looks across and sees Mr Kaye sitting up, talking and brushing his teeth. What should the nurse do first?
o: Go to him, assess him and check the electrodes and leads
Put out a cardiac arrest call and bring the defibrillator
Silence the alarm and review the monitor trace later
Give a precordial thump to restore a normal rhythm
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Monitor traces must be interpreted with the patient. Movement such as tooth brushing commonly causes artefact resembling VF. The nurse should assess him directly and check electrode contact; a cardiac arrest is confirmed by assessing the patient (RCUK 2025), not by the monitor alone.

n.1: He is conscious and talking, so he is not in cardiac arrest.
n.2: Silencing without assessing the patient risks missing a genuine problem.
n.3: A precordial thump is not indicated in a conscious person and is not a response to artefact.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Abbott, 67, presses the call bell on a surgical ward with central chest tightness that started 10 minutes ago. She looks pale and clammy. After calling for help and checking her observations, which investigation should the nurse prioritise?
o: A peak flow reading to assess her breathing
A chest X-ray, requested for later in the day
A 12-lead ECG, shown promptly to the doctor
A troponin sample, sent before anything else
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A 12-lead ECG should be recorded as soon as possible in suspected acute coronary syndrome and shown promptly to a doctor so ischaemia or infarction can be identified (P3.11 undertake investigations and share findings; P3.12 act promptly).

n.0: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not chest pain suggestive of a cardiac cause.
n.1: A chest X-ray does not identify acute myocardial ischaemia and should not take priority.
n.3: Troponin is useful but takes time; the ECG gives immediate information.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: The laboratory reports a potassium of 6.4 mmol/L for Ms Lane, 35, with a note that the sample was haemolysed. She is well, with normal observations, and her potassium yesterday was normal. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Disregard the result and record it as laboratory error
Wait until tomorrow's routine bloods to see the trend
Treat it as genuine hyperkalaemia and start a cardiac arrest alert
Inform the doctor and arrange a repeat sample
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Haemolysis releases potassium from red cells and can falsely raise the result. The finding should still be reported to the doctor and a repeat sample taken promptly to confirm or exclude true hyperkalaemia (P3.12).

n.0: A haemolysed result is unreliable but cannot simply be dismissed without repeating it.
n.1: Waiting until tomorrow could leave true hyperkalaemia unrecognised.
n.2: She is well and has no arrest; a haemolysed result needs urgent confirmation, not an emergency call.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A nurse is recording a 12-lead ECG for Mr Ford, 76, who is cold and shivering. The trace has a wandering, fuzzy baseline in several leads. What is the best way to improve the recording?
o: Accept the trace, as shivering does not affect how it is interpreted
Warm him, help him relax and lie still, then check electrode contact
Increase the paper speed and record the trace again at once
Record the trace with him standing to reduce the shivering
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Muscle tremor, movement and poor electrode contact cause artefact. Making the person warm, comfortable and still, usually lying or semi-recumbent, with clean dry skin and good electrode contact, gives an interpretable trace (Annexe B 2.3).

n.0: Artefact can mimic or hide abnormalities, so the trace may not be interpretable.
n.2: Changing paper speed alters the appearance of the trace and does not remove tremor artefact.
n.3: Standing increases muscle activity and movement; ECGs are recorded with the person at rest.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Booth, 58, has type 2 diabetes treated with gliclazide. Before lunch he is sweaty and shaky but alert and able to swallow. His capillary blood glucose is 3.3 mmol/L. What should the nurse do first?
o: Withhold his gliclazide and recheck at the next meal
Call 999 and place him in the recovery position
Give his lunch now and recheck the glucose in 1 hour
Give 15-20 g of glucose tablets by mouth and recheck
Assessment & Care Planning.w: RCUK First aid guidelines 2025: treat hypoglycaemia when capillary glucose is below 4.0 mmol/L; if awake and able to swallow give 15-20 g glucose or dextrose tablets by mouth, repeat the measurement after treatment (repeat treatment if no improvement after 15 minutes), then give a snack once recovered.

n.0: Medication review may follow, but the low glucose needs treating now.
n.1: He is alert and can swallow; 999 and the recovery position are for an unresponsive person.
n.2: A meal acts too slowly; quick-acting glucose is needed first, then a longer-acting snack.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Dean, 49, has just eaten an orange and asks the nurse to check her blood glucose. The nurse plans to use the side of her fingertip. What should the nurse do before taking the sample?
o: Squeeze the finger firmly to produce a large drop
Ask her to wash and dry her hands
Clean her finger with an alcohol wipe and test while still wet
Use the first drop from the centre of the fingertip pad
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Sugar residue on the skin, for example from fruit, can give a falsely high capillary glucose reading. Washing and drying the hands with warm water removes residue and improves blood flow (Annexe B 2.10: measure and interpret blood glucose).

n.0: Firm squeezing dilutes the drop with tissue fluid and can give an inaccurate result.
n.2: Testing through wet alcohol can dilute the sample and alter the reading.
n.3: The pad is more painful and the problem of sugar on the skin remains.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Lowe, 81, lives in a care home and was admitted yesterday with a chest infection. He has had three episodes of loose stool since this morning, and the nurse records the latest one on his stool chart as watery with no solid pieces. Using the Bristol Stool Chart, which type is this?
o: Type 3
Type 7
Type 5
Type 1
Assessment & Care Planning.w: The Bristol Stool Chart runs from type 1 (separate hard lumps) to type 7 (watery, no solid pieces). Type 7 indicates diarrhoea; with new diarrhoea the nurse should assess for infection, isolate as required and send a specimen per local policy (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Type 3 is sausage-shaped with cracks on the surface, a normal stool.
n.2: Type 5 is soft blobs with clear-cut edges, not entirely liquid.
n.3: Type 1 is separate hard lumps, indicating constipation.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Grey, 34, has symptoms of a urinary tract infection and needs a urine sample sent for culture. She is independent and mobile. Which instruction should the nurse give?
o: Collect urine from the toilet bowl after passing it
Discard the first part of the stream and collect the midstream urine
Collect the last few drops of urine at the end of passing it
Collect the first part of the urine stream into a clean pot
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A clean-catch midstream specimen reduces contamination by skin and urethral organisms. The first part of the stream is discarded and the midstream portion collected into a sterile container, labelled and sent promptly (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: Urine from the toilet bowl is contaminated and unsuitable for culture.
n.2: The end of the stream is not the midstream sample required for culture.
n.3: First-catch urine carries urethral and skin organisms that contaminate a culture; it is the sample used for chlamydia testing, not for MSU culture.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Hale, 66, has a productive cough and the doctor requests a sputum sample for culture. Antibiotics have not yet been started. Which approach is most likely to give a useful specimen?
o: Ask him to cough deeply on waking and spit into a sterile pot
Collect the sample after the first dose of antibiotics
Ask him to spit saliva into a pot after his evening meal
Take a throat swab instead, as it is easier to collect
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A useful sputum specimen comes from a deep cough, ideally on waking when secretions have accumulated, placed in a sterile container and sent promptly. Collecting before antibiotics where possible improves the chance of identifying the organism (Annexe B 2.9; antimicrobial stewardship, NICE NG15).

n.1: Starting antibiotics first reduces the chance of growing the organism.
n.2: Saliva is not sputum and gives a contaminated, unhelpful sample.
n.3: A throat swab does not sample lower respiratory secretions.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Webb, 72, takes ibuprofen for arthritis. She vomits a moderate amount of dark brown material that looks like coffee grounds. Her pulse is 108 and her blood pressure is lower than earlier. What should the nurse do?
o: Send a stool sample to the laboratory for testing
Dispose of the vomit and offer her mouth care and a drink
Give an antiemetic and recheck all her observations in 4 hours
Escalate urgently as a possible upper GI bleed and keep a record
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Coffee-ground vomit suggests partly digested blood from an upper gastrointestinal bleed; NSAID use is a risk factor. With a rising pulse and falling blood pressure she needs urgent escalation (P3.12) and accurate recording of the amount and appearance (Annexe B 2.9).

n.0: A stool sample does not address an acute bleed with haemodynamic change.
n.1: Disposing of it without escalation ignores a possible bleed; oral fluids may need withholding pending review.
n.2: An antiemetic does not address a possible bleed, and 4-hourly observations are too infrequent.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Okoro, 24, has type 1 diabetes and has been vomiting since last night. Her urinalysis shows glucose 3+ and ketones 3+. She is breathing quickly and her capillary glucose is 22.6 mmol/L. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Encourage oral fluids and recheck her urine in 4 hours
Check her blood ketones and inform the doctor urgently
Record the results and send the urine for culture
Give her usual insulin dose and recheck in the morning
Assessment & Care Planning.w: High glucose with heavy ketonuria, vomiting and rapid breathing in type 1 diabetes suggests diabetic ketoacidosis, a medical emergency. The nurse should check capillary blood ketones per local protocol and escalate urgently (P3.11, P3.12; Annexe B 2.10).

n.0: Oral fluids and a 4-hour recheck delay treatment of possible ketoacidosis.
n.2: Culture does not address the immediate danger shown by the results.
n.3: Her usual dose does not treat ketoacidosis, and waiting until morning is unsafe.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Day, 77, has type 2 diabetes and an infection. He is drowsy and his glucose meter displays 'HI' instead of a number. What should the nurse do?
o: Record the reading as normal and recheck it before the next meal
Assume the meter is faulty and replace it next week
Repeat the test in 4 hours with a different finger
Inform the doctor and send a venous sample for laboratory glucose
Assessment & Care Planning.w: A 'HI' result means the glucose is above the meter's measurable range. In a drowsy person this needs urgent escalation and a laboratory glucose to establish the true value (Annexe B 2.10 and 2.5: manage and interpret blood glucose monitors).

n.0: 'HI' indicates a very high reading, not a normal one.
n.1: Assuming a fault without confirming the glucose risks missing a hyperglycaemic emergency.
n.2: Waiting 4 hours is unsafe in a drowsy person with a possible very high glucose.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mrs Cole, 76, is recovering from a stroke on a rehabilitation ward. She tells the nurse that her main wish is to be able to get to the bathroom by herself before she goes home. Which care plan goal best reflects a person-centred, evaluable plan?
o: She will walk to the bathroom with her frame and one helper by Friday
Staff will encourage Mrs Cole to mobilise as much as possible
Mrs Cole's mobility will be improved during her stay on the stroke unit
Mrs Cole will be independent in all activities before discharge
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NMC proficiency P3.5 requires person-centred, evidence-based plans with agreed goals. A good goal is centred on the person's own priority, specific, measurable and time-bound, so progress can be evaluated (P3.15).

n.1: This describes a staff action, not an outcome for Mrs Cole.
n.2: 'Improved mobility' is vague, with no measure or timescale to evaluate against.
n.3: Full independence in all activities is not her stated goal and is unlikely to be realistic or measurable.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Price, 69, has COPD, type 2 diabetes and depression. He is admitted with an exacerbation of COPD. His SpO2 is 85% on air and he is struggling to finish sentences; his capillary glucose is 11.2 mmol/L. Which need should the nurse prioritise first?
o: His dietary intake and weight
His raised blood glucose
His low mood and anxiety
His breathing and oxygenation
Assessment & Care Planning.w: When prioritising care for a person with comorbidities (P3.13), immediate threats to life come first. Severe hypoxaemia and breathlessness are an airway and breathing priority needing escalation and oxygen to a prescribed target; the other needs are addressed once he is stable.

n.0: Nutrition is important for recovery but is not the immediate priority.
n.1: A glucose of 11.2 mmol/L needs monitoring but is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxaemia.
n.2: His mood matters but is not the most urgent need while he is hypoxic.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Hunt, 55, has had the same leg ulcer care plan for three weeks. Measurements show the wound has not reduced in size, and she says the dressing leaks and stops her going out. What should the nurse do?
o: Reassess the wound with her and revise the plan, referring if needed
Ask her to stay at home more until the leaking settles down
Continue the plan, as wounds can take several months to heal
Change to a more absorbent dressing without discussing it with her
Assessment & Care Planning.w: P3.15: work in partnership to monitor, evaluate and reassess care plans, readjusting goals and documenting progress. Lack of progress and a poor experience for the person mean the plan should be reviewed with her, with referral (for example to tissue viability) if needed (P3.16).

n.1: Restricting her life to suit the dressing is not person-centred and does not address the problem.
n.2: Continuing an unchanged plan ignores evidence that it is not working.
n.3: Changing the plan without her involvement is not partnership working.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: During lunch, the nurse notices that Mr Jacobs, 83, who had a stroke last week, coughs and splutters each time he drinks water, and his voice sounds wet afterwards. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Stop oral intake per local policy and refer him to speech and language therapy
Record the coughing and review at the next weekly team meeting
Give him thickened fluids of the nurse's choosing and continue his meal
Ask his family to bring in his favourite soft foods to help him eat
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Coughing and a wet voice when drinking suggest unsafe swallowing and aspiration risk. Code 13.2 requires a timely referral to another practitioner when action, care or treatment is required, and P3.16 requires knowing when and how to refer safely: the speech and language therapist assesses swallowing, with intake managed per local dysphagia policy meanwhile.

n.1: Waiting a week leaves him at risk of aspiration pneumonia.
n.2: Choosing a fluid thickness without specialist assessment may still be unsafe.
n.3: Soft foods brought from home do not address the aspiration risk and may be unsafe.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: At the end of a shift, the nurse is evaluating Mrs Dunn's care plan for pain after a hip fracture. Which entry best documents her progress?
o: Pain management ongoing; patient seems a lot more comfortable this afternoon.
Patient complained of pain all morning but is settled now.
14:30 Pain 7/10 moving at 12:00; 3/10 at 13:00 after oxycodone. Plan continued.
Analgesia given as prescribed. Continue current plan as per care plan.
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Code 10.1-10.4: complete records accurately at the time, attributing, dating and timing entries without speculation. P3.15 requires documenting progress against goals; a timed, measured pain score before and after the intervention shows whether the plan is working.

n.0: 'Seems more comfortable' gives no measurement and is open to interpretation.
n.1: 'Complained' is judgemental, and the entry gives no times, scores or interventions.
n.3: This records an action but not its effect, so progress cannot be evaluated.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Simms, 64, has heart failure and is due for discharge. The team has drafted a plan for daily weights and fluid restriction. He says he does not own scales and finds it hard to remember fluid limits. What is the best next step?
o: Ask his neighbour to supervise his weights and fluid intake
Discharge with the plan as written, as it follows guidance
Revise the plan with him so it fits his life and resources
Tell him that he must follow the plan to avoid readmission
Assessment & Care Planning.w: Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with people receiving care, and P3.4-P3.5 require shared planning and agreed goals. A plan he cannot follow will not work; adapting it (for example arranging scales and simple prompts) makes it achievable.

n.0: Involving a neighbour without his agreement is not partnership and may breach confidentiality.
n.1: Following guidance does not help if the plan is not achievable for him.
n.3: Instructing him without addressing the barriers he describes is not shared decision-making.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Ms Reid, 38, has a learning disability, epilepsy and type 1 diabetes. She has missed three diabetes clinic appointments, and her carer says the waiting room makes her very anxious. What is the most appropriate response by the community nurse?
o: Write to her to say that further missed appointments will be noted
Discharge her from clinic, as she has not attended three times
Ask her carer to attend the clinic in her place to collect advice
Arrange reasonable adjustments such as a first or quiet appointment
Assessment & Care Planning.w: P7.5 requires responding to the challenges of person-centred care for people with complex needs, and the Equality Act 2010 s20 imposes a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. Adjusting the appointment removes the barrier to her care.

n.0: A warning letter does not address the cause of her non-attendance.
n.1: Discharging her penalises her for a barrier the service can adjust, worsening inequality.
n.2: Her carer cannot receive her care or examinations for her; she needs to be seen.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: A ward nurse is referring Mr Kaur, 70, to the community dietitian after finding he has lost 8% of his body weight in 3 months. Which action best supports a safe referral?
o: Ask his GP to make the referral so that it is from a doctor
Send the referral and let the dietitian explain it when they contact him
Send his entire hospital record so that the dietitian has all details
Explain the referral to him and include the reason, urgency and key findings
Assessment & Care Planning.w: P3.16: know when and how to refer safely. The person should understand and agree to the referral (Code 4.2), and the referral should give the reason, urgency and relevant findings, sharing the minimum necessary information (Caldicott principle 3).

n.0: Nurses can refer directly to a dietitian; routing via the GP adds delay.
n.1: He should know about and agree to the referral before it is sent.
n.2: Sending the whole record exceeds the minimum necessary information for the purpose.

Assessment & Care Planning.q: Mr Achebe, 62, is admitted to a medical ward with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. The nurse is starting his admission assessment and wants it to be person-centred and shared. Which opening approach best achieves this?
o: Ask his wife to describe his usual routine and difficulties
Review his medical notes and set goals for him to work on
Ask what matters most to him and what he hopes to achieve
Complete the trust checklist, then explain the plan to him
Assessment & Care Planning.w: NMC proficiency P3.4 requires a person-centred approach with shared assessment, planning, decision-making and goal setting; Code 3.3 asks nurses to act in partnership with the person. Starting with what matters to Mr Achebe puts him at the centre of the assessment.
