Fundamental Nursing Care.w: White plaques that wipe off leaving a red base suggest oral candidiasis (thrush), which needs assessment and antifungal treatment. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during oral care.

n.0: Firm brushing traumatises the mucosa and does not treat the infection.
n.1: Large-volume rinsing in an unconscious person risks aspiration.
n.3: Petroleum jelly does not treat infection and is not applied inside the mouth.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Lily, 83, wears full upper and lower dentures. She asks what she should do with them at night while in hospital. What is the best advice?
o: Keep them in overnight so that her gums keep their shape
Soak them in boiling water overnight to sterilise them
Remove, clean and store them in a labelled pot overnight
Wrap them in a tissue on her bedside table overnight
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Dentures should be removed and cleaned daily and generally left out overnight to rest the gums, stored in a labelled, named denture pot to prevent loss or damage (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wearing dentures overnight increases the risk of denture stomatitis and infection.
n.1: Boiling water can warp acrylic dentures.
n.3: Tissue-wrapped dentures are easily thrown away by mistake.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Fred, 72, has crusting around both eyelids after a viral illness. You are asked to clean his eyes. Which technique is correct?
o: Use one swab for each eye, wiping back and forth across the lid
Use one swab for both eyes, wiping from outer to inner corner
Use a fresh swab for each eye, wiping from inner to outer corner
Use a dry cotton bud inside the lower lid to remove crusts
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Eye care principles: use sterile saline and a separate swab for each eye, wiping once from the inner canthus outward, so that debris and infection are not carried into the tear duct or the other eye (Annexe B 4.5).

n.0: Wiping back and forth reintroduces debris to the eye.
n.1: Sharing a swab and wiping inward risks cross-infection and moving debris into the tear duct.
n.3: Inserting a cotton bud inside the lid risks corneal injury.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Agnes, 79, has type 2 diabetes with reduced sensation in her feet. Her toenails are long and thickened, and she asks you to cut them during her bath. What is the most appropriate action?
o: File her nails down after soaking her feet for 20 minutes
Explain the risk and refer her to the podiatry service
Ask a healthcare support worker to cut them carefully
Cut her nails straight across with sterile nail clippers
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: People with diabetes and reduced sensation are at high risk of foot ulceration from minor trauma, so thickened nails should be cut by a podiatrist. Annexe B 4.5 includes deciding when to refer during nail care.

n.0: Prolonged soaking softens skin and can cause maceration in a person with diabetes.
n.2: Delegating a task that needs specialist assessment does not reduce the risk.
n.3: Cutting thickened nails in a person with diabetic neuropathy risks injury and ulceration.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Raymond, 74, takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. He usually wet shaves with a blade razor and asks for help to shave while in hospital. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply pressure to any cuts for 30 seconds afterwards
Use an electric razor to reduce the risk of bleeding
Postpone shaving until his anticoagulant is stopped
Use a new disposable blade razor and press gently
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 4.3: when assisting with shaving, consider risks such as anticoagulation. An electric razor reduces the risk of cuts and bleeding in people taking anticoagulants such as apixaban.

n.0: This responds to cuts rather than preventing them.
n.2: His anticoagulant is needed for stroke prevention and shaving is part of his personal care.
n.3: A blade razor still risks cuts that bleed more with anticoagulation.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Cathy, 66, has a new itchy, raised red rash on her trunk two days after starting a new antibiotic. She is alert, her observations are normal and her lips and tongue are not swollen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Advise her to stop the antibiotic once she is at home
Wait until the rash has spread before reporting it
Give the next dose and apply an emollient to the rash
Withhold the next dose and inform the prescriber promptly
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: A new rash after starting a medicine may be an adverse drug reaction. Without anaphylaxis features, withhold the next dose pending review and inform the prescriber promptly; document it and consider a Yellow Card report (Annexe B 4.4; P4.15).

n.0: Advice to stop treatment needs prescriber review and does not address her current care.
n.1: Delay risks progression of a drug reaction.
n.2: Giving another dose of a possible cause risks a more serious reaction.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Dolores, 88, is frail and drowsy after a stroke. She has a dry, coated tongue and cracked lips, takes nothing by mouth and has an unsafe swallow. Which oral care plan is most appropriate?
o: Daily chlorhexidine mouthwash rinses by mouth
Lemon and glycerine swabs every two hours
Gentle mouth care with a soft brush and lip balm
Mouth care whenever her relatives request it
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: People who are nil by mouth and drowsy need frequent oral assessment and gentle care with a soft toothbrush, moistening and lip care. Lemon and glycerine dry the mouth further and mouthwashes risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow (Annexe B 4.5; NICE NG31 advises frequent mouth and lip care).

n.0: Rinses she cannot spit out risk aspiration with an unsafe swallow.
n.1: Lemon and glycerine swabs dry the mucosa further and can damage teeth.
n.3: Oral care is a planned nursing intervention based on assessment, not on request.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Monica, 55, had abdominal surgery five days ago. Her wound edges are now red and swollen, the area is hot and tender, and there is cloudy discharge. Her temperature is 38.4°C. Which conclusion best fits these findings?
o: The wound is in the normal maturation phase
The wound is showing signs of a moisture lesion
The wound shows a normal inflammatory response
The wound shows signs of infection
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Increasing redness, swelling, heat, pain, purulent or cloudy exudate and fever at day 5 indicate wound infection, which needs escalation and review. Mild early inflammation in the first few days is normal, but it should be settling, not worsening (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Maturation (remodelling) is a late phase lasting months and does not cause fever and pus.
n.1: Moisture lesions are caused by incontinence or sweat on the skin, not surgical wound infection.
n.2: Normal inflammation is mild and settles early; worsening signs with fever suggest infection.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Which is the correct order of the phases of wound healing?
o: Inflammation, haemostasis, maturation, proliferation
Proliferation, haemostasis, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, proliferation, inflammation, maturation
Haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation, maturation
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Wounds heal through overlapping phases: haemostasis (clotting), inflammation (clearing debris and bacteria), proliferation (granulation tissue and epithelialisation) and maturation or remodelling (collagen reorganisation, which can last months).

n.0: Haemostasis comes first, and proliferation precedes maturation.
n.1: Proliferation follows inflammation; it does not begin the process.
n.2: Inflammation precedes proliferation, not the other way round.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: You are preparing to redress Stan's surgical wound using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT). Which principle is central to ANTT?
o: Completing the dressing within 5 minutes
Protecting key parts and key sites from touch
Cleaning the wound with an antiseptic each time
Wearing sterile gloves for every dressing change
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: ANTT is based on identifying and protecting key parts (for example the inside of the dressing) and key sites (the wound) by not touching them directly or indirectly, with hand hygiene and an aseptic field. Glove choice depends on whether key parts must be touched.

n.0: Speed is not the defining principle of ANTT.
n.2: Routine antiseptic cleansing is not a principle of ANTT and can harm tissue.
n.3: Sterile gloves are needed when key parts must be touched; non-sterile gloves are used otherwise.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Bob, 69, has a wound drain after hip surgery. In the first hour on the ward it drained 30 mL. In the last 30 minutes it has drained 350 mL of fresh blood, his pulse has risen to 118 and BP has fallen to 96/60 mmHg. What is the priority?
o: Change the drain bottle and document
Milk the drain tubing to keep it patent
Escalate urgently as possible haemorrhage
Clamp the drain and recheck in 1 hour
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: A sudden large volume of fresh blood with rising pulse and falling BP suggests haemorrhage. NEWS2: pulse 111-130 = 2, systolic 91-100 = 2; together with the clinical picture this needs an urgent medical response (RCP 2017; Annexe B 4.7).

n.0: Changing the bottle and documenting does not address the haemorrhage.
n.1: Milking the drain does not address active bleeding and shock.
n.3: Clamping without medical instruction can hide bleeding, and an hour's wait is unsafe.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Pat, 75, has a venous leg ulcer with no red flags. Mild compression was started at her first visit, and strong compression bandaging is now being considered. Before strong compression is applied, what assessment must be completed?
o: A wound swab for culture and sensitivity
A Doppler ankle brachial pressure index
A full blood count to check for anaemia
A capillary blood glucose measurement
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NWCSP Leg Ulcer Recommendations (2023): with no red flags, mild compression (up to 20 mmHg) can start straight away, but a full assessment including a Doppler ankle brachial pressure index (ABPI), within 14 days, is needed before strong compression (40 mmHg or more), because strong compression on a limb with arterial insufficiency can cause ischaemia (Annexe B 4.6 pressure bandaging).

n.0: A wound swab is not needed to decide on compression and is taken only with signs of infection.
n.2: FBC does not assess arterial supply to the limb.
n.3: Glucose is relevant to healing but does not determine whether compression is safe.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ken, 63, has interrupted sutures in a healing abdominal wound. The plan says to remove them today. When you remove the first two alternate sutures, the wound edges begin to gape. What should you do?
o: Remove all remaining sutures and apply adhesive strips
Remove the rest and redress the wound in 24 hours
Stop, leave the other sutures and inform the surgeons
Remove the rest and apply a tight pressure bandage
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Removing alternate sutures first allows the wound to be checked for adequate healing. If the edges separate, stop, leave the remaining sutures in place, support the wound and inform the team for review (Annexe B 4.6).

n.0: Removing all sutures from a gaping wound risks dehiscence.
n.1: Removing the remaining sutures risks wound dehiscence.
n.3: A pressure bandage does not replace adequate wound closure.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Joy, 58, has negative pressure wound therapy (a vacuum dressing) on a leg wound. The pump alarms for a leak and the dressing is no longer collapsed. What should you do first?
o: Find and seal the leak, then confirm the seal
Switch the pump off and leave the dressing in situ
Increase the pressure setting on the pump
Remove the dressing and apply gauze until tomorrow
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Vacuum dressings must maintain a seal to work. Check the dressing and connections for the leak, seal it per the manufacturer's instructions and confirm the dressing collapses. If therapy cannot be restored within the time stated in local policy, the dressing should be changed (Annexe B 4.6).

n.1: Leaving an inactive vacuum dressing in place risks infection and maceration.
n.2: Raising the pressure does not fix a leak and may harm the wound.
n.3: Removing it without trying to restore the seal is premature and loses therapy.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Frances, 84, has a sacral pressure ulcer. A routine wound swab grows Staphylococcus aureus. The ulcer has no increased pain, redness, heat or exudate, and she has no fever. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Repeat the swab daily until it shows no growth
Start systemic antibiotics because the swab is positive
Apply a topical antiseptic routinely to the ulcer
Continue current care without starting antibiotics
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG179: do not offer systemic antibiotics to adults based on positive wound cultures without clinical evidence of infection, and do not routinely use topical antiseptics or antimicrobials on pressure ulcers. Wounds are commonly colonised.

n.0: Repeated swabs of a colonised wound are unhelpful and do not guide care.
n.1: Systemic antibiotics without clinical infection contribute to resistance (NICE NG15).
n.2: CG179 advises against routine topical antiseptics on pressure ulcers.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Eileen, 78, is admitted to a medical ward with a chest infection. Under NICE CG32, when should she be screened for malnutrition while she is an inpatient?
o: Weekly, starting on day 7 of her stay
On admission and at discharge
On admission and weekly thereafter
On admission and when she loses weight
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32 (updated 2017): screen all hospital inpatients on admission and weekly thereafter; outpatients at their first clinic appointment; care home residents on admission and when there is clinical concern.

n.0: Waiting until day 7 delays identifying those already malnourished.
n.1: Screening only at admission and discharge misses deterioration during the stay.
n.3: Waiting for weight loss means malnutrition is found late.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Which contemporary tool is most widely used in UK adult care settings to screen for malnutrition?
o: The Braden scale for predicting risk
The 4AT rapid assessment test
The Waterlow risk assessment score
The 'MUST' screening tool
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: 'MUST' (BAPEN) combines BMI, unplanned weight loss and acute disease effect to give a low, medium or high risk of malnutrition, with a management plan for each (Annexe B 5.2).

n.0: Braden assesses pressure ulcer risk.
n.1: The 4AT screens for delirium.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ernest, 81, has Parkinson's disease with a tremor and struggles to get food to his mouth. He is eating less than half his meals. Which intervention should be tried first to help him eat?
o: Provide adapted cutlery, a plate guard and help
Give his meals later, when the ward is quieter
Refer him for insertion of a nasogastric feeding tube
Prescribe oral nutritional supplements three times a day
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 5.3: assist with eating and drinking and use feeding and drinking aids. Adapted cutlery, plate guards and non-slip mats, plus assistance (for example via a red tray system or protected mealtimes), address the cause of his poor intake.

n.1: Delaying meals does not address his difficulty and may mean food is cold.
n.2: Enteral feeding is not indicated when oral intake can be improved with help.
n.3: Supplements may follow, but his barrier is a physical one that aids can address first.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: According to NICE CG32, which finding indicates that an adult is malnourished?
o: BMI under 18.5 kg/m²
BMI between 20 and 25 kg/m²
Unintentional weight loss of 3% in 6 months
Eating normally for the past 5 days
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32 defines malnutrition as BMI under 18.5 kg/m²; or unintentional weight loss over 10% in 3-6 months; or BMI under 20 kg/m² with unintentional weight loss over 5% in 3-6 months.

n.1: BMI 20-25 is within the healthy range.
n.2: 3% weight loss is below the CG32 thresholds.
n.3: Normal intake is not a malnutrition criterion.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Derek, 59, has a history of alcohol misuse. He has eaten almost nothing for 7 days and his BMI is 17.8 kg/m². Nutrition support is planned. Using NICE CG32 criteria, what is his refeeding risk and the appropriate starting approach?
o: High risk: start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day with thiamin
Low risk: start at full requirements of 25-35 kcal/kg/day
Moderate risk: start at 50% of requirements without thiamin
No risk: offer normal ward meals without any monitoring
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32: high refeeding risk includes two or more of BMI under 18.5, weight loss over 10%, little or no intake for over 5 days, or alcohol misuse. Derek has three. Start at a maximum of 10 kcal/kg/day, increasing slowly, and give thiamin and vitamin B before and during the first 10 days, with electrolyte monitoring.

n.1: Full requirements in a high-risk person can precipitate refeeding syndrome.
n.2: He meets the high-risk criteria, and thiamin is needed.
n.3: Unmonitored feeding ignores his high refeeding risk.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Gloria, 72, has been prescribed oral nutritional supplements twice daily. On the ward round you notice the supplement bottles are left unopened on her table each day. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her family to bring in food from home and stop recording intake
Stop the supplements because she clearly does not want them
Sign the chart for the supplements because they were supplied
Explore why with her and review the plan with the dietitian
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Effective nutrition support requires monitoring that it is actually taken (NICE CG32 monitoring). Explore reasons (taste, fullness, opening the bottle, timing) and review with Gloria and the dietitian. Recording a supplement as taken when it was not would be inaccurate (Code 10.3).

n.0: Food from home may help, but intake must still be monitored and recorded.
n.1: Stopping without exploring reasons or involving the dietitian may leave her malnourished.
n.2: Recording unopened supplements as given falsifies the record.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Philip, 66, is drowsy after surgery and has had no food for 6 days. His BMI is 23 kg/m² and he has no other refeeding risk factors. Nutrition support is planned. Under NICE CG32, what is the maximum initial intake for the first 2 days?
o: His full estimated requirements
No more than 50% of his estimated requirements
No more than 25% of his estimated requirements
No more than 10 kcal/kg/day
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32: people who have eaten little or nothing for more than 5 days should have nutrition support started at no more than 50% of requirements for the first 2 days, before increasing if clinical and biochemical monitoring reveals no refeeding problems. The 10 kcal/kg/day limit is for those at high refeeding risk.

n.0: Full requirements after more than 5 days of little intake risk refeeding problems.
n.2: 25% is lower than the CG32 recommendation for this group.
n.3: 10 kcal/kg/day is the starting level for people at high refeeding risk, which he is not.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Nadia, 34, has a learning disability and is admitted with pneumonia. Her carer says she eats best with familiar foods, small portions and verbal prompting. Ward staff often place her tray and leave. Her intake is now poor. What is the best action?
o: Use the carer's advice in her plan and support her at meals
Ask the carer to come in at every mealtime to feed her
Refer her for a swallowing assessment before her next meal
Start oral supplements and continue placing her tray
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 5.3 and the Equality Act 2010 s20: make reasonable adjustments and give assistance with eating. Personalising meals and providing prompting and support is the nursing team's responsibility and addresses the cause of her poor intake.

n.1: Carers may help, but meeting her nutritional needs remains the ward's responsibility.
n.2: There is no indication of a swallowing problem; the issue is support with eating.
n.3: Supplements do not address the lack of support at mealtimes.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Tony, 70, is on a fluid balance chart. Over 24 hours his intake is 1,200 mL oral and 1,000 mL IV. His output is 1,400 mL urine and 300 mL from a nasogastric tube. What is his fluid balance?
o: Positive 800 mL
Positive 500 mL
Negative 200 mL
Negative 500 mL

n.0: Positive 800 mL omits the 300 mL nasogastric loss.
n.2: Negative 200 mL does not match the totals recorded.
n.3: Negative 500 mL reverses intake and output.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: You are mentoring a newly registered nurse who is about to care for several people receiving intravenous fluids on a surgical ward. She asks you to remind her of the framework NICE CG174 uses for IV fluid therapy. Which list correctly gives the '5 Rs'?
o: Resuscitation, rehydration, restriction, review and removal of lines
Rehydration, resuscitation, replacement, review and recording
Routine maintenance, rest, reassessment, recording and referral
Resuscitation, maintenance, replacement, redistribution, reassessment
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG174 (updated 2017): the 5 Rs are Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution and Reassessment.

n.0: Rehydration, restriction and removal are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.1: Rest, review and record are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.
n.2: Rest, recording and referral are not part of the CG174 5 Rs.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Marion, 85, lives in a care home and has had diarrhoea for 3 days. Staff say she has been drinking very little and seems more tired than usual. You are assessing her hydration status on admission. Which combination of findings most suggests dehydration?
o: Ankle oedema, crackles in the lungs and weight gain
Dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and tachycardia
Moist mouth, pale dilute urine and normal skin turgor
Raised blood pressure, bounding pulse and polyuria
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Dehydration commonly presents with dry mucous membranes, thirst, reduced and concentrated urine, tachycardia and postural hypotension (Annexe B 5.4). CG174 indicators of fluid need include HR over 90 and systolic under 100.

n.0: Oedema, crackles and weight gain suggest fluid overload.
n.2: A moist mouth and pale dilute urine suggest adequate hydration.
n.3: Raised BP and bounding pulse do not indicate dehydration.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Jean, 48, is nil by mouth for 24 hours before planned surgery and has no cardiac, renal or nutritional problems. The junior doctor asks you to check the volume she is prescribing for routine maintenance. Under NICE CG174, what is the daily routine maintenance water requirement for an adult?
o: 60-70 mL/kg/day
40-50 mL/kg/day
10-15 mL/kg/day
25-30 mL/kg/day
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG174: routine maintenance is 25-30 mL/kg/day of water, about 1 mmol/kg/day each of potassium, sodium and chloride, and 50-100 g/day of glucose.

n.0: 60-70 mL/kg/day risks fluid overload.
n.1: 40-50 mL/kg/day exceeds adult maintenance needs.
n.2: 10-15 mL/kg/day would cause dehydration in most adults.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Harold, 79, has heart failure and is receiving IV fluids. Overnight he becomes breathless with RR 26, SpO2 92% on air, crackles at both lung bases and new ankle swelling. His fluid balance is positive 2,300 mL over 24 hours. What should the nurse do first?
o: Increase the infusion rate to correct the dehydration
Give a prescribed diuretic before informing anyone
Stop the infusion, sit him up and escalate urgently
Continue the infusion and recheck in 4 hours
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Breathlessness, crackles, oedema and a large positive balance suggest fluid overload. Stop the infusion, sit him upright, give oxygen to target and escalate urgently: NEWS2 RR 26 = 3 and SpO2 92% = 2 gives at least 5 (RCP 2017). CG174 asks for fluid mismanagement to be reported as an incident.

n.0: More fluid worsens overload.
n.1: Treatment decisions need urgent medical review; giving a diuretic first delays escalation.
n.3: Continuing the infusion worsens overload and 4 hours is too long.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Linda, 64, has IV fluids running through a volumetric infusion pump. The pump alarms 'downstream occlusion'. What should you check first?
o: The line, clamps and cannula site for a blockage
The pump's battery level and mains connection
The fluid bag for an air bubble near the top
The prescription chart for the next bag due
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: A downstream occlusion means resistance between the pump and the patient: check for closed clamps, kinked tubing and the cannula site (phlebitis, infiltration or a positional cannula) before restarting (Annexe B 5.9).

n.1: Battery alarms are separate from occlusion alarms.
n.2: Air at the top of the bag is above the pump and does not cause a downstream occlusion.
n.3: The prescription does not explain an occlusion alarm.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Asif, 55, weighs 70 kg and is nil by mouth after surgery. He needs routine IV maintenance fluids. Using NICE CG174, what is the appropriate total daily water range?
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG174: 25-30 mL/kg/day. 70 kg x 25 = 1,750 mL; 70 kg x 30 = 2,100 mL. CG174 also notes that intake rarely needs to exceed 3 L/day.

n.0: 700-1,050 mL uses 10-15 mL/kg/day, below CG174 maintenance.
n.2: 3,500-4,200 mL is well above maintenance and risks overload.
n.3: 2,800-3,500 mL uses 40-50 mL/kg/day, above maintenance.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Edith, 90, is frail, weighs 45 kg and has chronic kidney disease. Routine IV maintenance fluids are prescribed at 30 mL/kg/day. What should the nurse do?
o: Double the rate to protect her kidneys from dehydration
Give the fluids as prescribed, as this is the standard rate
Query the prescription, as a lower rate may be needed
Change her to oral fluids without consulting the prescriber
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG174: consider prescribing less fluid (for example 20-25 mL/kg/day) for people who are older or frail, or who have renal or cardiac impairment. Raising a concern about a prescription supports safe practice (Code 18, RPS/RCN 2019).

n.0: Doubling the rate risks serious fluid overload.
n.1: Standard rates may cause overload in frail people with renal impairment.
n.3: Changing the route without the prescriber is outside a nurse's authority.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Hilda, 74, has had a nasogastric tube inserted for feeding after a stroke. You aspirate gastric contents and test them on CE-marked pH paper. Which reading confirms gastric placement so that feeding can start?
o: pH 8.5 or above
pH 6.0 or below
pH 7.0 or above
pH 5.5 or below
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32: gastric tube position is confirmed by pH 5.5 or below on pH paper. Position must be confirmed after placement and before each use by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary (rec 1.7.17).

n.0: pH 8.5 is alkaline and suggests a non-gastric position.
n.1: pH 6.0 is above the 5.5 threshold and does not confirm gastric placement.
n.2: pH 7 or above may indicate the tube is in the lung or intestine.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Stanley, 83, has a nasogastric tube for feeding after a stroke. The tube was confirmed in the stomach by X-ray yesterday and is secured at 60 cm at the nostril. He needs medicines, flushes and feeds today. Under NICE CG32, when must the tube position be confirmed?
o: Before the first feed of each day
When the person reports discomfort
After placement and before each use
After placement and then once a day
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32 rec 1.7.17: confirm the position of all nasogastric tubes after placement and before each use (each feed, flush or medicine) by aspiration and pH paper, with X-ray if necessary.

n.0: A single check at the start misses later displacement from coughing, vomiting or movement.
n.1: Displacement may cause no symptoms, so checks cannot wait for discomfort.
n.3: Daily checks miss displacement between uses.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: A ward manager is reviewing last month's incident reports with the team. She explains that some incidents are classed as Never Events because strong national safety barriers exist to prevent them. Which of the following incidents is classed as a Never Event in NHS England?
o: A fall resulting in a hip fracture on a ward
A missed dose of a prescribed antibiotic
Misplaced nasogastric tube not detected before use
A category 3 pressure ulcer acquired in hospital
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: The NHS England Never Events list (2018, updated 2021, still active) includes misplaced naso- or oro-gastric tubes not detected before use, as strong national barriers (pH testing and X-ray protocols) exist.

n.0: Inpatient falls are serious incidents but are not on the Never Events list.
n.1: Missed doses are medication incidents but are not Never Events.
n.3: Pressure ulcers are reported as incidents but are not Never Events.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Roger, 61, is on an oncology ward having chemotherapy. He says he feels nauseated before each meal and has been leaving most of his food. He has a prescription for a regular antiemetic. Which nursing action is most appropriate first?
o: Encourage large meals to settle his stomach
Withhold all food until the nausea fully resolves
Give the prescribed antiemetic before meals and review it
Offer strong-smelling hot food to stimulate appetite
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 5.5: identify and manage nausea and vomiting. Give prescribed antiemetics at a time that covers meals, assess the response, and use measures such as small frequent meals and reducing food odours.

n.0: Large meals worsen nausea; small frequent meals are better tolerated.
n.1: Withholding all food risks malnutrition.
n.3: Strong food smells often worsen nausea.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Frank, 70, has a nasogastric tube. Before his morning feed you aspirate and the pH is 6.5. He takes a proton pump inhibitor. He is comfortable with normal observations. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Start the feed, as the pH is close to the safe range
Withhold the feed and follow local policy on X-ray
Use the whoosh test to confirm the tube position
Flush with 50 mL of water and start feeding
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: A pH above 5.5 does not confirm gastric placement. Do not feed; follow local protocol, which may involve waiting and retesting, or an X-ray. CG32 rec 1.7.17 notes that pH may be invalid with acid suppression, which local protocols must address. Air auscultation (the whoosh test) is not a safe method.

n.0: Feeding with an unconfirmed tube position risks feed entering the lungs.
n.2: The whoosh test is unreliable and was removed from practice by the NPSA in 2005.
n.3: Flushing an unconfirmed tube risks fluid entering the lungs.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ida, 79, is being fed through a nasogastric tube. During the feed she starts coughing, becomes breathless and her SpO2 falls from 96% to 89%. What should the nurse do first?
o: Slow the feed rate and recheck her saturation
Flush the tube with water to clear any blockage
Stop the feed, sit her up and call for urgent help
Check the tube length mark and continue feeding
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Sudden coughing, breathlessness and desaturation during a feed suggest aspiration or tube misplacement. Stop the feed, sit her upright, give oxygen and get urgent help (Annexe B 5.7; misplaced tubes are a Never Event).

n.0: Continuing a slower feed risks further aspiration.
n.1: Flushing adds more fluid to a possibly misplaced tube.
n.3: Continuing feeding is unsafe until the cause is established.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Kamal, 50, has short bowel syndrome after surgery and is receiving parenteral nutrition through a multi-lumen central venous catheter on a surgical ward. You are planning his care for the shift. Which practice is correct?
o: Speed up the rate if the infusion falls behind
Take blood samples from the nutrition lumen
Use a dedicated lumen for the parenteral nutrition
Give IV antibiotics through the same lumen
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG32 rec 1.8.8: in hospital, parenteral nutrition is given through a dedicated catheter or a free dedicated lumen of a multi-lumen central catheter. Handle it with aseptic technique and do not use the lumen for other drugs or sampling, which risks infection and incompatibility (Annexe B 5.7).

n.0: Catching up the rate risks hyperglycaemia and fluid overload.
n.1: Sampling from the PN lumen risks infection and inaccurate results.
n.3: Mixing drugs with PN risks incompatibility and contamination.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Nora, 67, has a nasogastric tube. You cannot obtain an aspirate after trying the recommended measures, such as turning her onto her side and waiting before retrying. What should you do next?
o: Give the feed slowly while watching her closely for distress
Push the tube a further 10 cm and attempt aspiration again
Follow local protocol and seek a decision on X-ray confirmation
Inject air and listen over the stomach with a stethoscope
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: If no aspirate can be obtained, the tube must not be used until position is confirmed. CG32 rec 1.7.17 says position is confirmed by aspiration and pH paper with X-ray if necessary, and local protocols must cover failure to aspirate.

n.0: Feeding without confirming position risks pulmonary feeding.
n.1: Advancing the tube blindly without confirmation risks misplacement.
n.3: Air auscultation is unreliable and not a safe check.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Joseph, 77, has a long-term urinary catheter and is being cared for in a nursing home. Staff have positioned his drainage bag on the floor beside the bed so that it drains well. According to NICE CG139, how should the bag be positioned?
o: Below the level of the bladder and off the floor
Above the level of the bladder on the bed frame
Clamped and lying on the mattress beside him
On the floor beside the bed for free drainage
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG139: keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder to prevent backflow, and not in contact with the floor to reduce contamination; use a stand or hanger.

n.1: Above bladder level allows reflux of urine into the bladder.
n.2: Clamping and placing at bladder level risks reflux and obstruction.
n.3: Contact with the floor increases the risk of contamination.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Rita, 80, has a urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker asks whether a routine bladder washout would prevent infection. According to NICE CG139, what is the best response?
o: Yes, a weekly saline washout prevents infection
Yes, a daily washout is needed to keep it patent
No, but antibiotics should be given to prevent it
No, washouts must not be used to prevent infection
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE CG139: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infection. Daily meatal hygiene with soap and water and a closed drainage system are the key measures.

n.0: Routine washouts break the closed system and do not prevent infection.
n.1: Daily washouts are not recommended for infection prevention.
n.2: Antibiotic prophylaxis is not routinely used and contributes to resistance (NICE NG15).

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Cyril, 82, has not opened his bowels for 6 days despite oral laxatives and is uncomfortable. The doctor has prescribed a phosphate enema, and Cyril has given consent after you explained the procedure. In what position should he be placed for administration?
o: Supine with legs raised
Right lateral with legs straight
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Left lateral with knees flexed
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: The left lateral position follows the anatomy of the sigmoid colon and rectum, allowing the enema to flow along the bowel by gravity (Annexe B 6.5).

n.0: Supine makes insertion and retention difficult.
n.1: Right lateral works against the anatomy of the descending and sigmoid colon.
n.2: Prone is uncomfortable and does not aid flow into the sigmoid colon.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Brian, 68, reports changes in his bowel habit since starting a new medicine, alternating between hard pellets and loose stools. You want to record his bowel pattern consistently so that the team can track changes over the coming week. Which tool is commonly used to describe and record the form of stools?
o: The Abbey pain assessment scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale score
The Waterlow risk assessment scale
The Bristol Stool Form Scale
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: The Bristol Stool Form Scale classifies stools from type 1 (separate hard lumps, suggesting constipation) to type 7 (entirely liquid), supporting assessment of bowel patterns (Annexe B 6.4).

n.0: The Abbey scale assesses pain in people who cannot self-report.
n.1: The GCS assesses consciousness.
n.2: Waterlow assesses pressure ulcer risk.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Mary, 74, had a hip replacement 8 hours ago. She has not passed urine since surgery, says she needs to go but cannot, and has lower abdominal discomfort. Which action is most appropriate first?
o: Restrict her fluids until she passes urine
Give her a laxative to relieve the discomfort
Insert a catheter without discussing it with her
Assess her bladder volume with a bladder scanner
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 6.4: recognise and respond to retention. A bladder scan assesses residual volume to guide whether catheterisation is needed, which is then performed with her consent and in line with local policy.

n.0: Restricting fluids does not treat retention and risks dehydration.
n.1: A laxative does not address urinary retention.
n.2: Catheterisation needs assessment and valid consent (Code 4.2).

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ali, 66, had a colostomy formed 2 days ago. On inspection the stoma is dark purple-black and dry. It was red and moist yesterday. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a smaller appliance to reduce swelling
Clean it with antiseptic and recheck in 24 hours
Record it as a normal post-operative change
Report it urgently to the surgical team
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: A healthy stoma is moist and red or pink. A dusky, purple or black stoma suggests ischaemia or necrosis and needs urgent surgical review (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: A tight appliance could worsen ischaemia.
n.1: Antiseptic does not address ischaemia, and waiting 24 hours risks necrosis progressing.
n.2: This is not a normal change; a healthy stoma stays moist and red.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Phyllis, 85, on a medical ward, has had three episodes of loose, watery stool (Bristol type 7) since this morning with no obvious cause. She started antibiotics 5 days ago. What is the priority action?
o: Wait for two more episodes before sending a sample
Give her prescribed loperamide and continue to monitor her
Move her nearer the toilet in the shared bay
Isolate her in a single room and send a stool sample
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Unexplained diarrhoea, especially after antibiotics, may be infective (for example C. difficile). Isolate promptly in a single room with contact precautions, send a stool sample, and use soap and water for hand hygiene (NIPCM; Annexe B 6.4).

n.0: Delay increases the risk of spread and delays diagnosis.
n.1: Antidiarrhoeals can be harmful in suspected C. difficile and do not reduce spread.
n.2: Staying in a shared bay risks transmission to other patients.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Eric, 72, has a new ileostomy. He is preparing for discharge and asks how to fit his appliance. Which advice is correct?
o: Clean the skin with alcohol wipes before each change
Cut the flange well larger than the stoma to avoid rubbing
Measure the stoma and cut the flange slightly larger than it
Leave the appliance on for a week to protect the skin
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: The aperture should be cut just larger than the measured stoma (usually 2-3 mm) so that effluent does not contact the skin, re-measuring as post-operative swelling settles. Ileostomy output is corrosive, so a close fit protects skin (Annexe B 6.6).

n.0: Alcohol dries and stings the skin; warm water is used.
n.1: A large gap exposes skin to corrosive effluent and causes excoriation.
n.3: Ileostomy appliances are emptied and changed regularly, not left for a week.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Beryl, 84, is admitted to an older people's ward after a fall at home. A colleague suggests completing a falls risk prediction score to decide whether she needs falls prevention. What does NICE NG249 (2025) recommend?
o: Offer an assessment if she falls again on the ward
Offer a comprehensive falls assessment and plan
Complete the prediction tool and act on a high score
Use the prediction tool weekly to monitor her risk
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE NG249 (2025): do not use falls risk prediction tools to predict a person's risk of falling. Offer all hospital inpatients aged 65 and over (or 50-64 at higher risk) a comprehensive, multifactorial falls assessment and management plan.

n.0: She already qualifies for assessment as an inpatient aged 65 or over.
n.2: NG249 advises against using prediction tools to identify risk.
n.3: Repeating a prediction tool does not make it a valid basis for care.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: As part of a multifactorial falls assessment for Stanley, 79, which cardiovascular check does NICE NG249 include?
o: Twelve-lead ECG at rest
Lying and standing BP
Peak expiratory flow
Ankle brachial pressure index
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE NG249: the multifactorial falls assessment includes lying and standing blood pressure to detect orthostatic hypotension, alongside medication review, cognition, continence, vision, footwear, gait and balance.

n.0: An ECG may be needed in some people but is not the standard NG249 component listed.
n.2: Peak flow assesses airway obstruction, not falls risk.
n.3: ABPI assesses arterial supply before leg compression, not falls.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Hugh, 70, has had a stroke and cannot bear weight. He needs to be moved from bed to chair. Which approach is safest?
o: Lift him under the arms with two staff members
Use a drag lift with one person on each side
Use a hoist with an assessed sling
Ask him to stand and pivot using a frame
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 7.2-7.3: use moving and handling equipment for people with impaired mobility. A person who cannot bear weight needs a hoist with a correctly sized and assessed sling, operated by trained staff per the handling plan. Underarm drag lifts injure patients and staff.

n.0: Lifting under the arms is a drag lift, which risks shoulder injury to him and back injury to staff.
n.1: A drag lift is an unsafe technique and not part of contemporary practice.
n.3: He cannot bear weight, so a standing pivot transfer is unsafe.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: According to NICE NG89, which person should not be offered anti-embolism stockings for VTE prophylaxis?
o: A person with peripheral arterial disease
A person having elective hip replacement
A person with a BMI of 32 kg/m²
A person with a previous DVT
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE NG89 rec 1.3.1: do not offer anti-embolism stockings to people with suspected or proven peripheral arterial disease, peripheral arterial bypass grafting, peripheral neuropathy, fragile skin, dermatitis, gangrene, recent skin graft, severe oedema, material allergy or major limb deformity.

n.1: Hip replacement patients may be offered stockings when indicated.
n.2: Obesity is a VTE risk factor and is not a contraindication to stockings.
n.3: Previous DVT raises VTE risk and is not a contraindication to stockings.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Joan, 87, is wearing anti-embolism stockings after surgery. She has significantly reduced mobility and spends most of the day in bed. Under NICE NG89, how often should her skin be inspected?
o: When she reports pain or discomfort in her legs
Once a day when the stockings are removed for washing
Once a week when the stockings are changed for new ones
2 or 3 times a day, especially heels and bony prominences
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE NG89: remove stockings daily for hygiene and skin inspection; in people with significantly reduced mobility, poor skin integrity or sensory loss, inspect the skin 2 or 3 times a day, particularly over heels and bony prominences. Stop stockings if there is marking, blistering or discolouration.

n.0: Waiting for symptoms misses early damage; NG89 sets routine checks 2 or 3 times a day for people with significantly reduced mobility.
n.1: Daily removal and inspection is the minimum for everyone; she needs more frequent checks because of her significantly reduced mobility.
n.2: Weekly inspection would miss pressure damage.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Ivy, 82, has fallen on the ward and is lying on the floor. She is alert, says her hip hurts and her right leg looks shortened and externally rotated. What should the nurse do?
o: Help her to stand with two staff and walk her back to bed
Leave her on the floor until her family arrive
Use a standing hoist to lift her straight back into the chair
Keep her still, get her reviewed and use flat-lift equipment
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: After a fall, check for injury before moving. A shortened, externally rotated leg suggests a hip fracture: keep her still, call for medical review, give analgesia as prescribed and use flat-lifting equipment such as a scoop stretcher, in line with local post-fall protocols and Annexe B 7.3.

n.0: Standing a person with a suspected fracture risks further injury and pain.
n.1: Waiting for family delays medical review and pain relief.
n.2: A standing hoist needs weight bearing, which is unsafe with a suspected fracture.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Sidney, 76, has fallen twice in the past year at home and could not get up without help after the second fall. His GP practice nurse sees him for a routine review. What does NICE NG249 recommend?
o: Refer him for a bone scan without other assessment
Offer him a comprehensive falls assessment and management
Give him a leaflet on falls and review him in a year
Advise him to stay in his chair to avoid further falls
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: NICE NG249: in the community, offer a comprehensive falls assessment and management to people who have fallen in the past year and meet any criterion, such as being unable to get up independently or having 2 or more falls in the year. Sidney meets both.

n.0: Osteoporosis risk is part of the assessment, but not the whole of it.
n.2: A leaflet alone does not meet his assessed needs.
n.3: Reducing activity increases deconditioning and falls risk; exercise programmes are recommended.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Lillian, 89, has dementia and gets out of bed at night. Her son asks for bed rails to be put up to stop her falling. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Assess the risks first, as rails can harm her if she climbs
Put the rails up and add a lap belt in her chair by day
Refuse the request because bed rails are not allowed
Put the rails up straight away, as her son has asked
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 7.4: use safety devices appropriately. Bed rails must be individually risk-assessed; for a person with dementia who mobilises, they may cause entrapment or a higher fall from climbing over. Alternatives include a low bed, crash mat or sensor alarm, discussed with her and her family.

n.1: A lap belt is a restriction needing capacity and best-interests consideration, not a routine add-on.
n.2: Bed rails can be used after individual assessment.
n.3: A relative's request does not replace an individual risk assessment.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Arthur, 82, is in a four-bed bay and needs help to use a commode. The curtains around his bed space do not fully close and a visitor is sitting at the next bed. Which action best protects his privacy and dignity?
o: Help him quickly so that he is exposed for as short a time as possible
Delay the commode until visiting time has finished in an hour
Ask the visitor to look away while you help him onto the commode
Close the gap with a dignity clip and tell him before starting
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 3.4 requires privacy and dignity at all times, and Code 1.1 requires dignity in all care. Secure the screens fully (for example with dignity clips) and explain what you are doing before starting personal care.

n.0: Speed reduces exposure but leaves him visible through the gap.
n.1: Delaying elimination is uncomfortable, undignified and risks incontinence.
n.2: Relying on a visitor to look away does not provide privacy.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Doris, 76, is unconscious after a stroke and needs her bed linen changed. Two staff are available. Which technique is most appropriate?
o: Roll her to each side in turn, changing half the sheet each time
Lift her out to a chair while the bed is stripped and remade
Change the top sheet and add an extra pad underneath her
Leave the soiled sheet until she regains consciousness
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 3.2: bed-making for an unconscious or immobile person is done with the person in the bed, rolling them to each side with enough staff and appropriate handling aids, keeping the airway clear and maintaining dignity.

n.1: Transferring an unconscious person to a chair is unsafe and unnecessary.
n.2: Adding pads over soiled linen leaves her lying on moisture and risks pressure damage.
n.3: Leaving soiled linen risks skin damage and infection and is undignified.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: Frank, 70, says he cannot sleep on the ward because of noise and lights. He is not in pain. Which intervention should be tried first?
o: Move his evening medicines to midnight so that he wakes less
Request a hypnotic medicine for him to take every night
Encourage him to nap during the day to make up for lost sleep
Reduce noise and light at night and offer an eye mask and earplugs
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Annexe B 3.6: support rest and sleep with non-pharmacological measures first, such as a quiet, dark environment, eye masks and earplugs, and a routine. Hypnotics carry risks, including falls in older people.

n.0: Moving medicines to midnight adds a night-time disturbance and may be clinically inappropriate.
n.1: Hypnotics are not first line and increase falls and confusion in older people.
n.2: Daytime napping can worsen night-time insomnia.

Fundamental Nursing Care.q: According to the NMC Code (2018), which of the following is listed among the fundamentals of care that nurses must deliver?
o: Medicines reconciliation
Discharge planning
Health education
Bladder and bowel care
Fundamental Nursing Care.w: Code 1.2 (NMC 2018): fundamentals of care include nutrition, hydration, bladder and bowel care, physical handling and making sure people are kept in clean and hygienic conditions.

n.0: Medicines reconciliation is not one of the Code's listed fundamentals.
n.1: Discharge planning is important but is not in the Code's list of fundamentals.
n.2: Health education is not in the Code's list of fundamentals of care.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: You observe Jake, a first-year student nurse, using alcohol-based handrub. He applies a small amount, rubs his palms together for about 10 seconds, misses his thumbs and fingertips, and wipes the residue on his tunic. What feedback is most appropriate?
o: Apply a second dose and rub palms for a further 10 seconds
Cover all surfaces, including thumbs and fingertips, for 20 to 30 seconds until dry
Rinse the handrub off under running water after 15 seconds of firm rubbing
Rub all hand surfaces for 40 to 60 seconds, then dry them with a paper towel
Infection Prevention & Control.w: The WHO handrub technique adopted in NIPCM appendix 2 covers all surfaces of the hands, including thumbs and fingertips, and takes 20 to 30 seconds, with hands left to dry naturally. 40 to 60 seconds is the duration for handwashing with soap and water.

n.0: A second dose rubbed on the palms still misses the thumbs and fingertips that he omitted.
n.2: Handrub is not rinsed off; rinsing removes the product before it has acted.
n.3: 40 to 60 seconds is the handwash duration; handrub is rubbed until dry and is not towel-dried.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Jean, 82, was admitted from a care home with a chest infection and is in a six-bed bay. Overnight she has had three episodes of watery diarrhoea (Bristol type 7) with no laxatives prescribed. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Keep her in the bay with curtains drawn and send a stool sample before deciding on placement
Give the as-required loperamide and review placement if symptoms continue beyond 48 hours
Move her to a single room with contact precautions now and inform the IPC team
Move her to a single room once a stool sample confirms or excludes C. difficile toxin
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Unexplained diarrhoea is a cross-infection risk (NIPCM ch 2.1), so the nurse should isolate promptly on suspicion, start contact precautions, document the decision and seek IPC team advice, then send a stool sample. Antibiotics for her chest infection make C. difficile a real possibility. Waiting for results leaves other patients exposed.

n.0: Drawn curtains do not contain spread from a patient with infective diarrhoea; the sample is needed, but isolation should not wait for it.
n.1: Antimotility drugs are not appropriate in suspected infective diarrhoea and delaying isolation for 48 hours risks an outbreak.
n.3: Isolation should happen on suspicion; delaying until laboratory confirmation exposes the bay in the meantime.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ben, a staff nurse on a respiratory ward, has developed red, cracked skin across the backs of both hands after several weeks of frequent hand hygiene. He asks his ward manager for advice. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Use soap and water instead of handrub for routine care until his hands heal
Seek occupational health advice and use his own emollient regularly, including on breaks
Apply hand cream from the communal tub in the staff room after each patient contact
Wear non-sterile gloves for routine care tasks so his skin is protected
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.2 skin care: dry hands thoroughly, use an emollient hand cream regularly (for example during breaks and off duty), do not use communal tubs, and staff with skin problems should seek advice from occupational health or their GP. Damaged skin harbours organisms and may need further intervention or reporting.

n.0: Alcohol handrub is recommended for routine hand hygiene and is generally less drying than repeated soap and water.
n.2: NIPCM advises against communal tubs of hand cream because they can become contaminated.
n.3: Gloves are not recommended where no body fluid exposure is anticipated; overuse increases infection risk and does not replace hand hygiene.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: In a GP surgery waiting room, the practice nurse notices Colin, 56, coughing repeatedly into his hands. He has a fever and says he has no tissues. Other patients are seated close by. Which action best applies respiratory and cough hygiene?
o: Give tissues, a bin and a facemask, and seat him at least 1 metre from others
Ask him to cough into his hands and seat him at least 2 metres from others
Give him an FFP3 respirator to wear until he is called in for his appointment
Ask him to wait outside the building in his car until the nurse is ready to see him
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.3 and ch 2: cover the nose and mouth with a disposable tissue, dispose of it promptly and clean hands; outpatients with respiratory symptoms should be asked to wear a facemask if tolerated and be separated from others by at least 1 metre. Prioritising his appointment also helps.

n.1: Coughing into hands contaminates them; the crook of the arm is the fallback, and the NIPCM distance is 1 metre, not the pandemic-era 2 metres.
n.2: NIPCM states an FFP3 respirator must not be worn by an infectious patient, as it filters incoming rather than expelled air.
n.3: Sending a febrile patient to wait outside delays assessment and is not a standard respiratory hygiene measure.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ravi, 64, is prescribed his routine subcutaneous enoxaparin injection. He has intact skin at the injection site and no known infection. The nurse has prepared the syringe and checked the prescription. Which personal protective equipment approach is appropriate for giving this injection?
o: Wear non-sterile gloves and decontaminate them between patients
Wear non-sterile gloves and an apron for the injection
Perform hand hygiene; gloves are not routinely needed
Wear sterile gloves because the skin will be punctured
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.4 lists administering routine intradermal, subcutaneous and intramuscular injections among tasks where gloves should not routinely be worn because no exposure to blood or body fluids is anticipated. Hand hygiene is still required, and glove use stays a clinical risk assessment.

n.0: NIPCM states gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub or soap between uses; they are changed instead.
n.1: Gloves and apron are for anticipated exposure to blood or body fluids, which a routine SC injection does not involve.
n.3: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures such as catheter insertion, not routine SC injections.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Before entering the room of Margaret, 71, who has influenza and needs help to wash, Ade gathers an apron, a fluid-resistant surgical mask, goggles and non-sterile gloves. In which order should Ade put this equipment on?
o: Mask, eye protection, gloves, then apron
Apron, mask, eye protection, then gloves
Apron, gloves, eye protection, then mask
Gloves, apron, mask, then eye protection
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 6 sets the order for putting on PPE as apron or gown, FRSM or respirator, eye protection, then gloves. Gloves go on last so that they are not contaminated while the other items are adjusted.

n.0: The apron goes on first; putting it on last means pulling it over gloves and face protection.
n.2: The mask is fitted before eye protection and gloves; adjusting a mask with gloved hands risks contamination.
n.3: Putting gloves on first means they touch the apron ties, mask and goggles while fitting them.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ade has finished helping Margaret, who has influenza, to wash. He is wearing gloves, an apron, goggles and a fluid-resistant surgical mask. In which order should he remove this PPE?
o: Mask, eye protection, apron, then gloves
Eye protection, gloves, mask, then apron
Apron, gloves, mask, then eye protection
Gloves, apron, eye protection, then mask
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM appendix 6: remove gloves, then apron or gown, then eye protection, then the FRSM or respirator, followed immediately by hand hygiene. The most contaminated items (gloves and the front of the apron) come off first.

n.0: Removing the mask first means touching the face with contaminated gloves still on.
n.1: Handling goggles before glove removal transfers contamination from the gloves to the face area.
n.2: Gloves are the most contaminated item and come off before the apron, not after it.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Winston, 69, has a long-term urinary catheter. A healthcare support worker is about to empty his drainage bag into a single-use jug. There is a small risk of splashing. Which PPE is most appropriate for this task?
o: Sterile gloves and a disposable apron to protect the closed system
A disposable apron, with hand hygiene once the bag is emptied
Non-sterile gloves, a long-sleeved gown and an FFP3 respirator
Non-sterile gloves and apron, plus eye protection if splashing is likely
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves are worn when exposure to body fluids is anticipated, aprons protect clothing when contamination is likely, and eye or face protection is worn when splashing to the face is anticipated. Sterility is not needed to empty a drainage bag.

n.0: Sterile gloves are for sterile sites and aseptic procedures; emptying a bag via the outlet needs non-sterile gloves.
n.1: Contact with urine is anticipated, so gloves are needed as well as the apron.
n.2: Gowns are for extensive splashing and FFP3 respirators for airborne risks; neither applies to emptying a catheter bag.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Nadia is about to irrigate a large infected leg wound for Doreen, 81. Splashing of wound fluid towards her face is likely. There are no full-face visors on the ward. Which facial protection should Nadia wear?
o: A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with separate eye protection
A Type II surgical mask and her own prescription glasses
A Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask without eye protection
An FFP3 respirator without separate eye protection
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: where splashing of blood or body fluids onto the face is anticipated and a full-face visor is not available, wear a Type IIR FRSM with eye protection. Regular corrective spectacles are not considered eye protection.

n.1: A Type II mask is not fluid resistant, and corrective spectacles do not count as eye protection.
n.2: The mask protects the nose and mouth, but the eyes remain exposed to the expected splashes.
n.3: An FFP3 respirator protects against airborne particles; it does not protect the eyes from splashes.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Wearing non-sterile gloves and an apron, Sam has just emptied the stoma bag of Kofi, 47. Sam now needs to give Kofi mouth care before leaving the bed space. What should Sam do before starting the mouth care?
o: Pull a second pair of gloves over the first pair and continue
Keep the same gloves, as both tasks are for the same patient
Remove the gloves, perform hand hygiene and put on new gloves
Apply alcohol handrub over the gloves, then continue with mouth care
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 1.4: gloves must be changed after completing a procedure or task even on the same patient, and hand hygiene must be performed between glove changes. Gloves must not be decontaminated with handrub.

n.0: Double gloving is not recommended for routine care and still leaves the contaminated outer layer touching the mouth.
n.1: Gloves are changed between tasks on the same patient, so contamination from the stoma is not carried to the mouth.
n.3: NIPCM states gloves are not decontaminated with handrub or soap and water between uses.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Lucy, 58, has confirmed seasonal influenza and is in a single room under droplet precautions. A nurse needs to stand beside her bed to take observations; no aerosol generating procedure is planned. What respiratory protection should the nurse wear when within 1 metre of Lucy?
o: No mask is needed for brief observations
A fluid-resistant surgical mask
A fit-tested FFP3 respirator
A Type II surgical mask
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.4: an FRSM must be worn by staff providing care within 1 metre of a patient when droplet precautions apply. FFP3 respirators are considered for airborne pathogens and for AGPs on patients with infections spread by the airborne or droplet route.

n.0: Droplet precautions require an FRSM within 1 metre, however short the contact.
n.2: An FFP3 respirator is for airborne precautions or AGPs; routine observations on a droplet-precautions patient need an FRSM.
n.3: A Type II mask is not classed as fluid resistant; droplet precautions call for an FRSM.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Daniel, a staff nurse with a full beard, is asked to care for Tariq, 30, who has suspected measles and is in a negative-pressure room. Daniel passed an FFP3 fit test two years ago when he was clean-shaven. What is the most appropriate course of action?
o: Wear a powered respirator hood in place of the tight-fitting FFP3
Wear two fluid-resistant surgical masks layered over each other
Wear the same FFP3 model and perform a fit check on entry
Wear a Type IIR fluid-resistant surgical mask with a visor
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Measles spreads by the airborne route, so respiratory protective equipment is needed. NIPCM ch 2.4 states facial hair must not cross the respirator sealing surface and staff must pass a fit test for any tight-fitting RPE; powered respirator hoods are an alternative when fit testing cannot be achieved.

n.1: Layering surgical masks does not create a sealed respirator and gives no airborne protection.
n.2: A beard crossing the seal means a tight-fitting respirator cannot seal, and a fit check does not replace a valid fit test.
n.3: An FRSM with a visor protects against droplets and splashes, not airborne particles.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: During a ward teaching session on transmission-based precautions, a student nurse asks which route of transmission is responsible for most cross-infection in care settings, including spread via equipment and the patient's surroundings. Which answer is correct?
o: Airborne transmission via aerosols
Droplet transmission over short distances
Blood-borne transmission via sharps injuries
Contact transmission, direct or indirect
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2 defines contact precautions as preventing spread by direct contact with the patient or indirectly from the immediate care environment, including care equipment, and states this is the most common route of cross-infection transmission.

n.0: Airborne spread applies to a smaller group of organisms such as measles and TB.
n.1: Droplet spread is important for respiratory pathogens but NIPCM names contact as the most common route.
n.2: Sharps injuries carry blood-borne virus risk to staff, but are not the main route of cross-infection between patients.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: A medical ward has one free single room. The nurse in charge must decide which of four patients should move into it. Applying NIPCM single-room prioritisation, which patient should be moved first?
o: Edith, 92, who is frail and has been admitted with a hip fracture
Ann, 66, with pneumonia, a dry cough and on day 4 of antibiotics
Derek, 70, with vomiting and diarrhoea and suspected norovirus
Kevin, 59, with leg cellulitis fully contained by a dry dressing
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 flags diarrhoea and vomiting as a cross-infection risk and directs that single rooms are prioritised for infectious patients most likely to transmit to others; norovirus spreads rapidly in bays. Prioritisation is reviewed daily with IPC team input.

n.0: Frailty raises Edith's risk of acquiring infection, but she is not an infection source needing isolation.
n.1: Ann is on treatment with a dry cough and poses a lower transmission risk than active vomiting and diarrhoea.
n.3: Contained, dressed cellulitis presents a low transmission risk with standard precautions.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Single rooms are full on a respiratory ward. Two patients with the same confirmed respiratory virus are to be cohorted in a bay. Under current NIPCM guidance, what is the minimum separation between their beds?
o: At least 0.5 metres between the bed spaces
At least 3 metres between the bed spaces
At least 2 metres between the bed spaces
At least 1 metre between the bed spaces
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 states cohorted infectious patients should be separated by at least 3 feet (1 metre) with the door closed. Droplet precautions use at least 1 metre; the 2 metres introduced during COVID-19 has reverted to 1 metre in all areas.

n.0: Half a metre is below the 1 metre minimum for separation in a cohort.
n.1: 3 metres exceeds the NIPCM standard; the distance given is 3 feet, which is about 1 metre.
n.2: 2 metres was a COVID-19 measure that NIPCM says has returned to 1 metre.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Gordon, 74, is in a single room with a suspected respiratory infection and needs a chest X-ray. The radiology department cannot bring a portable machine today. He is stable and can tolerate a mask. How should the nurse arrange his transfer?
o: Postpone the X-ray until his infection status has been confirmed
Transfer him without a mask and clean the wheelchair once the journey is complete
Ask him to wear an FFP3 respirator during the transfer and X-ray
Ask him to wear a surgical mask if tolerated and inform radiology of his status
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: infectious patients are transferred only when clinically necessary, and should wear a surgical mask in communal areas during transfer if tolerated; the receiving department and transport staff must be made aware of the precautions needed.

n.0: The X-ray is clinically needed, and transfer with precautions is appropriate rather than delaying diagnosis.
n.1: Without a mask he exposes others in corridors and waiting areas; cleaning afterwards does not prevent that exposure.
n.2: FFP3 respirators filter incoming air and must not be worn by infectious patients.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Four patients on an elderly care ward have laboratory-confirmed norovirus. All single rooms are occupied. The IPC team agrees a cohort bay. Which plan for the cohort is most appropriate?
o: Place them together in one bay with the door closed and dedicated equipment
Place them together with a neutropenic patient who also has diarrhoea
Place them with two patients who have diarrhoea that is not yet confirmed
Keep each in their current bay with curtains drawn and contact precautions
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1-2.2: cohorting is considered when single rooms are short and two or more patients have the same confirmed infection; doors stay closed and reusable equipment is dedicated to the cohort area. Immunosuppressed patients and those with different or unconfirmed infections must not be mixed in.

n.1: NIPCM states patients at increased risk of adverse outcomes, such as those who are immunosuppressed, must not be cohorted with others.
n.2: Unconfirmed diarrhoea may be a different infection; cohorts are formed from patients with the same confirmed infection.
n.3: Leaving infected patients in mixed bays exposes susceptible patients; curtains do not contain norovirus.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Ellen, 77, who had C. difficile infection, has been discharged home from a single room. The domestic team asks the nurse what terminal cleaning is required. Which instruction is most appropriate?
o: Use detergent wipes on surfaces and send the curtains as used linen
Clean with a 10,000 ppm available chlorine solution and leave the curtains in place
Clean with neutral detergent and change the curtains at the next routine change
Remove the curtains as infectious linen and clean with 1,000 ppm available chlorine
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.3 terminal decontamination: bag and remove waste, manage curtains and bedding as infectious linen, decontaminate equipment, then clean with a combined detergent and 1,000 ppm available chlorine solution (or detergent followed by 1,000 ppm), working from high to low and least to most contaminated.

n.0: Curtains from an infectious patient's room are infectious linen, and wipes alone are not a terminal clean.
n.1: 10,000 ppm is the strength for blood spills; terminal cleaning uses 1,000 ppm, and curtains are removed.
n.2: Detergent alone does not meet the terminal clean standard, and curtains from an isolation room are removed as infectious linen.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Grace, 68, is admitted to a surgical ward. Three months ago she was an inpatient in a hospital abroad after a car accident. She has no symptoms of infection. What is the most appropriate placement while admission screening is arranged?
o: A single room with contact precautions while screening for CPE
A bay with other patients recently treated abroad, pending results
An open bay, after starting prophylactic broad-spectrum antibiotics
An open bay, with screening repeated if she develops a fever
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1 lists patients who have been inpatients in any hospital in the UK or abroad as a possible cross-infection risk for multidrug-resistant organisms such as carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales (CPE). She should be placed in a single room with contact precautions pending screening, and the decision documented.

n.1: Cohorting is for patients with the same confirmed infection; unscreened patients may carry different organisms.
n.2: Prophylactic antibiotics do not clear carriage and drive resistance, contrary to NICE NG15 stewardship.
n.3: CPE carriage is usually symptomless, so waiting for a fever leaves the bay exposed.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Alfred, 86, has delirium and MRSA and is nursed in a single room. With the door closed he becomes distressed and has twice tried to climb out of bed. The healthcare support worker suggests propping the door open. What should the nurse do?
o: Keep the door closed and increase checks on Alfred to hourly
Move Alfred back to the open bay where staff can see him
Prop the door open and mention the change at the next handover
Document a risk assessment and agree the door plan with the IPC team
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NIPCM ch 2.1: isolation room doors should remain closed, and if this is not possible a documented risk assessment is needed, with IPC team advice on precautions. Alfred's falls risk and distress must be balanced against transmission risk.

n.0: Hourly checks do not address the falls risk and distress that the closed door is causing.
n.1: Moving him to a bay exposes other patients to MRSA without IPC team assessment.
n.2: Changing isolation conditions needs a documented risk assessment, not an informal handover note.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Tom, a nursing associate, is preparing an intravenous antibiotic to give through the peripheral cannula of Joan, 59, using aseptic non-touch technique (ANTT). Which item is a Key-Part that must be protected from touch?
o: The tip of the syringe that connects to the cannula hub
The skin of Joan's forearm well away from the cannula
The outer barrel of the syringe held during preparation
The plastic tray used as the general aseptic field
Infection Prevention & Control.w: In the ANTT framework, Key-Parts are the parts of equipment that, if contaminated, are likely to infect the patient, such as syringe tips, needles and line connections. They are protected by non-touch technique and aseptic fields.

n.1: Key-Sites are open wounds and insertion sites; intact skin away from the cannula is neither a Key-Site nor a Key-Part.
n.2: The barrel is handled normally; only the parts that contact the patient or the sterile fluid path are Key-Parts.
n.3: The tray is the general aseptic field that supports Key-Part protection; it is not itself a Key-Part.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Nadia is redressing a deep cavity wound on the sacrum of Ruth, 80. She is wearing non-sterile gloves and using ANTT, but realises she will need to touch the wound bed with her fingers to place the packing. What should she do?
o: Change to sterile gloves, as the Key-Site will be touched directly
Moisten the non-sterile gloves with sterile saline before packing
Rub alcohol handrub onto the gloves before touching the wound
Continue with the non-sterile gloves, as she cleaned her hands first
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Under ANTT, if a Key-Site or Key-Part must be touched directly, sterile gloves are needed so that the hands do not contaminate it (a Surgical-ANTT approach). NIPCM ch 1.4 also requires sterile gloves for contact with a sterile site or body cavity.

n.1: Saline does not sterilise gloves; the gloves would still contaminate the wound bed.
n.2: Gloves are not decontaminated with handrub, and this does not make them sterile.
n.3: Non-sterile gloves are acceptable when Key-Sites are not touched; here she must touch the wound bed directly.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Sophie is about to insert a peripheral intravenous cannula into the forearm of Malik, 45. She has selected the vein and performed hand hygiene. According to NICE CG139, how should she prepare the skin at the insertion site?
o: Clean with a 70% alcohol wipe, then palpate the vein again
Clean with sterile 0.9% sodium chloride and pat the skin dry with gauze
Apply povidone-iodine and wipe it off before inserting
Clean with chlorhexidine in 70% alcohol and allow it to dry
Infection Prevention & Control.w: NICE CG139: decontaminate the skin at the insertion site with chlorhexidine gluconate in 70% alcohol before inserting a peripheral vascular access device or PICC. The solution must dry to work, and the cleaned site is not re-palpated.

n.0: Re-palpating the vein after cleaning contaminates the Key-Site, and alcohol alone is not the CG139 product.
n.1: Saline cleans but does not decontaminate the skin.
n.2: CG139 specifies chlorhexidine in alcohol; wiping antiseptic off before it has acted also defeats it.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: After inserting a peripheral cannula into the hand of Agnes, 88, the nurse needs to secure and cover the site. Which type of dressing is recommended so that the site can be inspected?
o: A sterile hydrocolloid dressing over the hub
A sterile gauze dressing and crepe bandage
Non-sterile adhesive tape over a gauze square
A sterile transparent semipermeable dressing
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Vascular access device care (NICE CG139 and the IPC facts sheet) uses a sterile, transparent, semipermeable membrane dressing so the insertion site can be observed for signs of infection or phlebitis without removing it.

n.0: Hydrocolloid dressings are for wounds; they are opaque and not designed for cannula sites.
n.1: A bandage over gauze prevents regular inspection of the insertion site.
n.2: Non-sterile tape and gauze hide the site and are not a sterile covering for a Key-Site.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: Rajesh, 52, is on day 3 of intravenous antibiotics through a forearm cannula. He reports pain at the site, and you see redness and swelling tracking along the vein. He still needs intravenous antibiotics. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Apply a warm compress and reassess the site at the end of the shift
Leave the cannula in place and record the findings in the care plan
Flush the cannula with 0.9% sodium chloride and continue if it is patent
Remove the cannula and arrange resiting at a different site
Infection Prevention & Control.w: Pain, erythema and swelling at a cannula site indicate phlebitis on a visual infusion phlebitis assessment, which calls for removal of the device. As IV therapy is still needed, a new cannula is resited elsewhere using ANTT, and the findings are documented.

n.0: A compress may ease symptoms after removal, but delaying removal leaves an infected device in place.
n.1: Documentation is needed, but leaving the cannula in place does not manage the phlebitis.
n.2: Patency does not rule out phlebitis; continuing to use an inflamed site risks thrombophlebitis and bloodstream infection.

Infection Prevention & Control.q: On a ward round you notice that the urinary drainage bag of Bernard, 79, is lying on the floor beside his chair, and later it is hooked over the bed rail above his waist while he is repositioned. What is the correct positioning of the drainage bag?
o: Level with the bladder to reduce traction on the catheter
Above the bladder when moving, then below it when seated
