n.0: Temporary registration is for people staying in an area for a short time; having no fixed address does not restrict her to it, and she is entitled to full registration.
n.2: Directing routine care to the emergency department is inappropriate and deepens inequality of access.
n.3: Lack of proof of address is not a reason to refuse registration.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Jamie, 24, has a learning disability and is admitted with abdominal pain. He brings a hospital passport describing how he communicates. On the ward round, staff talk to his mother and ignore Jamie. What should his nurse do?
o: Ask his mother to explain the ward round decisions to Jamie later
Allow the conversation to continue, as his mother knows him best
Share the passport details and invite staff to speak directly to Jamie
Ask the learning disability liaison nurse to attend the next ward round
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Nurses advocate for people who are vulnerable or disabled and make reasonable adjustments (P7.9; Code 3.4; Equality Act 2010 s20). Using the hospital passport and speaking directly to Jamie in his preferred way respects his rights, involves him in decisions and supports any capacity assessment (MCA 2005 s1(3)).

n.0: Passing information on later excludes Jamie from the conversation about his own care.
n.1: His mother's knowledge is valuable, but Jamie must be involved directly in decisions about his care.
n.3: Liaison nurses offer valuable support, but the nurse should advocate for Jamie now rather than wait.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Leo, 19, is autistic and attends a busy emergency department with a wrist injury. He is covering his ears, rocking and becoming more distressed in the noisy waiting room. His triage category means he may wait two hours. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Suggest he returns tomorrow when the department is likely to be quieter
Move him up the triage queue ahead of patients with more urgent needs
Ask him to wait outside the department until a cubicle becomes free
Offer a quieter space to wait and explain clearly what will happen next
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Reasonable adjustments remove disadvantage arising from disability without compromising others' safety: a quieter waiting space and clear, predictable information reduce sensory overload while clinical priority is maintained (Equality Act 2010 s20; P3.7; P7.9). Two steps: recognise sensory distress, then select a proportionate adjustment.

n.0: Delaying treatment of an injury is not a reasonable adjustment and may worsen the outcome.
n.1: Triage order is based on clinical urgency; changing it could harm patients with more urgent needs.
n.2: Sending him outside removes him from observation and is not an adjustment that maintains his care.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Edna Fox, 83, is medically fit for discharge after a urinary tract infection. Before admission she managed alone at home. She will now go home with a new package of carers visiting twice a day for personal care. Which discharge pathway applies?
o: Pathway 1
Pathway 2
Pathway 3
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Hospital discharge and community support guidance (DHSC/NHS England, updated January 2024): pathway 1 is discharge home or to the usual place of residence with new or additional health and/or social care needs (P4.18; P7.10).

n.1: Pathway 2 is a community bed-based setting with recovery support, not home.
n.2: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new or additional care needs; Mrs Fox needs a new care package.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Gordon Bailey, 79, is recovering from a hip fracture repair. He is not yet safe at home but the team expects he will be able to return home after a few weeks of rehabilitation in a community hospital bed. Which discharge pathway is this?
o: Pathway 3
Pathway 2
Pathway 1
Pathway 0
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Pathway 2 is discharge to a community bed-based setting with dedicated recovery support, where short-term care helps the person recover before living independently or receiving longer-term care (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Pathway 3 is a new residential or nursing home placement for people likely to need long-term care.
n.2: Pathway 1 is discharge home with new support; Mr Bailey is not yet ready to go home.
n.3: Pathway 0 is home with no new needs.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Rita Holmes, 87, lived alone before a fall and is now medically fit for discharge but still slow and unsteady. At the board round, a doctor suggests arranging a permanent nursing home place directly from the ward. What does current discharge guidance in England advise?
o: Discharge her home with no support and review her needs if she falls
Arrange the permanent place now, as hospital is the best place to assess needs
Discharge her for a period of recovery, then assess her long-term needs
Keep Mrs Holmes in hospital until she has fully recovered her mobility
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under discharge to assess, long-term needs are assessed once the person has reached optimal recovery, not in hospital. Other than in exceptional circumstances, no one should be discharged directly into a permanent care home placement for the first time without an opportunity to recover first (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P4.18). Two steps: recognise she is medically fit, then apply discharge to assess.

n.0: She has clear new needs; discharge without support is unsafe.
n.1: Assessing long-term needs in hospital, before recovery, tends to overestimate need; the guidance advises against it.
n.3: Staying in hospital once medically fit risks deconditioning and delays recovery.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Claire Bennett, 42, who has multiple sclerosis, is due for discharge after a relapse. During discharge planning, Sunil, her nurse, learns that her 14-year-old son provides much of her care at home. What should Sunil do?
o: Ask Claire to arrange more help from other family members before discharge
Plan the discharge around the son's school hours, as he already provides her care
Leave the son out of discussions, as he is under 18 and cannot be a carer
Involve the son appropriately and notify the local authority so it can assess him
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NHS trusts must involve unpaid carers, including young carers, in discharge planning as soon as feasible (Care Act 2014 s74 as amended by the Health and Care Act 2022). Where a young carer is identified, the local authority should be notified so it can carry out a young carer's needs assessment, including whether caring is appropriate or excessive (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Other support may help, but the young carer still needs to be identified and referred for assessment.
n.1: Relying on a child's care without assessment may place excessive responsibility on him and ignores safeguarding considerations.
n.2: Young carers are recognised in law and must be identified and involved appropriately, not excluded.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Leonard Ross, 74, is going home after a stroke. His wife, Margaret, will help him with washing and dressing. She tells the nurse she is already exhausted and worried about coping. What should the nurse tell her?
o: She should wait to see how she copes for the first few weeks at home
She can apply for a carer's assessment once he has been home a month
She has a right to a carer's assessment from the local authority
She can ask the GP to prescribe something to help her sleep better
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Under section 10 of the Care Act 2014, where a carer appears to have needs for support, the local authority must carry out a carer's assessment. For a new caring role this should ideally happen before caring begins, organised so as not to delay discharge (Hospital discharge and community support guidance, 2024; P7.10).

n.0: Waiting risks carer breakdown; carers' needs should be assessed early.
n.1: There is no one-month waiting period; the local authority's duty arises when it appears she may have needs.
n.3: Sleep problems may need attention, but this does not address her support needs as a carer.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mr Kwabena Asante, 66, is to be discharged on a newly started oral anticoagulant after a pulmonary embolism. Which final check before he leaves best supports a safe discharge?
o: He has been told to read the patient leaflet supplied with his tablets
He understands his medicine, has a supply, and follow-up is arranged
His observations are within normal limits on the morning of discharge
He has a copy of the discharge letter to hand in to his GP practice
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Safe discharge on a high-risk medicine requires the person to understand the medicine and its risks, have an adequate supply, and have follow-up arranged with information shared with primary care (P4.18 coordinate safe discharge; NICE NG5 medicines-related communication at transfer; Code 7 and 8.3 keep colleagues informed when sharing care).

n.0: A leaflet does not confirm understanding of a high-risk new medicine.
n.2: Stable observations are needed but do not address the medicines and follow-up risks of anticoagulation.
n.3: Relying on the patient to carry the letter delays information reaching the GP; discharge information should be sent directly.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: Mrs Joan Pike, 90, has social care needs and has been in hospital for a week with heart failure. Several professionals are involved and her daughter is confused about who to contact about discharge plans. According to NICE NG27, what should be in place?
o: A weekly letter to the daughter from the consultant in charge
A named discharge coordinator as the central point of contact
A rule that her daughter contacts the ward sister each morning
A referral to the hospital complaints team to manage contact
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: NICE NG27 (2015) recommends a hospital-based multidisciplinary team and a named discharge coordinator who is the central point of contact for the person and their family during discharge planning (P7.10; P4.18).

n.0: A weekly letter is too infrequent and does not provide a single coordinating contact.
n.2: This places responsibility on the family rather than giving them a coordinator.
n.3: Her daughter's confusion is a coordination problem, not a complaint to be managed.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward wants to evaluate how well it plans discharges for people with complex care needs who go home with new support. Which approach would best capture the quality of their experience?
o: Count the number of discharges completed before midday each week
Review the ward's length-of-stay figures against other medical wards
Phone people and carers after discharge to ask about their experience
Audit how many discharge letters reached GPs within 24 hours
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: The quality of people's experience of complex care is best evaluated by asking them and their carers directly about the discharge and transition, including whether support started as planned (P7.7 monitor and evaluate the quality of people's experience of complex care; P6.9).

n.0: Discharge timing is a process measure that says little about the person's experience.
n.1: Length of stay measures efficiency, not experience.
n.3: Letter timeliness is an important process measure but does not capture the experience of people and carers.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: During a team meeting, Ellie, a nurse three months after registration, says that leadership is something for ward managers and that her job is to look after her own patients. How does the NMC Code describe leadership for registrants?
o: All registrants have opportunities to show leadership whatever their role
Leadership is required where a nurse is formally in charge of a shift
Leadership is expected once a nurse is appointed to a band 6 role or above
Leadership is expected after completing a recognised leadership course
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Code standard 25 (provide leadership to make sure people's wellbeing is protected and to improve their experiences) applies to every registrant; the NMC states that all registrants have opportunities to show leadership regardless of formal position (P5.6 exhibit leadership potential).

n.1: Being in charge adds responsibilities (Code 25.1), but leadership is expected of all registrants at all times.
n.2: The Code links leadership to professional practice, not to pay band or grade.
n.3: Courses can develop leadership skills, but the Code's expectation does not depend on them.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: A ward is moving from paper charts to electronic observations next month. Several experienced nurses tell Raj, the ward manager, that the system will slow them down and they do not want it. Which approach is most likely to support the change?
o: Ask the nurses who object to work on other wards during the changeover
Involve staff early, explain the reasons, act on concerns and pilot it
Delay the change until every member of the team agrees to it
Set a firm start date and tell staff the system is mandatory from that day
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Effective change management involves the people affected: explaining why the change is needed, listening to and addressing concerns, and testing the change on a small scale so staff can shape it (P5.1 principles of leadership and organisational culture; AnnexA.4.2.1 strengths-based approaches to managing change).

n.0: Removing staff who raise concerns loses their expertise and damages trust in the team.
n.2: Waiting for unanimous agreement can block necessary safety improvements indefinitely.
n.3: Imposing change without engagement tends to increase resistance and workarounds.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: At her appraisal, Joy, a healthcare assistant, is praised by families for her skill in calming people living with dementia who are distressed. Her line manager, Paul, wants to use a strengths-based approach to developing the team. What should Paul do?
o: Concentrate the appraisal on the areas where Joy needs to improve
Move Joy to the dementia unit so that her skills are used there
Ask Joy to spend less time with families so she can do other tasks
Agree a plan for Joy to share her approach and support colleagues
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Strengths-based team development recognises what people do well and builds on it, for example by enabling a team member to share skills and act as a resource, which improves care and motivation (AnnexA.4.2.1; P5.2 strength-based approaches in teams).

n.0: Development needs matter, but a strengths-based approach starts from what the person does well.
n.1: Moving her removes the skill from the team rather than building on it within the team.
n.2: Reducing the activity she excels at undermines a strength that benefits patients and families.

Leading & Coordinating Care.q: On a leadership study day, students are asked to distinguish leadership from management. Which activity is best described as leadership rather than management?
o: Preparing the ward's off-duty rota for the next four weeks
Setting a shared vision for care and motivating the team
Recording and reviewing staff sickness absence each month
Monitoring the ward's monthly spending against its budget
Leading & Coordinating Care.w: Management is concerned with planning, organising and controlling resources (rotas, budgets, absence); leadership is concerned with direction, vision and influencing and motivating people. Nurses need both (P5.1 principles of effective leadership and management).

n.0: Rota planning organises resources, a management task.
n.2: Absence monitoring is a management process.
n.3: Budget monitoring is a management control activity.

Mental Health Law.q: Joseph, 52, has paranoid psychosis and is refusing all contact with services. His sister, who lives in another city, asks the community mental health nurse who can make the application for him to be detained under section 2. Which answer is correct?
o: The police officer who later detains him under section 136
The consultant psychiatrist or his general practitioner
An approved mental health professional or nearest relative
Any registered mental health nurse who has assessed him
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 11(1) of the Mental Health Act 1983, an application for admission under Part 2 is made by an approved mental health professional (AMHP) or the nearest relative. Doctors provide the medical recommendations; they do not make the application.

n.0: Section 136 is a police power to remove a person to a place of safety; the police do not make section 2 applications.
n.1: Doctors provide the two medical recommendations; the application itself is made by an AMHP or the nearest relative.
n.3: A registered nurse who is not an AMHP cannot make a Part 2 application; nurses of the prescribed class have only the section 5(4) holding power.

Mental Health Law.q: An approved mental health professional last saw Priya, 41, in person 16 days ago. Two doctors have now recommended section 3. The AMHP asks the community nurse whether the application can be completed today without visiting Priya again. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Yes, because the 28-day limit for personal contact has not passed
Yes, because the doctors' examinations were within the last 5 days
No, because the AMHP must have seen her personally within 14 days
No, because a fresh nearest relative consultation is due every 7 days
Mental Health Law.w: Section 11(5) requires the applicant to have personally seen the patient within the 14 days ending with the date of the application. Sixteen days have passed, so the AMHP must see Priya again before applying, whatever the dates of the medical examinations.

n.0: There is no 28-day personal-contact window; 28 days is the maximum length of section 2 detention.
n.1: Recent medical examinations do not satisfy the separate requirement that the applicant has seen the patient within 14 days (s11(5)).
n.3: There is no 7-day rule on nearest relative consultation; the issue here is the 14-day personal-contact rule for the applicant.

Mental Health Law.q: Daniel, 27, has a learning disability and no other mental disorder. He has become withdrawn but shows no aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. The team is considering long-term detention for treatment under section 3. What should the mental health nurse advise?
o: Section 3 is available if his nearest relative does not object
Section 3 is unavailable because his disability is not associated with such conduct
Section 3 is unavailable because people with learning disability are excluded from the Act
Section 3 is available because learning disability is a disorder of the mind
Mental Health Law.w: Section 1(2A) and (2B) of the Mental Health Act 1983 provide that, for section 3 and other longer-term powers, learning disability alone is not a mental disorder unless associated with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct. Section 2 is not in that list, so assessment remains possible. (The 2025 Act will go further but those provisions are not in force.)

n.0: The nearest relative's view does not cure the missing statutory condition; without the conduct qualification section 3 cannot be used.
n.2: People with learning disability are not excluded from the Act; section 2 remains available and section 3 is possible where the conduct qualification is met.
n.3: Learning disability is within the general definition, but for section 3 it counts only with abnormally aggressive or seriously irresponsible conduct (s1(2A)-(2B)).

Mental Health Law.q: A nurse consultant on a recovery ward asks whether she could become a patient's responsible clinician (RC) under the Mental Health Act 1983. Which statement is accurate?
o: The RC is the approved clinician with overall responsibility for the case
The RC is the AMHP who made the application for detention
The RC is the hospital manager who authorises leave and discharge
The RC must be a consultant psychiatrist on the GMC specialist register
Mental Health Law.w: Under the 1983 Act as amended in 2007, the responsible clinician is the approved clinician with overall responsibility for the patient's case. Approved clinicians may come from medicine, nursing, psychology, occupational therapy or social work, so a suitably approved nurse can be an RC.

n.1: The AMHP makes the application and has a separate, independent role; the AMHP is not the RC.
n.2: Hospital managers are the detaining authority and hear reviews; the RC is the clinician who grants section 17 leave.
n.3: Since 2008 the RC role is not limited to doctors; any approved clinician, including an approved nurse, can hold it.

Mental Health Law.q: Kwame, 23, is admitted under section 2 of the Mental Health Act 1983 after his first episode of psychotic symptoms. His mother asks the admitting nurse how long the section can last. Which answer is correct?
o: Up to 72 hours, unless a second doctor's recommendation is received
Up to 6 months, renewable for a further 6 months
Up to 28 days, renewable once for a further 28 days
Up to 28 days, and it cannot be renewed
Mental Health Law.w: Section 2(4) of the Mental Health Act 1983 authorises detention for assessment for up to 28 days from admission. It cannot be renewed; if further detention is needed the team must consider section 3.

n.0: Seventy-two hours is the limit for section 4 (emergency application) or section 5(2), not section 2.
n.1: Six months, renewable, is the initial period for section 3 treatment detention.
n.2: Section 2 has no renewal provision; continued detention requires a section 3 application.

Mental Health Law.q: Grace, 45, has had bipolar disorder for 20 years and is well known to the ward. She is relapsing into mania, refusing her established treatment plan and needs admission. Which section is generally most appropriate under the Code of Practice?
o: Section 4, because the admission is clinically urgent
Section 2, because every new admission begins with assessment
Section 3, because her diagnosis and treatment needs are established
Section 5(2), because she can be held and assessed on the ward
Mental Health Law.w: COP15 paragraphs 14.27-14.28: section 3 should be used where the nature and current degree of the disorder, the essential elements of the treatment plan and the likelihood of accepting informal treatment are already sufficiently established; section 2 is for when these are unclear and need in-patient assessment. Grace's illness and treatment are well established.

n.0: Section 4 is for urgent necessity where waiting for a second doctor would cause undesirable delay; nothing suggests that here.
n.1: The Code does not require every admission to start on section 2; section 2 suits cases where assessment is genuinely needed.
n.3: Section 5(2) applies to an informal in-patient already on a ward; Grace is not yet an in-patient.

Mental Health Law.q: An approved mental health professional consults Liam's nearest relative, his father, about an application for section 3. His father objects in writing. What is the legal effect?
o: The father's objection delays the application for 72 hours
The AMHP cannot make the section 3 application while the objection stands
The objection means Liam must be detained under section 2 instead
The AMHP may proceed if both doctors record that the objection is unreasonable
Mental Health Law.w: Section 11(4) provides that an AMHP may not make a section 3 application if the nearest relative has notified the AMHP or the local authority that they object. The route is an application to the county court to displace the nearest relative (s29).

n.0: There is no 72-hour delay rule; the objection bars the application. Seventy-two hours relates to the NR's discharge notice under s25.
n.2: Section 2 may be used where its own criteria are met, but the objection does not require it; that would need clinical justification, not a workaround.
n.3: Doctors cannot override the objection; displacement of an unreasonable nearest relative is a matter for the county court under section 29.

Mental Health Law.q: Gemma, 30, is depressed with suicidal thoughts. She has capacity, agrees she needs hospital care and is willing to be admitted. A junior doctor suggests section 2 'to be safe'. What is the most appropriate course?
o: Admit under section 2 because of the suicide risk
Admit informally and review if her consent changes
Admit under section 4 pending a second recommendation
Admit under section 3 so treatment can be given
Mental Health Law.w: Under the least restrictive principle (COP15 chapter 1 and chapter 14) informal admission should be considered first where a person with capacity consents. Detention criteria require that detention is necessary; a consenting capable person can usually be admitted informally.

n.0: Risk alone does not justify detention if a capable person consents; the least restrictive option is informal admission.
n.2: Section 4 is for urgent necessity with one doctor available; it is not a precaution for a consenting patient.
n.3: Section 3 requires that treatment cannot be provided unless she is detained, which is not met when she consents.

Mental Health Law.q: An approved mental health professional is assessing Mo, 38, for section 2. Mo's wife, his nearest relative, says she does not want him detained. What should the community nurse understand about her view?
o: It prevents the section 2 application in the same way as section 3
It allows the AMHP to delay the decision by up to 14 days
It requires a tribunal decision before the application
It must be considered, but it does not prevent a section 2 application
Mental Health Law.w: For section 2 the AMHP must take practicable steps to inform the nearest relative (s11(3)), but the NR has no power to block it. The objection bar in section 11(4) applies to section 3 and guardianship. The NR can later order discharge under section 23, subject to the RC's barring report (s25).

n.0: The statutory objection bar applies to section 3 and guardianship, not to section 2.
n.1: There is no 14-day delay power; 14 days is the period within which the applicant must have seen the patient and the s2 tribunal window.
n.2: No tribunal decision is needed before an application; tribunals review detention after it begins.

Mental Health Law.q: Ravi, 34, has been detained under section 2 for 25 days. He still needs treatment for psychosis and is refusing it and asking to leave. What is the most appropriate legal step?
o: Consider a section 3 application before the section 2 expires
Continue treating him under section 63 once day 28 has passed
Use section 5(2) to hold him once the section 2 expires
Make a fresh section 2 application for a further 28 days
Mental Health Law.w: Section 2 lasts up to 28 days and cannot be renewed (s2(4)). COP15 14.28 says section 3 should be used where the patient is already detained under section 2, so an AMHP application for section 3 with two medical recommendations should be considered before the section 2 lapses.

n.1: Section 63 authority depends on a live detention; it cannot authorise treatment once the section 2 has expired.
n.2: Section 5(2) applies to informal in-patients; using it to extend an expiring section 2 is not a proper use of the power (COP15 ch18).
n.3: Section 2 cannot be renewed, and COP15 14.28 states a new section 2 application cannot be used to extend it.

Mental Health Law.q: Bethany, 50, is detained under section 3. Her first renewal took effect 5 months ago and the next renewal is due. If renewed, how long will the next period of detention be?
o: Two years
Six months
Three months
One year
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 20 of the 1983 Act a section 3 lasts up to 6 months, may be renewed for a further 6 months, and then for periods of 1 year at a time. Bethany has had the initial 6 months and one 6-month renewal, so the next renewal is for 1 year. (The 2025 Act's shorter periods are not in force.)

n.0: Renewals after the first are for 1 year at a time, not 2 years.
n.1: Six months applies to the initial period and the first renewal; she has already had both.
n.2: Three-month periods are a Mental Health Act 2025 change that is not in force.

Mental Health Law.q: A student asks what extra condition must be met for section 3 that is not required for section 2. Which answer is correct?
o: Appropriate medical treatment must be available for the patient
Two medical recommendations must be provided
The patient must have a diagnosed mental disorder
The patient must be at risk to their own health or safety or to others
Mental Health Law.w: Section 3(2)(d) requires that appropriate medical treatment is available. Section 2 has no such test because its purpose includes assessment. Both sections need a mental disorder, risk-related grounds and two medical recommendations.

n.1: Both section 2 and section 3 need two medical recommendations; section 4 needs one.
n.2: Section 2 also requires a mental disorder of a nature or degree warranting detention, although a final diagnosis is not needed.
n.3: Both sections include grounds relating to the patient's health or safety or the protection of others.

Mental Health Law.q: At 22:00 Sean, 36, an informal in-patient on an acute ward, suddenly packs his bag and says he will 'end it tonight'. No doctor can attend quickly. The registered mental health nurse invokes section 5(4). For how long can Sean be held under this power?
o: Up to 72 hours, or until the approved mental health professional arrives if sooner
Up to 6 hours, renewable once by a second nurse of the prescribed class
Up to 6 hours, or until a doctor or approved clinician with s5(2) power arrives if sooner
Up to 24 hours, with a possible 12-hour extension by the duty doctor
Mental Health Law.w: Section 5(4) allows detention for up to 6 hours or until a doctor or approved clinician able to use section 5(2) arrives, whichever is earlier. It cannot be renewed (COP15 18.25).

n.0: Seventy-two hours is the maximum for the doctor's or approved clinician's section 5(2) power, not the nurse's.
n.1: Section 5(4) cannot be renewed by any nurse (COP15 18.25, 18.38).
n.3: Twenty-four hours plus a 12-hour extension is the place of safety limit under sections 135 and 136.

Mental Health Law.q: Hannah, a registered adult nurse on a medical ward, cares for Peter, 70, an informal patient receiving treatment for a depressive illness who is trying to leave and talking about suicide. She asks whether she can use the nurse's holding power. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, because any registered nurse can use section 5(4) on a hospital ward
No, because section 5(4) cannot be used on a general medical ward
No, because she is not a nurse of the prescribed class
Yes, if the duty psychiatrist confirms the decision by telephone
Mental Health Law.w: The prescribed class for section 5(4) is nurses registered on sub-parts 1 or 2 of the NMC register whose field is mental health or learning disabilities (COP15 ch18 footnote, SI 2008/1207). An adult nurse is not in that class, so she should urgently contact the doctor in charge, who may use section 5(2).

n.0: Section 5(4) is restricted to the prescribed class of mental health and learning disabilities nurses.
n.1: Section 5(4) can be used on any hospital ward for an in-patient receiving treatment for mental disorder; the bar here is her field of registration.
n.3: Telephone confirmation from a psychiatrist cannot give the power to a nurse outside the prescribed class.

Mental Health Law.q: Zainab, a registered mental health nurse, is phoned by the consultant psychiatrist, who is off site. He tells her to 'put Mr Ali on a 5(4)' because Mr Ali is asking to go home. Zainab has just spoken to Mr Ali, who is calm and agrees to stay until the morning. What should she do?
o: Ask a second nurse to invoke section 5(4) on her behalf
Invoke section 5(4) and record that it was on the consultant's instruction
Invoke section 5(4) because the consultant has instructed it
Make her own assessment and not invoke the power on these facts
Mental Health Law.w: Using section 5(4) is the personal decision of the nurse, who cannot be instructed to use it by anyone else (COP15 18.27). The criteria require that the patient needs to be immediately prevented from leaving; Mr Ali has agreed to stay, so the criteria are not met.

n.0: The criteria are not met because Mr Ali agrees to stay; asking a colleague to use the power avoids the personal decision the Code requires.
n.1: Recording the instruction does not make it lawful; the nurse must personally judge that the criteria are met.
n.2: Nobody can instruct a nurse to use section 5(4); the decision is the nurse's own (COP15 18.27).

Mental Health Law.q: Nadia, 19, is waiting in the emergency department for a mental health liaison assessment and says she is leaving. The emergency medicine doctor says he will 'use a section 5(2)'. What is the nurse's best response?
o: Section 5(2) can be used for up to 6 hours in the department
Section 5(2) can be used once the liaison psychiatrist agrees
Section 5(2) cannot be used because she is not an in-patient
Section 5(2) can be used because she is on hospital premises
Mental Health Law.w: Section 5(2) applies to hospital in-patients. COP15 18.8 states that the power cannot be used for an out-patient attending an accident and emergency department. Other lawful options (for example the Mental Capacity Act if she lacks capacity) must be considered instead.

n.0: Six hours is the nurse's section 5(4) limit; section 5(2) lasts up to 72 hours and in any case does not apply in ED.
n.1: Agreement from a psychiatrist does not make an emergency department attender an in-patient.
n.3: Being on hospital premises is not enough; the person must be an in-patient (COP15 18.7-18.8).

Mental Health Law.q: At 14:00 on Monday a registered mental health nurse records section 5(4) for Callum, 28. The duty doctor arrives at 15:30, examines him and furnishes a section 5(2) report. When does the section 5(2) holding power expire at the latest?
o: 15:30 on Thursday
14:00 on Thursday
15:30 on Wednesday
20:00 on Monday
Mental Health Law.w: Where a doctor or approved clinician uses section 5(2) after a nurse's section 5(4), the 72 hours run from the time the nurse made the section 5(4) record (s5(5); COP15 18.35). 14:00 Monday plus 72 hours is 14:00 Thursday.

n.0: The 72 hours run from the nurse's 5(4) record at 14:00, not from the doctor's report at 15:30.
n.2: Fifteen-thirty on Wednesday is only 48 hours after the report; the limit is 72 hours from 14:00 Monday.
n.3: 20:00 on Monday is the end of the 6-hour section 5(4) period, which lapsed when the doctor arrived.

Mental Health Law.q: Oliver, 40, an informal patient on an acute ward with severe depression, says he wants to go home now. The ward doctor is on the next ward and can come within 5 minutes. Oliver is willing to talk with the nurse meanwhile. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Let Oliver leave and ask the police to carry out a welfare check
Call the doctor to attend now and talk with Oliver while waiting
Invoke section 5(4) at once and then call the ward doctor
Lock the ward door until the doctor has assessed Oliver
Mental Health Law.w: Section 5(4) is for when it is not practicable to secure the attendance of a doctor or approved clinician who can use section 5(2). COP15 18.29 asks the nurse to weigh the doctor's likely arrival time and to try to persuade the patient to wait. Here the doctor can attend in 5 minutes and Oliver is engaging.

n.0: Allowing a severely depressed patient who may be at risk to leave without assessment fails to manage the risk when a doctor is minutes away.
n.2: The power is not appropriate when a doctor with section 5(2) power can attend within minutes and the patient is willing to wait.
n.3: Locking an informal patient in without legal authority is an unlawful restriction of liberty.

Mental Health Law.q: A registered mental health nurse invoked section 5(4) for Leah, 33, at 01:00. By 07:00 no doctor or approved clinician has attended. Leah still wants to leave. What is the correct position?
o: She becomes held under section 5(2) for 72 hours from the nurse's record
She is no longer detained and the delay should be reported as a serious failing
The nurse may renew section 5(4) for a further 6 hours while chasing a doctor
The nurse in charge may now apply under section 4 until the doctor arrives
Mental Health Law.w: If no doctor or approved clinician able to make a section 5(2) report attends within 6 hours, the patient is no longer detained and may leave if not prepared to stay. This should be treated as a serious failing, reported and investigated locally (COP15 18.36).

n.0: Section 5(2) requires a report by the doctor or approved clinician; it does not follow automatically from 5(4).
n.2: Section 5(4) cannot be renewed (COP15 18.25, 18.38).
n.3: Section 4 is an emergency application by an AMHP or nearest relative with a medical recommendation; a nurse cannot impose it.

Mental Health Law.q: At 23:00 an approved mental health professional assesses Kofi, 31, at home. He is acutely psychotic and threatening to harm his neighbour. One doctor has examined him and recommends admission; a second doctor cannot attend until the next afternoon. Which section best fits?
o: Section 2, with the second medical recommendation added the next afternoon
Section 5(2), because he urgently needs to be held pending assessment
Section 136, because his behaviour poses an immediate risk to his neighbour
Section 4, because waiting for a second doctor would cause undesirable delay
Mental Health Law.w: Section 4 allows an emergency application with one medical recommendation where it is of urgent necessity and waiting for a second recommendation would cause undesirable delay. It lasts 72 hours from admission unless the second recommendation is received, converting it to section 2.

n.0: A section 2 application needs two medical recommendations before the application is made.
n.1: Section 5(2) applies to people who are already hospital in-patients, not people at home.
n.2: Section 136 is a police power that cannot be used in a person's home (s136(1)-(1A)).

Mental Health Law.q: Police find Marcus, 32, on a bridge parapet in the town centre, distressed and responding to voices. They use section 136 and bring him to the health-based place of safety, arriving at 18:00. Without any extension, when does the authority to detain him end?
o: 18:00 the next day
06:00 two days later
06:00 the next day
18:00 three days later
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 136(2A) the permitted period is 24 hours beginning with arrival at the place of safety: 18:00 the next day. An extension of up to 12 hours is possible under section 136B. The old 72-hour limit was replaced in December 2017.

n.1: Thirty-six hours would require a 12-hour extension authorised by the examining doctor; without it the limit is 24 hours.
n.2: Twelve hours is the maximum extension under s136B, not the basic period.
n.3: Seventy-two hours was the pre-December 2017 limit and still appears in the 2015 Code, but the Act now allows 24 hours.

Mental Health Law.q: Officers are called to a house where Jess, 26, is in her own back garden, shouting that her family are poisoning her. Neighbours are alarmed. An officer asks the street triage nurse whether section 136 can be used. What is the correct answer?
o: No, because section 136 needs a warrant from a magistrate
Yes, because the garden is outdoors and visible from the street
Yes, because her family are at risk inside the house
No, because a garden used with her home is excluded from section 136
Mental Health Law.w: Section 136(1A) allows the power anywhere except a house, flat or room where a person is living, or a yard, garden, garage or outhouse used with it. Jess's private garden is excluded. If a warrant is needed to remove her, an AMHP can apply for one under section 135(1).

n.0: Section 136 needs no warrant; section 135 is the warrant-based power.
n.1: Being outdoors or visible from the street does not matter; a garden used with a dwelling is expressly excluded (s136(1A)(b)).
n.2: Risk to family does not bring a dwelling within section 136; other powers (for example s135 or police common-law powers to prevent harm) must be considered.

Mental Health Law.q: Ellis, 15, is detained under section 136 late at night and the health-based place of safety is full. The custody sergeant offers a cell at the police station. What should the mental health nurse advise?
o: A police station may be used if an inspector authorises it
A police station may be used for up to 12 hours with a parent present
A police station cannot be used as a place of safety for a child
A police station may be used if a nurse checks her every 30 minutes
Mental Health Law.w: Section 136A(1) prohibits removing a person under 18 to, or keeping them at, a police station as a place of safety. An alternative place of safety, such as an emergency department or a children's ward, must be found.

n.0: Inspector authorisation is part of the adult test under the 2017 regulations; it cannot be applied to under-18s.
n.1: There is no time-limited exception for children with a parent present; the bar in s136A is absolute for under-18s.
n.3: Thirty-minute welfare checks are a condition for adults in police stations, not a route to use one for a child.

Mental Health Law.q: Victor, 44, is detained under section 136. He is violently assaulting staff and officers. No health-based place of safety in the area can safely manage him. Which set of conditions allows a police station to be used for an adult?
o: He is intoxicated, a superintendent approves, and custody staff check on him at least once an hour
A high risk of absconding, the AMHP agrees, and detention is extended to 36 hours from the outset
Any assault on staff, the custody sergeant agrees, and a doctor reviews him within 4 hours of arrival
Imminent risk of serious injury or death, no safe alternative, clinician available, inspector authorises
Mental Health Law.w: The Mental Health Act 1983 (Places of Safety) Regulations 2017 allow a police station for an adult only where behaviour poses an imminent risk of serious injury or death, no other place of safety can reasonably be expected to detain the person because of that risk, a healthcare professional will be present or available, and an officer of at least inspector rank authorises it.

n.0: Intoxication is not a ground; superintendent approval relates to a s136B extension at a police station, and welfare checks are by a healthcare professional every 30 minutes.
n.1: Absconding risk is not a ground, and an AMHP does not authorise use of a police station.
n.2: An assault alone is not enough; the test is imminent risk of serious injury or death, and authorisation is by an inspector, not the custody sergeant.

Mental Health Law.q: Before deciding to use section 136, an officer telephones the mental health crisis line and speaks to a registered nurse about Ayo, 37, who is sitting on a railway platform edge. Why does the Act require this contact?
o: The officer must consult a health professional first if practicable
The nurse then becomes responsible for arranging Ayo's transport
The nurse must authorise the detention before it becomes lawful
The call to the nurse starts the 24-hour permitted detention period
Mental Health Law.w: Section 136(1C) requires the constable, if practicable, to consult a registered medical practitioner, registered nurse, approved mental health professional or other prescribed person before removing or keeping someone at a place of safety. The decision remains the officer's.

n.1: Consultation does not transfer conveyance responsibility to the nurse.
n.2: The nurse advises; the decision to use section 136 remains with the constable.
n.3: The 24 hours begin on arrival at the place of safety (or the decision to keep the person there), not with the phone call.

Mental Health Law.q: An approved mental health professional has serious concerns that Doreen, 79, who lives alone with severe self-neglect and possible psychosis, will not allow anyone into her flat. What is the lawful route to gain entry and, if necessary, remove her for assessment?
o: Ask her GP to complete a section 5(2) report
Ask a magistrate for a section 135(2) warrant to retake her
Apply to a magistrate for a section 135(1) warrant
Ask the police to use section 136 at her front door
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 135(1) a justice of the peace may, on information on oath from an AMHP, issue a warrant for a constable to enter premises, by force if needed, and remove the person to a place of safety. The constable must be accompanied by an AMHP and a registered medical practitioner (s135(4)).

n.0: Section 5(2) applies to hospital in-patients and is used by the doctor or approved clinician in charge of their treatment, not a GP at home.
n.1: Section 135(2) is for retaking a patient already liable to be detained; Doreen is not.
n.3: Section 136 cannot be used in a dwelling, including at the door of the person's own flat (s136(1A)).

Mental Health Law.q: Noor, 30, is brought under section 136 to an emergency department at 10:00 for urgent treatment of an overdose and is transferred to the health-based place of safety at 16:00. Assuming no extension, until when can she be detained?
o: 16:00 the next day
04:00 the next day
10:00 the next day
22:00 the next day
Mental Health Law.w: Section 136(3)-(4) allows transfer between places of safety, but detention at the later place ends no later than the end of the permitted period, which is 24 hours from arrival at the first place of safety (s136(2A)). 10:00 plus 24 hours is 10:00 the next day.

n.0: The clock does not restart on transfer; it runs from arrival at the first place of safety.
n.1: Four o'clock is 12 hours after the transfer; there is no 12-hour basic period.
n.3: Twenty-two hundred would be 36 hours from arrival, which needs a 12-hour s136B extension.

Mental Health Law.q: At 02:00 Ryan, 22, arrives at a health-based place of safety under section 136. He is so heavily intoxicated that the doctor cannot assess him. Who can extend his detention and what is the latest time it could then end?
o: The doctor responsible for his examination, to 02:00 the day after next
The doctor responsible for his examination, to 14:00 the next day
The duty inspector, to 14:00 the next day
The AMHP, to 14:00 the next day
Mental Health Law.w: Section 136B allows the registered medical practitioner responsible for the examination to authorise up to 12 further hours if the person's condition makes assessment within 24 hours impracticable. 02:00 plus 24 hours plus 12 hours is 14:00 the next day.

n.0: A further 24 hours is not available; the maximum extension is 12 hours.
n.2: Police officers do not extend health-based place of safety detention; a superintendent's approval is needed only when assessment is at a police station.
n.3: The AMHP cannot authorise an extension; s136B gives the power to the examining doctor.

Mental Health Law.q: Femi, 29, detained under section 3, asks the nurse in charge on a Saturday for two hours' unescorted leave to visit his sister. Nothing about leave is recorded in his notes. The responsible clinician is off duty. What should the nurse do?
o: Grant the leave, as the nurse in charge can authorise short leave
Grant escorted leave, because escorted leave needs no authorisation
Explain that leave must be granted by the responsible clinician
Ask the hospital managers to authorise the leave by phone
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 17(1) leave of absence for a detained patient is granted by the responsible clinician, who sets any conditions. Nurses cannot grant section 17 leave; the nurse should explain this and contact the RC or the covering approved clinician if appropriate.

n.0: The nurse in charge has no power to grant section 17 leave, however short.
n.1: Escorted leave is still section 17 leave and needs the RC's authority (s17(3)).
n.3: Hospital managers do not grant leave; the power belongs to the RC.

Mental Health Law.q: Lena, 41, detained under section 3, is on 5 days' overnight section 17 leave at home. Her husband rings the ward: she has stopped eating and is hearing voices telling her to harm herself. The responsible clinician decides she must return. How is the leave revoked?
o: By a magistrate's warrant under section 135(1)
By notice in writing to Lena or the person in charge of her
By an AMHP application under section 2
By a verbal instruction to her husband from the ward nurse
Mental Health Law.w: Section 17(4) allows the RC, where necessary for the patient's health or safety or the protection of others, to revoke leave and recall the patient by notice in writing given to the patient or the person in charge of them.

n.0: A section 135(1) warrant is for people not already liable to be detained; s135(2) may be needed only if entry to retake her is refused.
n.2: Lena is already liable to be detained under section 3, so a new section 2 application is not needed.
n.3: Revocation is the RC's power and must be in writing; a nurse's verbal instruction does not revoke leave.

Mental Health Law.q: Malik, 35, has been detained under section 3 for 4 months and is ready to spend 3 weeks at home on section 17 leave before possible discharge. What must the responsible clinician do before granting this leave?
o: Obtain written consent to the leave from his nearest relative
Refer his case to the tribunal before the leave begins
Arrange a SOAD certificate to cover his medication on leave
Consider whether a community treatment order would suit him better
Mental Health Law.w: Section 17(2A)-(2B): longer-term leave (more than 7 consecutive days) may not be granted unless the RC first considers whether the patient should be placed on a community treatment order under section 17A instead.

n.0: The nearest relative's consent is not a legal requirement for section 17 leave.
n.1: There is no requirement to refer to a tribunal before granting leave.
n.2: A SOAD certificate depends on the 3-month rule for medication, not on granting leave; the leave rule is to consider a CTO.

Mental Health Law.q: Stephen, 24, is detained under section 2 and is being discharged home next week. His mother asks if he can be put on a community treatment order 'to make sure he takes his tablets'. What is the nurse's correct response?
o: No, a CTO needs section 3 or an unrestricted hospital order
Yes, a CTO can be made for 28 days to match his section
Yes, a CTO can be made if an AMHP agrees in writing
Yes, a CTO can be made if his nearest relative applies
Mental Health Law.w: Section 17A allows a CTO for a patient liable to be detained under section 3 or an unrestricted Part 3 hospital order. A patient on section 2 is not eligible.

n.1: A CTO lasts 6 months initially; there is no 28-day CTO.
n.2: AMHP agreement is required for a CTO, but it cannot make a section 2 patient eligible.
n.3: Nearest relatives cannot apply for a CTO; it is made by the RC.

Mental Health Law.q: Dr Shah, the responsible clinician, wants to place Abi, 38, on a community treatment order on leaving hospital from section 3. Which agreement is legally required before the order can be made?
o: Approval of the proposed order by the First-tier Tribunal
The written agreement of an approved mental health professional
The written consent of Abi's nearest relative to the order
The agreement of Abi's named community mental health nurse
Mental Health Law.w: Section 17A(4) requires the RC's opinion that the criteria are met and an AMHP's written statement agreeing with that opinion and that it is appropriate to make the order.

n.0: Tribunals review CTOs after they are made; they do not approve them in advance.
n.2: The nearest relative's consent is not required for a CTO.
n.3: Care coordinators are consulted, but the statutory agreement is the AMHP's.

Mental Health Law.q: Jamal, 31, is on a community treatment order with a discretionary condition to avoid cannabis. A urine test shows cannabis, but his mental state is stable, he attends appointments and accepts his depot. Can the responsible clinician recall him on this basis?
o: No, because conditions about drug use cannot lawfully be set
Yes, because breaching any CTO condition is a ground for recall
Not for this breach; recall needs hospital treatment need and risk
Yes, because a positive drug test shows a need for hospital care
Mental Health Law.w: Section 17E(1) allows recall if the patient requires medical treatment in hospital and there would be a risk of harm without recall; section 17E(2) allows recall for breach of the mandatory section 17B(3) conditions (making himself available for examination). Breach of a discretionary condition may be taken into account (s17B(6)) but does not by itself justify recall.

n.0: Conditions may be set to prevent risk of harm to the patient's health (s17B(2)); a cannabis condition can be lawful.
n.1: Only breach of the mandatory examination conditions in s17B(3) is a stand-alone ground for recall.
n.3: A positive test is not the statutory test; s17E(1) needs a need for medical treatment in hospital and a risk of harm, and Jamal is stable.

Mental Health Law.q: Ruth, 46, on a community treatment order, is recalled to hospital and arrives at 09:00 on Monday. By when must the responsible clinician either release her or revoke the CTO?
o: 09:00 on Tuesday
09:00 on Thursday
09:00 on Wednesday
09:00 the following Monday
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 17F a recalled community patient may be detained for up to 72 hours. Within that time the RC must release her (she remains on the CTO) or revoke the CTO with AMHP agreement. 09:00 Monday plus 72 hours is 09:00 Thursday.

n.0: Twenty-four hours is the place of safety period, not the recall period.
n.2: Forty-eight hours is short of the 72-hour maximum in section 17F.
n.3: Seven days is not a recall limit under the Act.

Mental Health Law.q: After 48 hours' assessment following recall, Ruth's responsible clinician decides she needs a longer in-patient admission. An AMHP agrees that the CTO should be revoked. What is the legal effect?
o: Her section 3 revives, with a new 6-month period
The CTO is suspended and she remains informally
A fresh section 3 application must now be made
A new section 2 begins, lasting up to 28 days
Mental Health Law.w: When a CTO is revoked (RC order with AMHP agreement, s17F(4)), the detention provisions that applied before the CTO reapply (s17G(3)), usually section 3. Section 17G(5) treats the patient as admitted under the treatment application on the day of revocation, so a new 6-month period under section 20 starts.

n.1: Revocation means detention in hospital, not informal status.
n.2: No fresh application is needed; the original section 3 revives on revocation.
n.3: Revocation revives the previous detention; it does not create a section 2.

Mental Health Law.q: Kayleigh, 27, detained under section 2, refuses her prescribed oral antipsychotic on day 5 of admission. She is distressed and responding to voices. Under which provision can the medication be given without her consent?
o: Section 57, with her nearest relative's agreement
Section 63, by or under the direction of the approved clinician
Section 5 of the Mental Capacity Act, in her best interests
Section 58, after a SOAD has certified it
Mental Health Law.w: Section 63 allows medical treatment for mental disorder (other than treatments under s57, s58 and s58A) to be given to a detained patient without consent by or under the direction of the approved clinician in charge. In the first 3 months of medication, the s58 safeguard does not yet apply.

n.0: Section 57 covers psychosurgery and surgical hormone implants, and the nearest relative has no consent role.
n.2: MCA s28 prevents the MCA from authorising treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA.
n.3: The section 58 SOAD safeguard applies only once 3 months have passed since medication was first given in the current period of detention.

Mental Health Law.q: Aaron, 33, has been detained under section 3 since 2 January and first received antipsychotic medication on 4 January. On 10 April he refuses it, and the approved clinician believes it is still needed. What is required to continue the medication lawfully?
o: The written consent of his nearest relative
Continue under section 63, which covers medication throughout detention
A best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act
A certificate from a second opinion appointed doctor
Mental Health Law.w: Section 58 applies once 3 months have passed since medication for mental disorder was first given in the current detention (4 January to 4 April). After that, a patient who refuses or lacks capacity can be given medication only if a SOAD certifies it is appropriate. Aaron refuses on 10 April, beyond 3 months.

n.0: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment under Part 4.
n.1: Section 63 is limited by section 58 after the 3-month period; a SOAD certificate is now required.
n.2: MCA s28 excludes Part 4 treatment for mental disorder from MCA authority.

Mental Health Law.q: Bernadette, 68, detained under section 3, has severe depression. She has capacity and clearly refuses electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). She is eating and drinking and is not in danger. The team believe ECT would help. What is the legal position?
o: ECT cannot be given while she has capacity and refuses
ECT can be given if her nearest relative agrees
ECT can be given under section 63 because she is detained
ECT can be given if a SOAD certifies it as appropriate
Mental Health Law.w: Section 58A provides that ECT cannot be given to a capable adult who refuses. The only exception is urgent treatment under section 62 to save life or prevent serious deterioration, which does not apply on these facts.

n.1: The nearest relative has no power to consent to ECT on her behalf.
n.2: ECT is governed by section 58A, so section 63 cannot authorise it.
n.3: A SOAD can certify ECT for a patient who lacks capacity, not override a capable adult's refusal.

Mental Health Law.q: A trainee nurse asks which of the following grounds under section 62 (urgent treatment) can justify giving ECT without the usual section 58A safeguards. Which answer is correct?
o: To reduce a high risk of the patient absconding
To alleviate serious suffering by the patient
To prevent a serious deterioration in his condition
To prevent the patient behaving violently to others
Mental Health Law.w: Section 62(1A) restricts urgent ECT to the first two section 62 grounds: immediately necessary to save life, or (if not irreversible) to prevent a serious deterioration. Alleviating serious suffering and preventing violence or danger apply to medication under s58, not ECT.

n.0: Absconding risk is not a ground under section 62.
n.1: Alleviating serious suffering is a section 62 ground for medication, but s62(1A) excludes it for ECT.
n.3: Preventing violence or danger is a section 62 ground for medication, but not for ECT.

Mental Health Law.q: Raj, 52, detained under section 3, has schizophrenia and has developed cellulitis in his leg. He has capacity to decide about antibiotics, understands the risks and refuses them. A colleague says, 'He's sectioned, so we can treat him anyway.' What is the nurse's best response?
o: The Act authorises treatment of any condition while he is detained
His nearest relative can consent to the antibiotics for him
The Act does not cover unrelated physical illness, so his refusal stands
A SOAD can authorise the antibiotics because he is detained
Mental Health Law.w: Treatment under section 63 must be medical treatment for mental disorder (including its symptoms or manifestations). Cellulitis is unrelated to his mental disorder, so the ordinary law applies: a capable adult can refuse. The team should keep offering treatment, explain risks and record the discussion.

n.0: The Mental Health Act authorises treatment for mental disorder, not unrelated physical illness.
n.1: The nearest relative has no power to consent to treatment for an adult.
n.3: SOAD certificates relate to Part 4 treatment for mental disorder, not physical treatment.

Mental Health Law.q: Nikita, 40, has been detained under section 3 for 5 months. She lacks capacity to consent to her antipsychotic. A staff nurse suggests documenting a Mental Capacity Act best interests decision instead of waiting for a SOAD visit. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: The MCA can be used as an interim until the SOAD visits
Part 4 treatment is outside the MCA, so a SOAD is needed
The MCA can be used because she lacks capacity to consent
The MCA can be used if an IMCA has first been consulted
Mental Health Law.w: Section 28 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 states that the MCA does not authorise treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA. After 3 months, a detained patient who lacks capacity needs a SOAD certificate under section 58 (or s62 if urgent).

n.0: There is no interim MCA route pending a SOAD; urgent treatment uses section 62.
n.2: Lack of capacity does not bring Part 4 treatment within the MCA; s28 excludes it.
n.3: Consulting an IMCA does not overcome the s28 exclusion.

Mental Health Law.q: A second opinion appointed doctor (SOAD) visits Jordan, 45, detained under section 3, to consider certifying his medication. Under section 58, whom must the SOAD consult before certifying?
o: The hospital managers and his responsible clinician
His nearest relative and his independent mental health advocate
Two other doctors who are not involved in his care
A nurse and another professional who is neither a nurse nor a doctor
Mental Health Law.w: Section 58(4) requires the SOAD, before certifying, to consult two other persons professionally concerned with the patient's medical treatment: one a nurse and the other neither a nurse nor a registered medical practitioner. Neither may be the RC or the approved clinician in charge.

n.0: Hospital managers are not consultees, and the RC cannot be one of the two statutory consultees.
n.1: The SOAD may speak to family and advocates, but the statutory consultees are two professionals.
n.2: Neither consultee may be a doctor besides the SOAD; one must be a nurse.

Mental Health Law.q: Toby, 17, is detained under section 3 with severe depression. He has capacity and consents to electroconvulsive therapy recommended by his team. His parents also agree. What else is legally required before ECT can be given (outside an emergency)?
o: The written consent of both of his parents
A Court of Protection order
A SOAD certificate that the treatment is appropriate
The approved clinician's certificate of his consent
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 58A, ECT for a patient under 18 who consents still needs a SOAD certificate confirming that he is capable of consenting and that the treatment is appropriate. For capable adults the approved clinician can certify consent instead.

n.0: Parental consent is not the s58A safeguard; for a consenting under-18 a SOAD must certify capacity and appropriateness.
n.1: The Court of Protection is not involved in Part 4 ECT for a detained patient.
n.3: Approved clinician certification is available for capable consenting adults, not under-18s.

Mental Health Law.q: Patrick, 49, has just been detained under section 2. He is very thought-disordered and cannot follow the nurse's explanation of his rights. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Give the leaflet to his nearest relative instead, as he lacks capacity
Explain orally and in writing now, record it and repeat it later
Ask the IMHA to give his rights on the nurse's behalf the next day
Wait until he is well enough before giving him any information about his rights
Mental Health Law.w: Section 132 requires the hospital managers to take practicable steps, as soon as practicable after detention starts, to make sure the patient understands the section, its effects and the right to apply to a tribunal, orally and in writing. If he cannot understand, the attempt is recorded and repeated at intervals until he does.

n.0: The nearest relative is sent a copy unless the patient objects, but this does not replace telling the patient.
n.2: The IMHA supports the patient but does not take over the hospital managers' s132 duty, usually discharged by nurses.
n.3: The duty arises as soon as practicable after detention starts; delaying any attempt fails the s132 duty.

Mental Health Law.q: Siobhan, 36, is detained under section 3. She is unmarried and has lived with her younger brother, who cares for her, for 10 years. Her mother lives in Spain and her father lives nearby. Who is her nearest relative under section 26?
o: Her mother, because she is the elder of the two parents
Her younger brother, as he lives with and cares for her
Her father, because parents rank above brothers and sisters
Whichever of her parents Siobhan chooses to nominate
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 26(4), a relative with whom the patient ordinarily resides or who cares for her is preferred over others. Her brother lives with and cares for her, so he is her nearest relative. Her mother is also excluded because she is not resident in the UK (s26(5)(a)).

n.0: Her mother lives abroad and is treated as dead for this purpose (s26(5)(a)); she is also displaced by the carer rule.
n.2: The list order (parents before siblings) is overridden where a relative lives with or cares for the patient (s26(4)).
n.3: Patients cannot choose their nearest relative under the 1983 Act; nomination is a 2025 Act change not in force.

Mental Health Law.q: Marek, 55, detained under section 3, has lived with his partner Anna for 2 years; they are not married. His adult son lives across town. Marek is not married to anyone else. Who is his nearest relative?
o: His son, because Anna has not lived with him for 5 years
His son, because a child comes above a partner who is not a spouse
His son, because he is the eldest blood relative
Anna, because she has lived with him as if married for over 6 months
Mental Health Law.w: Section 26(6) treats a person living with the patient as husband, wife or civil partner for at least 6 months as a spouse. Anna therefore ranks first in the list, above his son.

n.0: The 5-year rule applies to a non-relative who lives with the patient (s26(7)), not a partner living as a spouse.
n.1: A cohabitee of 6 months or more counts as a spouse and ranks above a son (s26(6)).
n.2: Age only breaks ties within the same category; a spouse equivalent ranks first.

Mental Health Law.q: Ade, 42, is detained under section 3. On Monday at 10:00 his nearest relative gives the hospital managers written notice that she will discharge him. The responsible clinician believes Ade would be likely to act dangerously to himself if discharged. What should happen?
o: The AMHP can veto the discharge by applying for section 2
The RC must apply to the county court within 7 days to stop the discharge
Ade must be discharged at 10:00 on Monday
The RC can make a barring report within 72 hours, stopping the discharge
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 25 the nearest relative must give at least 72 hours' written notice. Within that period the RC can bar the discharge by reporting that the patient would be likely to act in a manner dangerous to himself or others. The NR then cannot order discharge again for 6 months but can apply to a tribunal.

n.0: A new section 2 would not be a lawful way to defeat an NR order; the statutory route is the RC's barring report.
n.1: No county court application is needed to bar discharge; the RC uses a barring report under s25.
n.2: The NR's order takes effect after 72 hours' notice, and can be barred by the RC within that time.

Mental Health Law.q: A ward nurse is checking which patients qualify for an independent mental health advocate (IMHA). Which patient is a qualifying patient?
o: Sam, held under section 136 at a place of safety
Ash, held under section 4 before a second recommendation
Bo, held by a nurse under section 5(4)
Lee, detained under section 2 on an acute ward
Mental Health Law.w: Under sections 130A-130C qualifying patients include those liable to be detained under the Act (including section 2 and section 3), CTO and guardianship patients. Short-term powers (s4 before conversion, s5(2), s5(4), s135, s136) are excluded.

n.0: People held under section 136 are excluded from IMHA eligibility.
n.1: Section 4 patients qualify once the second recommendation converts the section; before that they are excluded.
n.2: Patients held under the section 5 holding powers are excluded.

Mental Health Law.q: Daisy, 21, was admitted under section 2 on 1 March. On 17 March she asks the nurse how to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal. What is the most accurate advice?
o: Apply now, as section 2 patients may apply at any time
The window has closed; seek a managers' hearing or NR discharge
Wait until the section 2 is converted into a section 3
Apply now, because her responsible clinician supports an appeal
Mental Health Law.w: Under section 66(2) a section 2 patient may apply to the tribunal within the first 14 days of detention (1-14 March). On 17 March that window has passed, but she can ask for a hospital managers' hearing (s23) and her nearest relative can order discharge (s23, s25).

n.0: The section 2 application must be made within 14 days of admission.
n.2: She has no need to wait for a section 3, which would give a fresh right to apply but may never happen.
n.3: The RC's support does not reopen the 14-day statutory window.

Mental Health Law.q: Callum, 30, has been detained under section 3 for 6 months and has not applied to the tribunal. The section has just been renewed. What must the hospital managers do?
o: Ask the nearest relative whether to apply
Wait for Callum to apply at his next opportunity
Arrange a hospital managers' hearing in place of a tribunal
Refer his case to the tribunal
Mental Health Law.w: Section 68(1)-(2) requires the hospital managers to refer a patient to the tribunal if no application or reference has been made to the tribunal in the first 6 months of detention (s68(1)-(3)). Thereafter, a referral is required if there has been no tribunal for 3 years (1 year if under 18).

n.0: The duty to refer is the managers', not dependent on the nearest relative.
n.1: Section 68 requires the managers to refer him; waiting for him to apply would breach that duty.
n.2: A managers' hearing is a separate review and does not replace the s68 duty.

Mental Health Law.q: Mia, 16, has been detained under section 3 for 18 months. Her last tribunal hearing was 13 months ago and she has not applied since. What must the hospital managers do?
o: Wait until 3 years have passed since her last tribunal hearing
Refer her now, as over a year has passed since the last hearing
Refer her when her section 3 is next due for renewal
Refer her case to the tribunal when she reaches age 18
Mental Health Law.w: Section 68(6) requires the managers to refer a patient whose case has not been considered by a tribunal for 3 years, or 1 year if the patient is under 18. Mia is 16 and her last hearing was 13 months ago.

n.0: Three years is the adult referral interval; the interval for under-18s is 1 year.
n.2: The referral duty is not tied to renewal dates.
n.3: Her age now triggers the shorter interval; waiting until she is 18 would breach s68(6).

Mental Health Law.q: A discharge coordinator is reviewing four patients leaving an acute ward this week. Which patient is entitled to after-care under section 117 of the Mental Health Act 1983?
o: Dev, discharged after a section 4 that was not converted
Cara, an informal patient admitted after a section 136
Ava, discharged from section 2 after 20 days
Ben, detained under section 3 for 4 months
Mental Health Law.w: Section 117(1) applies to people detained under section 3, 37, 45A, 47 or 48 who then cease to be detained and leave hospital. Sections 2, 4, 5, 135 and 136 do not give an entitlement.

n.0: Section 4 is not a qualifying section.
n.1: Section 136 is a police power and does not give entitlement, and informal admission does not qualify.
n.2: Section 2 is not one of the qualifying sections in s117(1).

Mental Health Law.q: Grace, 48, is leaving hospital after detention under section 3. Her daughter asks who is legally responsible for providing her section 117 after-care. What is the correct answer?
o: The integrated care board and local social services authority
The local authority housing department for her home area
Her GP practice, as the lead for her ongoing community care
The NHS trust whose hospital detained her under section 3
Mental Health Law.w: Section 117(2) places a joint duty on the integrated care board and the local social services authority to provide or arrange after-care, in co-operation with voluntary agencies, until both are satisfied it is no longer needed.

n.1: Housing may be part of after-care, but the duty belongs to the ICB and the social services authority jointly.
n.2: Primary care is part of her care, but the GP practice does not hold the s117 duty.
n.3: The detaining trust may deliver services but the statutory duty sits with the ICB and the local social services authority.

Mental Health Law.q: Liam, 33, is on a community treatment order and has been well for a year. The local authority proposes to end his section 117 after-care because he is 'stable'. What is the correct legal position?
o: After-care can end if the local authority decides he no longer needs it
After-care ends once he has had 12 months of stability
After-care can end once his CMHT care coordinator agrees
After-care cannot be ended while he remains on the CTO
Mental Health Law.w: Section 117(2) provides that the ICB and local authority cannot be satisfied that a community patient no longer needs after-care while he remains on a CTO (COP15 33.6). Even afterwards, both bodies must agree.

n.0: Both the ICB and the local authority must be satisfied, and neither can be while he remains on a CTO (s117(2)).
n.1: There is no automatic end after an arbitrary period (COP15 33.21).
n.2: The care coordinator's view informs the decision but cannot end after-care during a CTO.

Mental Health Law.q: Mo, 45, previously detained under section 3, has been well for 2 years and is discharged from the community mental health team to his GP. He still lives in supported accommodation arranged under section 117. What should happen to his after-care?
o: It transfers to his GP, who decides whether it should continue
It continues while he needs services related to his disorder
It ends on his discharge from the community mental health team
It ends now that 2 years have passed without any readmission
Mental Health Law.w: COP15 33.20-33.21: after-care continues until both the ICB and local authority are satisfied it is no longer needed. It should not be withdrawn solely because the person is discharged from specialist services or an arbitrary period has passed. Suitable alternative accommodation must be in place before withdrawal.

n.0: The GP does not hold the s117 duty; it remains with the ICB and local authority.
n.2: Discharge from specialist services is listed in COP15 33.21 as an improper sole reason to end after-care.
n.3: An arbitrary period passing is also not a valid sole reason (COP15 33.21).

Mental Health Law.q: Ruby, 39, was detained under section 3. Her section was discharged by the tribunal, but she chose to stay on the ward informally for 3 more weeks before going home. Is she entitled to section 117 after-care?
o: No, because her section was discharged by the tribunal
Yes, because she ceased to be detained and then left hospital
Yes, for a fixed period of 6 weeks after she leaves hospital
No, because she left the hospital as an informal patient
Mental Health Law.w: Section 117(1) applies to qualifying patients who cease to be detained and, whether or not immediately after so ceasing, leave hospital. COP15 33.9 confirms patients who remain informally after detention ends are still entitled once they leave.

n.0: The way detention ended, including tribunal discharge, does not affect entitlement.
n.2: There is no 6-week limit; after-care lasts until both bodies agree it is no longer needed.
n.3: Leaving as an informal patient does not remove entitlement; the Act covers leaving 'whether or not immediately'.

Mental Health Law.q: Kwesi, 28, has just been admitted under section 3. A student asks when section 117 after-care planning should begin. What is the most accurate answer?
o: As soon as he is admitted to hospital
On the day he is discharged from hospital
When the responsible clinician first grants section 17 leave
At his first tribunal hearing
Mental Health Law.w: COP15 33.10: although the duty to provide after-care begins when the patient leaves hospital, planning should start as soon as the patient is admitted, so services are identified in good time for discharge.

n.1: Planning on the day of discharge is too late; the Code says it should start on admission.
n.2: Leave is a later step; planning should already be under way from admission.
n.3: Tribunals expect after-care information, but planning should not wait for a hearing.

Mental Health Law.q: Ella, 50, entitled to section 117 after-care, declines the support worker visits offered on discharge. Three months later she asks for help again. What is the correct position?
o: She must now pay for the services because she first declined them
She must be readmitted under section 3 to regain her entitlement
She lost her entitlement when she declined services at discharge
She can receive services, as declining did not end entitlement
Mental Health Law.w: COP15 33.24: patients are under no obligation to accept after-care, but unwillingness to accept services does not mean they have no need, and should not preclude them from receiving services under section 117 if they change their minds.

n.0: Declining services first does not convert entitlement into a chargeable service.
n.1: Entitlement continues without a new detention.
n.2: Declining services does not end the s117 duty; both bodies must be satisfied that she no longer needs after-care.

Mental Health Law.q: Tariq, 41, is leaving hospital after section 3. His team proposes a place in supported accommodation because his psychosis affects his ability to manage a tenancy. Can this be provided as section 117 after-care?
o: No, because section 117 after-care covers health services
No, because housing is a duty of the local housing department
Yes, because anyone leaving section 3 is entitled to housing
Yes, if it meets a need arising from his disorder and reduces risk
Mental Health Law.w: Section 117(6) defines after-care as services meeting a need arising from or related to the mental disorder and reducing the risk of deterioration (and readmission). COP15 33.4 says this should be read broadly and can include supported accommodation.

n.0: After-care includes social care, employment support and accommodation where they meet the statutory purpose (COP15 33.4).
n.1: Housing generally is a housing authority matter, but supported accommodation meeting a need related to his mental disorder can be s117 after-care.
n.2: There is no general entitlement to housing; accommodation is after-care when it meets a need arising from the disorder and reduces risk of deterioration.
