Mental Health Law.q: In October 2026, a preceptee nurse reads that the Mental Health Act 2025 received Royal Assent in December 2025. She asks how it relates to the 1983 Act she uses on her ward. Which statement is accurate?
o: It replaced the 1983 Act on 6 April 2026 under the first commencement regulations
It applies to new admissions, while the 1983 Act covers existing patients
It amends the 1983 Act, and most of its changes await commencement regulations
It repealed the 1983 Act in full on Royal Assent
Mental Health Law.w: The Mental Health Act 2025 (c. 33) amends the Mental Health Act 1983. Royal Assent was 18 December 2025. Only a few provisions are in force (technical provisions; some restricted-patient and tribunal provisions from 18 February 2026; ss51-52 from 6 April 2026 under SI 2026/385). The 1983 Act as amended remains the working law.

n.0: SI 2026/385 commenced only sections 51 and 52 on 6 April 2026, not a wholesale replacement.
n.1: There is no split by admission date; the 1983 Act as amended applies to all patients.
n.3: The 2025 Act amends the 1983 Act; it did not repeal it on Royal Assent.

Mental Health Law.q: Lucy, 31, detained under section 3, has read that patients can now choose a 'nominated person' instead of a nearest relative. She wants her best friend to take that role today. What should the nurse explain?
o: She can nominate her friend, but the AMHP must approve the choice
Nominated persons are not yet in force; section 26 decides her nearest relative
She can nominate her friend in writing to the hospital managers now
The nominated person scheme applies to informal patients but not to detained patients
Mental Health Law.w: Sections 24-28 and Schedule 2 of the Mental Health Act 2025 will replace the nearest relative with a nominated person chosen by the patient, but they are not in force in October 2026. The nearest relative is still identified under section 26 of the 1983 Act.

n.0: No AMHP approval process exists because the scheme is not in force.
n.2: The nomination scheme has not been commenced, so a written nomination has no legal effect yet.
n.3: The scheme is not in force for any patient, informal or detained.

Mental Health Law.q: Ellis, 24, is autistic with no other mental disorder. He is showing seriously irresponsible conduct linked to his autism, and his team are considering section 3. A colleague says the 2025 Act has removed autism from section 3. What is the position in October 2026?
o: Section 3 can be used for autism if he is under 18
Section 3 is barred for autistic people under the 2025 Act
Section 3 remains legally available if all the 1983 Act criteria are met
Section 3 can be used for autism if a care, education and treatment review agrees
Mental Health Law.w: Sections 3-4 and Schedule 1 of the 2025 Act, which will stop autism and learning disability alone being grounds for section 3, are not in force. Autism is a mental disorder under s1(2) of the 1983 Act and is not subject to the learning disability conduct qualification, so section 3 remains legally available if all its criteria are met.

n.0: Age makes no difference to the current section 3 criteria.
n.1: The removal of autism from section 3 has not been commenced.
n.3: CETR duties are part of the uncommenced 2025 reforms; current section 3 rests on the 1983 Act criteria.

Mental Health Law.q: A police officer tells a street triage nurse that police stations 'can no longer be used as places of safety' since the 2025 Act. Kenny, 40, is detained under section 136 and is extremely violent. What is the accurate position in October 2026?
o: Police stations may be used for up to 72 hours in exceptional cases
Police stations are banned for everyone under section 48 of the 2025 Act
Police stations are available for adults and children if an inspector authorises
Police stations remain available for adults under the strict 2017 conditions
Mental Health Law.w: Section 48 of the 2025 Act, which will remove police stations as places of safety, is not in force. For adults, the Places of Safety Regulations 2017 still permit a police station in exceptional circumstances (imminent risk of serious injury or death, inspector authorisation, healthcare professional available). Under-18s cannot be taken to a police station (s136A).

n.0: The limit is 24 hours plus up to 12 hours, not 72 hours.
n.1: Section 48 of the 2025 Act has not been commenced.
n.2: Under-18s are barred from police stations as places of safety by s136A, whatever the authorisation.

Mental Health Law.q: Which provision of the Mental Health Act 2025 was in force by 6 April 2026 under the first commencement regulations (SI 2026/385)?
o: The four statutory principles in the Code of Practice
HRA duties for private providers of care arranged under the Act
The nominated person replacing the nearest relative in law
The shorter 3-month initial detention period for section 3
Mental Health Law.w: SI 2026/385 brought section 51 (Human Rights Act 1998 extended to private providers of care arranged under the MHA, new s142C) and section 52 (review of CQC notification for under-18 in-patients) into force on 6 April 2026.

n.0: Sections 1-2 (the statutory principles) are not in force.
n.2: The nominated person provisions (ss24-28, Sch 2) are not in force.
n.3: Section 29 (shorter section 3 periods) is not in force.

Mental Health Law.q: Sanjay, 50, has been detained under section 3 since 1 June and first received medication on 2 June. On 10 August he refuses it. A colleague says a SOAD is now needed because 'the rule changed to 2 months'. What is correct in October 2026?
o: A SOAD certificate is needed now, as 2 months have passed
A SOAD certificate is needed because he is refusing at any stage
No SOAD certificate is needed while he is detained under section 3
No SOAD certificate is needed until 3 months from 2 June
Mental Health Law.w: Section 14 of the 2025 Act, which will cut the section 58 period from 3 months to 2 months, is not in force. Under section 58 of the 1983 Act, the SOAD safeguard applies from 3 months after medication was first given (2 September). On 10 August, medication can still be given under section 63.

n.0: The 2-month rule is an uncommenced 2025 Act change.
n.1: Refusal within the first 3 months does not trigger section 58; section 63 applies.
n.2: Section 58 applies to section 3 patients after the 3-month period.

Mental Health Law.q: Asif, 36, detained under section 2 on 1 October, asks on 18 October whether he can still apply to the tribunal, as he heard the window is now 21 days. What is the correct answer?
o: Yes, because the 2025 Act extended the window to 21 days
Yes, because section 2 patients may apply up to day 28
No, because section 2 patients must wait for a managers' referral
No, because the 14-day window under the 1983 Act has passed
Mental Health Law.w: Section 30(1) of the 2025 Act, which will extend the section 2 tribunal window from 14 to 21 days, is not in force. Under section 66(2) of the 1983 Act, Asif had to apply within 14 days of admission (by 14 October). He can still seek a hospital managers' hearing.

n.0: The 21-day window is an uncommenced 2025 Act change.
n.1: The window is 14 days, not the full 28 days of the section.
n.2: Section 2 patients may apply themselves within 14 days; s68 referrals concern section 3 and other longer-term patients.

Mental Health Law.q: In October 2026 a ward induction pack states that 'therapeutic benefit' is now a statutory principle in section 118 that all decisions under the Act must follow. What correction should the practice educator make?
o: The 2025 Act principles apply to CTO patients and the Code principles to others
None; the principles were added to the Code by SI 2026/385 in April 2026
The 2025 Act principles await commencement; the 2015 Code's five principles apply
None; the 2025 Act principles came into force on Royal Assent
Mental Health Law.w: Sections 1-2 of the 2025 Act will put four statutory principles (choice and autonomy, least restriction, therapeutic benefit, the person as an individual) into section 118, but they are not in force in October 2026. The 2015 Code's five guiding principles still apply.

n.0: There is no split by patient group; the 2025 principles are not in force for anyone.
n.1: SI 2026/385 commenced sections 51 and 52 only.
n.3: Royal Assent commenced only technical provisions (ss53-57), not the principles.

Mental Health Law.q: Ellie, a first-year student on an acute admissions ward in England, asks her practice supervisor how the Mental Health Act 1983 defines 'mental disorder'. Which answer is accurate?
o: Any mental illness of a nature or degree that warrants detention in hospital
Any disorder or disability of the mind
Any condition listed in the mental and behavioural chapter of ICD-11
A diagnosed psychotic, mood or personality disorder of moderate severity
Mental Health Law.w: Section 1(2) of the Mental Health Act 1983 (as amended in 2007) defines mental disorder as 'any disorder or disability of the mind'. The single broad definition replaced the four old categories in 2008.

n.0: 'Nature or degree' warranting detention is part of the section 2 and section 3 grounds, not the definition of mental disorder itself.
n.2: The Act does not import a diagnostic manual; ICD-11 is a clinical classification, not the statutory definition.
n.3: The Act does not limit the definition to particular diagnoses or a severity threshold; it uses one broad definition.

Mental Health Law.q: Tom, 34, is admitted informally with alcohol dependence and no other mental health problem. He wants to leave the ward to drink. A newly qualified nurse suggests the team detain him under the Mental Health Act 1983. What should the nurse in charge explain?
o: Dependence on alcohol is not itself a mental disorder under the Act
Alcohol dependence qualifies for section 2 but not for section 3
The nurse may hold him under section 5(4) while he is intoxicated
Alcohol dependence counts as a mental disorder once it is severe
Mental Health Law.w: Section 1(3) of the Mental Health Act 1983 states that dependence on alcohol or drugs is not considered a disorder or disability of the mind. A person can be detained only if they also have a mental disorder (for example a psychosis or alcohol-related brain injury) and the other criteria are met.

n.1: Section 1(3) applies to the whole definition, so dependence alone supports neither section 2 nor section 3.
n.2: Section 5(4) needs a mental disorder as well as the other criteria; intoxication with dependence alone does not meet it.
n.3: Severity does not change the position: section 1(3) excludes dependence on alcohol or drugs from the definition altogether.

Mental Health Law.q: On an acute ward, the team agree a care plan with Amara, 29, who is detained under section 3. She chooses her named nurse's visiting times and her views on medication are recorded and acted on where possible. Which Mental Health Act Code of Practice (2015) guiding principle does this most directly reflect?
o: Respect and dignity
Empowerment and involvement
Purpose and effectiveness
Efficiency and equity
Mental Health Law.w: The 2015 Code (chapter 1) sets five guiding principles: least restrictive option and maximising independence; empowerment and involvement; respect and dignity; purpose and effectiveness; efficiency and equity. Involving the patient fully in planning and giving weight to her views is empowerment and involvement.

n.0: Respect and dignity concerns respecting diversity and treating people without discrimination; participation in planning is the empowerment principle.
n.2: Purpose and effectiveness concerns care that is meaningful, evidence-based and aimed at recovery goals, not patient participation.
n.3: Efficiency and equity concerns fair, efficient use of resources and equal access, not involvement in decisions.

Mental Health Law.q: A ward manager proposes a local procedure that differs from the Mental Health Act Code of Practice (2015) because 'the Code is only guidance'. Which statement about the legal status of the Code is accurate?
o: It binds approved clinicians but not nurses or other staff
It is statutory guidance and any departure needs cogent, recorded reasons
It is advisory, so staff may follow their own local policy instead
It is primary legislation, so departing from it is a criminal offence
Mental Health Law.w: The Code is issued under section 118 of the Mental Health Act 1983. Professionals must have regard to it and should depart from it only for cogent reasons, which must be recorded. It remains the current Code in October 2026.

n.0: The duty to have regard to the Code applies to all professionals and hospital managers acting under the Act, including nurses.
n.2: The Code is statutory guidance that professionals must have regard to; local policy cannot simply override it.
n.3: The Code is guidance under section 118, not an Act of Parliament; departure is not an offence but must be justified by cogent reasons.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Ana, 42, has bipolar disorder and is in a manic episode. She wants to sign over her house to a man she met yesterday. She currently lacks capacity for this decision, and the transfer is not urgent. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Treat her as lacking capacity for all financial decisions until discharge
Support her and reassess when well, as the decision can wait
Ask her nearest relative to make the decision on her behalf
Make a best interests decision now to block the transfer permanently
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific and can fluctuate in mental illness (MCA s2; COP15 13.21). Where a decision can wait until the person is likely to regain capacity, it should be deferred and reassessed (MCA s4(3)).

n.0: Capacity is decision-specific; a blanket finding for all financial decisions breaches the MCA.
n.2: The nearest relative has no power to make decisions for her; that would need an attorney, deputy or court.
n.3: Where a decision can wait, the person should be given the chance to decide when capacity returns (s4(3)).

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Peter, 55, is an informal in-patient with depression. He has capacity and decides to stop his antidepressant, against advice. He is not asking to leave and shows no new risk. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the medication under section 63, as he is an in-patient
Respect his decision, explore his reasons and inform the team
Use section 5(4) so the medication can be given
Give the medication covertly in his best interests
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: A capable informal patient can refuse treatment. Section 63 applies to detained patients, not informal ones. The nurse should explore reasons (for example side effects), give information, record the discussion and inform the team.

n.0: Section 63 applies to detained patients, not informal patients.
n.2: Section 5(4) is for preventing an informal patient leaving, not for imposing medication, and its criteria are not met.
n.3: Covert medication is never appropriate for a person with capacity; it may be considered only for people who lack capacity, under the MCA.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: In October 2026, a care home manager tells the community mental health nurse that she will 'apply for Liberty Protection Safeguards' for a resident with dementia whose care amounts to a deprivation of liberty. What should the nurse advise?
o: No authorisation is needed in care homes since the 2025 Act
LPS now applies in care homes, and DoLS applies in hospitals
LPS replaced DoLS in April 2026, so an LPS application is right
DoLS remains in force, so a DoLS authorisation is the route
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: The Liberty Protection Safeguards in the Mental Capacity (Amendment) Act 2019 have not been implemented. DoLS (MCA Schedule A1) remains the system for authorising deprivation of liberty in hospitals and care homes in October 2026.

n.0: The Mental Health Act 2025 does not remove the need for authorisation of deprivation of liberty in care homes.
n.1: There is no split in which LPS covers care homes; LPS is not in force anywhere.
n.2: LPS has not been commenced; DoLS is still in force.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Sophie, 14, is assessed in CAMHS for possible informal admission. The nurse asks how her ability to consent should be judged. Which answer is correct?
o: By Gillick competence, as she is under 16
By the section 131 test used for 16-17s
By the Mental Capacity Act test, as for adults
By her parents' view, because she is under 16
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: For under-16s, competence to consent is judged using Gillick competence (Gillick v West Norfolk and Wisbech AHA [1986]). The MCA generally applies to people aged 16 and over (MCA s2(5)). Section 131 deals with 16-17-year-olds.

n.1: Section 131(2)-(4) applies to 16-17-year-olds, not to a 14-year-old.
n.2: The MCA generally applies from age 16, so it is not the test for a 14-year-old.
n.3: Parental views matter, but competence is about Sophie's own understanding.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: At a serious incident review after Michael, 29, a detained patient, took his life on the ward, the panel discusses which Human Rights Act 1998 Article places a positive duty on the hospital to take reasonable steps to protect patients from a real and immediate risk of suicide. Which Article is it?
o: Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 8, right to respect for private and family life
Article 2, right to life
Article 5, right to liberty and security
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Article 2 (right to life) includes a positive operational duty on the state, including NHS hospitals, to take reasonable steps to protect a person in its care, such as a detained patient, from a real and immediate risk to life that it knows or ought to know about.

n.0: Article 3 concerns torture and inhuman or degrading treatment, not the duty to protect life.
n.1: Article 8 protects privacy and family life; protecting life is Article 2.
n.3: Article 5 protects liberty and governs lawful detention, not protection from suicide.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Tunde, 40, is an informal patient. Ward staff stop him at the door and tell him he cannot go out, although no holding power or detention has been used. Which Human Rights Act right is most directly engaged?
o: Article 5, right to liberty and security
Article 10, freedom of expression
Article 14, protection from discrimination
Article 8, right to respect for private life
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Article 5 protects the right to liberty; any deprivation must follow a procedure prescribed by law. Preventing an informal patient from leaving without legal authority (for example s5(2) or s5(4)) is an unlawful interference with liberty.

n.1: Freedom of expression is not engaged by preventing him from leaving.
n.2: Article 14 requires discrimination in the enjoyment of another right; nothing suggests discrimination here.
n.3: Article 8 may be engaged by some restrictions, but stopping someone leaving is primarily a liberty issue.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A ward introduces a rule that no patient may receive visits from children, whatever their individual risk. Leanne, 32, detained under section 3, has two young children and no safeguarding concerns. Which right is most directly engaged by the rule as applied to her?
o: Article 2, the right to life
Article 3, prohibition of degrading treatment
Article 5, the right to liberty and security
Article 8, right to private and family life
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Article 8 protects private and family life. A blanket ban on children visiting, not based on individual risk, interferes with family life and must be justified as necessary and proportionate. The Code warns against blanket restrictions (COP15 ch8).

n.0: Article 2 concerns protection of life; there is no risk to life here.
n.1: Article 3 covers serious ill-treatment; a visiting rule interferes with family life rather than reaching that threshold.
n.2: Article 5 is engaged by her detention itself, not by the visiting rule.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A nurse audits mental health detentions in her trust and finds that Black patients are detained at much higher rates than White patients. Which NHS England framework is designed to help trusts address this inequality?
o: The Workforce Race Equality Standard (WRES)
The Triangle of Care for carers and families
The Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework
The Community Mental Health Framework (2019)
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: The Patient and Carer Race Equality Framework (PCREF) is NHS England's anti-racism framework for mental health providers, aimed at improving racial equity in access, experience and outcomes, including use of the Mental Health Act, where Black people are consistently over-represented.

n.0: The Workforce Race Equality Standard concerns staff, not patients and carers; PCREF is the patient-focused framework.
n.1: The Triangle of Care is a carers' partnership framework, not a race equality framework.
n.3: The Community Mental Health Framework reshapes community services; it is not the race equality framework.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Grace, 46, has had recurrent depression and severe anxiety for many years, which substantially affect her daily life. At an outpatient clinic she asks to wait in a quiet room because the busy waiting area triggers panic attacks. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Decline unless she brings a GP letter confirming her diagnosis
Decline, because mental illness is outside the Equality Act 2010
Agree, as the Equality Act requires reasonable adjustments
Agree, but record it as a one-off favour rather than a duty
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Under the Equality Act 2010, a mental health condition with a substantial and long-term adverse effect on day-to-day activities can be a disability, and services have a duty to make reasonable adjustments. A quiet waiting space is a simple reasonable adjustment.

n.0: Requiring a GP letter before a simple adjustment is a barrier; the duty is to make reasonable adjustments.
n.1: Mental health conditions can meet the Equality Act definition of disability.
n.3: Treating it as a favour misunderstands the legal duty to make reasonable adjustments.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: During handover, a nurse refers to a new admission as 'the schizophrenic in bed 4'. Which response from the nurse in charge best challenges stigma?
o: 'It is fine to use diagnoses as shorthand during a busy handover.'
'Call him "the psychotic patient" until the diagnosis is confirmed.'
'Say "Mr Osei, who has schizophrenia"; he is more than his diagnosis.'
'Use his bed number, to protect his confidentiality.'
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Person-first language that uses the person's name and describes a condition the person has, rather than defining them by it, reduces stigma and supports dignity (Code standards 1 and 20). Defining people by diagnosis or bed number dehumanises them.

n.0: Labels defining a person by their diagnosis reinforce stigma, however busy the handover.
n.1: This replaces one diagnostic label with another and still defines him by his illness.
n.3: Referring to people by bed number depersonalises them and does not address the stigmatising language.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Ravi, 37, is detained under section 3 in an independent hospital, with his care arranged and paid for by the NHS. In October 2026 he asks whether the hospital must act compatibly with his human rights. What is the accurate answer?
o: No, because the CQC protects his rights in an independent hospital
Yes, as the 2025 Act extended HRA duties to such providers in April 2026
Yes, once the remaining provisions of the 2025 Act are commenced
No, because the Human Rights Act binds NHS bodies, not private ones
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 51 of the Mental Health Act 2025 (new s142C of the 1983 Act), in force from 6 April 2026 under SI 2026/385, makes private providers of care arranged under the MHA subject to the Human Rights Act 1998 in providing that care.

n.0: The CQC regulates providers but does not replace the provider's own HRA duties.
n.2: Section 51 was commenced on 6 April 2026; it does not wait for the rest of the Act.
n.3: Section 51 of the 2025 Act now extends HRA duties to private providers of MHA-arranged care.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Kemi, 22, is restrained and secluded for long periods, sometimes without clothing, and staff mock her during restraint. Which Human Rights Act right is most clearly at risk of breach?
o: Article 6, the right to a fair trial and fair hearing
Article 9, freedom of thought, conscience and religion
Article 3, prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment
Article 12, the right to marry and to found a family
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Article 3 is an absolute right prohibiting torture and inhuman or degrading treatment. Humiliating restrictive practices such as mocking a restrained patient or unjustified removal of clothing in seclusion risk breaching it. NG10 says people in seclusion should keep their clothing.

n.0: Article 6 concerns fair hearings, not treatment during restraint.
n.1: Article 9 concerns freedom of belief, not humiliating treatment.
n.3: Article 12 concerns marriage and is not relevant here.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A nurse on an acute ward in England is completing training on the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018. Which intervention falls within the Act's definition of 'use of force'?
o: Asking a patient to move to a quieter lounge, which he agrees to do
Giving IM medication intended to subdue a patient's movement
Offering oral PRN medication that the patient accepts after discussion
Placing a patient on continuous observation within arm's length
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 1 of the 2018 Act defines use of force as physical, mechanical or chemical restraint or isolation. Chemical restraint is the use of medication intended to prevent, restrict or subdue movement of any part of the patient's body, as with rapid tranquillisation.

n.0: A voluntary move to another room involves no restraint or imposed isolation.
n.2: Oral medication accepted voluntarily is not given with the intention of subduing movement and involves no force.
n.3: Observation does not itself restrain movement or impose seclusion or segregation.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Which of these settings is a 'mental health unit' covered by the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018?
o: A GP surgery that runs a weekly mental health clinic
A crisis café run by a mental health charity in the evenings
A registered residential care home for older people living with dementia
An independent hospital giving NHS-funded psychiatric in-patient care
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 1 defines a mental health unit as an NHS hospital in England providing in-patient treatment for mental disorder, or an independent hospital in England providing such treatment where at least some of it is for the purposes of the NHS.

n.0: Outpatient primary care settings do not provide in-patient treatment for mental disorder.
n.1: A non-hospital crisis service does not provide in-patient treatment and is outside the Act.
n.2: Care homes are not hospitals and are outside the Act's definition.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A trust that runs five mental health wards asks how it must meet section 2 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018. Which arrangement complies?
o: A separate responsible person, employed by the trust, for each ward
One suitably senior responsible person, employed by the trust, for all
Each of the five ward managers acting as responsible person on a rota
A CQC inspector appointed as the responsible person for the trust
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 2 requires an organisation operating a mental health unit to appoint a responsible person, employed by it and of an appropriate level of seniority. An organisation with more than one unit must appoint a single responsible person for all its units.

n.0: Where an organisation runs more than one unit, it must appoint a single responsible person for all of them.
n.2: A rota of ward managers does not meet the requirement for one appointed, suitably senior responsible person.
n.3: The responsible person must be employed by the operating organisation, not the regulator.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Jamie, 26, is admitted to a mental health unit. When must he be given information about his rights in relation to the use of force, under the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018?
o: After force has been used on him for the first time
As soon as reasonably practicable after admission
At his first First-tier Tribunal hearing
Within 28 days of admission, at his first ward round
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 4 requires the responsible person to give each patient information about their rights in relation to the use of force as soon as reasonably practicable after admission, and to take reasonably practicable steps to make sure the patient is aware of and understands it.

n.0: Information is given on admission, before any force is used, so patients know their rights.
n.2: Tribunals review detention; the duty to give use of force information applies on admission.
n.3: There is no 28-day period; the duty is as soon as reasonably practicable after admission.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Following a planned restraint to give Dom, 33, his IM medication, the nurse in charge completes the use of force record. Under section 6 of the 2018 Act, which detail must the record include?
o: Whether de-escalation was attempted before force was used
The patient's nearest relative's views on the restraint
The names of all other patients on the ward at the time
The cost of the staff time involved
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 6(5) requires the record of each non-negligible use of force to include the reason, place, date and duration, the type of force, whether it formed part of the care plan, the patient's characteristics, the outcome and any efforts made to avoid the need for force, such as de-escalation (s6(5)(o)). Records are kept for 3 years (s6(6)).

n.1: The nearest relative's views are not a required field in the s6 record.
n.2: Recording other patients' names would breach confidentiality and is not required.
n.3: Staff costs are not part of the statutory record.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A new healthcare assistant starts on a psychiatric intensive care unit. Under section 5 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018, what training must she receive?
o: Restraint holds training, completed within her first year
None, as the section 5 duty covers registered nurses
Use of force training with de-escalation, soon after starting
Breakaway training, as she has been rostered for night shifts
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 5 requires the responsible person to give all staff in the unit training in the appropriate use of force as soon as reasonably practicable after joining, with refresher training at regular intervals. Content includes patient involvement, avoiding discrimination, de-escalation, risks of force and the impact of trauma.

n.0: The training is much broader than restraint holds and must be given as soon as reasonably practicable, not within a year.
n.1: The duty covers all staff working in the unit, including healthcare assistants.
n.3: Training applies to all staff in the unit; shift pattern does not change the content or timing.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Police officers attend an acute ward at staff request to help manage Sam, 30, who is assaulting other patients. What does section 12 of the Mental Health Units (Use of Force) Act 2018 require of the officers?
o: To obtain the responsible clinician's consent before entering
To complete the unit's section 6 use of force record themselves
To hand Sam over to ward staff before they use any force
To wear and run a body camera when reasonably practicable
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 12 (in force 18 August 2022) requires a police officer assisting staff in a mental health unit who has a body camera to wear it and keep it operating at all times when reasonably practicable, unless special circumstances justify not doing so.

n.0: No RC consent is required for police to enter when assisting staff.
n.1: Recording under section 6 is the responsible person's duty for the unit.
n.2: The Act does not require officers to hand over before acting; it regulates recording of their involvement.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A ward manager reviews the unit's use of force records from 2 years ago before an inspection. Under section 6 of the 2018 Act, for how long must these records be kept?
o: 3 years
1 year
6 months
8 years
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 6(6) requires each use of force record to be kept for 3 years from the date it was made.

n.1: One year is too short under s6(6).
n.2: Six months is too short under s6(6).
n.3: Eight years is not the statutory period in s6(6).

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Darren, 35, is shouting in the ward corridor, pacing and jabbing his finger at staff about a cancelled visit. Four staff members gather round, each trying to calm him at once. According to NICE NG10, what should happen?
o: One staff member takes the lead in communicating with him
All four staff keep talking to him so he feels well supported
Security staff are called to stand beside him
Staff withdraw until he calms down on his own
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.18: if a service user becomes agitated or angry, one staff member should take the primary role in communicating with them, assess safety, seek clarification and negotiate a non-confrontational resolution. Several people talking at once can overwhelm and provoke.

n.1: Multiple people speaking at once is confusing and can escalate agitation; NG10 recommends a single lead.
n.2: Bringing security alongside early can be perceived as threatening and is not a de-escalation technique.
n.3: Withdrawing entirely leaves an agitated person unsupported and does not use de-escalation skills.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Kieran, 28, is agitated in the ward lounge and is holding a kitchen knife he took from the activity room. He is not attacking anyone. The nurse leading de-escalation wants the knife removed safely. What does NICE NG10 advise?
o: Ask him to hand the knife directly to the nurse
Approach quickly from behind to take the knife
Ask him to put the knife down in a neutral place
Ask other patients to persuade him to give it up
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.7: if a service user is carrying a weapon, ask them to place it in a neutral location rather than hand it over. Handing it over brings the weapon close to staff and can be misread as a threatening movement.

n.0: Handing over a weapon brings it into close contact with staff; NG10 advises a neutral location instead.
n.1: Approaching from behind is likely to startle him and increase the risk of injury.
n.3: Involving other patients places them at risk and is not a recognised de-escalation step.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Bella, 24, becomes increasingly agitated in a busy dining room. The nurse wants to help her calm down somewhere quieter. Which location does NICE NG10 advise against using routinely for de-escalation?
o: A quiet area of the ward garden
The seclusion room
Her own bedroom with staff support
A designated comfort room
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.14 and 1.3.20: separate agitated service users from others using quiet areas, bedrooms, comfort rooms or gardens, and use a designated calming area. Do not routinely use the seclusion room for de-escalation, because the person may perceive it as threatening.

n.0: Gardens and quiet areas are suitable de-escalation spaces in NG10.
n.2: Bedrooms are listed in NG10 1.3.14 as places to aid de-escalation, ensuring staff are not isolated.
n.3: A comfort room is one of the spaces NG10 suggests for calming.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: During a morning shift, a nurse notices that Omar, 44, who is usually sociable, is sitting alone, clenching his fists, staring at another patient and muttering. What is the most appropriate first action?
o: Move the other patient off the ward for the rest of the day
Increase his observation level to continuous and inform security
Approach calmly, say he seems upset and ask what is troubling him
Offer him PRN lorazepam straight away to prevent an incident
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.13 and 1.3.17: build a close working relationship, sensitively monitor changes in mood or composure that may lead to aggression, and communicate respect and empathy. Early engagement on noticing warning signs is the first step before any restrictive measure.

n.0: Removing another patient disrupts their care and does not address Omar's distress.
n.1: Observation should be used after positive engagement fails (NG10 1.4.12); jumping to continuous observation and security is premature.
n.3: PRN medication is part of de-escalation, but the first step is to engage and understand what is wrong.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Lewis, 30, detained under section 3, demands to go to the shop now. His section 17 leave has been suspended by his responsible clinician after a recent incident. He becomes angry. Which response by the nurse best avoids escalating this flashpoint?
o: 'That's the decision, so you'll have to wait for the ward round.'
'You know the rules. Keep shouting and you will lose more privileges.'
'I can see you're frustrated. Leave is paused; can I help another way?'
'Fine, I will walk you to the shop now if you calm down first, okay?'
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Refusing a request is a known flashpoint (NICE NG10 1.3.15). The nurse should acknowledge feelings, explain clearly and respectfully, and offer realistic choices, using verbal and non-verbal skills to avoid provoking aggression (NG10 1.3.17).

n.0: A flat refusal without empathy or alternatives is dismissive and likely to provoke further anger.
n.1: Threats of sanctions are confrontational and likely to escalate; restrictive responses must never be used as punishment (NG10 1.4.6).
n.3: Taking him out would breach the RC's suspension of leave under section 17.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Taylor, 22, was admitted yesterday. The admitting doctor has written up PRN haloperidol 'for agitation' without discussing it with Taylor. According to NICE NG10, what is good practice for PRN medication used to prevent violence?
o: Review PRN use monthly at the person's care programme review
Leave the maximum daily dose open so the night team can be flexible
Tailor it to her needs with a set maximum dose and dose interval
Prescribe it on admission for everyone so it is to hand if needed
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.10-1.3.11: do not prescribe PRN routinely or automatically on admission; tailor it to individual need with discussion where possible; specify the rationale, maximum daily dose (within BNF when combined with regular and RT doses) and the interval; and review at least weekly, considering stopping it if unused.

n.0: NG10 1.3.11 requires MDT review of PRN at least once a week, not monthly.
n.1: The maximum daily dose must be specified so it does not inadvertently exceed the BNF maximum.
n.3: NG10 1.3.10 says not to prescribe PRN routinely or automatically on admission.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Ruth, 50, is shouting and has thrown a chair across the lounge, missing other people. Staff have tried talking with her in a quiet room and she declined PRN medication. She now picks up another chair and moves towards a patient. What does NICE NG10 say about using a restrictive intervention at this point?
o: It cannot be used now, because she declined PRN medication
It is not allowed until a doctor has assessed her in person
It is now justified: preventive steps failed and harm is likely
It should be held back until she has actually injured someone
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.5: use a restrictive intervention only if de-escalation and other preventive strategies, including PRN medication, have failed and there is potential for harm if no action is taken. De-escalation should continue throughout the intervention.

n.0: Declining PRN does not prevent other proportionate restrictive interventions where risk is imminent.
n.1: Waiting for a doctor before acting would leave a patient at risk of imminent harm; a doctor should be informed but need not attend first.
n.3: NG10 requires potential for harm, not that someone has already been injured.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: While talking with Jade, 26, who is becoming angry, a newly qualified nurse wants to use non-verbal de-escalation skills. Which approach is most appropriate?
o: Fold your arms to show you are calm and in control
Stand directly in front of her, close up, holding steady eye contact
Stand at a slight angle, keep a safe distance, with relaxed open hands
Stand between her and the door to stop her walking off
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.12 and 1.3.19: recognise the importance of personal space and use self-management of body posture and eye contact. An angled stance at a safe distance with open hands appears non-threatening and allows both people an exit route.

n.0: Folded arms can be read as defensive or dismissive.
n.1: A face-on, close stance with fixed eye contact invades personal space and can feel confrontational.
n.3: Blocking the exit can make her feel trapped and increase the risk to both.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Aaron, 31, has been held in standing manual restraint for 12 minutes after assaulting a nurse. He is still struggling. The team lead considers the options. What does NICE NG10 recommend?
o: Release him and call the police to take over the restraint
Take him to the floor face down so the struggle ends quickly
Consider rapid tranquillisation or seclusion instead
Continue standing restraint until he has stopped struggling
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.29-1.4.30: do not routinely use manual restraint for more than 10 minutes, and consider rapid tranquillisation or seclusion as alternatives to prolonged (over 10 minutes) manual restraint.

n.0: Handing over to police is not an NG10 alternative and may increase risk.
n.1: NG10 advises avoiding the floor and, if prone is needed, using it for the shortest time; it is not a way to end prolonged restraint.
n.3: NG10 1.4.29 advises against routinely restraining for more than 10 minutes; prolonged restraint raises the risk of harm.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: During a manual restraint of Nia, 25, one nurse is designated as the lead. According to NICE NG10, which is the lead's responsibility?
o: Completing the incident form while the restraint continues
Applying firm pressure to Nia's back to keep her still
Drawing up rapid tranquillisation while the others hold her
Making sure her head, neck, airway and vital signs are protected
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.32: one staff member should lead throughout and ensure other staff can protect and support the head and neck, check that airway and breathing are not compromised, monitor vital signs and are supported. NG10 1.4.25 forbids pressure on the rib cage, neck or abdomen.

n.0: Documentation follows the incident; during restraint the lead coordinates safety.
n.1: Pressure on the back or rib cage can compromise breathing and is prohibited by NG10 1.4.25.
n.2: The lead stays focused on coordinating the restraint and the person's safety, not preparing medication.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Isla, 38, an informal patient, suddenly attacks staff and another patient. As a last resort she is placed in seclusion to prevent harm to others. What must happen next?
o: Transfer her to the emergency department for review
Continue seclusion for up to 24 hours before review
Arrange a Mental Health Act assessment immediately
Ask her to sign consent to the use of seclusion
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Seclusion should be used only for patients detained under the Act. If an informal patient is secluded in an emergency as a last resort, an assessment for detention under the Act should be undertaken immediately (COP15 26.106; NICE NG10 1.4.46).

n.0: Transfer to ED is not indicated; seclusion is not used in emergency departments, and the priority is MHA assessment.
n.1: There is no 24-hour period; an MHA assessment must be arranged immediately and reviews start at once.
n.3: Consent does not legitimise seclusion; the need is for a lawful framework via MHA assessment.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Ben, 29, detained under section 3, has been placed in seclusion. A nurse is observing him. According to the Mental Health Act Code of Practice, how often must a written record of his behaviour be made?
o: At least every hour
At least every 30 minutes
At least every 15 minutes
At least every 2 hours
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 26.118-26.123: a suitably skilled professional should be within sight and sound of the seclusion area at all times, and a record of the patient's behaviour should be made at least every 15 minutes.

n.0: Hourly is the minimum for written records in long-term segregation, not seclusion.
n.1: Thirty minutes matches low-level intermittent observation, not the seclusion record.
n.3: Two-hourly is the frequency for nursing reviews of seclusion, not the observation record.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Seclusion of Marcus, 34, was started by the nurse in charge of the ward at 21:00. The responsible clinician is not on site. By when should the first medical review take place?
o: At the next morning's ward round
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 26.116: if seclusion is authorised by the professional in charge of the ward (or a non-medical approved clinician), the RC or duty doctor should attend to undertake the first medical review within 1 hour of the start of seclusion, and without delay if the patient is new or unknown, or their presentation has changed.

n.0: Thirty minutes is not the Code's standard; the first medical review is within 1 hour.
n.2: Four hours is the interval for continuing medical reviews, not the first review.
n.3: Waiting for ward round breaches the 1-hour requirement.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Chloe, 27, has been in continuous seclusion since 08:00. It is now 16:00. What review does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice require at this point?
o: A review by the CQC Mental Health Act reviewer
A further two-hourly nursing review by any nurse
A tribunal referral by the hospital managers
A prompt independent multidisciplinary review
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 26.141: an independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours consecutively or 12 hours intermittently within 48 hours. Members should not have been involved in the incident that led to seclusion, and include an IMHA if she has one.

n.0: The CQC monitors use of the Act but does not carry out case reviews of seclusion.
n.1: Nursing reviews continue every 2 hours but must be by two registered nurses, and they do not replace the independent MDT review at 8 hours.
n.2: Seclusion does not trigger a tribunal referral.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Two hours after seclusion begins, a nursing review of Jordan, 30, is due. Who should carry it out, according to the Code of Practice?
o: A healthcare assistant together with a student nurse
The duty doctor together with the nurse in charge
Two registered nurses, one not involved in the decision
One registered nurse, who authorised the seclusion
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 26.134: nursing reviews take place at least every 2 hours from the start of seclusion, by two registered nurses, at least one of whom was not directly involved in the decision to seclude.

n.0: Unregistered staff and students cannot carry out the nursing review.
n.1: The two-hourly review is a nursing review; medical reviews are separate.
n.3: The review needs two registered nurses, including one independent of the decision.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: After Aisha, 33, was restrained and given rapid tranquillisation, the risk has now been contained. According to NICE NG10, what should happen next?
o: A written warning to Aisha about her future behaviour
An immediate debrief that includes a nurse and a doctor
A formal disciplinary review of the staff involved
A debrief held at the next monthly team meeting
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.55: once risks are contained, conduct an immediate post-incident debrief including a nurse and a doctor to address physical harm, ongoing risks and emotional impact. A formal external post-incident review should follow within 72 hours (1.4.62), aimed at learning, not blame.

n.0: Warnings are punitive; restrictive interventions must not be used to punish, and the patient should be offered support to discuss the incident.
n.2: Reviews aim at learning and improvement, not assigning blame; disciplinary action is not the default step.
n.3: The debrief should be immediate, not delayed to a monthly meeting.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Nathan, 40, is at risk of becoming aggressive but does not pose an immediate risk. The team places him on high-level intermittent observation using NICE NG10 definitions. How often should staff check on him?
o: Continuously within eyesight
Once every 15 to 30 minutes
Within arm's length of a designated nurse
Once every 30 to 60 minutes
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.11: high-level intermittent observation is used when a person is at risk of becoming violent or aggressive but not an immediate risk; frequency is once every 15 to 30 minutes. Low-level intermittent (baseline) is every 30 to 60 minutes.

n.0: Continuous observation within eyesight is for an immediate threat.
n.2: Arm's length is a form of continuous observation, for higher risk.
n.3: Every 30 to 60 minutes is low-level intermittent, the baseline level.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Maya, 19, has made a serious attempt to strangle herself on the ward and remains intent on harming herself. The team decide she needs continuous observation. According to NICE NG10, what does this involve?
o: Being kept in the seclusion room with the door locked
Checks every 15 minutes, recorded on an observation chart
Staying within eyesight or arm's length of a designated nurse
Checks every 5 minutes by whichever staff member is free
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.11: continuous observation means the person is kept within eyesight or at arm's length of a designated one-to-one nurse, with immediate access to other staff. Seclusion must not be used solely to manage self-harm (COP15 26.108).

n.0: Seclusion should never be used solely to manage self-harm (COP15 26.108).
n.1: Fifteen-minute checks are intermittent, not continuous, observation.
n.3: Frequent checks by any staff member are still intermittent and lack a designated observer.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A healthcare assistant has been doing continuous one-to-one observation of Leon, 22, for 2 hours and is starting to lose concentration. According to NICE NG10, what should happen?
o: Leon's observation level should be reduced to intermittent
She should observe from the nurses' station to rest
Another staff member should take over so she can have a break
She should continue to the end of the 12-hour shift
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.20: no individual should undertake continuous observation above the general level for longer than 2 hours; if needed for longer, ensure regular breaks. Fatigue reduces vigilance and engagement.

n.0: Observation levels are changed on clinical grounds, not because the observer is tired.
n.1: Observing from a distance does not meet continuous observation requirements.
n.3: Continuous observation for a whole shift without breaks breaches NG10 1.4.20 and is unsafe.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A student nurse is allocated to continuous observation of Tom, 35. She sits by his door reading her notes and does not speak to him. What feedback should her practice supervisor give?
o: She should stand inside his room, facing him throughout
Observation should include active, positive engagement with Tom
This is appropriate, because talking may disturb him
She should record his position every 5 minutes without talking
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.19: staff undertaking observation should take an active role in engaging positively with the service user, be approachable, listen and convey that the person is valued. Observation is therapeutic engagement, not just watching.

n.0: Standing over him at all times is intrusive and not what positive engagement means.
n.2: Passive watching misses the therapeutic purpose of observation (NG10 1.4.19).
n.3: Recording position without engagement is custodial, not therapeutic.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Priya, 28, is placed on high-level intermittent observation after expressing suicidal thoughts. She asks the nurse why staff keep checking on her. What should the nurse explain, according to NICE NG10?
o: Why she is observed, its aims, how long and what will end it
That observation will continue until her next tribunal hearing
That this observation level is standard for all new admissions
That staff may not discuss observation decisions with patients
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.15: give the person information about why they are under observation, the aims, how long it is likely to last and what needs to be achieved for it to stop. With her agreement, tell her carer about the aims and level of observation.

n.1: Observation is reviewed clinically and is not tied to tribunal dates.
n.2: Observation should be individualised; this level is based on her risk, not routine for all admissions.
n.3: NG10 requires staff to explain observation to the person.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: At 03:00 a nurse doing 15-minute intermittent observations sees Gary, 46, lying still in bed with his covers pulled over his head. He has been expressing suicidal thoughts. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Confirm he is breathing and lying safely, entering if unsure
Shine a torch into his face to check that he responds to light
Wait and check again at the next scheduled 15-minute time
Record 'asleep in bed' and move on to the next patient's check
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Observation should confirm the person's safety, not just their presence. Staff should check for signs of breathing and a safe position, and enter the room if this cannot be confirmed. Most in-patient suicides are by hanging or strangulation, so covered heads and stillness warrant close checking.

n.1: Shining a torch in his eyes is unnecessarily intrusive when breathing can be checked by looking closely or entering quietly.
n.2: Waiting another 15 minutes when safety is unconfirmed risks missing a ligature or other harm.
n.3: Recording 'asleep' without confirming breathing and safety misses the purpose of observation.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: The night nurse is handing over continuous observation of Dee, 30, to the day nurse. According to NICE NG10, how should the handover be done?
o: By written note left on the observation chart
At the nurses' station, away from Dee, to protect confidentiality
After Dee has been asked to go to her room
Including Dee in the discussion where possible
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.21: when handing over to another staff member during observation, include the service user in the discussion if possible. This supports collaboration and avoids gaps in continuous observation.

n.0: A written note alone risks a gap in observation and misses involving Dee.
n.1: Handing over away from Dee risks a gap in continuous observation and excludes her.
n.2: Sending Dee away breaks continuous observation and excludes her from the discussion.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: The nurse in charge increases Kofi's observation from general (low-level intermittent) to continuous at 23:00 because of new suicidal intent. What else does NICE NG10 require?
o: Seek his nearest relative's consent to the change of level
Tell his psychiatrist or the on-call doctor as soon as possible
Make a referral to the tribunal for an independent review of it
Wait for the next ward round before informing the doctor
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.4.22: tell the psychiatrist or on-call doctor as soon as possible if observation above the general level is carried out. Decisions, reasons and who will review them should be recorded (1.4.16, 1.4.18).

n.0: The nearest relative's consent is not required for observation decisions.
n.2: Observation changes are clinical decisions and do not involve the tribunal.
n.3: Waiting for ward round delays medical awareness; NG10 requires informing the doctor as soon as possible.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: After one patient used a phone charger cable to self-harm, a ward manager proposes removing all mobile phones and chargers from every patient on the acute ward indefinitely. What does the Mental Health Act Code of Practice advise?
o: Apply the ban to detained patients and exempt informal patients
Apply the ban to every patient, as ward safety must come first
Apply the ban until the next CQC inspection has approved it
Avoid a blanket ban; restrict on individual risk and record it
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 8.5-8.7 and 8.19-8.20: blanket restrictions (including banning mobile phones and chargers) should be avoided unless justified as necessary and proportionate to individually identified risks; their impact on each patient should be documented. A blanket phone ban may breach Article 8.

n.0: Restricting by legal status is still a blanket restriction without individual risk assessment.
n.1: Safety concerns must be met by individualised, proportionate measures; a blanket ban may breach Article 8.
n.2: The CQC does not approve restrictions; they must be justified individually and authorised by hospital managers (COP15 8.9).

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Stella, 52, is an informal patient with capacity on an acute ward whose main door is locked for the safety of other patients. She asks whether she is allowed to go out. What is the correct response?
o: No, because the ward has a locked door policy for all patients
Yes, once her consultant has given written permission to go
No, unless she signs a form agreeing to be back within an hour
Yes, she may leave when she wishes; staff will open the door
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 8.11: an informal patient with capacity on a locked ward must be told the locked door policy, who to speak to if they wish to leave, and must be able to leave at any time unless held under section 5 or an application for detention is made.

n.0: A locked door cannot prevent an informal patient from leaving without legal authority.
n.1: An informal patient does not need a consultant's permission to leave.
n.2: Conditions such as a return time cannot be imposed on an informal patient's right to leave.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Staff need to search the belongings of Jake, 23, because there is a reasonable suspicion that he has brought illicit drugs onto the ward. According to NICE NG10, who should carry out the search?
o: Two staff members, at least one the same sex as Jake
One staff member of any sex, to minimise intrusion
Ward security staff, without nursing involvement
The police, as drugs are suspected
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.3: searches should be undertaken by two members of staff, at least one of whom is the same sex as the person being searched. NG10 1.3.4 adds seeking consent, explaining throughout, protecting dignity and recording.

n.1: NG10 recommends two staff, including one of the same sex, to protect the person and staff.
n.2: Searching is a clinical procedure carried out by trained staff under the organisation's policy, not by security alone.
n.3: Police involvement may follow local policy, but searching on the ward is by trained staff.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Before searching the room of Maria, 34, for suspected ligature materials, what should staff do first, in line with NICE NG10?
o: Ask another patient whether Maria has hidden anything in there
Remove all her belongings to the office and search them later
Give her the policy summary, seek consent and explain each step
Search while she is out at therapy so she is not upset by it
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.4: provide the summary of the search policy, seek consent, explain what is being done and why throughout, protect dignity and privacy, and record what was searched, why, how and the disposal of items.

n.0: Asking another patient breaches confidentiality and is not part of a lawful search process.
n.1: Wholesale removal of belongings is disproportionate and does not seek consent.
n.3: Searching without her knowledge bypasses consent and explanation required by NG10.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Femi, 37, detained under section 3, refuses to allow a search of his bag, which staff believe contains a knife. What does NICE NG10 recommend next?
o: Discharge him from the ward because he refused the search
Hold a multidisciplinary review of the need to use force
Return the bag to him, because he has refused the search
Search the bag by force immediately, before he can use it
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: NICE NG10 1.3.5: if a service user refuses to be searched, carry out a multidisciplinary review of the need to search using physical force and explore the consequences in advance; use physical force only as a last resort. If force is used, debrief and external review follow (1.3.6). Immediate danger is managed with de-escalation and the safety steps in 1.3.7-1.3.8.

n.0: Discharging a detained patient for refusing a search is not lawful or appropriate.
n.2: Ignoring a suspected weapon fails to manage risk to Femi and others.
n.3: Force should be a last resort after MDT review, not the first response.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: During a ward environmental check, a nurse finds that a new wardrobe in the bedroom of Kai, 20, who has recent suicidal thoughts, has a rail that could be used as a ligature point. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
o: Make Kai safe now (room or observation) and report it
Tell Kai not to use the rail and record that he agreed
Note the rail on the list for the next annual ligature audit
Remove the wardrobe herself using tools borrowed from estates
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: A newly identified ligature point is an immediate environmental risk. The nurse should mitigate it at once (for example a safer room or a change in observation) and report it through the local ligature and incident process so it can be removed. Ligature risk management is a key in-patient suicide prevention measure.

n.1: An agreement not to use the rail does not manage the risk and is not a safety measure.
n.2: Waiting for the annual audit leaves a known risk in place for a patient with suicidal thoughts.
n.3: Dismantling fittings without estates support risks injury and leaves debris; the risk should be mitigated and reported.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Sanjay, 45, detained under section 3, is recovering from psychosis and has a job interview next week. The team worries he may relapse under stress. Which approach best reflects positive risk-taking?
o: Refuse any leave until all risk of relapse has resolved
Agree escorted leave with a nurse waiting outside the interview
Plan the leave with him, with warning signs and a contingency
Ask his employer to postpone the interview until his discharge
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Positive risk-taking weighs potential benefits against harms and plans collaboratively with the person, using a contingency plan. This reflects the least restrictive and empowerment principles of the Code (COP15 ch1). The RC grants the leave under section 17.

n.0: Waiting for zero risk is unrealistic and unduly restrictive.
n.1: Escorting may be more restrictive than his risk requires and may undermine his chances.
n.3: Asking the employer to postpone breaches confidentiality and limits his recovery.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: A ward is short of staff on a Sunday. The nurse in charge suggests locking the door of the communal lounge so fewer staff are needed to supervise patients. What does the Code of Practice say?
o: Locking areas is acceptable if patients are told in advance
Locking clinical areas because of low staffing is not acceptable
Locking areas is acceptable on weekends
Locking areas is acceptable if recorded on Datix
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 8.13-8.14: hospitals should not lock patients in clinical areas simply because of inadequate staffing; safety should be ensured by adequate staffing, positive engagement and observation. The shortage should be escalated.

n.0: Telling patients in advance does not justify a restriction driven by staffing shortfall.
n.2: There is no weekend exception in the Code.
n.3: Recording an incident does not make a staffing-driven restriction acceptable.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Winston, 81, has Alzheimer's disease and severe depression with food refusal. He lacks capacity to decide on admission. The team agree that his care on a psychiatric ward will amount to a deprivation of liberty. He repeatedly says, 'I'm not going in there,' and pushes staff away. Which legal framework applies to admit him for treatment of his mental disorder?
o: A DoLS authorisation under the Mental Capacity Act
Sections 5 and 6 of the Mental Capacity Act
The Mental Health Act, because he objects to admission
Informal admission with his daughter's agreement
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: COP15 13.49-13.56 and Figure 5: where a person lacking capacity objects to admission or treatment for mental disorder in hospital, and meets section 2 or 3 criteria, they are ineligible for DoLS (MCA Schedule 1A) and only the Mental Health Act is available. Where in doubt, treat the person as objecting (13.51).

n.0: An objecting person who meets MHA criteria for hospital treatment of mental disorder is ineligible for DoLS (Schedule 1A).
n.1: Sections 5-6 protect acts of care but cannot authorise a deprivation of liberty (COP15 13.35).
n.3: A person lacking capacity who will be deprived of liberty should never be admitted informally (COP15 13.53), and a relative cannot consent for him.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Freya, 34, has schizophrenia and is becoming unwell. She has capacity to decide about admission, understands the risks and refuses to come into hospital. A colleague suggests a best interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act. What should the nurse explain?
o: She has capacity, so the MCA is unavailable; consider the MHA
The MCA applies if her nearest relative agrees to admission
The MCA can hold her for 72 hours while an AMHP is found
The MCA applies because her decision to refuse is unwise
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: The MCA applies only to people who lack capacity for the decision (MCA s1-2). A capable person's refusal of admission cannot be overridden under the MCA; an unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity (s1(4)). If MHA criteria are met, an MHA assessment is the lawful route (COP15 Figure 5).

n.1: The nearest relative has no power to authorise MCA best interests decisions.
n.2: There is no 72-hour MCA holding power; 72 hours relates to MHA s4 and s5(2).
n.3: An unwise decision does not mean a person lacks capacity (MCA s1(4)).

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Jasmine, 17, has severe anorexia nervosa. She has capacity under the Mental Capacity Act to decide about admission and refuses informal admission to a specialist unit. Her mother signs consent for the admission. What is the legal position?
o: Her capable refusal cannot be overridden by her mother's consent
Her mother's consent is enough to admit her informally
Her mother's consent is valid for her until Jasmine turns 18
Her mother can consent if two doctors agree admission is needed
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Section 131(4) of the Mental Health Act 1983 provides that where a 16- or 17-year-old has capacity and does not consent to informal admission, they cannot be admitted informally on the basis of consent from a person with parental responsibility. If admission is necessary, the MHA should be considered. For 16-17-year-olds, capacity is judged under the Mental Capacity Act (s131(5)).

n.1: Section 131(4) prevents parental consent overriding a capable 16-17-year-old's refusal.
n.2: Parental consent cannot override a capable 16-17-year-old's refusal of informal admission at any point before 18.
n.3: Medical agreement does not convert parental consent into authority; the MHA would be needed.

Restrictive Practice and Safety.q: Callum, 16, has capacity and wants to be admitted informally to an adolescent unit for severe depression. His father objects and says he will not allow it. What is the legal position?
o: Callum cannot be admitted while his father objects to it
His own consent is enough, despite his father's objection
Callum can be admitted under section 2 to resolve the dispute
Callum can be admitted once a court order has been obtained
Restrictive Practice and Safety.w: Under section 131(2)-(3), a 16- or 17-year-old with capacity can consent to informal admission even if a person with parental responsibility disagrees. The team should still involve and support his father.

n.0: Section 131 makes a capable 16-17-year-old's consent sufficient regardless of parental objection.
n.2: Detaining a consenting, capable young person to settle a family disagreement is not a proper use of section 2.
n.3: No court order is needed where a capable 16-17-year-old consents.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Wu, 38, has schizophrenia and is detained under section 3. She tells the nurse, 'The voices are part of my illness and the tablets help with them, but I don't need to be in hospital, I could manage at home.' How should her insight be recorded?
o: No insight, as she disagrees with the team's plan for her admission
Full insight, as she correctly names her illness and its treatment
Partial insight, as she accepts illness and medication but not admission
Insight not rated, as she is still hearing voices at present
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Insight is not all or nothing. Ms Wu recognises that her experiences are due to illness and that treatment helps, but does not accept the need for hospital care. This is partial insight, recorded with her own words under the insight heading of the MSE (FACTS s7).

n.0: She accepts that the voices are an illness and that medication helps, so 'no insight' understates her awareness.
n.1: Full insight would include accepting the need for the current treatment setting, which she does not.
n.3: Insight is rated whatever the current symptoms; ongoing voices do not prevent it being assessed.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Byrne, 45, is seen in a crisis assessment suite. He speaks very fast and loudly, and the nurse struggles to interrupt him. What he says stays on one topic, his job, and is logical and easy to follow. Which finding should the nurse record?
o: Flight of ideas, recorded under thought form
Perseveration, recorded under thought form
Pressure of speech, recorded under speech
Loosening of associations, recorded under thought form
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Pressure of speech is rapid, increased speech that is hard to interrupt and is recorded under speech (rate, volume, quantity). As his ideas stay on one logical topic, there is no evidence of a thought form disorder (FACTS s7).

n.0: Flight of ideas needs rapid shifts between topics; his content stays on one theme and is logical.
n.1: Perseveration is inappropriate repetition of the same word or idea, not rapid, logical speech.
n.3: Loosening of associations makes speech hard to follow; his content is easy to follow.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Ali, 23, is being assessed after a first presentation of psychosis. Several times he stops abruptly mid-sentence, stares ahead, then says he cannot remember what he was saying because his thoughts 'were taken out of my head'. How should the nurse record this?
o: Poverty of speech, recorded as a negative symptom of his psychosis
Loosening of associations, recorded under thought form as derailment
Thought block, with thought withdrawal recorded as a delusional belief
Distractibility, recorded under cognition as poor sustained attention
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A sudden break in the train of thought is thought block (thought form). His explanation that thoughts are removed from his head is thought withdrawal, a delusion of thought interference recorded under thought content. Recording both gives an accurate MSE (FACTS s7).

n.0: Poverty of speech is reduced quantity of speech overall, not an abrupt stop that he explains as thoughts being removed.
n.1: Derailment is a slide between loosely linked topics; Mr Ali's thought stops completely.
n.3: Distractibility describes attention drawn to other stimuli; he describes his thoughts being taken, which is not a cognitive deficit.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: During a mental state examination, Mr Hughes, 52, tells the nurse he hears a man's voice telling him to hurt his mother, who visits later today. He looks frightened and says he has managed to ignore it so far. What should the nurse do next?
o: Ask about the commands and his ability to resist, then inform the team now
Reassure him the voice is not real and move on to the next heading
Record it under perception and discuss it at tomorrow's ward round
Give his prescribed PRN antipsychotic and document the voice's content
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Command hallucinations to harm a named person need immediate exploration (content, frequency, intent, ability to resist, how he feels about them) and prompt escalation so that the team can formulate the risk and plan, including the planned visit. Risk is recorded alongside the MSE and acted on, not just documented (FACTS s6-7; NMC P3.3, P4.10).

n.1: Dismissing the experience damages engagement and leaves the risk unassessed.
n.2: Waiting until tomorrow leaves a risk to a named person, who visits today, without a plan.
n.3: PRN medication may form part of the plan, but exploring the risk and informing the team come first.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Reid, 50, is referred to a community mental health team with low mood. The nurse is completing a biopsychosocial assessment with him. Which information belongs in the social part of the assessment?
o: His thyroid function results and current medicines
His housing, debts and close relationships
His family history of bipolar disorder
His beliefs about himself and his coping style
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A biopsychosocial assessment considers biological factors (physical health, medicines, genetics), psychological factors (thoughts, beliefs, coping) and social factors (housing, money, work, relationships, support). Housing, debt and relationships are social factors (NMC P3.4).

n.0: Thyroid function and medicines are biological factors.
n.2: A family history of mental illness is a biological (genetic) vulnerability factor.
n.3: Beliefs about self and coping style are psychological factors.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: The nurse is writing a 5 Ps formulation with Ms Kerr, 27. She experienced neglect in childhood, became low after losing her job two months ago, now drinks wine every night to get to sleep and has stopped seeing friends. Her sister visits often and helps her. How should her nightly drinking be classified?
o: A precipitating factor
A predisposing factor
A protective factor
A perpetuating factor
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: In a 5 Ps formulation, perpetuating factors keep the problem going. Drinking to sleep and withdrawing from friends maintain low mood. Childhood neglect is predisposing, the job loss is precipitating, and her sister's support is protective.

n.0: The precipitating factor is the trigger, her job loss, not the drinking that followed.
n.1: Predisposing factors are longer-standing vulnerabilities, such as her childhood neglect.
n.2: Protective factors reduce the problem, such as her sister's support; nightly drinking maintains it.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Lewis, 44, completes a PHQ-9 questionnaire at his assessment with NHS Talking Therapies and scores 17. Using the threshold applied in NICE NG222, how is the severity of his depression categorised?
o: Less severe depression, as NICE uses a cut-off of 20
Severe depression, which means he needs referral for admission
Less severe depression, as a score of 17 counts as mild
More severe depression, as the score is 16 or more
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG222 groups subthreshold and mild depression as 'less severe' and moderate and severe as 'more severe', using a PHQ-9 score of 16 or more to indicate more severe depression. A scale score informs, but does not decide, the setting of care.

n.0: NG222 uses 16, not 20, as the threshold between less and more severe depression.
n.1: A PHQ-9 score does not determine admission; the decision rests on a full assessment of needs and safety.
n.2: A score of 17 is at or above 16, so it falls in more severe depression.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Doyle, 31, completes a PHQ-9 at a GP practice mental health clinic. Her total score is 8, but she scores 2 on the item about thoughts that she would be better off dead or of hurting herself. What should the nurse do next?
o: Ask her directly about suicidal thoughts and any plans today
Repeat the PHQ-9 at the next appointment to check the trend
Record mild depression and offer guided self-help materials
Ask her to complete a GAD-7 to check for co-existing anxiety
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A positive answer to the PHQ-9 item on thoughts of death or self-harm must be explored directly, whatever the total score. The scale is an aid; it does not measure risk, and the nurse needs to understand her thoughts, intent and plans and act on them (NICE NG225 1.6; NG222).

n.1: Waiting for the next appointment delays exploring possible suicidal thoughts.
n.2: Treating the total score alone overlooks her reported thoughts of death or self-harm.
n.3: Screening for anxiety does not address the thoughts of death she has just disclosed.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Ahmed, 36, has worried about everything for eight months and scores 13 on the GAD-7 questionnaire at her first appointment with a mental health nurse. How should the nurse interpret the score?
o: As minimal anxiety, as clinical concern starts at a score of 15
As a confirmed diagnosis of GAD, so an SSRI should be started
As a low suicide risk, as anxiety scores predict suicidal acts
As a probable anxiety disorder, needing a full clinical assessment
