Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A GAD-7 score of 10 or more suggests a probable anxiety disorder, but rating scales are aids to assessment: they support, and do not replace, a clinical assessment and diagnosis, and they do not predict suicide (NICE CG113; NG225 1.6).

n.0: A score of 13 is above the usual threshold of 10 for a probable anxiety disorder.
n.1: A screening score does not make a diagnosis or decide treatment; CG113 also offers psychological interventions before drugs.
n.2: Scales do not predict suicide; NG225 advises against using tools to predict suicide.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Fox, 48, is admitted to an acute mental health ward with depression. As part of his assessment he scores 22 on the AUDIT questionnaire and says he drinks from the morning onwards. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Give brief advice on drinking and repeat the AUDIT in a year
Record hazardous drinking and address it once his mood has improved
Assess dependence and withdrawal risk and seek specialist alcohol input
Advise him to stop drinking completely from today to help his mood
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: An AUDIT score above 15 indicates the need for a fuller assessment (NICE CG115 1.2.2.6), and scores of 20 or more suggest possible dependence. Morning drinking suggests dependence, so withdrawal risk must be assessed (for example with CIWA-Ar) and specialist advice sought before any reduction.

n.0: Brief advice suits lower-risk drinking; a score of 22 with morning drinking needs assessment now.
n.1: Delaying assessment risks unplanned withdrawal on the ward and ignores a factor maintaining his depression.
n.3: Stopping abruptly when dependent can cause seizures or delirium tremens; withdrawal must be assessed and planned.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: A student nurse asks why the community team writes a formulation for Mr Price, 39, rather than relying on his questionnaire scores. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: It gives a risk rating used to set his level of observation
It turns his symptoms into a score to compare with population norms
It replaces his diagnosis with a description agreed by the team
It explains how his difficulties developed and persist, to guide care
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A formulation is a shared, person-centred explanation of how a person's difficulties developed and are maintained, including strengths and protective factors. It guides the care plan (NICE CG178 care planning; NG225 1.6.6 on risk formulation; NMC P3.4).

n.0: Formulation is not a risk rating; NICE advises against global low, medium or high ratings to decide care.
n.1: Producing a score is the role of a rating scale, not a formulation.
n.2: A formulation sits alongside a diagnosis; it does not replace it.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Bell, 33, is admitted with psychosis. She says she was well until last week. Her partner, whom she has agreed the team can speak to, describes six months of her withdrawing from friends, sleeping poorly and stopping work. How should the nurse use this information?
o: Set the partner's account aside, as Ms Bell is the person assessed
Ask the partner to complete a depression questionnaire for her
Record the partner's account as collateral history beside her own
Use the partner's account in place of Ms Bell's, as more reliable
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Collateral history from a family member or carer, gathered with consent, adds to the person's own account and can reveal a prodromal period. Both views are recorded and the person remains at the centre of the assessment (NMC P3.4; NICE CG178; Triangle of Care).

n.0: She agreed to the contact, and the partner's information may show a significant prodrome.
n.1: Self-report questionnaires are completed by the person; a proxy score would not be valid.
n.3: Her own account remains central; collateral history adds to it rather than replacing it.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Jake, 19, is brought to his GP practice by his mother. For three weeks he has been hearing voices commenting on him, believes he is being followed and has stopped going to college. He has no previous contact with mental health services. What should the practice nurse advise the GP to do?
o: Start a low-dose antipsychotic today and review him in four weeks
Refer him without delay to the early intervention in psychosis service
Review him in three months to see whether the symptoms settle
Refer him to NHS Talking Therapies for a course of individual CBT
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE CG178 says early intervention in psychosis (EIP) services should be open to everyone with a first episode of psychosis and should assess people without delay. Antipsychotics should not be started in primary care for a first presentation unless in consultation with a consultant psychiatrist (CG178 1.3.2.1).

n.0: CG178 advises against starting antipsychotics for first-presentation psychosis in primary care without a consultant psychiatrist.
n.2: Delay prolongs untreated psychosis; CG178 requires assessment without delay.
n.3: Talking Therapies treats common mental health problems; first-episode psychosis needs specialist EIP care including CBT for psychosis.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Grant, 42, has bipolar disorder. Her sister reports that she has not slept for three nights, has spent thousands of pounds online and talks non-stop. Ms Grant tells the community nurse that she has been chosen to save the world. Which presentation is this most consistent with?
o: Agitated depression with guilt
Cyclothymia with elevated mood
Hypomania with grandiose ideas
Mania with psychotic features
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Elevated mood with reduced need for sleep, reckless spending and pressured speech, together with a grandiose delusion, indicates mania with psychotic features. Psychotic symptoms exclude hypomania. NICE CG185 advises urgent specialist assessment when mania is suspected.

n.0: Her mood is elevated and grandiose, not low, so agitated depression does not fit.
n.1: Cyclothymia is long-standing, milder mood instability without psychosis.
n.2: Hypomania does not include psychotic features or marked impairment; she has a grandiose delusion.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Evans, 76, is usually independent and has no psychiatric history. Over the last 24 hours on an older adults' ward he has started seeing insects on the walls, is unsure of the day and drifts in and out of conversation. What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Delirium, needing a 4AT and a search for a cause
Late-onset psychosis, needing an antipsychotic
Lewy body dementia, needing a memory clinic referral
Psychotic depression, needing a PHQ-9 and review
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Acute onset over hours, fluctuating attention, disorientation and visual hallucinations point to delirium, which is a medical emergency. NICE CG103 recommends assessment (the 4AT is widely used) and identifying and treating underlying causes such as infection, medicines or dehydration.

n.1: Psychosis rarely starts over hours with fluctuating attention in an older person with no history; an antipsychotic would also miss the physical cause.
n.2: Dementia develops over months; this change happened over a day.
n.3: There is no low mood reported, and a fluctuating, acute picture suggests delirium.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mrs Nolan, 58, has severe depression and is an informal inpatient. She has refused food and most fluids for three days, saying she is 'rotting inside' and deserves to die. Her urine output has fallen. What should the nurse do first?
o: Encourage fluids and review her intake at the end of the week
Record her beliefs as overvalued ideas in the care plan
Refer her for a course of high-intensity CBT on the ward
Escalate now for urgent medical and psychiatric review
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Nihilistic delusions with refusal of food and fluids indicate psychotic depression with both physical risk (dehydration, falling urine output) and suicide risk. This needs urgent escalation for medical and psychiatric review (NMC P4.10; NICE NG222 on psychotic depression).

n.0: Waiting several days risks serious dehydration and kidney injury.
n.1: A belief that she is rotting inside is a nihilistic delusion, not an overvalued idea, and recording it does not address the risk.
n.2: Psychological therapy cannot address the immediate physical danger and suicide risk.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Liam, 22, is brought to the emergency department by friends. He has used cocaine over the weekend, has not slept and believes people are trying to kill him. His heart rate is 128 beats per minute and his temperature 38.4 C. What should the mental health liaison nurse do first?
o: Give oral haloperidol to reduce his paranoid ideas
Refer him to the drug service for follow-up next week
Arrange admission to a psychiatric ward for his psychosis
Make sure he has full observations and a medical review
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Tachycardia and fever after stimulant use may indicate stimulant toxicity, which is a physical emergency. Physical assessment and medical review come before psychiatric care planning (NMC P4.10: recognise and escalate physical deterioration).

n.0: Giving an antipsychotic without medical review risks harm, as antipsychotics can affect temperature regulation and heart rhythm.
n.1: Follow-up may help later, but his abnormal observations need assessment now.
n.2: A psychiatric admission before medical assessment could miss life-threatening stimulant toxicity.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Anna, 31, has bipolar disorder and a relapse plan she wrote with her community nurse. Her early warning signs are sleeping less, writing through the night and becoming irritable. At a home visit she says she has slept four hours a night this week and has started a novel. What should the nurse do?
o: Recognise her early warning signs and follow the agreed relapse plan
Advise her to take extra lithium tonight to settle her sleep
Reassure her that a few short nights are common and review in a month
Advise her to stop her medication for a week to see if it is the cause
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Early warning signs in a person's relapse signature allow early action. Acting on the plan agreed with Anna (for example increased contact, sleep strategies, medication review with the prescriber) respects her expertise and reduces the risk of full relapse (NICE CG185 on relapse prevention).

n.1: Changing a lithium dose needs a prescriber and level monitoring; extra doses risk toxicity.
n.2: Her own early warning signs are present; waiting a month risks a full manic relapse.
n.3: Stopping medication suddenly increases relapse risk; lithium in particular should be withdrawn gradually.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Doran, 35, tells his practice nurse that for five days he has felt full of energy, needs only four hours of sleep and is more productive at work. His colleagues have noticed but he is working normally. There are no unusual beliefs or perceptual experiences. Which description fits best?
o: Hypomania, as there is no marked impairment or psychosis
Cyclothymia, as his mood has been raised for under a week
Mania, as his mood has been elevated for more than four days
Mania, as he is sleeping much less than he usually does
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Hypomania is elevated mood and activity lasting at least four days without marked impairment of functioning and without psychotic features. Mania involves marked impairment, psychosis or hospitalisation, and usually lasts at least a week (standard diagnostic criteria; NICE CG185 distinguishes mania and hypomania).

n.1: Cyclothymia is a pattern of mood instability over at least two years, not a single five-day episode.
n.2: Four days of elevated mood is the hypomania duration; mania also needs marked impairment, psychosis or admission.
n.3: Reduced need for sleep occurs in both hypomania and mania, so it does not decide between them.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: A community mental health nurse takes a call from Ms Rowe, 25, who is known to the team. She says she took 40 paracetamol tablets an hour ago after an argument, now regrets it and feels physically fine. What should the nurse advise?
o: Wait at home for a crisis team visit later this afternoon
Monitor herself at home, as she feels physically well
Book an urgent GP appointment for tomorrow morning
Go to the emergency department now, by ambulance if needed
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Paracetamol overdose may cause no early symptoms while liver damage develops, and treatment depends on blood levels and timing. She needs emergency medical assessment now (NICE NG225 1.7.4; BNF/TOXBASE emergency treatment of poisoning), with psychosocial assessment alongside physical care.

n.0: Waiting delays time-critical assessment and treatment for paracetamol poisoning.
n.1: Feeling well does not exclude serious paracetamol toxicity, which often has no early symptoms.
n.2: Waiting until tomorrow could miss the window for effective treatment.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Hart, 47, is seen by a mental health nurse after telling his GP he has thought about ending his life. The nurse completes a psychosocial assessment and writes a risk formulation. Which content best describes a risk formulation as NICE NG225 intends it?
o: A total score from a validated suicide risk scale, placed in a band
His historic, current, future and protective factors, linked to a plan
A list of his diagnoses and the medicines prescribed for each one
A rating of low, medium or high risk with a review date
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 says mental health professionals should undertake a risk formulation in every psychosocial assessment, exploring historic, changeable and current, future and protective factors (1.5.10, 1.6.6), and focusing on the person's needs and safety rather than a prediction.

n.0: NG225 1.6.1 advises against using risk tools and scales to predict suicide.
n.2: Diagnoses and medicines may inform the formulation, but on their own they do not explain his risk or guide a plan.
n.3: Global low, medium or high risk stratification is not recommended for predicting suicide or deciding care (NG225 1.6.3-1.6.4).

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Ellis, 55, is under the community mental health team after a suicide attempt. During his psychosocial assessment he mentions that the final hearing in his divorce is next Tuesday. Under NICE NG225, how should this be recorded in his formulation?
o: As a protective factor
As a historic factor
As a fixed static factor
As a future factor
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.5.10 asks assessors to explore historic, changeable and current, and future factors, including specific upcoming events or circumstances, plus protective factors. An upcoming court hearing is a future factor that may raise distress and should shape the plan around that date.

n.0: A stressful hearing is not protective; protective factors reduce risk, such as supportive relationships.
n.1: Historic factors are past events, such as a previous suicide attempt.
n.2: Static factors cannot change; a dated upcoming event is a future, time-specific factor.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Quinn, 40, was admitted to an acute mental health ward after a suicide attempt and is being discharged home today. Her risk formulation identifies an ongoing risk of suicide. Under NICE NG53, when should she be followed up after discharge?
o: Within 48 hours of discharge
At her first outpatient clinic
Within 7 days of discharge
Within 14 days, by her GP
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG53 says follow up a person within 7 days of discharge, and within 48 hours if a risk of suicide has been identified (1.6.7-1.6.8). The period soon after discharge carries high suicide risk.

n.1: An outpatient clinic may be weeks away, leaving the highest-risk period without contact.
n.2: Seven days is the general standard; an identified suicide risk needs follow-up within 48 hours.
n.3: NG53 suggests a GP appointment within 2 weeks in addition to, not instead of, early follow-up.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Byrne, 63, has been an inpatient with severe depression for three weeks and has been very distressed. Today he seems calm, has given his watch to another patient and thanks staff 'for everything'. A colleague suggests reducing his observation level. What should the nurse do?
o: Begin planning his discharge as he is recovering
Agree, as his mood has clearly improved today
Explore with him now what the change means
Record an improved mood and continue the plan
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A sudden, unexplained change after weeks of severe distress, together with giving away belongings and thanking staff 'for everything', may signal a decision to end his life rather than recovery. NICE NG10 1.4.17 says decisions on observation levels take into account the person's current mental state and current risk assessment, and NG225 1.6.5 focuses assessment on his safety, so the nurse should explore the change with him now and share concerns with the team before any change to observations (NMC P3.10).

n.0: Discharge planning on these facts ignores warning signs of suicidal intent.
n.1: Reducing observations on the basis of apparent calm could remove support at a time of high risk.
n.3: Recording 'improved mood' without exploring the warning signs leaves the risk unassessed.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: A ward manager asks a newly registered nurse why the trust no longer uses a suicide risk scale to allocate low, medium or high risk to patients. Which explanation is most accurate?
o: Scales take too long to complete properly in busy clinical areas
Scales are completed and interpreted by psychiatrists
Scales are validated for teenagers but not for adults
Scales predict poorly, and many who die were judged at low risk
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG225 (1.6) advises against using risk tools, scales or global risk stratification to predict suicide or to decide treatment or discharge, because they have poor predictive value. National confidential inquiry data show most patients who die by suicide were judged at low risk at their last contact.

n.0: The reason is poor predictive value, not the time taken.
n.1: Who completes the scale is irrelevant; NG225 advises against their use for prediction by anyone.
n.2: There is no such age-based validation; NG225 applies to all ages.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mrs Lowe, 74, attends the emergency department after taking an overdose of her husband's tablets. She says it was 'a silly mistake' and wants to go home. She has arthritis, lives with her husband and has been low since a recent fall. Which approach to her assessment is most appropriate?
o: A brief screen, as overdoses in later life are mostly impulsive
Defer assessment until a memory clinic has ruled out dementia
Discharge with a GP letter, as she calls the overdose an accident
Psychosocial assessment by a clinician experienced with older people
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG225 1.5.12: older people who self-harm should be assessed by a professional experienced in assessing older people, paying attention to depression, cognitive impairment, physical ill health and frailty, and recognising higher rates of suicide after self-harm in older people.

n.0: Self-harm in older people carries higher suicide risk and needs full assessment, not a brief screen.
n.1: Cognitive assessment can be part of the psychosocial assessment; delaying it until a memory clinic leaves her risk unassessed.
n.2: Her account does not replace a psychosocial assessment, which NG225 says should happen at the earliest opportunity.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Price, 29, has been on an acute ward for six weeks after self-harm. She asks for unescorted time off the ward to visit her daughter, and the team considers this as therapeutic risk-taking. Under NICE NG225, which condition should be met first?
o: Her parents sign to accept responsibility for her safety
Her risk scale score has fallen from the high into the low band
It follows a psychosocial assessment and is agreed with the team
A senior nurse has rated her as low risk on the ward form
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.14: therapeutic risk-taking should only be used after a psychosocial assessment, involve the relevant professionals, draw on the person's strengths and what matters to them, focus on positive outcomes and be revisited as part of ongoing assessment.

n.0: Responsibility for the clinical decision stays with the team; families cannot take it on by signing a form.
n.1: Risk scales should not be used to decide treatment (NG225 1.6.2).
n.3: Global low, medium or high ratings should not determine care (NG225 1.6.4).

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Ward, 36, tells his community mental health nurse that he has thought about suicide every day this week. He is calm and talking openly. To build his risk formulation, what should the nurse explore next?
o: His plans, intent, access to means and what has stopped him
Whether he will agree to a no-harm contract today
His PHQ-9 score, to place him in a risk category
Whether his GP already knows, before asking anything more
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: After suicidal thoughts are disclosed, the nurse explores plans, intent, access to means and protective factors (what has kept him safe). This builds the risk formulation and safety plan (NICE NG225 1.5.10, 1.6.5-1.6.6, 1.7.1).

n.1: No-harm contracts are not an evidence-based safety measure and do not replace assessment and a safety plan.
n.2: Questionnaire scores should not be used to categorise suicide risk (NG225 1.6).
n.3: Pausing to check what the GP knows delays the assessment the nurse is in a position to do now.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Jones, 24, is in a busy emergency department cubicle after cutting her forearm. The mental health liaison nurse arrives to carry out her psychosocial assessment. Ms Jones asks quietly whether a woman could do the assessment, because she does not want to talk to a man. What should happen?
o: Assess her in the cubicle with the curtain closed to avoid delay
Ask her to wait until the morning when more staff will be on duty
Arrange a private room and offer a female clinician to assess her
Explain that the clinician on duty is the one who must assess her
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG225 says psychosocial assessment should take place in a private, designated area where the person cannot be overheard, with the option of a healthcare professional of the same sex when the person requests this (1.5, 1.7.15).

n.0: A curtained cubicle does not allow her to speak in confidence without being overheard.
n.1: The assessment should happen at the earliest opportunity, not be put off overnight.
n.3: NG225 provides for a same-sex assessor on request; refusing it may stop her disclosing.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Dale, 28, has attended the emergency department 12 times in three months after self-harm. At a team meeting a colleague suggests asking the police for a community protection notice to reduce her attendances. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask security to direct her to her GP the next time she attends
Offer physical treatment and withhold assessment until she engages
Support the notice, as frequent attendance blocks care for others
Arrange a multidisciplinary review with her to agree a joint plan
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG225 1.7.5 says not to use aversive, punitive or criminal justice approaches such as community protection notices for frequent self-harm. For frequent episodes, 1.5.17 recommends a multidisciplinary review with the person to agree a joint plan, a care coordinator, a care plan and a safety plan.

n.0: Turning her away from the department is a punitive approach and leaves her needs unassessed.
n.1: Withholding assessment is punitive; a liaison professional should see her at every attendance (NG225 1.7.14).
n.2: NG225 specifically advises against community protection notices and other criminal justice approaches for frequent self-harm.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Cole, 22, has self-harmed by cutting several times a week for a year. At her community appointment she asks the nurse whether there is a tablet she could take to stop the urges. Which response is in line with NICE NG225?
o: Ask the prescriber about starting an SSRI to reduce the urges
Explain that naltrexone is the first-line medicine for self-harm
Explain no tablet treats self-harm itself, and discuss therapy
Ask the prescriber for PRN lorazepam to take when urges arise
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.10: do not offer drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm. Instead offer a structured, CBT-informed psychological intervention tailored to self-harm (1.11.3), while treating any coexisting condition in line with its own guideline.

n.0: An SSRI might treat coexisting depression, but NG225 does not recommend drugs to reduce self-harm itself.
n.1: No medicine, including naltrexone, is recommended as a treatment for self-harm.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are not a treatment for self-harm and may disinhibit and add overdose risk.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Stone, 35, has self-harmed three times this year. After his psychosocial assessment, the community team plans his treatment. Which psychological intervention does NICE NG225 recommend for adults who self-harm?
o: Single-session psychological debriefing after each new episode
Dialectical behaviour therapy adapted for adolescents
Psychodynamic psychotherapy lasting at least 12 months
A structured CBT-informed intervention, usually 4 to 10 sessions
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.3: offer a structured, person-centred, CBT-informed psychological intervention (for example CBT or problem-solving therapy) tailored for adults who self-harm, starting as soon as possible and typically lasting 4 to 10 sessions.

n.0: Debriefing after each episode is not a recommended self-harm treatment.
n.1: DBT-A is considered for young people with significant emotional dysregulation and frequent self-harm, not adults.
n.2: Long-term psychodynamic therapy is not the intervention NG225 recommends for self-harm.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Leah, 15, is under the children and young people's mental health service. She self-harms several times a week and has intense, rapidly changing emotions that she finds hard to manage. Which intervention should the team consider under NICE NG225?
o: Psychological debriefing sessions with her family
Fluoxetine with a monthly medication review
A CBT-informed programme designed for adults
Dialectical behaviour therapy adapted for adolescents
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.4: for children and young people with significant emotional dysregulation difficulties who have frequent episodes of self-harm, consider dialectical behaviour therapy adapted for adolescents (DBT-A), taking age and any transition into account.

n.0: Psychological debriefing is not a recommended intervention for self-harm.
n.1: Drug treatment is not offered as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm (1.11.10).
n.2: The CBT-informed intervention in 1.11.3 is specified for adults.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Ross, 26, is an inpatient engaged in recovery-focused care. He is not yet able to resist the urge to cut and asks whether the ward can give him clean blades so that he can do it more safely. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Supply sterile blades so that his self-harm is less risky
Remove his belongings and place him on continuous observation
Discuss wound care and delaying strategies, agreed with the team
Tell him that further self-harm will lead to his discharge
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 makes no recommendation on 'safer self-harm'. For someone in ongoing care who cannot yet resist urges, harm minimisation may be considered as part of overall recovery-focused care, agreed with the person and the multidisciplinary team, and includes wound hygiene and aftercare, distraction, coping and delaying strategies (1.11.11-1.11.12).

n.0: NG225 does not recommend providing means for 'safer self-harm'.
n.1: Blanket removal and continuous observation are restrictive; NG225 asks for the least restrictive measures, decided with the person (1.12.5-1.12.6).
n.3: Threatening discharge is a punitive approach that NG225 advises against.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Hill, 19, is on a general medical ward after self-harm, and the mental health and ward teams agree she needs close observation tonight. The ward is short-staffed, and the nurse in charge suggests asking the hospital security officer to sit with her. What should the nurse do?
o: Agree, as the security officer is available and nearby
Ask her mother to stay overnight and observe her
Request a member of staff trained in clinical observation
Ask a first-year student nurse to observe her instead
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NICE NG225 1.12.2: do not use staff who are untrained in clinical observation, such as security staff or trainees, to observe a person who has self-harmed. Observation should be by appropriately skilled and trained staff, engaging with the person (1.7.23, 1.14.4).

n.0: NG225 names security staff as unsuitable to undertake clinical observation.
n.1: Family may support her, but responsibility for clinical observation stays with trained staff.
n.3: Trainee staff are also named as unsuitable to undertake these observations.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Grey, 45, has twice taken overdoses of her prescribed antidepressant. She is now well engaged with her community nurse, and her GP plans to continue sertraline. Which prescribing approach best reflects NICE NG225?
o: Prescribe three months' supply to reduce visits to the surgery
Ask her partner to hold the tablets without discussing it with her
Agree smaller, weekly supplies with her through shared decisions
Switch her to a tricyclic antidepressant to improve her mood
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.13.1-1.13.2: consider toxicity in overdose (tricyclics are more dangerous) and use shared decision-making to discuss limiting the quantity supplied, for example weekly prescriptions, and returning unwanted medicines.

n.0: A large supply increases access to a means of overdose.
n.1: Changes should be agreed through shared decision-making, not arranged behind her back.
n.3: Tricyclic antidepressants are more toxic in overdose, which NG225 asks prescribers to take into account.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: A community mental health nurse is developing a safety plan with Ms Evans, 33, who has self-harmed after arguments with her partner. Which content best reflects what NICE NG225 says a safety plan should include?
o: Her risk score and the date of the next risk reassessment
A signed promise from her that she will not self-harm again
Her triggers, warning signs, coping strategies and crisis contacts
A list of the restrictions staff will apply if she self-harms
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.7: a safety plan recognises triggers and warning signs, identifies individual coping strategies, social contacts and settings for distraction, people who can help, contact details for services including out of hours, and ways to keep the environment safe.

n.0: Risk scores are not used to predict or decide care (NG225 1.6) and are not part of a safety plan.
n.1: A no-harm promise is not a safety plan and offers no strategies or contacts in a crisis.
n.3: A safety plan is a collaborative problem-solving tool, not a list of restrictions.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Patel, 44, has a safety plan that lists his care coordinator's office number, staffed 9am to 5pm. He tells the nurse that his urges to harm himself are worst late at night. How should the plan be improved?
o: Add out-of-hours crisis numbers and emergency contacts
Add the ward phone number so he can ask for admission
Advise him to wait until the team opens the next morning
Advise him to attend his GP practice when his distress rises
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.7 says a safety plan should include contact details for the mental health service, including out-of-hours services and emergency contact details, so that help is available when crises happen.

n.1: Ringing an inpatient ward to request admission is not a crisis pathway and may not offer support.
n.2: Waiting overnight leaves him without support at the time his risk is highest.
n.3: His GP practice is closed late at night, when his urges are worst.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Ali, 20, has written a safety plan with her nurse. She would like her sister and her care team to have a copy, but does not want her parents, with whom she lives, to see it. What should the nurse do?
o: Share it with her parents, as they are her next of kin
Give a copy to everyone in her household to keep her safe
Share it with her sister and the professionals she agrees to
Keep it in the team's records so no family members see it
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.11.8: the safety plan is held by the person and shared with family, carers and relevant professionals as decided by the person, so that it is accessible in a crisis. Ms Ali has capacity to decide who sees it.

n.0: 'Next of kin' gives no right to see her plan; she has chosen not to share it with her parents.
n.1: Sharing with her whole household overrides her decision about her parents.
n.3: She wants her sister to have a copy, and the plan should be accessible to her supporters in a crisis.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Young, 51, is being discharged today from an acute mental health ward to the care of the community team. Under NICE NG53, what should the hospital psychiatrist make sure happens with his GP?
o: A discharge letter is posted to the GP within 14 days
The GP is phoned at the first outpatient review
A discharge letter is emailed to the GP within 24 hours
Mr Young takes a copy of his drug chart to the GP
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG53 1.6.3: at discharge, within 24 hours a discharge letter is emailed to the person's GP (copy to the person), and within 24 hours the latest care plan goes to everyone involved; a fuller discharge summary follows within a week.

n.0: Fourteen days by post is too slow; NG53 sets 24 hours by email.
n.1: Waiting for an outpatient review leaves the GP without information during the high-risk early period.
n.3: A drug chart is not a discharge letter, and the responsibility sits with the hospital team.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Rae, 38, is in crisis with suicidal thoughts after a bereavement. She has no plan, wants to stay at home with her children and her mother has moved in to help. Her community nurse believes she needs intensive support this week. Which service is most appropriate?
o: Admission to an acute ward under section 2
NHS Talking Therapies guided self-help
A routine outpatient review in four weeks
The crisis resolution and home treatment team
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Crisis resolution and home treatment teams provide intensive support at home as an alternative to admission, which suits her wishes, support and level of need. This is the least restrictive option that meets her needs (MHA Code of Practice guiding principles; NICE CG178 1.4 for acute episodes).

n.0: Detention is not justified when intensive community care can meet her needs and she is engaging.
n.1: Low-intensity guided self-help is not suitable for a crisis with suicidal thoughts.
n.2: Four weeks is too long to wait when she needs intensive support this week.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: While developing a safety plan, Mr Reed, 52, a farmer, says that he holds a shotgun licence and keeps two guns at home. He has thought about using one when his distress is at its worst. What should the nurse do?
o: Discuss removing the guns with him and agree where they go
Advise him to keep the guns locked in their cabinet at home
Ask his wife to hide the cabinet key where he cannot find it
Record the guns and review them at his next appointment
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG225 1.7.1 and 1.11.7: establish the means of self-harm and, if accessible, discuss removing it through therapeutic collaboration, and keep the environment safe by working together to remove or restrict lethal means.

n.1: A locked cabinet in his home still gives him access to the guns.
n.2: Covert arrangements undermine trust and are not collaborative means restriction.
n.3: Waiting until the next appointment leaves lethal means available now.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Ford, 27, is preparing to leave an acute ward. The nurse is completing the care plan that will be sent to everyone supporting her after discharge. Which content does NICE NG53 say this plan should include?
o: The ward rules she agreed to follow on admission
Her possible relapse signs and where to go in a crisis
Her risk band and the scale used to calculate it
A record of incidents and restraint during her stay
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG53 1.5.20: the discharge care plan should include possible relapse signs, recovery goals, who to contact, where to go in a crisis, medication, physical health needs and the date of review, and a copy goes to everyone involved in her support.

n.0: Ward rules are not relevant to her support in the community.
n.2: Risk bands from scales should not determine care (NICE NG225 1.6) and are not part of the NG53 care plan.
n.3: Incident records are kept in her notes; the discharge plan focuses on recovery and crisis support.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mrs Shah, 66, lives with her husband, who is her main carer, and is due to be discharged from a mental health ward on Friday. She agrees that he can be involved. Her husband had a hip replacement during her admission. What should the nurse do?
o: Involve him, check his current needs and confirm the date early
Leave contact with her husband to the community team
Plan discharge around the support he gave her before admission
Inform her husband on Friday when she is ready to leave
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: NG53 1.5.22-1.5.23: recognise that carers' circumstances may have changed since admission, let carers know about discharge plans, discuss progress and readiness, and make sure they know the likely discharge date well in advance.

n.1: The inpatient team should involve carers in discharge planning, not defer it.
n.2: His hip surgery may have changed what support he can give, so the plan must reflect his current circumstances.
n.3: Telling him on the day does not allow planning; NG53 asks for the date to be known well in advance.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Okafor, 34, is admitted to an acute mental health ward. During his mental state examination he says, 'I feel fine, really happy.' He sits slumped, is tearful at times, makes little eye contact and speaks slowly and quietly. How should the nurse record this?
o: Mood and affect both recorded as euthymic until a rating scale is done
Mood recorded as low, because observation outweighs his own account
Affect recorded as happy, matching the words he uses about himself
Mood reported as happy, with an observed low affect that is incongruent
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: In the mental state examination (MSE) mood is the person's subjective report in their own words, and affect is what the clinician observes, including range and whether it matches the reported mood (congruence). Recording both, and noting the mismatch, gives the most accurate picture (FACTS s7; NMC P3.3).

n.0: Euthymic means normal mood; a rating scale does not replace recording what he says and what is observed.
n.1: Mood is defined by the person's own account, so it is recorded as he describes it; the nurse's observation belongs under affect.
n.2: Affect is the observed emotional state; his slumped, tearful presentation is not a happy affect.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Ms Patel, 29, is admitted with suspected mania. She speaks rapidly: 'I came by bus, bus stop, stop the war, war and peace, piece of cake, I baked a cake for the queen.' The nurse can follow how each idea links to the next through rhymes and puns. Which term best describes her thought form?
o: Thought block
Flight of ideas
Circumstantiality
Loosening of associations
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: Flight of ideas is rapid thinking in which topics shift quickly but the links can be followed, often through rhymes, puns or chance associations (clang associations). It is typical of mania and is recorded under thought form in the MSE (FACTS s7).

n.0: Thought block is a sudden interruption of the train of thought, not rapid, connected shifting.
n.2: Circumstantiality is over-inclusive detail that eventually reaches the point, not rapid jumps between topics.
n.3: In loosening of associations the links between ideas cannot be understood; here the nurse can follow each connection.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Green, 70, is in a dimly lit bay at night. He calls the nurse because a man is standing by the door. When the light is switched on, he laughs and says it is his coat hanging on the hook. How should this experience be described in his mental state examination?
o: A persecutory delusion
A pseudohallucination
An illusion
A visual hallucination
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: An illusion is a misperception of a real external stimulus (the coat), often in poor lighting, fatigue or delirium. A hallucination is a perception without any external stimulus. Both are recorded under perception in the MSE (FACTS s7).

n.0: A delusion is a fixed false belief; he corrected his perception as soon as the light came on.
n.1: A pseudohallucination is experienced as arising in the inner mind and recognised as not real; it is not a misperception of an object.
n.3: A hallucination occurs without an external stimulus; here a real object (the coat) was misperceived.

Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.q: Mr Adeyemi, 41, is firmly convinced that his neighbours have placed a transmitter in his wall to read his thoughts. When told that the landlord searched and found nothing, he says the neighbours removed it in the night. Under which mental state examination heading should the belief itself be recorded?
o: Cognition, as an impairment of orientation and memory
Thought form, as a disorder of the flow of thinking
Perception, as an auditory hallucination
Thought content, as a delusion
Assessment, Risk and Self-harm.w: A delusion is a fixed, false belief held with conviction despite evidence to the contrary and out of keeping with the person's cultural background. It is recorded under thought content, alongside overvalued ideas and obsessions (FACTS s7).

n.0: Nothing suggests disorientation or memory loss; the belief is a disturbance of thought content.
n.1: Thought form describes how thoughts are linked, for example flight of ideas; his belief concerns what he thinks.
n.2: He describes a belief, not hearing a voice or sound; perception covers hallucinations and illusions.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Ade, 26, has taken risperidone for six months. She tells the nurse her periods have stopped and she has noticed a milky discharge from her breasts. A pregnancy test is negative. Which side effect best explains her symptoms?
o: Weight gain disrupting her ovarian function
Low thyroid hormone caused by risperidone
Raised prolactin from dopamine D2 blockade
Antimuscarinic effects on her breast tissue
Psychopharmacology.w: Dopamine inhibits prolactin release, so dopamine-blocking antipsychotics raise prolactin. Risperidone is among those most likely to cause symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia: amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and reduced bone density (BNF). It should be reported for review.

n.0: Weight gain does not explain galactorrhoea; the combination points to raised prolactin.
n.1: Risperidone is not a recognised cause of hypothyroidism; that is a lithium effect.
n.3: Antimuscarinic effects cause dry mouth and constipation, not breast milk production.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Clarke, 45, has just been admitted to an acute mental health ward with psychosis and has a diagnosis of high blood pressure. The team plans to start an antipsychotic. Which investigation should be offered before the first dose, in addition to the baseline bloods?
o: An EEG to assess his seizure threshold
A bone density scan for prolactin effects
A chest X-ray to assess his heart size
An ECG, given his admission and hypertension
Psychopharmacology.w: NICE CG178 1.3.6.2: offer an ECG before starting antipsychotics if the SPC specifies it, if examination identifies cardiovascular risk such as hypertension, if there is a personal history of cardiovascular disease, or if the person is being admitted as an inpatient. Mr Clarke meets two criteria.

n.0: An EEG is not a routine baseline test before starting an antipsychotic.
n.1: Bone density is not a baseline test; prolactin is measured by blood test at baseline.
n.2: A chest X-ray is not part of the baseline antipsychotic checks and does not assess QT interval.

Psychopharmacology.q: A prescriber plans to start haloperidol for Mr Grant, 33, and asks the nurse whether procyclidine should be prescribed regularly from the first dose 'to stop side effects'. Which response best reflects BNF advice?
o: Use it if EPSE occur, not as routine prevention
Prescribe it regularly to prevent tardive dyskinesia
Prescribe it for everyone on a first-generation drug
Give it before each dose to prevent akathisia
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF says antimuscarinic drugs such as procyclidine can relieve parkinsonism and dystonia but should not be prescribed routinely as prophylaxis. They do not help tardive dyskinesia, and antimuscarinic side effects add to the burden.

n.1: Antimuscarinics do not prevent or treat tardive dyskinesia and may worsen it.
n.2: Routine prophylaxis for all first-generation drugs is not recommended.
n.3: Procyclidine is not an effective prevention for akathisia.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Hill, 72, started haloperidol six weeks ago for late-onset psychosis. Staff notice that she now shuffles when she walks, has a tremor in her right hand, is slow to start moving and has fallen once. What should the nurse do?
o: Record tardive dyskinesia and continue the current dose
Refer her to a neurologist for new Parkinson's disease
Report possible parkinsonism so her antipsychotic is reviewed
Give PRN procyclidine and continue the haloperidol unchanged
Psychopharmacology.w: Drug-induced parkinsonism (bradykinesia, tremor, rigidity) appears gradually, is more common in older women and increases falls risk. The BNF advises reviewing treatment to reduce exposure to high-dose, high-potency antipsychotics when parkinsonism is identified.

n.0: Tardive dyskinesia is orofacial involuntary movement after long-term use, not shuffling and tremor at six weeks.
n.1: The timing after starting haloperidol makes a drug cause likely; the first step is a medication review.
n.3: Adding an antimuscarinic in an older person without reviewing the cause adds confusion and falls risk.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Okoro, 34, started haloperidol five days ago on an acute mental health ward. He is now confused and sweating, his limbs are stiff throughout, his temperature is 39.2 C, his pulse is 124 and his blood pressure keeps changing between readings. Which complication of his medication is most likely?
o: Serotonin syndrome from interaction
Acute dystonic reaction to haloperidol
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) toxicity
Psychopharmacology.w: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is hyperthermia, fluctuating consciousness, muscle rigidity and autonomic dysfunction (tachycardia, labile blood pressure, sweating). It is rare but potentially fatal and can occur with any antipsychotic (BNF psychoses treatment summary).

n.0: Serotonin syndrome follows serotonergic drugs and features clonus and hyperreflexia; he has started an antipsychotic.
n.1: Acute dystonia is a localised muscle spasm; it does not cause fever, confusion or autonomic instability.
n.3: Antimuscarinic toxicity causes dry, flushed skin rather than sweating and does not cause generalised rigidity.

Psychopharmacology.q: A nurse on a mental health ward suspects neuroleptic malignant syndrome in Ms Burke, 41, who takes olanzapine. Her temperature is 38.9 C, she is rigid and drowsy, and her pulse is 118. Her next olanzapine dose is due now. What should the nurse do first?
o: Give the dose and recheck her observations in four hours
Withhold the olanzapine and get an urgent medical review
Give paracetamol and review her temperature in an hour
Give PRN procyclidine to relieve her muscle rigidity
Psychopharmacology.w: NMS is a medical emergency. The antipsychotic should be stopped (BNF: for at least 5 days and until symptoms resolve) and urgent medical assessment arranged, as the person may need transfer to acute medical care (NMC P4.10).

n.0: Giving more antipsychotic may worsen NMS, and four-hourly observations are too infrequent.
n.2: Paracetamol does not treat NMS and delays the essential steps of stopping the drug and escalating.
n.3: Procyclidine treats dystonia and parkinsonism; it does not treat NMS.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Field, 46, takes both an antipsychotic and an SSRI. She becomes febrile, sweaty and agitated, and the team must decide between neuroleptic malignant syndrome and serotonin toxicity. Which finding points most towards neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
o: Lead-pipe rigidity developing over days
Onset within hours of a dose increase
Inducible clonus with brisk reflexes
Shivering with diarrhoea and dilated pupils
Psychopharmacology.w: NMS usually develops over days with generalised 'lead-pipe' rigidity and slowed reflexes. Serotonin toxicity develops within hours of starting, increasing or combining serotonergic drugs, with neuromuscular excitability such as clonus, hyperreflexia, tremor and myoclonus, plus shivering and diarrhoea (BNF antidepressant treatment summary).

n.1: Rapid onset within hours is typical of serotonin toxicity.
n.2: Clonus and hyperreflexia are characteristic of serotonin toxicity.
n.3: Shivering, diarrhoea and dilated pupils are features of serotonin toxicity.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Price, 52, on a mental health ward, is rigid and confused after starting an antipsychotic. His observations are: respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96% on air, blood pressure 150/92, pulse 118, temperature 39.3 C, and new confusion. What is his NEWS2 score and the response required?
o: 11, needing six-hourly observations
6, needing an urgent ward review
9, needing an emergency response
4, needing hourly observations
Psychopharmacology.w: NEWS2: respiratory rate 21-24 = 2, SpO2 96% = 0, air = 0, systolic 150 = 0, pulse 111-130 = 2, new confusion = 3, temperature 39.1 or above = 2; total 9. A score of 7 or more triggers an emergency response, which on a mental health unit usually means emergency transfer to acute care (RCP NEWS2).

n.0: The total is 9, and any score of 7 or more needs an emergency response, not six-hourly observations.
n.1: The total is 9, not 6; new confusion alone scores 3.
n.3: The total is 9; a score of 4 would understate his deterioration.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Ellis, 29, developed neuroleptic malignant syndrome two days ago and his antipsychotic was stopped. His signs are improving, but his voices are returning and he is distressed. A doctor asks the nurse's view on restarting. Which plan best reflects BNF advice?
o: Restart the same dose today, as his psychosis is returning
Restart at half dose once his temperature is normal
Switch to a depot, as NMS does not occur with depot drugs
Restart after the signs fully resolve and at least 5 days off
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF advises stopping the antipsychotic for at least 5 days, preferably longer, and allowing the signs of NMS to resolve completely before any rechallenge, which is a specialist decision with close monitoring. His distress meanwhile needs non-antipsychotic support.

n.0: Restarting two days after NMS, before full resolution, risks recurrence.
n.1: A normal temperature does not mean NMS has fully resolved, and five days have not passed.
n.2: NMS can occur with any antipsychotic, including depot preparations.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Rowe, 37, takes aripiprazole. A colleague tells a student nurse that she cannot develop neuroleptic malignant syndrome because 'it only happens with the old drugs'. Which statement should the nurse give the student?
o: NMS is linked to first-generation drugs such as haloperidol
NMS appears after years of treatment, like tardive dyskinesia
NMS can occur with any antipsychotic, including newer drugs
NMS is a mild reaction that settles with an antimuscarinic
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF describes NMS as a rare but potentially fatal side effect of all antipsychotic drugs, first- and second-generation. Staff must recognise it whatever drug the person takes.

n.0: Although classically linked with high-potency first-generation drugs, NMS also occurs with second-generation drugs.
n.1: NMS usually develops early in treatment or after a dose change, not after years.
n.3: NMS is a medical emergency, and antimuscarinics do not treat it.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Webb, 45, is transferred from a mental health unit to an acute medical ward with neuroleptic malignant syndrome. He is febrile, rigid and sweating heavily, and his oral intake is poor. Which nursing care is most important while he is being treated?
o: Frequent observations, fluid balance and cooling as directed
Restrict his fluids to reduce the risk of fluid overload
Encourage him to walk to reduce his muscle stiffness
Use restraint to manage his confusion and agitation
Psychopharmacology.w: NMS causes hyperthermia, sweating, autonomic instability and risk of dehydration and kidney injury from muscle breakdown. Close monitoring, accurate fluid balance, cooling and prompt escalation of deterioration are key nursing care (NMC P4.10; BNF).

n.1: He is sweating with poor intake; fluid restriction would worsen dehydration and kidney risk.
n.2: Exertion does not relieve NMS rigidity and increases temperature and muscle breakdown.
n.3: Restraint can worsen hyperthermia and muscle injury and is not a treatment for confusion.

Psychopharmacology.q: At 02:00 on a stand-alone mental health unit, Mr Lyle, 60, has suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome with a NEWS2 score of 8. The on-call psychiatrist is 40 minutes away and the unit has no acute medical team. What should the nurse in charge do?
o: Recheck his observations in an hour before escalating
Wait for the on-call psychiatrist to assess him first
Give oral fluids and paracetamol and review at 06:00
Arrange emergency transfer to acute care by calling 999
Psychopharmacology.w: A NEWS2 score of 7 or more needs an emergency response with critical care competencies. On a unit without an acute medical team this means emergency transfer (999) under local policy, informing the on-call doctor in parallel (RCP NEWS2; NMC P4.10).

n.0: A score of 8 already requires an emergency response; waiting an hour delays it.
n.1: Waiting 40 minutes for a psychiatrist delays emergency care for a life-threatening condition.
n.2: Simple measures and a review hours later are unsafe for suspected NMS with a score of 8.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Kaye, 30, started clozapine ten weeks ago. She tells her community nurse she has had a sore throat since yesterday and feels shivery. Her temperature is 38.2 C. Her next routine blood test is due in five days. What should the nurse do?
o: Wait for her routine blood test, which is due in five days
Advise her to double her fluids and recheck her temperature
Arrange an urgent full blood count and medical review today
Advise paracetamol and rest, and review her at the next visit
Psychopharmacology.w: Clozapine can cause neutropenia and potentially fatal agranulocytosis. The BNF says patients must report symptoms of infection immediately, especially sore throat, fever or flu-like illness, so that an urgent full blood count can check the neutrophil count.

n.0: Waiting five days is unsafe when infection symptoms may signal neutropenia.
n.1: Fluids do not address the possibility of a dangerously low neutrophil count.
n.3: Treating the symptoms without a blood count could miss agranulocytosis, which can progress rapidly.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Ali, 34, has taken clozapine for 25 weeks and all his blood counts have been normal. He asks how often he now needs blood tests. Under the BNF monitoring schedule, what should the nurse tell him?
o: At least every 4 weeks from this point onwards
Every 3 months once his dose is stable
Weekly, while he continues to take clozapine
At least every 2 weeks until he reaches 1 year
Psychopharmacology.w: BNF: counts weekly for the first 18 weeks, then at least every 2 weeks, and if clozapine continues with a stable count after 1 year, at least every 4 weeks (and for 4 weeks after stopping), through the clozapine patient monitoring service.

n.0: Four-weekly testing starts after 1 year of stable counts.
n.1: Three-monthly testing is not part of the clozapine monitoring schedule.
n.2: Weekly testing applies to the first 18 weeks; at 25 weeks it is at least fortnightly.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Tan, 26, started clozapine four weeks ago on an acute ward. For three days his resting pulse has been around 120, and today he has chest discomfort, a mild fever and feels 'flu-ish'. What is the most important action?
o: Escalate urgently as possible myocarditis for medical review
Advise more fluids and recheck his pulse next week
Record a tachycardia, which is common during titration
Ask the prescriber to slow the next week's dose increases
Psychopharmacology.w: Fatal myocarditis with clozapine occurs most often in the first 2 months. The BNF says persistent tachycardia, especially in this period, should prompt checks for myocarditis; if suspected, clozapine is stopped and the person evaluated urgently by a cardiologist.

n.1: Delaying review risks missing a potentially fatal myocarditis.
n.2: Tachycardia can occur in titration, but persistent tachycardia with chest pain and fever needs urgent investigation.
n.3: Slowing the titration does not address possible myocarditis, which needs urgent assessment now.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Bell, 48, has taken clozapine for two years. He tells the nurse he has not opened his bowels for four days and his stomach feels bloated and uncomfortable. His evening clozapine is due in an hour. What should the nurse do?
o: Give his clozapine and advise a high-fibre diet
Offer an antimuscarinic medicine for his cramps
Explain that constipation is expected and will pass
Seek medical review before his next clozapine dose
Psychopharmacology.w: MHRA (October 2017): clozapine can cause potentially fatal intestinal obstruction, faecal impaction and paralytic ileus. Patients and carers should seek medical advice before taking the next dose if constipation develops; constipation must be recognised and actively treated.

n.0: Giving the dose without medical review ignores MHRA advice, and diet alone may not treat impaction.
n.1: Antimuscarinic drugs slow the gut further and increase the risk of obstruction.
n.2: Constipation on clozapine can progress to ileus and must be treated, not dismissed.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Day, 40, has been stable on clozapine for three years. Ten days ago she stopped smoking cigarettes and switched to an e-cigarette. She now feels very drowsy, is drooling more and is unsteady on her feet. What should the nurse do?
o: Encourage her to restart cigarettes to lower her clozapine
Report a possible raised clozapine level and request testing
Ask the prescriber to increase her clozapine dose
Reassure her that e-cigarettes affect clozapine like tobacco
Psychopharmacology.w: Tobacco smoke induces clozapine metabolism, so stopping smoking or switching to an e-cigarette can raise clozapine levels and cause toxicity. MHRA (August 2020) advises monitoring clozapine blood levels in this situation; the dose may need reducing.

n.0: Smoking cessation should be supported; the safe response is to check her level and adjust the dose.
n.2: Stopping smoking raises clozapine levels, so an increase would worsen toxicity.
n.3: E-cigarettes do not contain the tobacco smoke components that induce clozapine metabolism.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Nash, 38, takes clozapine 400 mg daily. He returns from a weekend at his sister's and says he forgot his tablets and has not taken any for three days. He asks for his usual dose now. What should the nurse do?
o: Give half the dose today and full dose tomorrow
Withhold it and ask the prescriber about re-titration
Give a double dose to make up the missed days
Give his usual 400 mg dose as prescribed for today
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF says that if clozapine is restarted after an interval of more than 48 hours it should begin again at 12.5 mg once or twice on the first day and be re-titrated, because tolerance to its cardiovascular and respiratory effects is lost.

n.0: Half the usual dose is far above the 12.5 mg restart dose after a 48-hour gap.
n.2: Doubling doses greatly increases the risk of toxicity.
n.3: After more than 48 hours off, a full dose risks severe hypotension, collapse and respiratory or cardiac arrest.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Ray, 31, has taken clozapine for six months and is otherwise well. He is embarrassed that he wakes with a wet pillow from drooling at night and asks whether something is wrong. Which response is most appropriate?
o: Explain it is a common effect and discuss treatment options
Withhold his clozapine until the drooling stops
Explain this means his clozapine dose is too low
Report it to the team as an early sign of agranulocytosis
Psychopharmacology.w: Hypersalivation is a very common clozapine side effect, often worse at night. It can be managed with practical measures and, if needed, medicine such as hyoscine hydrobromide prescribed off-label (BNF). Discussing it supports adherence.

n.1: Stopping clozapine for a common side effect risks relapse and, after 48 hours, re-titration.
n.2: Hypersalivation does not indicate a low dose.
n.3: Hypersalivation is not a sign of agranulocytosis, which presents with infection symptoms.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Hart, 44, has taken clozapine for eight months. Today's result from the monitoring service shows white cell count 3.4 x 10^9/L and neutrophils 1.3 x 10^9/L. He feels well. His morning dose is due. What should the nurse do?
o: Give the dose and repeat the blood test in a week
Withhold the dose and inform the prescriber urgently
Give the dose, as his white cell count is above 3.0
Halve the dose until his neutrophil count recovers
Psychopharmacology.w: BNF: if the leucocyte count falls below 3000/mm3 (3.0 x 10^9/L) or the absolute neutrophil count below 1500/mm3 (1.5 x 10^9/L), clozapine must be stopped permanently and the person referred to a haematologist. His neutrophils are 1.3 x 10^9/L, below the threshold.

n.0: Continuing clozapine with neutrophils below the threshold risks agranulocytosis.
n.2: The neutrophil count is below 1.5 x 10^9/L, which requires stopping even though the white cell count is above 3.0.
n.3: Dose reduction is not the response; the BNF requires clozapine to be stopped.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Kent, 42, takes modified-release lithium carbonate once daily at 22:00. He is due a serum lithium level this week and asks the community nurse when he should attend for the blood test. What should the nurse advise?
o: At 22:00 the next day, before his next dose
At 10:00 the morning after his evening dose
At 06:00, eight hours after his evening dose
At any time, as lithium levels stay constant
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF says lithium samples should be taken 12 hours post dose. A 22:00 dose therefore means a sample at about 10:00 the next morning. Taking it at another time gives a misleading level.

n.0: Twenty-four hours after the dose is too late and would give a falsely low level.
n.2: Eight hours after the dose is too early and would give a falsely high level.
n.3: Lithium levels vary through the dosing interval, which is why a standard 12-hour sample is used.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Ross, 58, takes lithium for bipolar disorder. She has had diarrhoea and vomiting for two days. At a home visit she has a coarse tremor, is unsteady when walking and her speech is slurred. Her evening lithium is due. What should the nurse do?
o: Give an anti-diarrhoeal medicine and continue her lithium
Give the dose with extra fluids and recheck her in a week
Reassure her that tremor is a common side effect of lithium
Withhold the dose and arrange an urgent level and review
Psychopharmacology.w: Diarrhoea and vomiting cause dehydration, which raises lithium levels. Coarse tremor (a fine tremor becoming coarse), ataxia and dysarthria are signs of toxicity, which require withdrawal of treatment (BNF). She needs an urgent level and medical review.

n.0: Treating the diarrhoea alone ignores signs of lithium toxicity.
n.1: Giving more lithium when toxicity is suspected could cause seizures, arrhythmias or kidney injury.
n.2: A fine tremor is common, but a coarse tremor with ataxia and slurred speech suggests toxicity.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Odell, 47, has taken lithium for six years. He tells his community nurse that he has hurt his back and plans to buy ibuprofen from the pharmacy. Which advice is most appropriate?
o: Ibuprofen is safe with lithium for up to two weeks
Ibuprofen is suitable if he drinks less fluid while using it
Avoid ibuprofen, as it can raise his lithium level
Ibuprofen is safe with lithium if he takes it with food
Psychopharmacology.w: NSAIDs such as ibuprofen reduce renal lithium clearance and can raise levels into the toxic range. NICE CG185 says to warn people taking lithium about over-the-counter NSAIDs, and the BNF lists the interaction; an alternative analgesic should be discussed.

n.0: Even short courses can raise lithium levels; the interaction does not depend on duration.
n.1: Reducing fluids increases the risk of lithium toxicity.
n.3: Taking ibuprofen with food protects the stomach but does not prevent the rise in lithium levels.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Ward, 35, has bipolar disorder and is starting lithium for the first time. She asks the nurse what blood level the team is aiming for. Under NICE CG185, what is the usual initial target?
o: 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L
1.0 to 1.5 mmol/L
0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L
0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 and the BNF recommend an initial serum lithium level of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L for people with bipolar disorder starting lithium. A level of 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L may be considered later after relapse or with subthreshold symptoms.

n.0: 0.8 to 1.0 mmol/L is considered later if response is sub-optimal, not as the starting target.
n.1: Levels above 1.0 mmol/L are above the recommended range and carry toxicity risk.
n.2: 0.4 to 0.6 mmol/L is the BNF initial target for people aged 65 and over and for unipolar depression.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Grey, 68, has taken lithium for three years. Her levels have been stable, the last one was 0.7 mmol/L and she takes no interacting medicines. How often should her serum lithium level now be checked?
o: Every 3 months, because she is aged over 65
Every 6 months, as her levels have been stable
Every week, as older people are at higher risk
Every 12 months, at her annual physical review
Psychopharmacology.w: Once stable, levels are checked every 3 months in the first year and every 6 months after that, but every 3 months for people aged 65 or over, those on interacting drugs, those at risk of renal or thyroid problems or raised calcium, those with poor control or adherence, or whose last level was 0.8 mmol/L or higher (BNF; NICE CG185 1.10.19-1.10.20).

n.1: Six-monthly testing would apply if she were under 65 with no other risk factors.
n.2: Weekly testing is for starting treatment or after dose changes, not stable maintenance.
n.3: Annual testing is too infrequent for lithium at any age.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Patel, 39, takes lithium and is going on holiday to southern Spain in July. She asks the nurse whether there is anything she needs to think about. Which advice is most important?
o: Take an extra dose if she misses one while she is travelling
Reduce salt in her diet to prevent fluid retention in the heat
Stop lithium during the holiday to avoid toxicity in the heat
Drink plenty and seek help if she has vomiting or diarrhoea
Psychopharmacology.w: Hot weather, sweating, vomiting, diarrhoea and alcohol can cause dehydration and lithium toxicity. The BNF advises maintaining adequate fluid intake, avoiding dietary changes in salt intake and seeking medical attention if dehydration occurs (CG185 1.10.17).

n.0: Doubling up after a missed dose increases toxicity risk.
n.1: Reducing salt raises lithium levels; the BNF advises avoiding changes in sodium intake.
n.2: Stopping lithium abruptly risks relapse; it should be reduced gradually when stopping is planned.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Lee, 55, has taken lithium for five years and his levels are in range. He tells the nurse he feels tired all the time, has gained weight and feels the cold more than his wife does. Which explanation and action is most appropriate?
o: Normal ageing; review this at his next annual check
Possible hypothyroidism; request thyroid function tests
Possible depressive relapse; ask for a dose increase
Possible lithium toxicity; withhold his lithium today
Psychopharmacology.w: Lithium commonly causes hypothyroidism. Tiredness, weight gain and cold intolerance with in-range levels suggest it, so thyroid function (part of the 6-monthly monitoring) should be checked and the result acted on (NICE CG185 1.10.21; BNF).

n.0: Attributing new symptoms to age risks missing a treatable lithium side effect.
n.2: Hypothyroidism can mimic low mood; thyroid function should be checked before any dose change.
n.3: His level is in range and the symptoms fit hypothyroidism rather than acute toxicity.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Shaw, 50, has been well on lithium for four years and, after discussion with his psychiatrist, has decided to stop it. He asks the nurse how this will be done. Which plan reflects NICE CG185?
o: Halve the dose for 1 week and then stop it completely
Reduce gradually over at least 4 weeks and watch for relapse
Stop over 3 days to limit time at a sub-therapeutic level
Stop it now and check his serum level after 3 months
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 1.10.25-1.10.26: stop lithium gradually over at least 4 weeks, preferably up to 3 months, and monitor for early signs of mania or depression during the reduction and for 3 months after stopping, because abrupt withdrawal increases relapse risk.

n.0: Halving the dose for 1 week and then stopping is a 1-week taper, well short of the minimum 4 weeks in CG185 1.10.25.
n.2: Stopping over 3 days is close to abrupt withdrawal and raises the risk of manic relapse.
n.3: Abrupt stopping risks relapse, and a level after stopping serves no purpose.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Kemp, 28, has bipolar disorder and could not tolerate lithium. Her psychiatrist is considering starting valproate for the first time. Under the MHRA safety measures set out in NICE CG185, what must happen before it is started?
o: Two specialists independently agree and document the need
A baseline plasma valproate level in the normal range
Her written consent and her GP's agreement to prescribe
A negative pregnancy test on the morning it is started
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 box 1 (MHRA): do not start valproate in anyone under 55 unless two specialists independently agree and document that there is no other effective tolerated treatment, or that the reproductive risks do not apply. For women able to have children, the Pregnancy Prevention Programme is also put in place where appropriate.

n.1: Valproate levels are not measured routinely and there is no baseline level before starting.
n.2: GP agreement is not the safeguard, and CG185 says valproate should not be started in primary care for bipolar disorder.
n.3: Pregnancy testing forms part of the Pregnancy Prevention Programme but does not replace the two-specialist requirement.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Jacobs, 30, has taken valproate for bipolar disorder for several years. He and his partner are thinking about having a baby next year, and he asks whether his medicine matters for him as a man. What should the nurse explain?
o: Use effective contraception during and for 3 months after
Stop valproate 1 week before trying to conceive
Use contraception for 1 month after stopping valproate
Contraception advice applies to women on valproate, not to men
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 box 1 (MHRA): advise men that effective contraception (condoms plus contraception used by a female partner) is recommended during valproate treatment and for 3 months after stopping, and discuss fertility risks and options with men planning a family within the next year, because of a possible link with neurodevelopmental disorders in their children.

n.1: Stopping a week before conception is not the advice, and valproate should be withdrawn gradually under specialist care.
n.2: The recommended period after stopping is 3 months, not 1 month.
n.3: MHRA advice now also covers men taking valproate.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Holt, 62, started valproate for bipolar disorder six months ago and is well. Her baseline weight, liver function tests and full blood count were normal. Under NICE CG185, which monitoring is due now?
o: A plasma valproate level, then every month
Weight, liver function tests and full blood count
An ECG and serum prolactin level
U&Es and thyroid function tests every 3 months
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 1.10.33: measure weight or BMI and carry out liver function tests and a full blood count after 6 months of valproate and then annually. Plasma valproate levels are not measured routinely unless there is evidence of ineffectiveness, poor adherence or toxicity (1.10.32).

n.0: Routine valproate levels are not recommended.
n.2: ECG and prolactin belong to antipsychotic monitoring, not valproate.
n.3: Three-monthly U&Es and thyroid tests relate to lithium monitoring in higher-risk groups.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Rees, 66, takes valproate. At a home visit his wife says he has been bruising easily for a week, and the nurse notices his eyes look yellow. He feels tired and off his food. What should the nurse do?
o: Seek urgent medical review for possible liver or blood toxicity
Advise more vitamin K foods and review him in a month
Advise him to drink more fluids to help clear the jaundice
Reassure them that bruising is a common harmless effect
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 1.10.30: advise people taking valproate and carers to recognise signs of blood and liver disorders and seek immediate medical help; stop valproate immediately if abnormal liver function or blood dyscrasia is detected. Jaundice and bruising need urgent assessment.

n.1: Dietary advice and a month's delay could allow serious liver failure or bleeding to progress.
n.2: Fluids do not treat liver injury, and the cause needs urgent investigation.
n.3: Bruising with jaundice and malaise suggests serious toxicity, not a harmless effect.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Wood, 33, started lamotrigine for bipolar depression three weeks ago and her dose is being slowly increased. She phones the community team to say a red, itchy rash has appeared on her chest and arms today. What should the nurse advise?
o: Use an emollient and continue the planned dose increases
Contact her prescriber today, as a rash in titration can be serious
Continue lamotrigine, as rashes are expected in the first month or so
Take an antihistamine and review the rash in one week
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 1.10.37: advise people taking lamotrigine to contact their doctor immediately if they develop a rash while the dose is being increased, as it can signal a serious skin reaction such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

n.0: Continuing dose increases with a new rash risks a serious skin reaction.
n.2: A rash during titration is a warning sign needing urgent medical advice, not an expected effect.
n.3: Waiting a week delays assessment of a possibly serious reaction.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Barr, 58, takes valproate for bipolar disorder. Her psychiatrist plans to add lamotrigine for persistent depressive symptoms. Which interaction should the nurse be aware of when the lamotrigine is started?
o: Valproate lowers lamotrigine levels, so higher doses are used
Lamotrigine raises valproate levels, so valproate is halved
Lamotrigine levels must be measured weekly during titration
Valproate raises lamotrigine levels, so titration is slower
Psychopharmacology.w: CG185 1.10.36: when starting lamotrigine be aware of its interaction with valproate and follow the SPC/BNF titration, which is slower because valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism and raises its levels (and rash risk). Lamotrigine levels are not measured routinely (1.10.38).

n.0: Valproate increases, not lowers, lamotrigine levels.
n.1: The clinically important effect is valproate raising lamotrigine levels, not the reverse.
n.2: CG185 says not to measure lamotrigine levels routinely.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Lane, 24, is about to start carbamazepine for bipolar disorder. She mentions that she takes the combined contraceptive pill and does not want to become pregnant. What should the nurse discuss with her and the prescriber?
o: Her pill will raise her carbamazepine to toxic levels
Carbamazepine can make her pill less effective
Carbamazepine increases the pill's contraceptive effect
Taking her pill at night prevents any interaction
Psychopharmacology.w: Carbamazepine is a hepatic enzyme inducer that speeds the metabolism of hormonal contraceptives and can make the combined pill unreliable; the BNF and FSRH advise discussing a method unaffected by enzyme inducers, such as an intrauterine method. It is also teratogenic, so effective contraception matters.

n.0: The interaction runs the other way: carbamazepine reduces contraceptive hormone levels.
n.2: Enzyme induction reduces, not increases, contraceptive effect.
n.3: Changing the time of day does not prevent enzyme induction.

Psychopharmacology.q: A practice nurse receives a phone request from a hospital doctor asking the GP practice to start valproate for Mr Dunn, 60, who has a new diagnosis of bipolar disorder and has not yet been seen by mental health services. What is the most appropriate response?
o: The GP can start it, as Mr Dunn is over the age of 55
The practice nurse can start it under a patient group direction
Valproate is not started in primary care for bipolar disorder
The pharmacist can start it after checking his liver function
Psychopharmacology.w: NICE CG185 1.2.8: do not start valproate in primary care to treat bipolar disorder. Treatment should begin under specialist mental health care, which also applies the MHRA safeguards and monitoring.

n.0: Being over 55 removes the two-specialist requirement but not the CG185 advice against starting it in primary care.
n.1: A patient group direction is not a route for starting a mood stabiliser for a new diagnosis.
n.3: Pharmacist checks do not make primary care initiation appropriate under CG185.
