Psychopharmacology.q: Ryan, 21, is prescribed sertraline today for more severe depression after an assessment with his GP. He has no history of self-harm. Under NICE NG222, when should his first review take place?
o: After 6 weeks
After 2 weeks
After 1 week
After 4 weeks
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222: review new antidepressant prescriptions usually within 2 weeks, but at 1 week if the person is aged 18 to 25 or there is a particular concern about suicide risk, because of the possible increase in suicidal thoughts early in treatment.

n.0: Six weeks is too late for a first review and leaves the early high-risk period unmonitored.
n.1: Two weeks is the usual review time for people over 25 without particular suicide concerns.
n.3: Four weeks is too late for a first review at his age.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Owen, 40, is starting citalopram for depression. She asks the nurse what to expect in the first few weeks. Which information is most important to give her?
o: She may feel more anxious early on and should report suicidal thoughts
She should stop the tablets if she feels more anxious in the first week
Her mood should improve within 2 to 3 days of starting
She can stop once she feels better, which is usually after a month
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF notes increased potential for agitation, anxiety and suicidal ideation in the first few weeks; NG222 advises warning people about this and about when to seek help. Benefit usually takes up to 4 weeks, and treatment continues for at least 6 months after remission.

n.1: Early anxiety is common and often settles; stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal symptoms, so she should seek advice instead.
n.2: Antidepressant effects usually take weeks, not days, to appear.
n.3: Treatment usually continues for at least 6 months after remission to reduce relapse.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Ball, 79, started sertraline three weeks ago. Her daughter reports she has become drowsy and muddled over two days. Her blood results show sodium 124 mmol/L (previously 139). What is the most likely explanation and response?
o: Possible SSRI-induced hyponatraemia; inform the prescriber urgently
Expected sedation from sertraline; give the dose at night instead
Progression of dementia; continue the sertraline as prescribed
Worsening depression; ask for the sertraline dose to be increased
Psychopharmacology.w: Hyponatraemia, usually in older people and possibly due to inappropriate ADH secretion, is associated with all antidepressants and more often with SSRIs. The BNF says to consider it in anyone who develops drowsiness, confusion or convulsions on an antidepressant.

n.1: Drowsiness with low sodium is a serious adverse effect, not expected sedation.
n.2: An acute change over two days with a falling sodium is not dementia progression.
n.3: Increasing the SSRI could worsen hyponatraemia.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Mann, 56, takes sertraline. Yesterday his GP added tramadol for back pain. Today he is agitated and sweating, with a tremor, jerking of his legs, brisk reflexes, diarrhoea and a temperature of 38.3 C. What is the most likely cause and response?
o: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; ask for dantrolene
Serotonin toxicity; withhold both drugs and get urgent review
A panic attack; give PRN lorazepam and reassure him
Antidepressant withdrawal; give an extra sertraline dose
Psychopharmacology.w: Serotonin toxicity can follow within hours of adding a second serotonergic drug (tramadol has serotonergic activity). Neuromuscular excitability, autonomic signs and altered mental state are characteristic. Treatment is withdrawing the serotonergic drugs, supportive care and specialist advice (BNF).

n.0: NMS follows antipsychotics and shows slow-onset rigidity, not clonus and hyperreflexia.
n.2: Fever, clonus and hyperreflexia are physical signs of toxicity, not panic.
n.3: He has not missed doses; extra sertraline would worsen serotonin toxicity.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Sharma, 35, has taken sertraline for four months and her depression went into remission a month ago. She tells the nurse she feels well and would like to stop her tablets now. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Stop the tablets now, as her symptoms have resolved
Continue for at least 6 months after remission, then review
Continue for at least 2 years before any review is needed
Halve the dose now and continue it as a maintenance dose
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 and the BNF advise continuing antidepressant treatment for at least 6 months after remission to reduce the risk of relapse, with a shared decision and gradual tapering when stopping.

n.0: Stopping one month after remission increases relapse risk and, if abrupt, withdrawal symptoms.
n.2: Two years without review is not the standard; treatment is reviewed regularly.
n.3: NG222 advises continuing at the dose that achieved remission unless there is good reason to reduce it.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Hale, 45, has depression and took an overdose of paracetamol last year. His GP is choosing an antidepressant and asks the practice nurse which option carries the lowest risk in overdose. Which is most appropriate?
o: Dosulepin, as it can be started by the GP
Sertraline, as SSRIs are safer in overdose
Lofepramine, as tricyclics are safest in overdose
Amitriptyline, as it also helps his sleep
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF states SSRIs are better tolerated and safer in overdose than other antidepressant classes; amitriptyline and dosulepin are particularly dangerous in overdose. NICE NG225 1.13.1 asks prescribers to consider toxicity in overdose for people who have self-harmed.

n.0: Dosulepin is particularly dangerous in overdose and should be started by a specialist.
n.2: Tricyclics, including lofepramine, carry more overdose risk than SSRIs, although lofepramine is less dangerous than other tricyclics.
n.3: Amitriptyline is particularly dangerous in overdose.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Ford, 61, has treatment-resistant depression and has been started on phenelzine by a specialist. He asks the nurse which foods he should avoid. Which advice is correct?
o: Mature cheese, yeast extracts and cured meats
Milk and dairy products within 2 hours of a dose
Grapefruit juice and other citrus fruit
Leafy green vegetables high in vitamin K
Psychopharmacology.w: Monoamine-oxidase inhibitors such as phenelzine have dangerous interactions with tyramine-rich foods (for example mature cheese, yeast extracts, cured or fermented meats), which can cause a hypertensive crisis (BNF antidepressant treatment summary).

n.1: Separating dairy from doses applies to some antibiotics, not MAOIs.
n.2: Grapefruit interacts with some other medicines but is not the MAOI tyramine risk.
n.3: Vitamin K foods are relevant to warfarin, not MAOIs.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Ray, 29, has taken fluoxetine alone for depression for six weeks. Her partner calls to say she has barely slept for four nights, is talking very fast and has spent her savings on a new business. She says she has 'never felt better'. What should the nurse do?
o: Ask for the fluoxetine dose to increase as her mood lifts
Advise that elation shows she is recovering well
Ask for a second antidepressant to stabilise her mood
Arrange urgent review, as mania may have been triggered
Psychopharmacology.w: Signs of mania on antidepressant monotherapy need urgent specialist review. NICE CG185 1.5.2: consider stopping the antidepressant and offer an antipsychotic. The episode may also indicate bipolar disorder.

n.0: Increasing the antidepressant could worsen mania.
n.1: Reduced sleep, pressured speech and reckless spending indicate mania, not recovery.
n.2: Adding another antidepressant may worsen mania.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Hart, 44, stopped her venlafaxine suddenly three days ago because she felt better. She now feels dizzy, gets 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, and is irritable and tearful. What is the most likely explanation?
o: An early relapse of her depression
Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms
A new generalised anxiety disorder
Serotonin toxicity from venlafaxine
Psychopharmacology.w: NICE NG222 1.4.13-1.4.14: stopping abruptly, missing doses or reducing can cause withdrawal symptoms such as dizziness, electric shock sensations, irritability, anxiety and low mood, usually within a few days. Venlafaxine is particularly associated with them (1.4.18).

n.0: Relapse does not usually happen as soon as an antidepressant is stopped, and electric shock sensations point to withdrawal.
n.2: The symptoms began within days of stopping venlafaxine, which fits withdrawal.
n.3: Serotonin toxicity follows starting, increasing or combining serotonergic drugs, not stopping one.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Kaur, 50, is reducing his sertraline with his GP's agreement. Four days after his last reduction he feels anxious and dizzy and tells the nurse he is frightened his depression is coming back. Which response best reflects NICE NG222?
o: These are common withdrawal symptoms rather than a relapse
These symptoms mean you have become addicted to sertraline
These symptoms will last for at least six months after stopping
This shows your depression has returned, so restart the full dose
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.19: if withdrawal symptoms occur, reassure the person that they are not having a relapse, that these symptoms are common, and that relapse does not usually happen as soon as an antidepressant is stopped or reduced.

n.1: Withdrawal symptoms do not mean addiction; they reflect the body adjusting to the change.
n.2: Withdrawal symptoms usually resolve within 1 to 2 weeks, although some last longer.
n.3: Early symptoms after a reduction are more likely withdrawal than relapse, so a full restart is not the first response.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Gill, 38, has taken citalopram for two years and has agreed with her prescriber to stop. The nurse is helping her understand the tapering plan. Which plan best reflects NICE NG222?
o: Reduce by the same fixed amount each week until it is stopped
Take the full dose on alternate days for a month, then stop
Stop abruptly, as tapering prolongs the withdrawal symptoms
Reduce by a share of the last dose, with smaller steps as it falls
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.16: reduce to zero step-wise, prescribing a proportion of the previous dose at each step (for example 50%), with smaller reductions (for example 25%) as the dose gets lower, using liquids if needed, at a pace led and agreed by the person.

n.0: Equal fixed reductions mean proportionally larger steps at low doses, where withdrawal is often worst.
n.1: Alternate-day dosing is suggested for fluoxetine 20 mg because of its long action, not for citalopram.
n.2: Abrupt stopping makes severe withdrawal symptoms more likely.

Psychopharmacology.q: A community mental health nurse is supporting four people who each plan to stop an antidepressant. Under NICE NG222, which person most needs particular care because of a higher risk of withdrawal symptoms?
o: Ms Boyd, on paroxetine for two years
Ms Dunn, on citalopram for two weeks
Mr Abbas, on fluoxetine 20 mg for two years
Mr Cole, on sertraline for three weeks
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.18: some commonly used antidepressants, such as paroxetine and venlafaxine, are more likely to be associated with withdrawal symptoms, so particular care is needed. Longer treatment also increases the risk (1.4.16).

n.1: Two weeks of citalopram is a very short course, which lowers the risk.
n.2: Fluoxetine's long action means it can sometimes be stopped more easily, for example with alternate-day dosing.
n.3: Sertraline for three weeks is a short course and not one NICE highlights as high risk.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Dee, 47, reduced his venlafaxine dose two weeks ago. He now has severe dizziness, nausea and 'brain zaps' and has had to stop working. His mood itself has been stable. What is the most appropriate plan to discuss with his prescriber?
o: Restart the previous dose, then taper later in smaller steps
Continue the reduction, as the symptoms will pass within days
Stop the remaining dose now to get the withdrawal over with
Switch straight to a different antidepressant at full dose
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.21: if withdrawal symptoms are more severe, consider restarting the original antidepressant at the previous dose and then reducing more slowly with smaller decrements once symptoms have resolved.

n.1: Severe symptoms lasting two weeks and stopping him working need action, not waiting.
n.2: Stopping abruptly would make his withdrawal symptoms worse.
n.3: An abrupt switch is not the NG222 response to severe withdrawal and may add new side effects.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Nash, 33, is tapering her sertraline. Four days after the latest step down she has a mild headache and some trouble sleeping, but is managing her usual activities. What should the nurse advise?
o: Ask the GP for a benzodiazepine to cover the symptoms
Return to her full original dose from today
Monitor, and contact the prescriber if symptoms worsen
Stop the remaining tablets, as she is intolerant of them
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.20: for mild withdrawal symptoms, monitor them, reassure that they are common and usually time-limited, and advise contacting the prescriber if they do not improve or get worse. The next step down should wait until symptoms have resolved or are tolerable (1.4.16).

n.0: Benzodiazepines are not recommended for managing antidepressant withdrawal and carry dependence risk.
n.1: Restarting the original dose is considered for severe, not mild, withdrawal.
n.3: Stopping abruptly would make withdrawal more likely and more severe.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Lowe, 41, takes fluoxetine 20 mg daily and wants to stop after a year of being well. She has read that stopping antidepressants can be difficult. Which approach does NICE NG222 describe for her?
o: Check her fluoxetine blood level weekly during the withdrawal
Taper more slowly than for paroxetine, as fluoxetine is short-acting
Switch her to paroxetine first, as it is easier to stop
Use a period of alternate-day dosing as a dose reduction
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.18: fluoxetine's prolonged duration of action means that, for people taking 20 mg a day, a period of alternate-day dosing can provide a suitable reduction; higher doses need a gradual schedule.

n.0: Blood levels are not used to manage antidepressant withdrawal.
n.1: Fluoxetine is long-acting; short half-life drugs such as paroxetine need slower tapering.
n.2: Paroxetine is more likely to cause withdrawal symptoms, not less.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Jay, 36, takes paroxetine. He tells his nurse that most Sundays he feels dizzy and irritable with 'zaps' in his head. On questioning, he often forgets his tablets on Friday and Saturday when he stays with his partner. What is the best explanation and response?
o: Missed doses cause withdrawal; agree ways to take them regularly
Weekend alcohol is causing serotonin toxicity; advise abstinence
Paroxetine is wearing off with tolerance; ask about a switch
His depression relapses at weekends; ask for a dose increase
Psychopharmacology.w: NG222 1.4.13: missing doses or not taking a full dose can cause withdrawal symptoms, and paroxetine is particularly associated with them (1.4.18). Exploring practical ways to support regular dosing is the person-centred response.

n.1: His symptoms follow missed doses; serotonin toxicity follows extra or combined serotonergic drugs.
n.2: The timing links to missed doses, not tolerance.
n.3: Dizziness and 'zaps' after missed doses fit withdrawal, not depressive relapse.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Faris, 24, is on his first admission to an acute ward and has never taken antipsychotic medication. Despite de-escalation he is hitting out at staff, and he has refused oral medication. The team decides rapid tranquillisation is needed. Under NICE NG10, which medication should be used?
o: IV diazepam on its own
IM haloperidol on its own
IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
IM lorazepam on its own
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.37-1.4.38: use either IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol combined with IM promethazine; if there is insufficient information to guide the choice, or the person has not taken antipsychotics before, use IM lorazepam.

n.0: IV use is exceptional in NG10 and diazepam is not one of the recommended options.
n.1: NG10 pairs haloperidol with promethazine; haloperidol alone raises the risk of acute dystonia.
n.2: Haloperidol with promethazine is an NG10 option, but not for someone who is antipsychotic-naive.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Young, 38, has taken antipsychotics for years and needs rapid tranquillisation after de-escalation has failed. He has no known heart disease. A doctor suggests IM haloperidol with promethazine, but the nurse checks the notes first. Which finding is the main reason to use IM lorazepam instead?
o: No ECG has been done since his admission
He is younger than 40 years of age
He is detained under section 2 of the Act
He took oral lorazepam once last year
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.39: if there is evidence of cardiovascular disease, including a prolonged QT interval, or no ECG has been carried out, avoid IM haloperidol with IM promethazine and use IM lorazepam instead.

n.1: Age under 40 is not a reason to avoid haloperidol with promethazine; young men are more prone to dystonia, which promethazine helps prevent.
n.2: Detention status gives the legal framework; it does not decide which drug is used.
n.3: Previous lorazepam use does not rule out haloperidol with promethazine.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Coe, 30, received IM lorazepam for rapid tranquillisation 30 minutes ago. She is now awake, calm and talking. She has no physical health problems, has not taken alcohol or drugs, was not restrained and received a standard dose. How often should her physical observations be done?
o: Every 4 hours for the whole of the next day
Every 15 minutes for the next 4 hours
Once, an hour after the injection was given
At least hourly until there are no concerns
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.45: after rapid tranquillisation, monitor side effects, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and level of consciousness at least every hour until there are no further concerns. 15-minute monitoring applies if any listed risk factor is present; none applies to Ms Coe.

n.0: Four-hourly checks are less frequent than the NG10 minimum of hourly.
n.1: 15-minute monitoring is for people who appear asleep or sedated, exceed the BNF maximum, have taken drugs or alcohol, have a physical health problem or were harmed by restraint.
n.2: A single check does not meet NG10, which requires ongoing monitoring until there are no concerns.

Psychopharmacology.q: A newly registered nurse is about to monitor Mr Lund, 45, after rapid tranquillisation on a mental health ward. Which set of observations does NICE NG10 specify, in addition to side effects?
o: Level of consciousness, pupil size and limb power
Pulse, blood pressure, capillary glucose and pain score
Pulse, BP, breathing, temperature, hydration, alertness
Respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and peak flow
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.45 lists pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, temperature, level of hydration and level of consciousness, plus side effects. Many trusts also record SpO2 and NEWS2, but the core set must be complete.

n.0: A neurological check alone omits the cardiovascular, respiratory, temperature and hydration observations.
n.1: Glucose and pain score are not the NG10 set, which also needs breathing, temperature, hydration and consciousness.
n.3: Breathing measures alone miss cardiovascular, temperature, hydration and consciousness monitoring.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Ince, 33, was given IM haloperidol with IM promethazine 20 minutes ago. He is awake and talking, but police reported he had been drinking heavily before he was brought to the ward. He has no other health problems. How often should his observations be done?
o: Hourly, because he is awake and talking
Every 4 hours, as the drugs are short-acting
Every 15 minutes, because he has taken alcohol
Every 30 minutes, as he received two drugs
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.45: monitor every 15 minutes if the person has taken illicit drugs or alcohol (or appears asleep or sedated, exceeded the BNF maximum dose, has a pre-existing physical health problem, or was harmed by restrictive intervention). Alcohol adds to sedation and respiratory risk.

n.0: Hourly monitoring is the baseline, but alcohol intake requires 15-minute monitoring even if he is awake.
n.1: Four-hourly monitoring is below the NG10 minimum in any case.
n.3: Two drugs do not set a 30-minute interval; alcohol triggers 15-minute monitoring.

Psychopharmacology.q: A doctor is writing a rapid tranquillisation prescription for Ms Pike, 29, on an acute ward. The nurse checks that it follows NICE NG10 and BNF advice. Which prescription is correct?
o: Up to four doses in 24 hours, given at the nurse's discretion
A single dose, not repeated until its effect has been reviewed
A combined 'oral or IM' entry so either route can be used
A regular four-hourly IM dose for the next 48 hours
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.44: write the initial rapid tranquillisation prescription as a single dose and do not repeat it until the effect of the initial dose has been reviewed. The BNF adds that oral and IM doses should be prescribed separately.

n.0: Open-ended repeat doses risk cumulative over-sedation before the first dose's effect is reviewed.
n.2: The BNF says oral and IM drugs should be prescribed separately.
n.3: Regular IM doses are not rapid tranquillisation and risk high-dose prescribing.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Dace, 35, received IM lorazepam 45 minutes ago because of severe violence. She has had no response and remains very agitated. She regularly takes an antipsychotic, and an ECG yesterday was normal. Under NICE NG10, what should the team consider next?
o: Further IM lorazepam every 15 minutes until calm
IM haloperidol with IM promethazine
An urgent team meeting before any further medicine
IV haloperidol for a faster onset of sedation
Psychopharmacology.w: NG10 1.4.40-1.4.41: if there is a partial response to IM lorazepam, consider a further dose; if there is no response, consider IM haloperidol with IM promethazine. An urgent team review is for when there is no response to both options (1.4.43).

n.0: A further lorazepam dose is for a partial response, and repeated 15-minute doses would risk respiratory depression.
n.2: An urgent team review is for no response to both lorazepam and haloperidol with promethazine.
n.3: IV administration is exceptional and carries more cardiac risk; NG10 next step is the IM combination.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Bryce, 40, has been detained under section 3 of the Mental Health Act for three weeks and has been receiving antipsychotic medication since admission. During a violent episode he refuses IM medication. Under which provision may rapid tranquillisation be given?
o: Section 63, as treatment for mental disorder
Section 5(4), the nurse's holding power
Section 58, with a SOAD certificate
The Mental Capacity Act, in his best interests
Psychopharmacology.w: Section 63 allows treatment for mental disorder (other than s57, s58 and s58A treatments) to be given to a detained patient without consent by or under the direction of the approved clinician. Medication only falls under s58 after 3 months from first administration in the current detention.

n.1: Section 5(4) holds an informal inpatient; it does not authorise treatment.
n.2: The s58 SOAD requirement starts after 3 months; he has received medication for three weeks.
n.3: MCA s28 prevents the MCA authorising treatment for mental disorder regulated by Part 4 of the MHA.

Psychopharmacology.q: A community mental health nurse is about to give Mr Ellis, 41, his fortnightly flupentixol decanoate depot, an oil-based antipsychotic, by deep intramuscular injection into the upper outer buttock. Which step does the product's summary of product characteristics (SPC) stress for oil-based injections such as this?
o: Give it into the subcutaneous fat of the abdomen instead
Aspirate first to check that no blood is drawn back
Massage the site firmly once the injection is complete
Use a shorter needle to keep the medicine superficial
Psychopharmacology.w: The Depixol (flupentixol decanoate) SPC states that, as with all oil-based injections, it is important to ensure by aspiration before injection that inadvertent intravascular entry does not occur. The route is deep intramuscular injection into the upper outer buttock or lateral thigh.

n.0: The SPC route is deep intramuscular injection, not subcutaneous.
n.2: Massage does not prevent intravascular entry, and some depot SPCs (for example olanzapine embonate) say not to massage the site.
n.3: A short needle risks depositing the oily depot superficially; the SPC requires a deep intramuscular injection.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Bain, 36, receives a depot antipsychotic every two weeks into the gluteal muscle. Today the nurse notices that the area used last time is firm and slightly tender. What is the most appropriate practice?
o: Give half the dose into each deltoid muscle today
Massage the firm area, then inject into it as usual
Use the same side again so the record stays simple
Use a different site and record each site given
Psychopharmacology.w: Rotating injection sites and documenting the site used for each dose reduces induration, pain and erratic absorption; the haloperidol decanoate SPC, for example, recommends alternating between the two gluteal muscles. The new site must be appropriate for the product (SPC) and checked before injecting.

n.0: Splitting a dose between sites, or using the deltoid, depends on the product licence and is not a response to induration.
n.1: Injecting into indurated tissue risks poor absorption and further injury.
n.2: Repeating a site that is already firm and tender worsens tissue damage and absorption.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Lake, 33, has schizophrenia and has recovered from an acute episode. Her care coordinator mentions that a depot injection is one option and she asks why it might be offered. Which explanation reflects NICE CG178?
o: Depots remove the need for physical health monitoring
Depots cause fewer side effects than any oral antipsychotic
Depots are given to everyone detained under section 3
She may prefer it, or it helps when missed doses are a concern
Psychopharmacology.w: CG178 1.5.5.3: consider depot or long-acting injectable antipsychotics for people who would prefer this after an acute episode, or where avoiding covert non-adherence is a clinical priority, taking into account the person's preferences and attitudes (1.5.6.1).

n.0: The same metabolic and physical monitoring applies to depot antipsychotics.
n.1: First-generation depots may cause more extrapyramidal effects; depots are not side-effect free.
n.2: Detention does not mean a depot; the choice depends on preference and clinical need.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Craig, 50, developed a tremor and stiffness after his first-generation depot antipsychotic was increased. The team decides to stop the depot. He asks whether the side effects will go away as soon as it is stopped. What should the nurse explain?
o: Side effects will be reversed at once by an antimuscarinic
Side effects may continue until the drug clears from the site
Side effects will stop within a few hours of the decision
Side effects can be ended by injecting a different depot
Psychopharmacology.w: The BNF notes that with depot antipsychotics, side effects may persist until the drug has been cleared from its depot site, which can take weeks. This is one reason doses and changes are made carefully.

n.0: An antimuscarinic may ease parkinsonism but does not reverse the effects immediately or remove the drug.
n.2: A long-acting depot keeps releasing drug for weeks, so effects do not stop within hours.
n.3: Another depot adds more antipsychotic exposure and would not end the current effects.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Grant, 59, has taken diazepam 10 mg daily for two years for anxiety. She tells her community nurse she is fed up with tablets and plans to stop them completely tomorrow. What should the nurse advise?
o: Support her plan to stop tomorrow, as she is motivated to do so
Swap to zopiclone, which can be stopped at any time safely
Halve the dose for three days and then stop it completely
Avoid stopping suddenly; agree a slow taper with the prescriber
Psychopharmacology.w: MHRA (January 2026) strengthened warnings on dependence, withdrawal and tolerance with benzodiazepines and Z-drugs and advises avoiding abrupt cessation. After long-term use a gradual, supported dose reduction agreed with the prescriber reduces withdrawal risks such as rebound anxiety and seizures.

n.0: Stopping suddenly after two years risks severe withdrawal, including seizures.
n.1: Z-drugs such as zopiclone also carry dependence and withdrawal risks and should not be stopped abruptly.
n.2: A three-day taper is far too rapid after long-term use.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Hill, 46, is prescribed methadone for opioid dependence and attends a community mental health clinic with severe anxiety. A doctor suggests regular lorazepam. Which concern should the nurse raise first?
o: The combination risks serotonin syndrome
Methadone will make his anxiety much worse over time
Combined use risks fatal respiratory depression
Lorazepam reduces the effect of methadone
Psychopharmacology.w: MHRA (March 2020): co-prescribing benzodiazepines with opioids increases the risk of profound sedation, respiratory depression and death. The decision needs careful review, alternatives and, if used, the lowest dose for the shortest time with monitoring.

n.0: Lorazepam is not serotonergic, so serotonin syndrome is not the main risk.
n.1: Methadone is not the main safety concern raised by adding lorazepam.
n.3: The danger is additive sedation and respiratory depression, not a reduced methadone effect.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Obi, 27, stopped his olanzapine a month ago because he gained a lot of weight and felt 'flat'. He tells his care coordinator he will not take it again. He is well at present. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Explore his concerns and review options with the prescriber
Explain that he will be detained if he refuses to take it
Ask his mother to mix crushed tablets into his meals
Arrange a depot injection so that doses cannot be missed
Psychopharmacology.w: Shared decision-making explores the person's experience, priorities and the side effects they are willing to tolerate, and reviews alternatives with the prescriber (NICE CG178 1.3.6.3; NG5 medicines optimisation; NMC Annexe A 3.1 motivational approaches).

n.1: Threatening detention is coercive and does not reflect the legal criteria or partnership working.
n.2: Covert administration to a person with capacity is unlawful and a breach of trust.
n.3: Imposing a depot without his agreement ignores his concerns and preferences.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Rae, 24, has a first episode of psychosis, and the team is about to start an antipsychotic. Before the first dose, the nurse joins the discussion with her. Which approach best reflects NICE CG178?
o: Let the team choose the drug so that she is not overwhelmed
Tell her side effects are rare and not worth worrying about
Advise her not to read the leaflet to avoid worrying her
Discuss which side effects she would most accept, and benefits
Psychopharmacology.w: CG178 1.3.6.3: treat antipsychotic medication as an explicit individual therapeutic trial, discussing and recording the side effects the person is most willing to tolerate, the expected benefits and risks, and the time to change in symptoms.

n.0: Drug choice should be made with the person, based on side-effect profiles and her preferences.
n.1: Side effects are common with antipsychotics; minimising them undermines informed consent and trust.
n.2: Discouraging her from reading information undermines informed, shared decisions.

Psychopharmacology.q: Tom, 19, was started on oral haloperidol yesterday on an acute mental health ward. This morning his neck is twisted to one side, his eyes are rolled upwards and he is frightened. His temperature and consciousness are normal. Which side effect is he most likely experiencing?
o: Acute dystonia
Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Psychopharmacology.w: Acute dystonia is an uncontrolled muscle spasm (for example torticollis or oculogyric crisis) that can appear within hours of starting an antipsychotic, especially a high-potency first-generation drug, and is more common in young men (BNF psychoses treatment summary). It needs prompt medical review.

n.1: Tardive dyskinesia develops after long-term or high-dose treatment, not the day after starting.
n.2: Akathisia is inner and motor restlessness, not a sustained muscle spasm.
n.3: NMS involves fever, rigidity, altered consciousness and autonomic instability; his temperature and consciousness are normal.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mr Sato, 28, had his risperidone dose increased ten days ago. He now paces the corridor, cannot sit through meals and says he feels 'restless inside'. A colleague thinks his psychosis is worsening and suggests giving his PRN antipsychotic. What should the nurse do?
o: Encourage him to rest in bed until the restlessness eases
Give his PRN antipsychotic for psychotic agitation
Report possible akathisia to the prescriber for review
Increase his observation level for rising aggression
Psychopharmacology.w: Akathisia (subjective and motor restlessness) typically starts hours to weeks after starting or increasing an antipsychotic and can be mistaken for psychotic agitation (BNF; NICE CG178 1.3.6.4). More antipsychotic may worsen it, so the prescriber should review the treatment.

n.0: Lying in bed does not relieve akathisia, which makes it hard to stay still.
n.1: Extra antipsychotic may worsen akathisia, which is the likely cause after a recent dose increase.
n.3: Treating restlessness as aggression without assessing the cause risks unnecessary restriction.

Psychopharmacology.q: Mrs Doyle, 68, has received a first-generation depot antipsychotic for 15 years. At her clinic visit the nurse notices repetitive lip-smacking, chewing movements and tongue protrusion that she seems unaware of. Which side effect is most likely?
o: Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Acute dystonia
Psychopharmacology.w: Tardive dyskinesia is abnormal involuntary movements of the lips, tongue, face and jaw developing on long-term or high-dose antipsychotic treatment; it is more common in older women and may be irreversible (BNF psychoses treatment summary). It should be reported for review.

n.1: Akathisia is restlessness with an urge to move, not orofacial movements.
n.2: Parkinsonism causes slowness, rigidity and tremor rather than lip-smacking and tongue movements.
n.3: Acute dystonia is a sustained spasm occurring within hours or days of starting treatment.

Psychopharmacology.q: Ms Lin, 30, started olanzapine for schizophrenia two weeks ago. Her baseline weight, waist, pulse, blood pressure, HbA1c and lipids were recorded. Under NICE CG178, how often should her weight be measured now?
o: At 12 weeks and then every year
Monthly for the first year of her treatment
Weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks
Every 6 months while she takes olanzapine
Psychopharmacology.w: CG178 1.3.6.4: weight weekly for the first 6 weeks, then at 12 weeks, at 1 year and annually, plotted on a chart. Olanzapine commonly causes early weight gain, so frequent early monitoring allows early intervention.

n.0: 12 weeks, 1 year and annually is the schedule for pulse, blood pressure, glucose and lipids, not weight in the early weeks.
n.1: Monthly weighing misses the weekly monitoring required in the first 6 weeks.
n.3: Six-monthly weighing would miss the rapid early weight gain olanzapine can cause.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Tom, 19, attends with low mood. His father has schizophrenia and Tom asks whether he will develop it too. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
o: It is not inherited, so your risk is the same as anyone else's
Your risk is about one in two because your father has the condition
A blood test can show whether you carry the gene for schizophrenia
Your risk is raised, but most children of affected parents are unaffected
Mental Health Conditions.w: SPEC.T2 lists genomics linked to MH conditions. Schizophrenia is polygenic: a first-degree relative raises lifetime risk (to roughly 10%), and environmental stressors interact with this vulnerability (stress-vulnerability model), so most children of affected parents are not affected.

n.0: Family history is a recognised risk factor, so his risk is higher than average.
n.1: One in two greatly overstates the risk from one affected parent.
n.2: No single gene or diagnostic genetic test exists; risk is polygenic.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Sam, 26, has a first episode of psychosis. After discussion he declines antipsychotic medication and says he wants to try talking therapy first. He is not at immediate risk. What is the most appropriate plan?
o: Request a Mental Health Act assessment to start medication
Offer family intervention and CBT and review the plan in 6 months
Explain that CBT cannot start until he accepts an antipsychotic
Offer family intervention and CBT and agree a review within 1 month
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.3.4: if the person still wants psychological interventions alone, offer family intervention and CBT, agree a time (1 month or less) to review treatment options including antipsychotics, and keep monitoring symptoms and functioning.

n.0: He is not at immediate risk and is engaging; compulsion is not justified on these facts.
n.1: Six months is far longer than the 1 month or less review NICE advises.
n.2: Psychological therapy is offered even if medication is declined.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Grace, 45, has schizophrenia and is showing early signs of relapse: poor sleep, suspiciousness and returning voices. She lives with a supportive partner, is not at immediate risk and wants to stay at home. Which is the most appropriate first option?
o: Referral back to the early intervention in psychosis service
Increasing her outpatient reviews to once a month
Referral to the crisis resolution and home treatment team
Informal admission to an acute inpatient ward
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.4.1: crisis resolution and home treatment teams are the first-line service for people in crisis, as an alternative to admission, where the person can be managed safely at home.

n.0: EIP is for first episode or first presentation; Grace has an established illness.
n.1: Monthly review is too slow a response to an acute relapse.
n.3: Admission is for when home treatment cannot manage the risk; here it can.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Holly, 20, is referred because she has become withdrawn, her college work has declined and she has had brief periods of hearing her name called. A clear diagnosis of psychosis cannot be made. Her mother asks if a low-dose antipsychotic would prevent psychosis. What should the nurse explain?
o: A low-dose antipsychotic is started to reduce the risk of transition
No treatment is offered until a diagnosis is confirmed
Individual CBT is offered; antipsychotics are not used for prevention
An antipsychotic is offered if symptoms last more than 2 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.2.3.1-1.2.3.2: for people at increased risk of psychosis offer individual CBT with or without family intervention, and do not offer antipsychotic medication to reduce the risk of or prevent psychosis. Monitor for up to 3 years if symptoms persist.

n.0: NICE advises against antipsychotics to prevent psychosis.
n.1: She is distressed with declining function, so CBT is offered now rather than waiting.
n.3: Duration of attenuated symptoms does not change the advice against preventive antipsychotics.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ella, 30, has had 5 days of elevated mood, needing 4 hours' sleep and starting several new projects at work. Colleagues find her talkative but she is still working. There are no delusions or hallucinations. Which term best describes her presentation?
o: Mania
Hypomania
Mania with psychotic features
Cyclothymia
Mental Health Conditions.w: Hypomania is a milder elevation of mood lasting several days without psychotic features and without marked impairment of functioning. Mania is more severe, impairs functioning or needs admission, and may include psychosis (ICD-11; CG185 uses both terms).

n.0: Her functioning is largely preserved, which points away from mania.
n.2: She has no delusions or hallucinations.
n.3: Cyclothymia is a persistent pattern of mood instability over at least 2 years, not a discrete episode.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Byrne, 38, is admitted with mania. In the busy day room he is loud, pacing and becoming more irritable as other patients come and go. He is not threatening anyone. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Encourage him to join the ward exercise group to use up energy
Offer him a quiet, low-stimulation area with calm, brief interaction
Move him to seclusion to reduce stimulation
Let him stay in the day room so he does not feel restricted
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.5.1: ensure people with mania or hypomania have access to calming environments and reduced stimulation. Short, calm interactions avoid adding to overarousal.

n.0: Group activity adds stimulation and is likely to escalate him.
n.2: Seclusion is for severe behavioural disturbance likely to cause harm to others; he is not threatening anyone.
n.3: Leaving him in an escalating environment ignores a clear trigger.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Adeyemi, 44, is on an acute ward with mania. She tells the nurse she has resigned from her job by email and plans to sell her house this week to fund a business idea. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Help her contact an estate agent because it is her choice
Tell her she lacks capacity for all decisions while on the ward
Advise her to delay major decisions until she has recovered
Ask her to make a lasting power of attorney while on the ward
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.5.1: advise people with mania or hypomania not to make important decisions until they have recovered. Lasting power of attorney can be discussed (1.1.5) but needs capacity and should not be made in the acute phase.

n.0: Facilitating an impulsive sale during mania risks serious financial harm she may regret.
n.1: Capacity is decision-specific (MCA s2); a blanket statement is wrong.
n.3: Making an LPA while acutely manic risks invalidity and exploitation; it belongs to a calmer, planned discussion.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Clarke, 52, has bipolar disorder and has been taking sertraline on its own for depression. He now presents with mania. What does NICE CG185 recommend?
o: Consider stopping the sertraline and offer an antipsychotic
Increase the sertraline dose to treat the mood instability
Continue the sertraline and add lamotrigine for mood
Continue the sertraline and add lorazepam for sleep
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.5.2: if a person develops mania or hypomania while taking an antidepressant as monotherapy, consider stopping the antidepressant and offer an antipsychotic (1.5.3), whether or not the antidepressant is stopped.

n.1: Antidepressants can drive mood elevation; increasing the dose may worsen mania.
n.2: CG185 1.5.12: do not offer lamotrigine to treat mania.
n.3: A benzodiazepine may help sleep but does not treat the mania; NICE recommends an antipsychotic.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ruth, 27, develops mania. She is not taking any antipsychotic or mood stabiliser. Which medicine does NICE CG185 recommend as an option?
o: Carbamazepine
Sertraline
Olanzapine
Lamotrigine
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.5.3: if a person develops mania and is not taking an antipsychotic or mood stabiliser, offer haloperidol, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone, considering preference, advance statements and physical health.

n.0: Carbamazepine is not among the first-line options for acute mania in CG185.
n.1: An antidepressant can worsen mania.
n.3: Lamotrigine is not used to treat mania (1.5.12).

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Lewis, 61, has taken lithium for bipolar disorder for 10 years and is admitted with a manic relapse. She says she has 'mostly' taken her tablets. What should happen first regarding her lithium?
o: Switch her to valproate as a more reliable mood stabiliser
Check her plasma lithium level to optimise treatment
Stop the lithium because it has failed to prevent relapse
Add an antidepressant to prevent a later depressive episode
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.5.8: if the person is already taking lithium, check plasma lithium levels to optimise treatment. Partial adherence is common and the level guides whether dose or adherence is the issue.

n.0: Valproate is not a first choice here and the level has not yet been checked.
n.2: One relapse does not mean lithium has failed; the level and adherence need checking first.
n.3: Adding an antidepressant during mania risks worsening the episode.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Kemi, 35, is preparing for discharge after an episode of mania. Her partner wants to know how they can spot problems earlier next time. Which intervention best reduces the risk of a future crisis?
o: Give her a general leaflet about bipolar disorder to read at home later
Advise her partner to call 999 at the first change in her mood
Agree a plan with them both of her early warning signs and actions
Arrange weekly lithium blood levels for the next year
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.4.1: develop a risk management plan jointly with the person and their carer covering triggers, early warning signs of relapse, their own coping strategies and how to get help. A personal relapse signature is more useful than generic information.

n.0: Generic information does not identify her personal relapse signature.
n.1: Emergency services are for emergencies; early warning signs need a graded plan.
n.3: Once stable, levels are every 3 months in the first year, not weekly, and do not identify early warning signs.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Shah, 47, has bipolar disorder and develops moderate depression. He is not currently taking any medicine for bipolar disorder. Which medication option does NICE CG185 recommend?
o: Mirtazapine on its own
Quetiapine on its own
Sertraline with lorazepam
Fluoxetine on its own
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG185 1.6.3: for moderate or severe bipolar depression in a person not taking a drug for bipolar disorder, offer fluoxetine combined with olanzapine, or quetiapine on its own. A psychological intervention for bipolar depression is also offered (1.6.1).

n.0: Antidepressant monotherapy risks switching into mania and is not recommended.
n.2: Neither drug addresses bipolar depression in line with CG185, and the SSRI is unprotected by an antimanic agent.
n.3: Fluoxetine is recommended combined with olanzapine, not as monotherapy.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Patel, 39, has had low mood and poor sleep for 6 weeks. His PHQ-9 score is 11, he is working and has no thoughts of self-harm. He has no preference about treatment. Which first-line option does NICE NG222 favour?
o: Guided self-help based on CBT principles
An SSRI started at his first appointment
Referral for psychodynamic psychotherapy
Individual CBT combined with an antidepressant
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG222 1.5: for less severe depression (PHQ-9 under 16) start with the least intrusive, most effective option; guided self-help is first in the NICE table. Do not routinely offer antidepressants first line unless the person prefers.

n.1: Antidepressants are not routinely first line for less severe depression.
n.2: Psychodynamic therapy is lower in the NICE order for less severe depression.
n.3: Combined CBT and an antidepressant is the first option for more severe depression.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ana, 33, has moderate depression. During her assessment she says she feels 'there is no point any more'. The student nurse is worried about raising suicide. What is the most appropriate approach?
o: Ask her directly whether she has thoughts of ending her life
Ask her partner privately whether she has mentioned suicide
Avoid the subject in case asking increases her risk
Wait for her to raise the topic when she feels ready
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG222: always ask people with depression directly about suicidal ideation and intent. Asking does not increase risk and allows safety planning (P3.10).

n.1: Collateral history can help but does not replace asking Ana herself.
n.2: Asking about suicide does not plant the idea or increase risk.
n.3: Waiting may miss serious risk that she is hinting at now.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Fisher, 50, has depression and has stopped going out, seeing friends or doing his woodwork. He is offered behavioural activation. Which description best fits this therapy?
o: Graded exposure to situations that trigger his panic
Practising mindfulness to notice thoughts without reacting
Exploring early relationships to gain insight into his low mood
Planning rewarding activities to reverse withdrawal and inactivity
Mental Health Conditions.w: Behavioural activation (an NG222 option for both less and more severe depression) targets the cycle of withdrawal and low mood by planning and monitoring activities that give pleasure or achievement.

n.0: Graded exposure is used for anxiety disorders, not as BA for depression.
n.1: This describes mindfulness-based approaches, used mainly to prevent relapse.
n.2: This describes psychodynamic therapy.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Green, 46, has a new episode of more severe depression (PHQ-9 of 20). She has no psychotic symptoms and is willing to try either talking therapy or medication. Which option is first in the NICE NG222 list for more severe depression?
o: Counselling for 8 sessions
Guided self-help with weekly telephone support
Individual CBT combined with an antidepressant
Group exercise over 10 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG222 1.6.1, table 2: all listed treatments can be first line, matched to preference, but the first in the NICE order is a combination of individual CBT and an antidepressant.

n.0: Counselling is an option but sits lower in the NICE order for more severe depression.
n.1: Guided self-help is in the less severe depression table, not the more severe one.
n.3: Group exercise is an option but sits low in the NICE order for more severe depression.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Wood, 68, has severe depression. He has stopped eating much and tells the nurse that his insides have rotted away and that he is already dead. His mood has not improved on sertraline. What does NICE NG222 recommend?
o: Stopping the sertraline and starting an antipsychotic in its place
Group behavioural activation as the next step
Specialist referral and an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic
Doubling the sertraline dose and reviewing him in 3 months
Mental Health Conditions.w: He has depression with psychotic (nihilistic) symptoms. NG222 1.12.1-1.12.2: refer to specialist mental health services and consider combining an antidepressant with an antipsychotic such as olanzapine or quetiapine.

n.0: NICE combines the drugs rather than replacing the antidepressant.
n.1: Group therapy does not address severe psychotic depression; psychological therapy follows improvement of psychotic symptoms.
n.3: A 3-month wait is unsafe with psychotic features and poor intake.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Hughes, 72, has severe depression. For 4 days she has taken almost no food or fluid, her urine output has fallen and she is becoming weaker. Two antidepressants have not helped. Which treatment should be considered?
o: Electroconvulsive therapy, as a rapid response is needed
Adding lithium augmentation and reviewing in 4 weeks
Referral for individual high-intensity CBT
Switching to an antidepressant from another class
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG222 1.13.1: consider ECT for severe depression when a rapid response is needed, for example when the depression is life-threatening because the person is not eating or drinking. Consent and MHA s58A safeguards apply.

n.1: Lithium augmentation also takes weeks; a rapid response is needed.
n.2: CBT is too slow and she is too unwell to engage.
n.3: Another antidepressant would take weeks to work; her condition is life-threatening now.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Ito, 31, completes a PHQ-9 with the nurse at his GP surgery. He scores 18. He has no suicidal thoughts and no psychotic symptoms. How should his depression be classified and managed under NICE NG222?
o: As more severe, discussing combined CBT and an antidepressant
As severe enough to need an urgent referral for ECT assessment
As less severe, with guided self-help offered first
As less severe, with active monitoring for the next 2 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: Step 1: NG222 uses a PHQ-9 cut-off of 16; 16 or more is 'more severe'. Step 2: offer a choice of more severe depression treatments, the first in the table being individual CBT with an antidepressant.

n.1: ECT is for severe life-threatening depression or when other treatments fail, not a PHQ-9 score.
n.2: A score of 18 is above the 16 cut-off, so this is not less severe.
n.3: Active monitoring is for people with less severe depression who do not want treatment.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Jonas, 40, sees the practice nurse for a review of his depression. He says he has written goodbye letters, has saved a supply of tablets and intends to take them this weekend. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Refer him urgently to specialist mental health services
Start an antidepressant and review him in 2 weeks
Give him a crisis line number and book a review next week
Refer him to NHS Talking Therapies for high-intensity CBT
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG222 1.2.9: if a person with depression presents considerable immediate risk to themselves, refer them urgently to specialist mental health services. Goodbye letters, means and a timed plan indicate high immediate risk (P3.10).

n.1: Medication does not address the immediate risk and takes weeks to work.
n.2: A crisis number and a week's wait leave him unsafe this weekend.
n.3: Talking Therapies is not a crisis service.

Mental Health Conditions.q: A week after a patient seriously assaulted a nurse on an acute ward, several staff report poor sleep and intrusive memories. Their symptoms are mild and below the threshold for acute stress disorder. The ward manager asks what NICE NG116 recommends to prevent PTSD. What is the best answer?
o: Practical support and active monitoring of their symptoms
Immediate referral of all staff for EMDR
A single group session to talk through the assault in detail
A short course of diazepam for the staff most affected
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG116 1.6.4-1.6.5: consider active monitoring for subthreshold symptoms within 1 month of a trauma; do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing for the prevention or treatment of PTSD.

n.1: EMDR is for diagnosed PTSD, typically more than 1 to 3 months after a trauma, not routine prevention.
n.2: This is psychologically-focused debriefing, which NICE advises against.
n.3: NG116 1.6.24: do not offer drug treatments, including benzodiazepines, to prevent PTSD.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Novak, 34, was in a serious car crash 4 months ago. He has flashbacks, nightmares, avoids driving and is constantly on edge. He is diagnosed with PTSD. Which treatment does NICE NG116 recommend first?
o: Non-directive supportive counselling
Regular lorazepam to reduce hyperarousal
Psychologically-focused debriefing
Individual trauma-focused CBT or EMDR
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG116 1.6.16 and 1.6.19: offer adults individual trauma-focused CBT (more than 1 month after the trauma), or EMDR for PTSD presenting more than 3 months after a non-combat trauma (1.6.19).

n.0: Non-trauma-focused counselling is not a NICE first-line treatment for PTSD.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are not a PTSD treatment and carry dependence risk.
n.2: NICE advises against debriefing to prevent or treat PTSD.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Leo, 12, has PTSD 4 months after a house fire. His mother asks whether medication would help. Which treatment does NICE NG116 recommend?
o: EMDR as his first treatment
An individual trauma-focused CBT intervention
Psychologically-focused debriefing at school
Sertraline with monthly review by his GP
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG116 1.6.11: offer individual trauma-focused CBT to 7 to 17 year olds presenting more than 3 months after a trauma. 1.6.14: do not offer drug treatments for PTSD in under-18s.

n.0: EMDR is considered for children only if they do not respond to or engage with trauma-focused CBT.
n.2: Debriefing is not recommended to prevent or treat PTSD.
n.3: Drug treatment is not offered for PTSD in under-18s.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Reid, 29, has generalised anxiety disorder. Her symptoms have not improved after education and active monitoring. She has no marked functional impairment. What is the most appropriate next step under NICE CG113?
o: A low-dose antipsychotic prescribed by her GP
A 4-week course of diazepam
Guided self-help based on CBT principles
Individual high-intensity CBT
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG113 step 2: for GAD not improved after step 1, offer a low-intensity psychological intervention such as individual non-facilitated or guided self-help, or psychoeducational groups.

n.0: Antipsychotics should not be offered for GAD in primary care.
n.1: Benzodiazepines are not used for GAD except short term in a crisis.
n.3: High-intensity CBT is step 3, for marked impairment or no improvement after step 2.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Daly, 41, has panic disorder with attacks several times a week. He asks his GP practice nurse whether he can have diazepam to take when an attack starts. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Arrange diazepam to take as needed during attacks
Explain diazepam worsens long-term outcome and discuss CBT
Suggest a sedating antihistamine at night
Suggest a low-dose antipsychotic to reduce the attacks
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG113: benzodiazepines are associated with a less good long-term outcome and should not be prescribed for panic disorder; sedating antihistamines or antipsychotics should not be prescribed either. CBT is the psychological treatment of choice.

n.0: NICE advises against benzodiazepines for panic disorder.
n.2: Sedating antihistamines should not be prescribed for panic disorder.
n.3: Antipsychotics should not be prescribed for panic disorder.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Kaur, 55, has GAD that has not improved with guided self-help. She prefers to try medication. Which drug does NICE CG113 suggest considering first?
o: Pregabalin
Quetiapine
Sertraline
Diazepam
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG113 1.2.23: if a person with GAD chooses drug treatment, offer an SSRI and consider sertraline first because it is the most cost-effective.

n.0: CG113 1.2.25: pregabalin is considered if SSRIs and SNRIs cannot be tolerated.
n.1: Antipsychotics are not offered for GAD in primary care.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are reserved for short-term crisis use.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Hassan, 23, has OCD. He fears contamination and washes his hands up to 50 times a day, often asking staff whether his hands are clean. Which psychological approach is central to his treatment?
o: Applied relaxation
Reassuring him whenever he asks
Trauma-focused CBT
Exposure and response prevention
Mental Health Conditions.w: NICE CG31: CBT including exposure and response prevention (ERP) is the core psychological treatment for OCD. Graded exposure to the feared trigger while resisting the compulsion breaks the cycle.

n.0: Applied relaxation is an option for GAD, not OCD.
n.1: Repeated reassurance acts like a compulsion and maintains the OCD.
n.2: Trauma-focused CBT treats PTSD.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Sophie, 26, has panic disorder and is on an acute ward. She suddenly feels her chest tightening, is breathing fast and has tingling fingers. Her observations and a recent ECG are normal and she says it feels like her usual attacks. What is the most appropriate nursing action?
o: Ask her to breathe in and out of a paper bag
Leave her in a quiet room to settle by herself
Stay with her and coach slow, steady breathing
Give her PRN lorazepam straight away
Mental Health Conditions.w: Having excluded a physical cause (normal observations, recent ECG, typical pattern), the priority is calm presence, slow controlled breathing and explaining that the symptoms are panic and will pass (Annexe A 3.6 CBT-informed techniques; CG113 discourages benzodiazepines for panic).

n.0: Paper-bag rebreathing is no longer recommended and can cause hypoxia.
n.1: Leaving her alone increases fear and removes support.
n.3: Benzodiazepines are not used for panic disorder and the attack can be managed without them.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Kayleigh, 25, has a diagnosis of emotionally unstable (borderline) personality disorder and no other mental health condition. She asks the community nurse for 'a tablet to stop my moods swinging'. What is the most accurate response?
o: Medication is not recommended to treat the disorder or its symptoms
A regular benzodiazepine will settle her mood over time
A long-term antipsychotic will reduce her emotional instability
A mood stabiliser is the first-line treatment for mood swings
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.3.5.1-1.3.5.2: drug treatment should not be used specifically for borderline personality disorder or its individual symptoms (such as emotional instability or self-harm), and antipsychotics should not be used for medium- or long-term treatment. Drugs may treat comorbid conditions.

n.1: Regular benzodiazepines are not recommended and carry dependence and overdose risk.
n.2: CG78 1.3.5.2: antipsychotics should not be used for medium- and long-term treatment of BPD.
n.3: Mood stabilisers are not recommended for BPD or its individual symptoms.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Evans, 32, has borderline personality disorder and is in a crisis. His GP and the crisis team agree to a short course of a sedative antihistamine. Following NICE CG78, what is the longest the course should run?
o: 1 week
Until his next outpatient review
2 weeks
4 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.3.5.4 and 1.3.7.3: short-term sedative medication may be considered cautiously in a crisis; the duration should be agreed with the person but be no longer than 1 week, with informed consent documented.

n.1: An open-ended course is not short term and could run well beyond 1 week.
n.2: Two weeks exceeds the CG78 limit.
n.3: Four weeks exceeds the CG78 limit and risks dependence and overdose.

Mental Health Conditions.q: At handover a staff nurse says about a newly admitted woman with borderline personality disorder: 'She is just attention seeking, she should not even be on this ward.' What is the most appropriate response?
o: Report the staff nurse to the NMC after handover
Leave the comment unchallenged to avoid conflict in the team
Challenge the comment: the diagnosis does not bar her from care
Agree that discharge would avoid reinforcing her behaviour
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.1.1.1: people with BPD should not be excluded from any health or social care service because of their diagnosis or because they have self-harmed. Code 3.4 and 20.2 and P1.14 require challenging discriminatory attitudes and stigma.

n.0: A single remark is first addressed locally; an NMC referral is disproportionate at this stage.
n.1: Leaving it unchallenged allows stigma to shape her care.
n.3: Discharge on the basis of the diagnosis is exclusion that CG78 prohibits.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Megan, 22, has borderline personality disorder and repeatedly self-harms by cutting. She and her team agree that reducing self-harm is the main priority. Which psychological treatment does NICE CG78 suggest considering?
o: Group psychoeducation over 4 sessions
A comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy programme
A brief 6-week course of solution-focused therapy
Psychologically-focused debriefing after each episode
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.3.4.5: for women with BPD for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, consider a comprehensive DBT programme.

n.0: Four sessions of psychoeducation is not a treatment for recurrent self-harm in BPD.
n.2: CG78 1.3.4.4: do not use brief psychological interventions (under 3 months) specifically for BPD outside a service with the 1.3.4.3 characteristics; for recurrent self-harm in women, 1.3.4.5 points to comprehensive DBT.
n.3: Debriefing is not a treatment for BPD or self-harm.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Brown, 36, has borderline personality disorder and arrives at the community mental health team in crisis after an argument with her partner, saying she cannot cope. What should the nurse do first?
o: Use her crisis plan and calm, validating open questions
Arrange an informal admission so she is kept safe
Advise her to come back to the team once she feels calmer
Ask her GP to increase her regular medication today
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.3.7.1: when a person with BPD presents in crisis, consult the crisis plan, maintain a calm, non-threatening attitude, try to understand the crisis from their view and use empathic open questioning with validating statements.

n.1: Admission is considered after alternatives such as home treatment, and risk has not yet been assessed.
n.2: Sending her away in crisis is unsafe and invalidating.
n.3: Drugs are not used for BPD symptoms; crisis sedation is short term and follows assessment.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Jade, 28, has borderline personality disorder. Over 2 days her distress and thoughts of self-harm have increased despite support from her care coordinator. She is not detained and lives with a friend. Which option should be considered first?
o: Referral to the early intervention in psychosis team
Referral to the crisis resolution and home treatment team
A routine outpatient appointment with her psychiatrist
Admission to an acute psychiatric inpatient ward
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.4.1.1: before considering admission to an acute inpatient unit for a person with BPD, first refer them to a crisis resolution and home treatment team or another local alternative to admission.

n.0: EIP is for first-episode psychosis.
n.2: A routine appointment is too slow for rising risk.
n.3: Admission is for risk that other services cannot manage; home treatment comes first.

Mental Health Conditions.q: On an inpatient unit, Ms Kowalski, who has borderline personality disorder, praises some nurses as 'the only ones who care' and criticises others. Staff have begun to disagree about her care plan. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Transfer her to another ward to break the pattern
Agree a consistent team approach in supervision and her care plan
Confront her at the next ward meeting about dividing the staff
Allocate her to the nurses she praises on each shift
Mental Health Conditions.w: Splitting is managed by a consistent, structured team approach agreed in the care plan and supported by supervision (CG78 1.1.8 and 1.3.4.3: explicit, integrated approach shared by the team).

n.0: A transfer moves the problem without a consistent plan.
n.2: Confrontation is likely to feel rejecting and does not address team inconsistency.
n.3: Favouring some staff reinforces splitting and leaves the team divided.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Ali, 30, has borderline personality disorder. Home treatment has not managed a serious risk to himself and the team now plans a short informal admission. Which action is in line with NICE CG78?
o: Set the length within the team and tell him when he arrives
Agree the purpose and likely length of stay with him first
Leave the length open until he says he feels ready to leave
Agree that he stays until he has stopped self-harming
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG78 1.4.1.3: when considering inpatient care, actively involve the person and agree the length and purpose of the admission in advance, based on a shared understanding of benefits and possible harms.

n.0: Deciding without him fails to involve him actively, as CG78 requires.
n.2: An open-ended stay is not agreed in advance and can increase dependence.
n.3: Stopping self-harm is not a defined, agreed endpoint.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Zara, 19, has restricted her eating for 8 months, exercises for hours daily and is frightened of gaining weight. Her BMI is 19. A practitioner suggests she is 'not underweight enough' for eating disorder treatment. What does NICE NG69 say?
o: Referral is appropriate after 12 months of restriction
Treatment is offered once her BMI falls below 17.5
She should be weighed monthly until her BMI is below 18.5
Single measures such as BMI must not decide access to care
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG69 1.2.8: do not use single measures such as BMI or duration of illness to determine whether to offer treatment for an eating disorder.

n.0: Duration of illness is also a single measure that must not gate treatment.
n.1: A BMI threshold for access is exactly the single measure NICE warns against.
n.2: Waiting for a lower BMI delays treatment and risks harm.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ollie, 15, is diagnosed with anorexia nervosa and lives with both parents, who are keen to help. Which treatment does NICE NG69 suggest considering first?
o: A group psychoeducation programme
Individual eating-disorder-focused CBT
An SSRI alongside regular dietetic advice
Anorexia-focused family therapy (FT-AN)
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG69 1.3.10: consider FT-AN for children and young people with anorexia nervosa. Individual CBT-ED or adolescent-focused psychotherapy are alternatives if FT-AN is unacceptable or ineffective.

n.0: Group psychoeducation is not a recommended treatment for anorexia in young people.
n.1: CBT-ED is an alternative for young people when FT-AN is not suitable.
n.2: NG69 1.3.24: do not offer medication as the sole treatment for anorexia nervosa.

Mental Health Conditions.q: A community nurse reviews Ms Hart, 24, who has anorexia nervosa. Which single finding is a red (high risk to life) flag on the MEED adult risk tool?
o: Heart rate of 38 beats per minute
Heart rate of 55 beats per minute
Tympanic temperature of 36.2°C
Postural heart rate rise of 15 beats per minute
Mental Health Conditions.w: MEED (RCPsych CR233) adult red flags include heart rate under 40, BMI under 13, temperature under 35.5°C, postural heart rate rise over 30, systolic BP under 90 and SUSS score 0 to 1.

n.1: A heart rate of 50 to 60 sits in the lower-risk band.
n.2: Above 36°C is low risk on the MEED tool.
n.3: A rise of 10 to 30 is amber, not red.

Mental Health Conditions.q: A nurse uses the SUSS test when assessing a young person with anorexia nervosa. What does this test assess?
o: Grip strength in the person's dominant hand
Walking speed over a measured 10 metres
Muscle power sitting up and rising from a squat
Postural drop in blood pressure on standing
Mental Health Conditions.w: The Sit Up Squat Stand (SUSS) test in the MEED tool scores proximal muscle power: rising from lying to sitting and from squatting to standing. A score of 0 to 1 is a red flag.

n.0: Grip strength is used in other nutrition assessments, not SUSS.
n.1: Walking speed is not part of SUSS.
n.3: Postural blood pressure is a separate MEED item.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Bella, 20, is in the third day of a refeeding plan on a specialist unit. She becomes weak and breathless and develops ankle oedema. Which action is the priority?
o: Check phosphate, potassium and magnesium urgently
Check her sodium and glucose and continue the plan
Increase her calories to speed up weight restoration
Stop feeding until her next weekly medical review
Mental Health Conditions.w: These are features of refeeding syndrome, which usually occurs in the first days of refeeding with low phosphate, potassium and magnesium. Urgent bloods and medical review guide correction (NG69 refeeding protocol referencing MEED).

n.1: Sodium and glucose miss the key electrolyte, phosphate.
n.2: Increasing calories now could worsen refeeding syndrome.
n.3: Stopping feeding for a week risks under-nutrition, which MEED also warns against.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Patel, 27, has anorexia nervosa. At clinic her BMI is 12.8, heart rate 42 and tympanic temperature 35.3°C. She is alert and wants to continue outpatient therapy. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange urgent medical admission for stabilisation
Repeat her weight and observations in 1 week
Refer her to a community dietitian for a meal plan
Increase her outpatient CBT-ED to twice weekly
Mental Health Conditions.w: Step 1: BMI under 13 and temperature under 35.5°C are MEED red flags (high impending risk to life). Step 2: NG69 1.10: admit people whose physical health is severely compromised for medical stabilisation and to start refeeding.

n.1: A week's delay is unsafe with red-flag findings.
n.2: Dietetic input alone does not manage acute medical instability.
n.3: More therapy does not address immediate medical risk.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Rhian, 23, has severe anorexia nervosa. Her physical health is at serious risk, she refuses admission and food, and the team agree she can only be treated safely as an inpatient. What does NICE NG69 recommend?
o: Follow the Mental Health Act 1983 framework
Respect her refusal because she is an adult
Wait for her to lose capacity before acting
Ask her parents to give consent on her behalf
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG69 1.12: if physical health is at serious risk, the person does not consent and can only be treated safely as an inpatient, follow the Mental Health Act 1983. Nasogastric feeding can be treatment for the mental disorder.

n.1: The MHA allows treatment of mental disorder without consent when the criteria are met.
n.2: Delay until capacity is lost puts her life at risk and the MHA does not require incapacity.
n.3: Parents cannot consent for an adult.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Clarke, 30, has bulimia nervosa with binge eating and vomiting several times a week. He is medically stable. Which treatment does NICE NG69 suggest considering first?
o: Fluoxetine as the main treatment
Bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help
Bulimia-nervosa-focused family therapy
Admission for supervised meals
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG69 1.5.2-1.5.4: for adults with bulimia, consider bulimia-nervosa-focused guided self-help; if unacceptable or ineffective after 4 weeks, consider individual CBT-ED. Do not offer medication as the sole treatment.

n.0: Medication should not be the sole treatment for bulimia.
n.2: FT-BN is offered to children and young people, not adults.
n.3: He is medically stable and does not need admission.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Leah, 29, gave birth 6 days ago. Her partner calls the community midwife: over 24 hours she has stopped sleeping, seems confused and has said the baby is 'not really hers'. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Arrange a perinatal team appointment for next week
Ask the health visitor to review her at the next visit
Reassure her partner that these are the baby blues
Refer her for specialist assessment within 4 hours
Mental Health Conditions.w: Sudden onset of confusion, sleeplessness and delusional ideas soon after birth suggests postpartum psychosis, a psychiatric emergency. CG192: refer to a secondary mental health service, preferably a specialist perinatal service, for immediate assessment (within 4 hours of referral).

n.0: A week's wait is unsafe in suspected postpartum psychosis.
n.1: Waiting for a routine visit delays an emergency assessment.
n.2: Baby blues cause tearfulness and mood swings, not confusion or delusions.

Mental Health Conditions.q: At her booking appointment, a midwife asks Freya, 26, about her mental health. What does one of the two depression identification questions in NICE CG192 ask about?
o: Feeling down, depressed or hopeless in the last month
Feeling low on most days over the whole past year
Any past treatment for depression or anxiety
Feeling unable to cope since the pregnancy began
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.5.4: at first contact or booking and in the early postnatal period, consider asking: 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by feeling down, depressed or hopeless?' and 'During the past month, have you often been bothered by having little interest or pleasure in doing things?'.

n.1: The NICE questions cover the past month, not the past year.
n.2: Past treatment is asked about separately (CG192 1.5.9) and is not an identification question.
n.3: Coping since pregnancy is not one of the two CG192 identification questions.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Osei, 34, has severe depression with suicidal thoughts 3 months after giving birth and needs inpatient care. She is breastfeeding. Where should she normally be admitted?
o: A psychiatric intensive care unit
An adult acute psychiatric ward
A specialist mother and baby unit
A general medical ward with mental health liaison
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.10.1: women who need inpatient care for a mental health problem within 12 months of childbirth should normally be admitted to a specialist mother and baby unit, unless there are specific reasons not to.

n.0: PICU is for severe disturbance needing intensive care, not the default perinatal setting.
n.1: A general adult ward separates mother and baby and lacks perinatal expertise.
n.3: A medical ward lacks specialist perinatal mental health care.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Lane, 28, takes valproate for bipolar disorder. She tells the community nurse she and her partner are hoping to start a family. What should she be advised?
o: To continue valproate and start folic acid
To stop valproate gradually under specialist advice
To stop valproate as soon as she is pregnant
To halve the valproate dose before trying to conceive
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.4.28: if a woman taking valproate is planning a pregnancy, advise her to gradually stop it because of the risk of fetal malformations and adverse neurodevelopmental outcomes after any exposure in pregnancy (MHRA valproate rules).

n.0: Folic acid does not remove valproate's risks.
n.2: Any exposure in pregnancy carries risk, so stopping should happen before conception.
n.3: A lower dose still carries fetal risk.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Grey, 31, has bipolar disorder and has been well on lithium for 3 years. She is now 6 weeks pregnant and remains well. What does NICE CG192 advise the team to consider?
o: Stopping the lithium today to protect the fetus
Continuing lithium with her usual 6-monthly levels
Stopping the lithium gradually over 4 weeks
Switching from lithium to valproate
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.4.35: if a woman taking lithium becomes pregnant and is well, consider stopping it gradually over 4 weeks, explaining that stopping may not remove the risk of fetal heart malformations and that relapse risk is high postnatally.

n.0: Abrupt stopping raises the risk of relapse.
n.1: If lithium continues, levels are monitored more often than usual in pregnancy.
n.3: Valproate must not be offered in pregnancy for a mental health problem.
