Mental Health Conditions.q: At booking, Ms Chen, 33, says she was treated for bipolar disorder 5 years ago and has been well since. What should the maternity and mental health team be particularly alert for?
o: Postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after birth
Postpartum psychosis from 3 to 6 months after birth
Postnatal depression starting about 6 months after birth
Baby blues continuing beyond the first 6 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192: if a woman has past or present severe mental illness or a first-degree relative with severe perinatal mental illness, be alert for possible symptoms of postpartum psychosis in the first 2 weeks after childbirth.

n.1: Onset is usually within the first 2 weeks, not months later.
n.2: Her main risk is early postpartum psychosis.
n.3: Baby blues settle within about 2 weeks; this is not the specific risk for her history.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Ahmed, 27, is 4 weeks postnatal. At a contact she answers 'yes' to one of the depression identification questions. She has no thoughts of harm and no signs of severe illness. What is the most appropriate next step?
o: Ask her GP to start an antidepressant at this visit
Repeat the questions at her next routine contact
Use the EPDS or PHQ-9 as part of a fuller assessment
Refer for specialist assessment within 4 hours
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.5.5: if a woman responds positively to either identification question, consider using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) or PHQ-9 as part of a full assessment, or refer to her GP (or to a mental health professional if severe illness is suspected).

n.0: Treatment follows a full assessment, not a single positive answer.
n.1: Deferring delays assessment of a positive screen.
n.3: The 4-hour assessment is for suspected postpartum psychosis.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Silva, 30, is 28 weeks pregnant and detained on an acute ward with mania. After de-escalation fails she is given rapid tranquillisation. What is the most appropriate care immediately afterwards?
o: Avoid seclusion and monitor her closely afterwards
Seclude her to reduce stimulation as for other patients
Give a long-acting benzodiazepine to avoid repeat doses
Use the standard restraint position without changes
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG192 1.8.23: a pregnant woman needing rapid tranquillisation is treated as per NG10 except that she should not be secluded after RT, restraint is adapted to avoid harm to the fetus and short half-life drugs are preferred, with paediatric and anaesthetic input.

n.1: CG192 states she should not be secluded after rapid tranquillisation.
n.2: A short half-life benzodiazepine is preferred because of floppy baby syndrome risk.
n.3: Restraint must be adapted to avoid harm to the fetus.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Doyle, 52, was admitted 3 days ago and stopped drinking on admission. He is now agitated, sweating, tremulous, disorientated and picking at things that are not there. Delirium tremens is diagnosed. Which treatment does NICE CG100 recommend first?
o: Oral lorazepam
Oral chlordiazepoxide
Oral haloperidol
Intravenous phenytoin
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG100 1.1.4.1: in delirium tremens, offer oral lorazepam first line; if symptoms persist or oral medication is declined, offer parenteral lorazepam or haloperidol.

n.1: Chlordiazepoxide is the usual assisted-withdrawal drug, but CG100 names oral lorazepam for delirium tremens.
n.2: Haloperidol is a second-line option if oral lorazepam fails or is declined.
n.3: Phenytoin is not used in alcohol withdrawal.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Byrne, 47, has alcohol dependence and is in acute withdrawal on a ward. She has a generalised seizure that stops after 2 minutes. Which medicine does NICE CG100 advise considering to reduce further seizures?
o: Haloperidol to reduce agitation
Phenytoin by intravenous infusion
A quick-acting benzodiazepine such as lorazepam
Carbamazepine as a long-term anticonvulsant
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG100 1.1.5: in alcohol withdrawal seizures, consider a quick-acting benzodiazepine (such as lorazepam) to reduce the likelihood of further seizures; do not offer phenytoin; review the withdrawal regimen.

n.0: Haloperidol can lower the seizure threshold and does not prevent further seizures.
n.1: CG100 1.1.5.3: do not offer phenytoin to treat alcohol withdrawal seizures.
n.3: Long-term anticonvulsants are not indicated for withdrawal seizures.

Mental Health Conditions.q: A nurse in a community alcohol service wants a validated scale to measure how severe a person's current alcohol withdrawal is. Which tool does NICE CG115 name for this?
o: SADQ-C
CIWA-Ar
AUDIT-C
FAST
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG115 1.2.1.4: use AUDIT (and its short forms) for identification and outcomes, SADQ or LDQ for severity of dependence, CIWA-Ar for severity of withdrawal and APQ for the problems arising from drinking.

n.0: SADQ-C measures severity of dependence, not current withdrawal.
n.2: AUDIT-C is a short form of AUDIT for identifying risky drinking.
n.3: FAST is a brief screening tool for hazardous drinking.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Kerr, 45, drinks about 20 units a day and has shaky mornings. At a community mental health review he says he will stop drinking completely tomorrow at home on his own. What is the most appropriate advice?
o: Halve his intake each day until he reaches zero
Switch to lower-strength drinks and keep the same volume
Stop completely tomorrow as he plans, with family support
Avoid a sudden stop and contact the local alcohol service
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG100 1.1.1.4: for people who are alcohol dependent but not admitted, offer advice to avoid a sudden reduction in alcohol intake and information on contacting local alcohol support services, because abrupt withdrawal risks seizures and delirium tremens.

n.0: Halving daily is still a rapid, unsupervised reduction.
n.1: This is not a planned assisted withdrawal and he remains dependent.
n.2: An abrupt stop in dependence risks dangerous withdrawal.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Shaw, 58, a dependent drinker, is brought to an acute mental health unit. He is confused, unsteady on his feet and has jerky eye movements on looking sideways. He has not eaten properly for weeks. What is the priority?
o: Give chlordiazepoxide and reassess tomorrow
Give parenteral thiamine as prescribed
Give intravenous glucose before any thiamine
Give oral thiamine with his breakfast
Mental Health Conditions.w: Confusion, ataxia and nystagmus suggest Wernicke's encephalopathy. CG100 1.2.1.4: offer parenteral thiamine (in the UK, Pabrinex) for suspected Wernicke's for at least 5 days unless excluded, then oral thiamine.

n.0: Withdrawal treatment does not treat thiamine deficiency.
n.2: Glucose before thiamine can precipitate or worsen Wernicke's.
n.3: Oral absorption is unreliable; suspected Wernicke's needs parenteral thiamine.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Fox, 50, drinks about 35 units a day and had a withdrawal seizure during a previous attempt to stop. He now wants to stop drinking. Which setting for assisted withdrawal does NICE CG115 suggest considering?
o: Inpatient or residential assisted withdrawal
Community assisted withdrawal with daily visits
Outpatient withdrawal with a fixed chlordiazepoxide pack
Self-managed reduction with weekly GP review
Mental Health Conditions.w: Step 1: identify risk factors. Step 2: CG115 1.3.4.5: consider inpatient or residential assisted withdrawal if the person drinks over 30 units a day, scores over 30 on SADQ or has a history of epilepsy or withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens. He has two.

n.1: Community withdrawal is for people without these higher-risk features.
n.2: Outpatient prescribing does not provide the monitoring his risk needs.
n.3: Unsupervised reduction is unsafe given his seizure history.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Lowe, 61, has alcohol dependence and liver impairment confirmed by her GP. She is to start assisted withdrawal. Which approach does NICE CG115 advise?
o: Chlordiazepoxide at the usual full starting dose
Diazepam at a higher dose to prevent any seizures
Clomethiazole managed by her GP at home
Lorazepam at a reduced dose with liver monitoring
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG115 1.3.5: chlordiazepoxide or diazepam are preferred generally, but with liver impairment consider a benzodiazepine needing limited liver metabolism (for example lorazepam), start at a reduced dose and monitor liver function. CG100: clomethiazole is inpatient only.

n.0: Chlordiazepoxide relies on liver metabolism and can accumulate.
n.1: Higher doses of a long-acting drug risk accumulation and oversedation.
n.2: Clomethiazole should be used in inpatient settings, not at home.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Ince, 40, scores 23 on AUDIT and drinks about 18 units a day. He has no history of seizures or delirium tremens, lives with a supportive partner and wants to stop. What does NICE CG115 suggest considering?
o: Advising him to stop drinking at once
Brief advice and a review in 3 months
Assessment for community-based assisted withdrawal
Inpatient assisted withdrawal as the first option
Mental Health Conditions.w: Step 1: over 15 units a day and AUDIT 20 or more. Step 2: CG115 1.3.4.1: consider assessment for and delivery of community-based assisted withdrawal, with no inpatient criteria present (under 30 units, no seizures or DTs, support at home).

n.0: Abrupt stopping without support risks dangerous withdrawal.
n.1: Brief advice is for hazardous drinking; he is likely dependent and needs assisted withdrawal.
n.3: He meets none of the inpatient criteria.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Reece, 27, has schizophrenia and uses cannabis most days. His referral to the community mental health team is returned with a note saying he must stop using cannabis before he can be accepted. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Accept the decision as it follows team criteria
Challenge it: substance use is not a reason to exclude him
Ask the substance misuse service to take him on instead
Advise him to stop cannabis and then re-refer him
Mental Health Conditions.w: NICE NG58: do not exclude people with severe mental illness from services because of their substance misuse. Mental health services keep responsibility and work jointly with substance misuse services.

n.0: Local criteria cannot override the NG58 principle of non-exclusion.
n.2: Substance services work alongside, not instead of, mental health care for SMI.
n.3: Requiring abstinence first is the exclusion NG58 warns against.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Kyle, 22, has had one episode of psychosis and smokes high-strength cannabis every day. He says it helps him relax and asks whether it matters. Which response is most accurate?
o: Cannabis affects mood but is not linked with psychosis
Cannabis eases psychotic symptoms, so it can be a coping aid
Cannabis can worsen psychotic symptoms and raise relapse risk
Cannabis harms mental health when combined with alcohol
Mental Health Conditions.w: Cannabis, especially high-potency forms, is associated with developing psychosis, more severe symptoms and higher relapse rates. Honest, non-judgemental information supports harm reduction (P2.4).

n.0: There is a well-established link between cannabis and psychosis.
n.1: Any short-term relaxation is outweighed by worsening psychosis and relapse.
n.3: The psychosis risk applies to cannabis use itself, not just combined with alcohol.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Lyons, 35, is found unresponsive in a ward toilet with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. Naloxone is given as part of the emergency response and she wakes. Ten minutes later she says she feels fine and wants to go home. What should the nurse explain?
o: She can leave now that the naloxone has reversed the overdose
She should rest in her room with hourly checks overnight
She can go home if a friend stays with her tonight
Naloxone can wear off before the opioid, so she needs monitoring
Mental Health Conditions.w: Naloxone has a shorter duration of action than many opioids, so opioid toxicity can return as it wears off. She needs continued close observation and medical review, with repeat doses as needed.

n.0: Recovery after naloxone can be temporary.
n.1: Hourly checks are too infrequent while re-sedation is possible.
n.2: A friend at home cannot provide monitoring or repeat naloxone if toxicity returns.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Dean, 31, has depression and injects heroin. He says he is not ready to stop. What is the most appropriate nursing response at this stage?
o: Offer harm reduction such as needle exchange and naloxone
Advise him to cut down gradually without other support
Explain his care will end unless he becomes abstinent
Avoid discussing drugs until he says he is ready to stop
Mental Health Conditions.w: Harm reduction meets people where they are: safer injecting, needle exchange, take-home naloxone and links to drug services, alongside motivational work (P2.4, NG58 person-centred approach).

n.1: Unsupported reduction is risky and offers no safety measures.
n.2: Making care conditional on abstinence excludes him (NG58).
n.3: Avoiding the subject misses the chance to reduce harm now.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Grant, 44, has bipolar disorder and alcohol dependence and is facing eviction for rent arrears. His care coordinator is reviewing his plan. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Pause his mental health care until housing is settled
Transfer the lead for his care to the alcohol service
Work with housing and alcohol services in his care plan
Leave the housing problem for him to sort out himself
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG58: the care coordinator works with other services to address social care, housing, physical and mental health needs as well as substance misuse. Do not exclude people from housing or other support because of coexisting SMI and substance misuse (P7.5 interagency working).

n.0: Pausing care leaves him unsupported at a high-risk time.
n.1: Mental health services keep a role for SMI; care is coordinated, not handed over.
n.3: Housing instability threatens his mental health and recovery and is part of coordinated care.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Ms Adebayo, 26, is referred with a first psychotic episode. She says she drinks heavily at weekends and uses cocaine. What is the most appropriate first step?
o: A joint assessment of her mental health and substance use
Await abstinence before assessing her psychosis further
Do a urine drug screen and refer on if it is positive
Treat the psychosis now and assess substance use later
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG58: undertake a comprehensive assessment of the person's mental health and substance misuse needs together, as each affects the other and both shape the care plan.

n.1: Requiring abstinence first excludes her from mental health care.
n.2: A drug screen is not a needs assessment and onward referral risks exclusion.
n.3: Leaving substance use until later misses a key factor in her psychosis and risk.

Mental Health Conditions.q: During a home visit to Ms Dale, 29, who has schizophrenia and uses heroin, a community nurse sees used needles on a low table where her 4-year-old son is playing. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Ask her to move the needles and take no further action
Discuss it at her next routine review in a month
Remove the immediate risk and raise a safeguarding concern
Wait for her consent before sharing any concern
Mental Health Conditions.w: NG58: ensure the safeguarding needs of people with coexisting SMI and substance misuse, their carers and wider family are met (think family). Make the child safe now, then follow local child safeguarding procedures.

n.0: A single request does not address an ongoing safeguarding risk.
n.1: A month's delay leaves the child at risk of needlestick injury and neglect.
n.3: Consent is not needed to share information to protect a child at risk of harm.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mr Webb, 38, takes methadone and has PRN diazepam prescribed for agitation on an acute ward. At 22:00 he asks for diazepam. He is drowsy, his speech is slurred and his respiratory rate is 10. What should the nurse do?
o: Withhold the diazepam and get an urgent medical review
Give the diazepam because he is asking for it now
Give half of the prescribed dose of diazepam instead
Omit his next methadone dose and give the diazepam
Mental Health Conditions.w: Benzodiazepines with opioids can cause fatal respiratory depression (MHRA 2020). He already shows sedation and a low respiratory rate, so the PRN must be withheld and he needs urgent medical review and close monitoring.

n.1: Giving it adds to existing respiratory depression.
n.2: A reduced dose still adds sedation to an opioid.
n.3: Changing a methadone dose is a prescriber decision, and giving diazepam still deepens his sedation.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Daniel, 24, has schizophrenia. His mother says he hears voices commenting on what he does, believes the neighbours are plotting against him, speaks very little in reply to questions and his talk sometimes jumps between unconnected topics. Which of his features is a negative symptom?
o: His belief that the neighbours are plotting
Talk that jumps between unconnected topics
His markedly reduced amount of speech
Voices commenting on what he is doing
Mental Health Conditions.w: Negative symptoms are a loss of normal function: alogia (poverty of speech), avolition, anhedonia, blunted affect and social withdrawal (CG178). Reduced speech is alogia.

n.0: A persecutory delusion is a positive symptom.
n.1: Loosening of associations is formal thought disorder, grouped with the positive symptoms.
n.3: Hallucinations are a positive symptom: an experience added to normal perception.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Mrs Okafor, 41, is seen by her GP. Over three weeks she has become convinced that her television is sending her messages and she hears a voice telling her she is worthless. She has no previous mental health history. Which referral is most appropriate?
o: An older adult community mental health team
An NHS Talking Therapies service
An early intervention in psychosis service
The community mental health team for routine assessment
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.3.1.1: early intervention in psychosis services should be open to everyone with a first episode or first presentation of psychosis, irrespective of age or duration of untreated psychosis, and should assess without delay.

n.0: She is 41; age does not route her away from EIP, and she is not an older adult.
n.1: Talking Therapies treats common anxiety and depression, not psychosis.
n.3: A routine CMHT referral would delay the specialist first-episode care NICE recommends.

Mental Health Conditions.q: Leon, 29, has a first episode of psychosis and agrees to cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp) alongside medication. He asks what the therapy will involve. How does NICE CG178 recommend it is delivered?
o: One to one over at least 6 planned sessions
In a group over 6 weekly sessions
One to one over at least 16 planned sessions
As guided self-help over 8 weeks
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.3.7.1: CBT for psychosis should be delivered on a one-to-one basis over at least 16 planned sessions and follow a treatment manual.

n.0: Six sessions is well below the 16-session minimum.
n.1: CG178 specifies individual, not group, CBTp, and 6 sessions is too few.
n.3: Guided self-help is a low-intensity option for common mental health problems, not CBTp.

Mental Health Conditions.q: The parents of Priya, 22, who has schizophrenia, have agreed to family intervention. Priya lives with them. According to NICE CG178, how should family intervention be delivered?
o: Over 3 months to 1 year with at least 10 planned sessions
Over 3 months to 1 year with at least 16 planned sessions
Over 6 weeks with at least 6 planned sessions
As a single psychoeducation session at discharge
Mental Health Conditions.w: CG178 1.3.7.2: family intervention should include the person if practical, last between 3 months and 1 year, and include at least 10 planned sessions.

n.1: Sixteen sessions is the CBTp minimum, not the family intervention minimum.
n.2: Six weeks and 6 sessions is too short and too few.
n.3: A single session is information giving, not family intervention.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Jones, 33, has taken clozapine for 2 years and smoked heavily until admission to a smoke-free ward 8 days ago. He is now very drowsy, drooling more than usual and had a brief jerking movement of his arm. What is the priority?
o: Record the drowsiness as a usual clozapine effect
Report urgently and request a clozapine level
Give his clozapine and recheck him in the morning
Encourage him to resume smoking to settle his levels
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: smoking induces clozapine metabolism, so stopping raises levels. Step 2: sedation, hypersalivation and myoclonus suggest toxicity; MHRA (2020) advises monitoring levels on stopping smoking, and urgent medical review is needed.

n.0: New myoclonus with sedation is a warning sign, not a usual effect.
n.2: Giving the next dose before review risks worsening toxicity, including seizures.
n.3: Restarting smoking is not a safe way to manage toxicity.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Barnes, 51, has schizophrenia. He tells a nurse on the ward he has had a heavy pain in his chest for an hour. A colleague says he often complains of aches when he is anxious. What should the nurse do?
o: Offer PRN lorazepam to help him settle
Assess the pain fully, including observations and an ECG
Reassure him that his anxiety is causing the discomfort
Ask him to mention it at tomorrow's ward round
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Attributing physical symptoms to mental illness (diagnostic overshadowing) contributes to the SMI mortality gap. Chest pain needs prompt physical assessment, observations and an ECG, with escalation as indicated (P2.5).

n.0: Sedation may mask a serious physical cause.
n.2: Reassurance without assessment could miss a cardiac event.
n.3: A day's delay with possible cardiac pain is unsafe.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Ellis, 58, takes quetiapine with an antidepressant for treatment-resistant depression. She is not on her GP's SMI register. Her daughter asks whether she needs physical health monitoring. What is the most accurate answer?
o: Yes, but monitoring starts after 1 year of treatment
No, because quetiapine has few metabolic effects
No, because she is not on the SMI register
Yes, because she takes an antipsychotic
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NHS England: everyone taking antipsychotics or mood stabilisers needs medication monitoring whether or not they are on the SMI register. NG222 1.4.33 sets baseline checks before starting an antipsychotic for depression.

n.0: Baseline checks happen before starting, with early follow-up.
n.1: Quetiapine can cause weight gain and metabolic changes.
n.2: Monitoring follows the medicine, not register status.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Kai, 24, has first-episode psychosis and has gained weight since starting an antipsychotic. He is worried about it and keen to change his lifestyle. What does NICE CG178 recommend his mental health provider offers?
o: Advice to stop the antipsychotic to reverse the weight gain
A repeat weight check at his annual review
A combined healthy eating and physical activity programme
Referral for bariatric surgery assessment
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG178 1.1.2.1: people with psychosis or schizophrenia, especially those taking antipsychotics, should be offered a combined healthy eating and physical activity programme by their mental healthcare provider.

n.0: Stopping without review risks relapse; any medication change is a shared decision with the prescriber.
n.1: Waiting a year allows further rapid weight gain.
n.3: Bariatric surgery is not a first response to early antipsychotic weight gain.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mia, 14, has been diagnosed with mild depression by a CAMHS practitioner. She does not want any treatment at the moment and the practitioner thinks she may recover without intervention. What does NICE NG134 recommend?
o: Starting fluoxetine at a low dose
Reassessment, normally within 2 weeks
Reassessment in about 3 months
Discharge to her GP with written advice
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG134: for children and young people with mild depression who do not want an intervention or may recover without one, arrange further assessment, normally within 2 weeks ('watchful waiting'). Antidepressants should not be used for initial treatment of mild depression.

n.0: Antidepressants are not used as initial treatment for mild depression in young people.
n.2: Three months is far longer than the 2-week reassessment NICE advises.
n.3: Discharge without follow-up misses deterioration.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Noah, 16, has moderate depression that has not responded to psychological therapy. After a multidisciplinary review an antidepressant is to be offered. Which does NICE NG134 recommend?
o: Fluoxetine alongside psychological therapy
A tricyclic antidepressant taken at night
Paroxetine combined with weekly CBT
Sertraline on its own as the first choice
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG134: when an antidepressant is prescribed for moderate to severe depression in a young person it should be fluoxetine, given with concurrent psychological therapy. Paroxetine, venlafaxine and tricyclics should not be used.

n.1: NG134: tricyclic antidepressants should not be used for depression in young people.
n.2: NG134: paroxetine should not be used for depression in children and young people.
n.3: Sertraline is a second-line alternative and antidepressants are not given without therapy.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Amelia, 17, has severe anorexia nervosa and the team recommend informal admission. She has capacity and agrees to admission, but her father objects and says he will not allow it. What is the legal position?
o: Her father's objection prevents informal admission
The decision must go to the Court of Protection
Her own consent to informal admission is sufficient
Both parents must agree before she can be admitted
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: MHA 1983 s131(2)-(4): a 16 or 17-year-old with capacity can consent to informal admission even if a person with parental responsibility disagrees, and a capable refusal cannot be overridden by parental consent.

n.0: A parent cannot override a capable 16 or 17-year-old's consent to informal admission.
n.1: The Court of Protection is not needed where she has capacity and consents.
n.3: Parental agreement is not needed when a capable 17-year-old consents.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ben, 17, has psychosis and is under CAMHS. He turns 18 next month and has just been readmitted in crisis. His CAMHS team proposes transferring him to adult services on his birthday. What does NICE NG43 advise?
o: Transfer him now, before he reaches 18
Time the transfer for when he is more stable
Keep him in CAMHS until he reaches 21
Transfer him on his 18th birthday as planned
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG43 1.2.3: the point of transfer should be developmentally appropriate, not based on a rigid age threshold, and take place at a time of relative stability for the young person.

n.0: Moving him mid-crisis is not a time of relative stability.
n.2: NICE does not set a fixed age of 21; transfer is planned around stability and need.
n.3: A transfer fixed to a birthday is a rigid age threshold during a crisis.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Chloe, 15, attends a school nursing drop-in. She is low in mood, wants to be referred for talking therapy and asks the nurse not to tell her parents. What should the nurse do first?
o: Inform her parents because she is under 16
Explain therapy must wait until she turns 16
Assess whether she understands enough to consent herself
Assess her capacity using the Mental Capacity Act test
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Under 16s can consent to treatment if they are Gillick competent: they have sufficient understanding and intelligence to understand what is proposed. Confidentiality is respected unless there is a risk of serious harm.

n.0: Being under 16 does not on its own require parental involvement.
n.1: Gillick competent under 16s can consent now.
n.3: The MCA applies from age 16; for under 16s Gillick competence is used.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Isla, 13, has moderate depression. After 6 sessions of a specific psychological therapy her symptoms have not improved. What does NICE NG134 recommend next?
o: Continue the same therapy unchanged for 6 more months
An MDT review, then consider fluoxetine with therapy
Start sertraline before any team review
Discharge her as therapy has not helped
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: NG134: if moderate to severe depression in a young person does not respond to psychological therapy after 4 to 6 sessions, carry out a multidisciplinary review. Step 2: offer fluoxetine (12 to 18 years) alongside continued psychological therapy.

n.0: Continuing unchanged ignores the lack of response after 4 to 6 sessions.
n.2: An MDT review comes first and fluoxetine is the recommended antidepressant.
n.3: Discharge leaves a young person with moderate depression untreated.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Josh, 15, is admitted to a paediatric ward after an overdose of paracetamol. He is medically stable. Who should carry out his psychosocial assessment, according to NICE NG225?
o: His GP at a follow-up visit after discharge
A CYP mental health professional skilled in self-harm
The adult liaison nurse covering the emergency department
The paediatric nurse caring for him on the ward
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG225: for children and young people who have self-harmed, ensure a mental health professional experienced in assessing children and young people who self-harm carries out the psychosocial assessment, with 24-hour CAMHS access and joint paediatric and CAMHS review on the ward.

n.0: Assessment should happen without delay, not after discharge.
n.2: NICE specifies age-appropriate expertise rather than adult services.
n.3: Paediatric nurses provide care but the psychosocial assessment needs CYP mental health expertise.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Erin, 16, self-harms several times a week and has significant emotional dysregulation. Her mother asks what treatment might help. What does NICE NG225 suggest considering?
o: Four sessions of solution-focused therapy
Fluoxetine to reduce the urge to self-harm
DBT adapted for adolescents (DBT-A)
A parenting skills group for her mother
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG225: for children and young people with significant emotional dysregulation and frequent self-harm, consider DBT-A. Do not offer drug treatment as a specific intervention to reduce self-harm.

n.0: A brief 4-session intervention is not the NG225 recommendation here.
n.1: NG225: do not offer drug treatment specifically to reduce self-harm.
n.3: Carer support helps but does not replace DBT-A for Erin.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Price, 84, has Alzheimer's disease and lives on an older adult mental health ward. Each evening she becomes restless, calls out and tries to leave the bay. She is not hurting herself or anyone else. What is the most appropriate first response?
o: Ask for PRN haloperidol to be prescribed for the evenings
Look for causes such as pain or unmet needs and adapt her care
Ask for regular risperidone to prevent the restlessness
Use bed rails in the evenings to keep her safe
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG97 1.7.2: offer psychosocial and environmental interventions to reduce distress as initial and ongoing management. Look for triggers such as pain, constipation, hunger, noise or boredom, and offer personalised activities (1.7.9).

n.0: Antipsychotics are reserved for risk of harm or severe distress and are not first line.
n.2: Regular antipsychotics are not used to prevent distress in dementia.
n.3: Bed rails are a restriction that can increase risk and do not address the cause.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Ward, 79, has Alzheimer's disease and was started on risperidone for severe distressing delusions. According to NICE NG97, how often at least should the need for the antipsychotic be reassessed?
o: Every 6 months
Every 12 months
Every 6 weeks
Every 12 weeks
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG97 1.7.6: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible time and reassess at least every 6 weeks to check whether the person still needs the medication.

n.0: 6 months is far too long given stroke and mortality risks.
n.1: Annual review would leave him exposed to harm without clear benefit.
n.3: 12 weeks is twice the NG97 interval.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Hill, 76, has dementia with Lewy bodies and frightening visual hallucinations. A locum doctor suggests haloperidol. What is the most important point for the nurse to raise?
o: Haloperidol works best if given as a long-acting depot
He should start an antidepressant before any antipsychotic
Hallucinations in dementia are treated first with a benzodiazepine
Antipsychotics can cause severe reactions in Lewy body dementia
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NG97 1.7.4: in dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson's disease dementia, antipsychotics can worsen motor features and in some cases cause severe antipsychotic sensitivity reactions. CG103 1.7.4 also highlights MHRA warnings on the cardiac and neurological risks of haloperidol, especially in these conditions.

n.0: A depot would prolong exposure to a drug that may cause a severe reaction.
n.1: Antidepressants do not treat hallucinations in Lewy body dementia.
n.2: Benzodiazepines are not first-line treatment for hallucinations in dementia.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Iqbal, 81, is on an older adult ward. A nurse is asked which change might indicate hypoactive delirium, which is often missed. Which is the best answer?
o: Pacing, shouting and pulling at her cannula
Low mood and early waking for several months
Withdrawal, slowed responses and reduced appetite
Memory loss that has worsened slowly over 2 years
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG103 1.3.2: be particularly vigilant for hypoactive delirium, often missed: withdrawal, slow responses, reduced mobility and movement, worsened concentration and reduced appetite.

n.0: These are features of hyperactive delirium.
n.1: Months of low mood and early waking suggest depression.
n.3: Slow decline over years suggests dementia.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Norris, 82, has vascular dementia. Over 2 days he has become much more confused than usual. His alertness fluctuates from drowsy to restless and he cannot keep his attention on a conversation. What should the nurse do?
o: Arrange a memory clinic review in 6 weeks
Assess for delirium and seek a physical cause
Request a higher dose of his usual medicines
Record it as a progression of his dementia
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: acute onset, fluctuating course and inattention point to delirium, which often occurs on top of dementia. Step 2: assess (4AT) and seek and treat causes such as infection, constipation, dehydration, pain or medicines (CG103).

n.0: Delirium needs prompt assessment, not a routine clinic appointment.
n.2: More medication could worsen delirium.
n.3: Dementia progresses gradually; a change over 2 days suggests delirium.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Grant, 74, was widowed 2 months ago. He has become slow, has lost weight, sleeps poorly and often answers 'I don't know' when tested on memory, though he can recall recent events when encouraged. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Depression with cognitive symptoms
Early-stage Alzheimer's disease
Hypoactive delirium
Behavioural frontotemporal dementia
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: In older adults, depression can present with apparent cognitive impairment. Recent onset after a loss, biological symptoms and 'don't know' answers with better effort-dependent recall point to depression rather than dementia.

n.1: Alzheimer's develops gradually and people often try to answer, with confabulation rather than 'don't know'.
n.2: There is no acute fluctuation or inattention to suggest delirium.
n.3: Frontotemporal dementia typically presents with personality or language change, not low mood after a loss.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Dunn, 86, has delirium. She is very distressed, believes staff are trying to poison her and is hitting out. Calm verbal and non-verbal de-escalation has not worked. She does not have Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia. What does NICE CG103 suggest considering?
o: Restraint until the delirium has resolved
Short-term haloperidol, usually 1 week or less
Regular haloperidol for 6 weeks, then review
Regular lorazepam for the next 2 weeks
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG103 1.7.3-1.7.4: de-escalate first; if ineffective and the person is distressed or a risk, consider short-term haloperidol (usually 1 week or less), starting at the lowest clinically appropriate dose and titrating cautiously, taking into account MHRA warnings on cardiac and neurological risks (especially in Parkinson's disease or Lewy body dementia).

n.0: Prolonged restraint is not a treatment and increases harm.
n.2: CG103 advises a short course, usually 1 week or less.
n.3: Benzodiazepines can worsen delirium and are not the CG103 recommendation here.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Lowe, 69, has schizophrenia and has been told he has advanced lung cancer. He wants to plan his future care. A colleague suggests his wishes cannot be relied on because of his diagnosis. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Postpone planning until his psychiatrist confirms he is well
Ask his sister to make the plan as his next of kin
Plan care with the team and inform him of the decisions
Support him to plan, assessing capacity for each decision
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: MCA 2005 s1(2): a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it; capacity is decision-specific. People with SMI should have equal access to advance care planning at the end of life (SPEC.T2).

n.0: Delay risks losing the chance to plan and assumes incapacity.
n.1: Next of kin have no legal power to decide for a capable adult.
n.2: Excluding him from decisions ignores the presumption of capacity.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: On his first day on an acute ward, Mr Cole, 40, meets his named nurse. They talk about why he has been admitted, what he hopes for and how they will work together. In Peplau's model, which phase is this?
o: Exploitation
Orientation
Resolution
Identification
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Peplau (1952): in orientation the nurse and patient meet, clarify roles and begin to identify the problem; then identification, exploitation (making full use of help) and resolution (ending).

n.0: Exploitation is when the patient makes full use of the help available.
n.2: Resolution is the ending of the relationship as needs are met.
n.3: Identification follows, when the patient begins to work with the nurse on the problem.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Bell, 33, has been on a rehabilitation ward for some weeks. She now books her own appointments, uses the ward groups well and asks the nurse for help when she needs it, becoming steadily more independent. Which Peplau phase best fits?
o: Identification
Orientation
Exploitation
Resolution
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: In Peplau's exploitation phase the person makes full use of the services and the relationship, moving towards independence before resolution.

n.0: Identification is when the person first starts to work on the problem with the nurse.
n.1: Orientation is the initial getting-to-know-you stage.
n.3: Resolution is the ending, when goals are met and the relationship closes.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Joel, 21, has psychosis. He tells the nurse that voices are saying he is evil and should be punished. He looks frightened. Which response by the nurse is best?
o: 'Let us talk about something else to take your mind off it.'
'I can hear them too, so let us talk about it together.'
'The voices are not real, so try not to listen to them.'
'That sounds frightening. What are they saying to you?'
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Acknowledge the person's experience and feelings without arguing or colluding, and explore content and impact (including risk from command hallucinations) with open questions (Annexe A 1.1 active listening).

n.0: Changing the subject misses distress and possible risk in what the voices say.
n.1: Pretending to hear them is collusion and is dishonest.
n.2: Dismissing the experience damages trust; the voices are real to him.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Hart, 55, is convinced that MI5 is poisoning the ward food and refuses meals. He asks the nurse to agree that he is being targeted. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Tell him he will be fed by tube if he keeps refusing
Acknowledge his fear and offer sealed food items
Explain firmly why MI5 would have no reason to target him
Agree with him so that he will trust the team
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Neither challenge nor collude with a delusion: acknowledge the emotion (fear), stay honest and offer practical options such as sealed or packaged food to meet nutritional needs.

n.0: Threats are coercive and damage the therapeutic relationship.
n.2: Arguing with a fixed belief tends to entrench it and harms engagement.
n.3: Agreeing colludes with the delusion and is dishonest.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Two weeks after discharge, a former patient sends a nurse a friend request on social media with a message thanking her for her care. What should the nurse do?
o: Decline the request to keep a clear boundary
Accept as he is no longer her patient
Accept it but avoid sending any messages
Report him to the police for contacting her
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NMC Code 20.6: stay objective and keep clear professional boundaries with people in your care, including former patients; 20.10: use social media responsibly. NMC social media guidance warns against relationships with service users online.

n.1: Boundaries apply to former patients as well.
n.2: Accepting still creates a personal connection that blurs boundaries.
n.3: A thank-you message is not a crime; this is disproportionate.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Okoro, 28, is due for discharge and tells her nurse she feels safest talking to her. She asks for the nurse's personal mobile number so she can text if she feels low at night. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Give the number and ask her to text in emergencies
Decline kindly and agree crisis contacts for night-time
Agree to call her each evening after the nurse's shift
Give a work email address and reply when off duty
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Code 20.6: clear professional boundaries. Sharing personal contact details creates dependence and an unsafe, unsupported route for crisis help. Agreeing crisis contacts in the safety plan meets the need safely.

n.0: Personal contact details blur boundaries and cannot guarantee a response in a crisis.
n.2: Personal calls after shifts cross professional boundaries.
n.3: Off-duty replies still create an informal, unsafe arrangement.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: During a one-to-one session, Mr Price, 45, who has depression, asks his nurse: 'Have you ever been depressed?' What is the most therapeutic response?
o: Share her own history of depression in detail
Answer briefly and refocus on his experience
Move on to the next topic without answering
Tell him personal questions are not allowed
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Self-disclosure should be limited and only used when it helps the person; the focus stays on the patient. A brief, warm acknowledgement keeps the relationship genuine while keeping the boundary (Annexe A 1.5).

n.0: Detailed disclosure shifts the focus to the nurse and burdens the patient.
n.2: Not responding can feel dismissive and harm trust.
n.3: A blunt refusal feels rejecting and can damage rapport.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Ahmed, 60, has been on a long-stay ward for a year and has a close working relationship with his named nurse. Discharge is planned in 6 weeks and he has started to become anxious when it is mentioned. What should the nurse do?
o: Promise to visit him at home after discharge
Avoid mentioning discharge so that he stays settled
Hand over his care on the day he is discharged
Discuss the ending early and plan community support
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: recognise anxiety about ending as part of Peplau's resolution phase. Step 2: plan the ending openly and early, linking him with community staff so the relationship closes safely.

n.0: Personal visits cross professional boundaries.
n.1: Avoidance leaves the anxiety unaddressed and makes the ending abrupt.
n.2: A same-day handover gives no chance to build new relationships.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Liam, 23, has depression. After failing his driving test he tells the nurse: 'I failed that, so I am a failure at everything I do.' Which thinking error is this?
o: Personalisation
Catastrophising
Mind reading
Overgeneralising
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Overgeneralisation draws a sweeping conclusion from a single event. Naming the thinking error is a CBT technique that helps the person examine and test the thought (Annexe A 3.6).

n.0: Personalisation takes responsibility for events outside one's control.
n.1: Catastrophising predicts the worst possible outcome.
n.2: Mind reading assumes knowledge of what others think.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Hale, 37, has social anxiety. She says: 'When I speak in meetings, everyone thinks I am stupid.' No one has said this to her. Which thinking error does this show?
o: Emotional reasoning
Black-and-white thinking
Mind reading
Overgeneralisation
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Mind reading is assuming you know what others are thinking, usually negatively, without evidence. In CBT the person is helped to look for evidence for and against the thought.

n.0: Emotional reasoning treats feelings as facts ('I feel stupid, so I am').
n.1: Black-and-white thinking sees things in extremes.
n.3: Overgeneralisation draws broad conclusions from one event.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: A student nurse asks what makes cognitive behavioural therapy different from other talking therapies. Which description is most accurate?
o: It offers unstructured, open-ended time to talk
It focuses mainly on improving relationships with other people
It links current thoughts, feelings, behaviour and body sensations
It explores unconscious conflicts from early childhood years
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CBT is structured, time-limited and collaborative, focuses on current problems and how thoughts, emotions, behaviour and physical sensations interact, and uses homework to practise new skills.

n.0: CBT is structured and goal-focused, not open-ended.
n.1: This describes interpersonal therapy.
n.3: This describes psychodynamic therapy.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Doyle, 50, drinks heavily. He says: 'I know the drinking is getting out of hand and I might cut down at some point, but not right now.' Which stage of change is he in?
o: Contemplation
Precontemplation
Action
Preparation
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Prochaska and DiClemente: in contemplation the person recognises a problem and is ambivalent about change but has not committed to act.

n.1: In precontemplation the person does not see a problem.
n.2: Action means the person is actively changing behaviour.
n.3: Preparation involves a commitment and plan to change soon.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: During a motivational interviewing session, Ms Kerr, 31, says: 'Everyone keeps nagging me about my smoking.' Which response is the best reflective statement?
o: 'You sound fed up with being told what to do.'
'You really need to stop smoking for your health.'
'Why don't you just try nicotine patches?'
'Have you had a cigarette today?'
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Reflective listening is a core MI skill (OARS). Reflecting her feeling reduces resistance and invites her to explore her own reasons for change, rather than triggering the 'righting reflex'.

n.1: Telling her what to do is the righting reflex and increases resistance.
n.2: Jumping to solutions skips her ambivalence and her own ideas.
n.3: A closed question does not reflect or explore her feelings.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Young, 25, contacts NHS Talking Therapies with mild anxiety for 2 months. She is working and has no risk concerns. Under the stepped care model, what is she most likely to be offered first?
o: Referral to the community mental health team
Assessment for a day hospital
High-intensity individual CBT
Low-intensity guided self-help
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NHS Talking Therapies uses stepped care: low-intensity interventions such as guided self-help (often with a psychological wellbeing practitioner) for milder problems, stepping up to high-intensity therapy if needed (CG113 stepped care).

n.0: CMHTs serve people with severe or complex needs.
n.1: Day hospital care is for severe illness, not mild anxiety.
n.2: High-intensity CBT is a later step for more severe or persistent problems.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ryan, 19, has early psychosis and smokes cannabis daily. He sees no problem with it and says it helps him relax. Which approach by the nurse is most consistent with motivational interviewing?
o: Give him a step-by-step plan to stop smoking it this week
Warn him he will be discharged unless he stops
Leave the subject until he raises it himself
With permission, explore its pros and cons for him
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: he is in precontemplation. Step 2: MI raises awareness with permission, explores what he values and dislikes about cannabis (decisional balance) and draws out ambivalence, rather than pushing action.

n.0: An action plan does not fit his stage and is likely to be rejected.
n.1: Threats provoke resistance and exclusion is not appropriate (NG58).
n.2: Avoidance misses the chance to raise awareness of a serious risk.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Ray, 46, has panic disorder. She avoids the local shop because she believes that if she goes in she will panic, collapse and be humiliated. Which CBT technique is most suited to testing this belief?
o: A planned behavioural experiment to test the prediction
Avoiding the shop until her anxiety settles
Reassurance that she will not collapse in the shop
Free association about her early memories
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Behavioural experiments are a CBT technique (Annexe A 3.6): the person predicts what will happen, tests it in a planned way and reviews the evidence, weakening catastrophic beliefs.

n.1: Avoidance prevents disconfirmation and keeps the fear going.
n.2: Reassurance gives short-term relief but maintains anxiety.
n.3: Free association is a psychodynamic technique, not CBT.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Nadia, 24, is starting a dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) programme. She asks her named nurse what skills she will learn in the group. Which is one of the four DBT skills modules?
o: Distress tolerance
Cognitive restructuring
Graded activity scheduling
Exposure and response prevention
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: DBT (Linehan) teaches four skills modules: mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness.

n.1: Cognitive restructuring is a core CBT technique, not a DBT module.
n.2: Activity scheduling belongs to behavioural activation for depression.
n.3: ERP is a CBT technique for OCD.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: A student asks how DBT differs from standard CBT. Which statement is most accurate?
o: It relies on medication to stabilise emotions first
It balances change strategies with acceptance and validation
It is a brief therapy delivered over 4 sessions
It focuses on interpreting unconscious childhood conflict
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: DBT combines CBT change strategies with acceptance, mindfulness and validation (the 'dialectic' between acceptance and change). Comprehensive DBT includes individual therapy, skills groups and phone coaching over many months.

n.0: DBT is psychological; drugs are not used for BPD itself (CG78).
n.2: Comprehensive DBT runs for months; brief interventions under 3 months are not advised for BPD (CG78).
n.3: Interpreting unconscious conflict is psychodynamic.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Reed, 27, has an intense urge to self-harm. Her nurse helps her hold a cold pack to her face and then do some paced breathing. Which DBT skills module do these techniques come from?
o: Distress tolerance
Mindfulness
Emotion regulation
Interpersonal effectiveness
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Cold temperature and paced breathing are part of the TIPP crisis-survival skills in DBT's distress tolerance module, used to get through an acute urge without making things worse (Annexe A 3.8).

n.1: Mindfulness builds present-moment awareness; TIPP is a distress tolerance skill.
n.2: Emotion regulation reduces emotional vulnerability over time rather than surviving a crisis.
n.3: Interpersonal effectiveness covers asking for what you need and saying no.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Tate, 30, is in a DBT programme. He finds it hard to ask the team for things he needs without either saying nothing or becoming angry. Which DBT module targets this?
o: Interpersonal effectiveness
Core mindfulness skills
Distress tolerance skills
Emotion regulation skills
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Interpersonal effectiveness skills (for example DEAR MAN) help a person ask for what they want and say no while keeping relationships and self-respect.

n.1: Mindfulness underpins all modules but does not target assertive requests.
n.2: Distress tolerance helps survive crises without making them worse.
n.3: Emotion regulation helps understand and change emotions.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Holly, 20, approaches a nurse on the ward. She says the urge to cut herself is very strong right now but she has not acted on it. She has a DBT crisis plan. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she goes to her room to rest until it passes
Ask for PRN medication to be given straight away
Stay and coach her in a distress tolerance skill
Explore her history of self-harm in detail now
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Supporting the person to use a skill from her crisis plan (distress tolerance: TIPP, distraction, self-soothing) helps her ride out the urge, which rises and falls, without acting on it (NG225 safety planning; Annexe A 3.8).

n.0: Being left by herself at peak urge increases risk.
n.1: Medication is not the first response and does not teach coping.
n.3: In-depth exploration during peak distress can heighten emotion; it fits later, when calm.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Kara, 26, who is in DBT, tells the nurse: 'No one understands how much this hurts.' Which response best reflects DBT validation?
o: 'You need to calm down before we can talk.'
'Lots of people have it much worse than you do.'
'After all you have been through, that makes sense.'
'I know exactly how you feel, I have been there.'
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Validation communicates that the person's emotions are understandable in context. It reduces emotional arousal and is a core DBT and CG78 approach (empathic, validating statements in crisis).

n.0: Demanding calm first is invalidating and may escalate her.
n.1: Comparison invalidates her experience and may increase distress.
n.3: Claiming to know exactly how she feels is presumptuous and shifts focus to the nurse.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Lane, 32, notices her moods are much harder to manage when she sleeps badly, skips meals and drinks alcohol. Her DBT therapist works with her on these areas. Which module does this belong to?
o: Emotion regulation
Interpersonal effectiveness
Distress tolerance
Radical acceptance
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Emotion regulation includes reducing vulnerability to strong emotions by looking after physical health, eating, sleep, exercise and avoiding mood-altering substances (PLEASE skills).

n.1: Interpersonal effectiveness concerns relationships and requests.
n.2: Distress tolerance is about surviving crises in the moment.
n.3: Radical acceptance is a distress tolerance skill, not a module.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Fox, 22, in a DBT programme, cut her arm last night. Her wound has been treated and she is now calm. Her care plan uses DBT principles. Which approach is most appropriate now?
o: Start continuous one-to-one observation indefinitely
Avoid discussing it so as not to reinforce it
Do a chain analysis of what led to the self-harm
Stop her leave as a consequence of the incident
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: deal with physical care and wait for calm. Step 2: behaviour chain analysis maps triggers, thoughts, feelings and actions to identify where skills could be used next time. Punitive responses are not part of DBT or NG225.

n.0: Indefinite observation is restrictive and not based on a current risk assessment.
n.1: Avoidance misses learning; DBT addresses self-harm directly.
n.3: Punitive restrictions damage engagement and are not therapeutic.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Evans, 38, has schizophrenia. During a review he says: 'More than anything I need to believe things can get better for me.' Which element of the CHIME recovery framework is he describing?
o: Connectedness with others
Empowerment and control
Hope and optimism
A positive identity
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CHIME (Leamy et al. 2011): Connectedness, Hope and optimism, Identity, Meaning in life and Empowerment are the processes of personal recovery.

n.0: Connectedness is about relationships, peer support and community.
n.1: Empowerment is about personal responsibility, control and focusing on strengths.
n.3: Identity is about rebuilding a positive sense of self beyond the illness.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Clarke, 45, still hears voices at times but works part time, has friends and says her life feels meaningful. A student says she cannot be 'in recovery' while she has symptoms. Which statement is most accurate?
o: Recovery means the full and lasting removal of all symptoms
Recovery is measured mainly by how rarely she is admitted
Recovery means a hopeful, satisfying life even with symptoms
Recovery begins once she has stopped all medication
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Personal recovery is a unique process of living a satisfying, hopeful and contributing life, even with ongoing symptoms; it differs from clinical recovery (symptom remission).

n.0: This describes clinical recovery, not personal recovery.
n.1: Admission rates are a service measure, not the person's recovery.
n.3: Recovery does not depend on stopping medication.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: At handover a nurse wants to describe a newly admitted man in line with recovery-focused, person-first language. Which phrase is most appropriate?
o: A chronic schizophrenic
A schizophrenic young man
A schizophrenia sufferer
A man who has schizophrenia
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Person-first language puts the person before the diagnosis and avoids defining them by it, reducing stigma (SPEC.T2 social stigma; Code 1.1 treat people with kindness, respect and compassion).

n.0: Labelling someone a 'chronic schizophrenic' is stigmatising and hopeless.
n.1: Using the diagnosis as an adjective defines him by the illness.
n.2: 'Sufferer' implies passivity and victimhood.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Shah, 29, has bipolar disorder. He says: 'People like me are mad. No one will employ me, so there is no point applying for jobs.' What is he describing?
o: Public stigma
Stigma by association
Structural stigma
Self-stigma
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Self-stigma (internalised stigma) is when a person accepts negative stereotypes about mental illness and applies them to themselves, lowering self-esteem and leading to the 'why try' effect.

n.0: Public stigma is the negative attitudes held by others in society.
n.1: Stigma by association affects family and carers.
n.2: Structural stigma is in policies and institutions.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Lewis, 34, has a history of sexual abuse and is admitted to a ward that searches belongings on admission. She becomes very anxious when the search is explained. Which approach is most trauma-informed?
o: Delay the search until a doctor has reviewed her
Do the search quickly so it is over for her sooner
Explain each step, offering choices and a female nurse
Search her room later while she is at a group
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Trauma-informed care aims to avoid retraumatisation by promoting safety, trust, choice, collaboration and empowerment: clear explanation, gender-sensitive staffing and as much control as possible.

n.0: A medical review is not needed for the search and does not address her fear.
n.1: Speed without explanation or choice can feel like a loss of control and retraumatise her.
n.3: Searching covertly breaks trust and is not transparent.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: A ward is introducing trauma-informed care. Which question best reflects the trauma-informed shift in how staff think about a person's distress?
o: 'Why are you behaving like this?'
'What is wrong with you?'
'What has happened to you?'
'What is your diagnosis?'
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Trauma-informed practice reframes distress as an understandable response to experiences, moving from 'what is wrong with you?' to 'what has happened to you?'.

n.0: This implies blame and can increase shame.
n.1: This frames the person as defective.
n.3: Focusing on diagnosis overlooks the experiences behind distress.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Aisha, 22, is recovering from a first episode of psychosis. She tells her care coordinator that her main goal is to return to her college course. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Focus her plan on taking her medication
Set goals for her based on the ward routine
Advise her to wait until she is free of symptoms
Build her care plan around her goal and strengths
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Recovery-oriented care is person-centred: plans are built around the person's own goals, strengths and hopes, with support for education and employment (CG178 EIP services; P4.2).

n.0: Medication may help, but a plan narrowed to it ignores her goals.
n.1: Professional-set goals undermine empowerment.
n.2: Waiting for no symptoms delays meaningful recovery.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Ford, 50, was discharged a month ago. He says he has lost touch with friends, feels isolated and that no one understands what he has been through. Which intervention most directly supports the 'connectedness' element of CHIME?
o: Giving him a leaflet on his diagnosis
Linking him with a peer support group
Increasing his antipsychotic dose
Arranging a review in 6 months
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Connectedness covers peer support, relationships and being part of the community. Peers with lived experience help reduce isolation and model hope (CHIME).

n.0: Information alone does not create relationships.
n.2: Medication changes do not address social isolation.
n.3: A distant review does not build connections.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: A mental health trust signs up to the Triangle of Care. A student nurse asks what the 'triangle' refers to. What is the best answer?
o: Joint working between health, housing and social care
The balance between risk, rights and recovery
Links between the GP, psychiatrist and care coordinator
A partnership of the service user, carer and professional
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: The Triangle of Care (Carers Trust) describes a therapeutic alliance between the service user, the carer and the professional, recognising carers as partners in care.

n.0: Interagency working matters but is not the Triangle of Care.
n.1: This is not the Triangle of Care.
n.2: This describes professional links, leaving out the service user and carer.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Shaw, 30, is an inpatient and has asked that no details of his care be shared with his family. His mother phones the ward, very worried, and asks how he is. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Ask her to call back once he has given consent
Share his care plan because she is his mother
Listen to her and give general information and support
Explain that you cannot discuss anything with her today
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Respecting his refusal means not sharing personal information, but staff can listen to carers, receive information from them and give general information about the condition, services and carer support (Triangle of Care; CG178 1.1.4).

n.0: Turning her away now ignores her distress and what she knows.
n.1: Being his mother does not override his refusal of consent.
n.3: Refusing any conversation fails the carer and loses information she may hold.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Patel, 41, has severe depression with suicidal thoughts but has a supportive partner and is willing to accept daily support at home. What is the main purpose of the crisis resolution and home treatment team for her?
o: To arrange her admission to an acute ward
To give intensive home support instead of admission
To complete her discharge from mental health services
To provide weekly psychotherapy sessions
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Crisis resolution and home treatment teams provide rapid assessment and intensive home-based treatment, available 24 hours, as an alternative to hospital admission where it is safe (CG178 1.4; CG78 1.4.1.1).

n.0: Their role is to avoid admission where home treatment is safe.
n.2: CRHT provides crisis care, not discharge.
n.3: Weekly therapy is not crisis care.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: During family work for Ben, 25, who has schizophrenia, the therapist notes that his father is often critical and hostile and his mother is very over-involved. Why is this important to address?
o: It is linked with better adherence to medication
High expressed emotion is linked with relapse
It shows that the parents caused his schizophrenia
It means the family should not be involved in his care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: High expressed emotion (criticism, hostility, emotional over-involvement) in families predicts relapse in schizophrenia. Family intervention reduces it and lowers relapse rates (CG178 family intervention).

n.0: High expressed emotion is linked with relapse, not better outcomes.
n.2: Family attitudes do not cause schizophrenia; this belief adds blame.
n.3: The aim is to support and involve the family, not exclude them.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mrs Green's son, 19, has just been diagnosed with schizophrenia. She is his main carer and feels out of her depth. What does NICE CG178 recommend for her?
o: Advice to arrange supported housing for her son
A carer-focused education and support programme
Referral to her GP for an antidepressant
Waiting until her son's family therapy starts
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG178 1.1.4.4: offer a carer-focused education and support programme, which may be part of family intervention, as early as possible to all carers, with a positive message about recovery.

n.0: Moving her son out does not meet her own support needs.
n.2: She needs support and information, not presumed medication.
n.3: NICE says to offer support as early as possible.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr King, 52, agrees that his sister, his main carer, can know about his medication and appointments but not about his past trauma. She asks the nurse why he was admitted last year. What should the nurse do?
o: Share everything as she is his main carer
Share the agreed information and not the past trauma
Share the trauma history as it may help her support him
Refuse to give her any information about him
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG178 1.1.4.2: negotiate early how information will be shared, and respect the agreement; consent can be partial. Information outside the agreement is not shared without a lawful basis (Code 5).

n.0: Being the main carer does not override his limits on consent.
n.2: Good intentions do not override his explicit refusal.
n.3: He has agreed to share some information, so refusing all of it is wrong.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: The partner of Ms Reid, 37, who has bipolar disorder, calls the community team. He says she has slept 2 hours a night for 4 days, is spending heavily and is talking very fast. When the nurse phones, Ms Reid says she is fine. What is the most appropriate action?
o: Accept that she is fine because she has capacity
Act on the partner's report and arrange a prompt review
Advise the partner to call 999 if she gets worse
Tell the partner the team cannot act without her consent
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: Step 1: these are early warning signs of mania, and carers often notice relapse first. Step 2: receiving information from a carer does not breach confidentiality; act on it with a timely assessment (CG185 1.4.1 relapse plans; Triangle of Care).

n.0: Lack of insight is common in early mania; her report alone does not rule out relapse.
n.2: Waiting for an emergency misses the chance to intervene early.
n.3: Staff can receive and act on carer information without breaching confidentiality.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Obi's son, 22, has had his first admission for psychosis. At his discharge meeting she asks what she should do if things go wrong at home. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Suggest she reads about psychosis on reputable websites
Give written and verbal information, with crisis contacts
Reassure her that the team will contact her if needed
Explain that information must wait until his consent
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG178 1.1.4.1: give carers written and verbal information in an accessible format about the diagnosis and management, recovery, carer support, the role of teams and services, and how to get help in a crisis.

n.0: Websites, even reputable ones, do not give her tailored information or local crisis routes.
n.2: Waiting to be contacted leaves her without a plan in a crisis.
n.3: General and crisis information can be given to carers without breaching confidentiality.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: A student nurse on a community mental health team asks why physical health checks are such a priority for people with severe mental illness. On average, how much earlier do people with SMI die than the general population?
o: 15 to 20 years
2 to 5 years
25 to 30 years
5 to 8 years
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: People with SMI die on average 15 to 20 years earlier, mostly from preventable physical conditions such as cardiovascular and respiratory disease; adults with SMI were 4.9 times more likely to die before 75 (OHID).

n.1: This greatly understates the mortality gap.
n.2: This overstates the gap.
n.3: This understates the gap.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Ford, 49, has schizophrenia and attends his GP practice for his annual SMI physical health check. Which test is one of the six core elements of this check?
o: A lipid profile
A thyroid function test
A full blood count
Liver function tests
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: NHS England: the annual SMI physical health check has six core elements: alcohol consumption, blood glucose or HbA1c, blood pressure, BMI, lipid profile and smoking status.

n.1: Thyroid function is monitored for lithium, not part of the six-element check.
n.2: FBC is used for clozapine monitoring, not the six-element check.
n.3: LFTs may be clinically indicated but are not one of the six core elements.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Mr Holt, 36, has schizophrenia and smokes 30 cigarettes a day. He has tried to stop twice before without success and now wants to try again. Which support is most appropriate under NICE CG178?
o: Nicotine replacement therapy with behavioural support
Advice that further attempts are unlikely to work
Bupropion with behavioural support
Advice to wait until his psychosis is in remission
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: CG178 1.1.2.3-1.1.2.4: offer help to stop smoking even if previous attempts were unsuccessful, following NICE tobacco guidance, except do not offer bupropion to people with psychosis. Be alert to changes in clozapine and olanzapine levels.

n.1: NICE says to offer help even if previous attempts have failed.
n.2: CG178 1.1.2.4: do not offer bupropion to people with psychosis to help them stop smoking.
n.3: There is no need to wait; help is offered now.

Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.t: Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeutic Care
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.q: Ms Akhtar, 42, has bipolar disorder. Her annual physical health check shows a raised BMI, raised blood pressure and an HbA1c in the prediabetes range. What is the most appropriate response?
o: Agree an intervention plan for each abnormal result with her
Advise her the results are expected with her medicines
Tell her the GP will deal with any physical problems
Record the results and repeat them at next year's check
Lifespan, Physical Health and Therapeuti.w: The Lester UK adaptation (endorsed by NHS England) says 'don't just screen, intervene': abnormal results should lead to action such as lifestyle support, referral and treatment. CG185 1.2.13: identify people with bipolar disorder who have hypertension, are obese or at risk of diabetes at the earliest opportunity and follow the relevant NICE guidance.

n.1: Treating abnormal results as expected is diagnostic overshadowing and delays treatment.
n.2: Mental health and primary care share responsibility for physical health in SMI.
n.3: Screening without acting leaves modifiable risks untreated.
